title: Epigrams
text: pr. I hope that in my little books I have observed such restraint that no one with a good conscience about himself can complain of them, since they make their jokes while keeping intact the respect owed even to persons of the humblest rank. This sense was so lacking in the old authors that they abused not only real names but great ones. Let my fame cost me less, and let wit be the very last thing approved in me. Far from the candour of our jests be the malicious interpreter, and let him not write my epigrams for me: it is a shameful thing to play the wit upon another man's book. As for the frank licence of the language—that is, the tongue of epigram—I would excuse it, were the precedent mine: but so writes Catullus, so Marsus, so Pedo, so Gaetulicus, so everyone who is read through. If, however, anyone is so ostentatiously severe that in his presence plain Latin may not be spoken on any page, he may content himself with the preface—or rather with the title. Epigrams are written for those who are in the habit of watching the Floralia. Let Cato not enter my theatre; or if he does enter, let him watch. I think I shall be within my rights if I close the preface with verses:

title: Epigrams
text:
Since you knew the sweet rite of merry Flora,
The festal games and the licence of the crowd,
Why, stern Cato, did you come into the theatre?
Or had you come for this alone—to walk out?
1. I
This is he whom you read, the man you ask for,
Martial, known the whole world over
For his witty little books of epigram:
To whom, devoted reader, the honour you have given
While he yet lives and feels it
Few poets have after their ashes.
2. II
You who long to have my little books with you wherever you go,
And want them as companions of a long road,
Buy these, that parchment compresses into small leaves:
Give book-cases to the great; one hand can hold me.
Yet, that you may not be ignorant where I am for sale, and wander
Astray through the whole city, with me for guide you shall be sure:
Look for Secundus, the freedman of learned Lucensis,
Behind the threshold of Peace and the forum of Pallas.
3. III
You would rather live in the bookshops of the Argiletum,
Little book, though our book-cases stand empty for you.
You do not know, alas, you do not know the disdain of Rome our mistress:
Believe me, the crowd of Mars is far too shrewd.
Nowhere are there greater sneers: young men and old
And boys too have the nose of a rhinoceros.
When you have heard a great "Bravo!" and are blowing kisses,
You will be tossed in a shaken blanket up to the stars.
But you, that you may not so often suffer your master's erasures
Nor have the grim pen mark down your jokes,
Long, you wanton thing, to flit through the airs of heaven:
Go, fly; but you could have been safer at home.
4. IV
If by chance, Caesar, you should touch our little books,
Lay aside the frown of the lord of the earth.
Your triumphs too are used to bearing jests,
And a general is not ashamed to be matter for a quip.
With the same look with which you watch Thymele and the mimic Latinus,
With that, I pray, may you read our songs.
Your censorship can permit harmless games:
Wanton is my page, but my life is honest.

title: Epigrams
text:
5. V
I give you a sea-fight, you give me epigrams:
You wish, I think, Marcus, to swim along with your book.
6. VI
While the eagle bore the boy through the airs of heaven,
The freight clung unharmed to the fearful talons:
Now its own prey prevails upon the lions of Caesar,
And the hare plays safe within the enormous mouth.
Which do you think the greater marvel? For each there stands
The highest author: these are Caesar's deeds, those Jove's.
7. VII
The Dove, the darling of my friend Stella—
Though Verona hear me say it—
Has beaten, Maximus, the Sparrow of Catullus.
My Stella surpasses your Catullus
By as much as a dove is greater than a sparrow.
8. VIII
That you follow the doctrines of great Thrasea and perfect Cato
In such a way that you would have yourself survive,
And do not rush bare-breasted upon drawn swords—
You do, Decianus, what I would wish you to do.
I have no use for the man who buys his fame with blood cheaply given;
The man I want is one who can be praised without dying.
9. IX
You wish to be thought a fine fellow and a great man at once, Cotta:
But the man who is a fine fellow, Cotta, is a trifling man.
10. X
Gemellus seeks the hand of Maronilla in marriage,
And longs and presses and entreats and gives.
Is she so lovely? No—nothing is more hideous.
What then is sought and pleases in her? She has a cough.
11. XI
Since the knight has been given his twice five coins, why
Do you alone, Sextilianus, drink twice ten times that?
By now the hot water would have failed the slaves who fetch it,
If you, Sextilianus, did not drink your wine neat.
12. XII
Where you go up to the Herculean heights of cool Tibur,
And the white Albula steams with its sulphurous waters,
The fourth milestone from the city marks the farms,
The sacred grove, and the acres dear to the Muses.
Here a rough portico used to offer shade in summer—
Ah, what an unheard-of crime that portico nearly dared!
For suddenly it collapsed in ruin, just when, beneath that pile,
Regulus had been carried by his pair of horses.
Surely Fortune feared our complaints,
Which were no match for so great a hatred.
Now even the losses please us; the very danger is worth so much:
Had the roof stood, it could not have proved the gods exist.

title: Epigrams
text:
13. XIII
When chaste Arria handed the sword to her own Paetus,
The blade she had herself drawn from her own vitals,
"If there be any faith," she said, "the wound I made does not pain me:
But the wound you will make, Paetus—that one pains me."
14. XIV
The dalliance, Caesar, the games and the sport of lions
We have seen—the arena gives you this too—
When the hare, caught again and again by the gentle tooth,
Came back, and ran at large through the open jaws.
How can the greedy lion spare the prey it has caught?
And yet it is said to be yours: therefore it can.
15. XV
O Julius, to be named before none of my companions,
If long fidelity and grey old loyalty count for anything,
Your sixtieth consul is now almost upon you,
And your life counts scarcely a few more days.
You will not do well to put off what you may see can be denied you,
And to reckon that alone yours which has already been.
Cares await you, and labours linked in chains;
Joys do not stay, but fly away in flight.
Grasp these with both hands and with your whole embrace:
Even so they often slip and flow from the depths of your lap.
It is not, believe me, the part of a wise man to say "I shall live":
Tomorrow's life is too late; live today.
16. XVI
Some things are good, some middling, more are bad,
Of those you read here: no otherwise, Avitus, is a book made.
17. XVII
Titus urges me to keep pleading cases,
And often tells me, "It is a great thing."
A great thing, Titus, is what the farmer does.
18. XVIII
Why does it please you, Tucca, to mix with old Falernian
The new must stored in Vatican jars?
What great good have the worst of wines done you?
Or what harm have the best of wines done you?
About us it is easy; but it is a crime to slaughter Falernian
And to give cruel poison to Campanian wine.
Your guests, perhaps, have deserved to perish:
But so precious a jar did not deserve to die.

title: Epigrams
text:
19. XIX
If I remember rightly, Aelia, you had four teeth:
One cough spat out two, and another two.
Now you can cough in safety the whole day long:
A third cough has nothing left to do there.
20. XX
Tell me, what madness is this? Before the summoned crowd that watches,
You alone, Caecilianus, devour the mushrooms.
What shall I pray for, worthy of so great a belly and gullet?
May you eat such a mushroom as Claudius ate.
21. XXI
When his right hand, aiming at the king, was deceived by the attendant,
He thrust it, doomed to perish, into the sacred fire.
But the kindly foe could not endure so cruel a marvel,
And bade the man, snatched from the flames, depart:
The hand that Mucius could burn with fire he scorned,
Porsena could not bear to look upon.
Greater is the fame and glory of the cheated right hand:
Had it not erred, it would have done less.
22. XXII
Why now, hare, do you flee the gentle mouth of a peaceful lion?
It has not learned to crush such tiny beasts.
Those claws are kept for mighty necks,
Nor does so great a thirst rejoice in thin blood.
The hare is prey for hounds; it does not fill those vast jaws.
The Dacian boy need not fear the arms of Caesar.
23. XXIII
You invite no one, Cotta, except a man you have bathed with,
And the baths alone furnish you a dinner-guest.
I used to wonder why you never asked me, Cotta:
Now I know—it was naked that I displeased you.
24. XXIV
You see that man there, Decianus, with unkempt hair,
Whose grim brow even you yourself dread,
Who talks of the Curii and the liberating Camilli?
Do not trust the face: he was married yesterday—as a bride.
25. XXV
Publish your little books at last, Faustinus, to the people,
And bring out the polished work of your learned heart,
Such as the Cecropian citadels of Pandion would not condemn
Nor our old men pass over in silence.
Do you hesitate to admit Fame as she stands before your doors,
And does it irk you to bear off the rewards of your own labour?
Let the pages, fated to outlive you, begin through you also
To live: glory comes too late to the ashes.

title: Epigrams
text:
26. XXVI
Sextilianus, you drink as much, all by yourself,
As five tiers of benches: you could be drunk so often on water;
Nor do you beg only the coins of neighbours sitting near you,
But the cash from benches further off.
This vintage is not pressed by Paelignian wine-presses,
Nor was that grape born on Tuscan slopes,
But the lucky jar of old Opimius is drained dry,
And the Massic cellar empties out its black casks.
Go beg the dregs of Laletania from a tavern-keeper,
If, Sextilianus, you drink more than ten times.
27. XXVII
Last night I had told you—
After ten half-pints downed, I think—
That you should dine with me today, Procillus.
At once you thought the thing as good as done,
And made a note of my unsober words
By a precedent far too dangerous:
"I hate a drinking-mate with a good memory," Procillus.
28. XXVIII
Whoever believes that Acerra reeks of yesterday's wine
Is mistaken: Acerra always drinks till dawn.
29. XXIX
Rumour reports, Fidentinus, that you recite my little books
To the public no otherwise than as your own.
If you want them called mine, I will send you the poems for nothing:
If you want them called yours, buy this—that they may not be mine.
30. XXX
Diaulus had been a surgeon, now he is an undertaker.
He began to be a doctor in the only way he could.
31. XXXI
To you, Phoebus, Encolpos vows all the hair from the crown of his head,
The darling of his master the centurion,
When Pudens shall have won the deserved reward of the first rank.
Cut the long locks soon, Phoebus,
While no down soils the tender face
And while the milk-white neck becomes the flowing mane;
And, that master and boy may long enjoy
Your gifts, make him shorn quickly, a man late.
32. XXXII
I do not love you, Sabidius, nor can I say why:
This only can I say—I do not love you.
33. XXXIII
Gellia does not weep for her lost father when she is alone,
But if anyone is present, the bidden tears leap forth.
He does not mourn who seeks to be praised for it, Gellia;
He grieves truly who grieves with no witness by.

title: Epigrams
text:
34. XXXIV
With your doors unguarded and forever open, Lesbia,
You sin, and do not hide your stolen pleasures,
And the onlooker delights you more than the lover himself,
Nor are your joys agreeable to you if they lie hidden.
But the courtesan drives off the witness with a curtain and a bolt,
And rarely does a chink gape in the brothel of Summemmius.
From Chione at least, or from Ias, learn some modesty:
Even the tombs hide their filthy harlots.
Does my censure seem to you too harsh?
I forbid you, Lesbia, to be caught—not to be had.
35. XXXV
You complain, Cornelius, that the verses I write are too little severe,
And not such as a schoolmaster might read aloud in class:
But these little books, like husbands with their wives,
Cannot please without a cock.
What if you bade me write a wedding-hymn
In language not of a wedding-hymn?
Who clothes the Floralia, and grants
To courtesans the modesty of the matron's robe?
This is the law laid down for jesting songs:
They cannot give pleasure unless they tickle.
So lay aside your severity, I beg,
And spare my sports and jokes,
And do not seek to castrate my little books.
Nothing is uglier than a Priapus gelded.
36. XXXVI
If to you, Lucanus, or to you, Tullus, there were given
Such a destiny as the Spartan sons of Leda have,
There would be a noble contest of devotion between the two,
Since each would wish to die before the other for his brother,
And the first to go down to the shades below would say:
"Live out your time, brother; live out mine."
37. XXXVII
You receive the burden of your belly in wretched gold—and feel no shame—
You drink from glass, Bassus: so it costs you more to shit.
38. XXXVIII
The book you recite, Fidentinus, is mine:
But when you recite it badly, it begins to be yours.
39. XXXIX
If there is anyone to be numbered among rare friends,
Of the kind that old fidelity and ancient fame have known;
If anyone is steeped in the arts of Cecropian and Latin Minerva,
And good with a true plainness of heart;
If anyone is a guardian of the right, an admirer of the honourable,
And one who asks the gods nothing with a secret mouth;
If anyone is upheld by the strength of a great mind:
May I perish if that man is not Decianus.

title: Epigrams
text:
40. XL
You who draw down your face and do not read these lines with pleasure,
May you envy everyone, you spiteful man, and no one envy you.
41. XLI
You think yourself a wit, Caecilius.
You are not, believe me. What then? A vulgar slave—
The kind that hawker across the Tiber is,
Who barters pale sulphur-matches
For broken glass; the kind who sells
Soaked chickpeas to the lounging crowd;
The kind who keeps and owns the vipers;
The kind the cheap boys of the salt-sellers are;
The kind that hoarse cook is who carries round
Steaming sausages through the lukewarm cook-shops;
The kind some second-rate street-poet is;
The kind that shameless dancing-master from Gades is;
The kind the chattering mouth of an aged catamite is.
So cease at last to seem to yourself
What only to yourself, Caecilius, you seem—
You who could outdo Gabba in your salt,
And Tettius Caballus himself.
It is not granted to everyone to have a nose:
He who jests with stupid impudence
Is no Tettius—but a horse.
42. XLII
When Porcia had heard the fate of her husband Brutus,
And her grief sought the weapons taken from her,
"Do you not yet know," she said, "that death cannot be denied?
I had believed my father taught this by his fate."
She spoke, and drank with eager mouth the burning coals.
Go now, you tiresome crowd, and deny her steel.
43. XLIII
We were twice thirty, Mancinus, summoned by you,
And nothing was set before us yesterday but a boar,
No grapes kept from the late-bearing vines,
Nor honey-apples to rival the sweet combs,
No pears that hang tied to the long broom-shoots,
Nor pomegranates that mimic short-lived roses;
Rustic Sassina sent no milk-white cones of cheese,
Nor came the olive from Picene jars:
The boar alone—and that the smallest, such as could be killed
By an unarmed pygmy.
And nothing was given from it; we all only looked on:
That is how the arena too serves us up a boar.
After such deeds, may no boar be set before you,
But may you be set before the boar that took Charidemus.

title: Epigrams
text:
44. XLIV
That the wanton runs of hares and the games of lions
Are carried by my larger sheet and my smaller,
And that I do the same thing twice—if that, Stella, seems
Too much to you, then you too serve me a hare twice over.
45. XLV
That the labour I publish may not perish in little books,
Let it rather be said, "Him then in answer he addressed."
46. XLVI
When you say, "Quick, do it if you're doing it," Hedylus, at once
My passion droops and falters, weakened.
Bid me wait: held back, I will go the faster.
Hedylus, if you're in a hurry, tell me—not to hurry.
47. XLVII
Lately he was a doctor, now Diaulus is an undertaker:
What the undertaker does, the doctor too had done.
48. XLVIII
From these jaws the keepers have not rescued bulls,
Through which the fleeing prey, the hare, goes and returns;
And, what is more wondrous, it comes out swifter than its foe,
And carries off something from so great a nobility.
It is not safer when it runs on the empty sand,
Nor is it shut up in its cage with such good faith.
If you seek to escape the bites of hounds, you reckless hare,
You have the mouth of a lion to flee to for refuge.
49. XLIX
Man not to be left unspoken among the Celtiberian peoples,
And glory of our Spain,
You shall see lofty Bilbilis, Licinianus,
Renowned for horses and for arms,
And old Caius white with snows, and Vadavero
Holy with its broken crags,
And the sweet grove of delicate Boterdus,
Which fruitful Pomona loves.
You shall swim the gentle ford of warm Congedus
And the soft lakes of the Nymphs,
And brace your slackened body in the brief
Salo, that hardens iron.
There Voberca itself shall offer to the man at lunch
Wild beasts to be shot close by.
You shall break the clear heat in the golden Tagus,
Shaded by the shadows of trees;
The chilly Derceita shall quench your greedy thirst,
And Nutha, that surpasses snows.
But when grey December and winter's unbridled storm
Bellow with the hoarse north wind,
You shall seek again the sunny shores of Tarraco
And your own Laletania.
There you shall slaughter does entangled in soft nets,
And boars bred at home,
And burst the cunning hare with a strong horse,
And leave the stags to your bailiff.
The neighbouring wood shall come right down to your hearth,
Ringed with grimy children.
The huntsman shall be called, and the guest shall come to you
At a shout from close at hand.
Nowhere a crescent-marked boot, nowhere the toga,
Nor garments rank with purple dye;
Far off the bristling Liburnian and the querulous client,
Far off the imperious commands of widows;
No pale defendant shall break your deep sleep,
But you shall sleep the whole morning through.
Let another earn a great and frantic "Bravo!":
Pity you the fortunate,
And enjoy true joy without pride,
While your Sura is being praised.
Not shamelessly does my life ask what is left to it,
When my fame has what is enough.

title: Epigrams
text:
50. L
If your cook, Aemilianus, is called Mistyllus,
Why should not mine be called Taratalla?
51. LI
No neck but the first will do for the fierce lions.
Why do you flee these teeth, you ambitious hare?
No doubt you wish them to descend from mighty bulls
To you, and to break necks they cannot see.
You must despair of the glory of a mighty fate:
You cannot die thus, a slender prey, beneath such a foe.
52. LII
I commend to you, Quintianus, my own books—
If I may still call them my own,
The books your poet recites:
If they complain of harsh slavery,
Come as their liberator and give security enough,
And, when that man calls himself their owner,
Say they are mine, manumitted by my hand.
If you cry this out three and four times,
You will put shame upon the plagiarist.
53. LIII
There is one page in our little books that is yours, Fidentinus—
But marked with the sure stamp of its true owner,
Which exposes your poems for the manifest theft they are.
So, set among them, a Lingonian hooded cloak, with its greasy nap,
Pollutes the city's violet-purple stuffs;
So Arretine pots violate vessels of crystal;
So, when by chance the black raven strays on the banks of Cayster,
It is laughed at among the swans of Leda;
So, where the sacred grove resounds with the many-voiced nightingale,
The wicked magpie offends the Cecropian laments.
Our books need no informer, no judge:
Your page stands against you and says to you, "You are a thief."
54. LIV
If, Fuscus, you have still any room to be loved—
For you have friends on this side, friends on that—
We ask one place, if one is left,
And do not refuse me because I am new to you:
All those old friends of yours were once new.
Only look at the one newly offered for the part,
And see whether the new friend can grow old in it.
55. LV
If you wish to know briefly the prayer of your Marcus,
Fronto, bright ornament of camp and toga,
This is what he seeks: to be the ploughman of his own, not a great, estate,
And he loves homely leisure among small things.
Does any man, fool that he is, court the painted cold of Spartan marble,
And carry the morning greeting "Good day,"
When he could—blessed with the spoils of wood and field—
Spread out his full nets before the hearth,
And draw up the leaping fish on the quivering line,
And bring out yellow honey from the red jar?
When his plump farm-wife loads his uneven table,
And ash, bought from no one, makes ready his own eggs?
Let no one love this life who does not love me—that is my wish—
And let him live, pale, among the duties of the town.

title: Epigrams
text:
56. LVI
The vintage, harassed by unceasing rains, is sodden:
You cannot, much as you wish, sell unwatered wine, tavern-keeper.
57. LVII
You ask, Flaccus, what sort of girl I would have, or not?
I want one neither too easy nor too hard.
What lies between, and between the two, is what I approve:
I want neither what torments nor what cloys.
58. LVIII
A slave-dealer asked me a hundred thousand for a boy:
I laughed, but Phoebus paid it on the spot.
This grieves my cock, and it complains of me in private,
And Phoebus is praised to my disgrace.
But my cock has just made Phoebus a present of
Two million: give me that, and I will buy at a higher price.
59. LIX
The dole at Baiae gives me a hundred farthings.
What does such starvation do amid such luxuries?
Give me back the dark baths of Lupus and Gryllus:
When I dine so badly, why, Flaccus, should I bathe so well?
60. LX
Though you enter the wide mouth of the grim lion, hare,
The lion still thinks its tooth is idle.
On what back will it rush, on what shoulders fall?
Where will it fix the deep wounds it deals to bullocks?
Why do you weary in vain the lord and king of the woods?
He feeds on nothing but the beast he has chosen.
61. LXI
Verona loves the verses of her learned bard,
Mantua is blessed in Maro,
The land of Aponus is reckoned rich in its Livy
And its Stella, no less than in Flaccus,
The rainy Nile applauds Apollodorus,
The Paeligni resound with Naso,
And eloquent Corduba speaks of its two Senecas
And of its one and only Lucan,
Merry Gades delights in its Canius,
Emerita in my Decianus:
In you, Licinianus, our Bilbilis shall glory,
And it will not be silent about me.
62. LXII
Laevina, chaste, and yielding to none of the ancient Sabine women,
And, though her husband is gloomy, gloomier still herself,
While she gives herself now to the Lucrine, now to Avernus,
And while she is often warmed by the waters of Baiae,
Fell into the flames: pursuing a young man, she left
Her husband and came as Penelope—and departed Helen.

title: Epigrams
text:
63. LXIII
You ask me to recite my epigrams to you. I will not.
You do not want to listen, Celer, but to recite.
64. LXIV
You are beautiful—we know it—and a girl, that is true,
And rich, for who can deny it?
But when you praise yourself too much, Fabulla,
You are neither rich nor beautiful nor a girl.
65. LXV
When I say "ficus," you laugh as at a barbarous word,
And bid me say "ficos," Laetilianus.
We will say "ficus" for the figs we know grow on the tree,
We will say "ficos," Caecilianus, for yours.
66. LXVI
You are mistaken, you greedy thief of my books,
Who think a poet can be made for the cost
That a copying and a cheap roll come to:
A "Bravo!" is not got for six or ten coins.
Seek out unpublished poems and rough drafts,
Which one man alone knows, and which the father of the virgin page
Keeps sealed in his book-case, himself the guardian,
Pages that have not yet bristled at a hard chin.
A book once known cannot change its master.
But if there is one with its brow not yet pumiced,
Not yet adorned with bosses and parchment wrapper,
Buy it: such I have; and no one will know.
Whoever recites another's work and seeks fame
Ought to buy not the book, but silence.
67. LXVII
"You are too free a man," you always tell me, Cerylus.
The man who says that against you, Cerylus—is he a free man?
68. LXVIII
Whatever Rufus does, it is nothing but Naevia to Rufus.
If he rejoices, if he weeps, if he is silent, of her he speaks.
He dines, he toasts, he asks, refuses, nods: there is one
Naevia; if there were no Naevia, he would be dumb.
When yesterday at dawn he was writing a greeting to his father,
"Naevia my light," he wrote, "Naevia my lamp, good morning."
Naevia reads this and laughs with downcast face.
There is more than one Naevia: why, you fool of a man, do you rave?
69. LXIX
Maximus, the Tarentos that once was wont to show a Pan
Now shows a Canius.

title: Epigrams
text:
70. LXX
Go and pay my respects for me, book: you are bidden to go,
Dutifully, to the gleaming home of Proculus.
You ask the way? I will tell you. You will pass the Castor
Near grey-haired Vesta and the home of the virgins;
Thence by the sacred slope you shall seek the venerable Palatine,
Where many an image of the supreme leader gleams.
Let not the radiant mass of the marvellous colossus delay you,
That rejoices to surpass the work of Rhodes.
Turn your way here, where stand the roofs of dripping Lyaeus
And the dome of Cybele with its painted Corybant.
Straightway on the left, with bright front, are the household gods
And the halls of the lofty house you must approach.
Make for this house: fear no pride, no haughty threshold:
No door stands more open with every post thrown wide,
Nor any that Phoebus and the learned sisters love more nearly.
If he says, "Why has he not come himself, then?"
You may excuse me thus: "Because, whatever the quality
Of what is read here, a mere caller could not have written it."
71. LXXI
Let Laevia be drunk in six measures, Justina in seven,
Lycas in five, Lyde in four, Ida in three.
Let every mistress be counted out in poured Falernian,
And, since none of them comes, you, Sleep, come to me.
72. LXXII
Do you think, Fidentinus, that by my verses you are a poet,
And do you wish to be believed so?
So Aegle thinks she has teeth,
With bones and Indian horn she has bought;
So Lycoris, who is blacker than a falling mulberry,
Pleases herself with white lead.
By the same reasoning by which you are a poet,
When you are bald, you will have a head of hair.
73. LXXIII
There was no one in the whole city who would touch
Your wife for free, Caecilianus, while it was allowed:
But now, with guards posted, there is a huge
Crowd of seducers: you are a man of resource.

title: Epigrams
text:
74. LXXIV
He was an adulterer: yet you could deny it, Paula.
Now, look, he is your husband: can you deny it now, Paula?
75. LXXV
The man who would rather give Linus half than lend him the whole,
Would rather lose the half.
76. LXXVI
O Flaccus, no cheap reward of my cares,
Hope and nursling of the Antenorean home,
Put off the Pierian songs and the choirs of the sisters;
None of those girls will give you a copper.
What do you seek from Phoebus? Minerva's chest has the cash;
She is the shrewd one, she alone lends to all the gods.
What can the ivy of Bacchus give? The tree of Pallas,
Black with weight, bows down its various foliage.
Besides waters, Helicon has nothing but garlands
And the lyres of the goddesses, and a grand but empty "Bravo!"
What have you to do with Cirrha? What with naked Permessis?
The Roman forum is nearer and richer.
There the coins ring out: but round our stages
And barren professors' chairs only kisses click.
77. LXXVII
Charinus is in fine health, and yet he is pale.
Charinus drinks sparingly, and yet he is pale.
Charinus digests well, and yet he is pale.
Charinus takes the sun, and yet he is pale.
Charinus dyes his skin, and yet he is pale.
Charinus licks a cunt, and yet he is pale.
78. LXXVIII
When the wasting plague gripped his undeserving throat
And the black pest crept over his very face,
With dry cheeks himself, exhorting his weeping friends,
Festus resolved to go to the Stygian pools.
Yet he did not defile his pious lips with hidden poison,
Nor torment his sad fate with lingering starvation,
But ended a holy life by a Roman death,
And sent forth his soul by a nobler pyre.
Fame may set this death above the fate of great Cato:
For of this man Caesar was the friend.
79. LXXIX
You always plead cases and always drive at business, Attalus:
Whether there is or is not something to drive at, Attalus, you always drive.
If business and cases fail, Attalus, you drive mules.
Attalus, that you may not lack something to drive—drive out your life.

title: Epigrams
text:
80. LXXX
The last night of your life, Canus, you went out to beg the dole:
You died, I think, Canus, because there was only one.
81. LXXXI
You know you were born of a slave, and sweetly confess it,
When you call your father master, Sosibianus.
82. LXXXII
This portico, scattered in much dust,
That unfolds its long ruins,
See by what a chance it lies, finished off.
For only just now Regulus had been
Carried beneath those roofs, and had withdrawn,
When suddenly it was overcome by its own weight,
And, after it had nothing to fear for its master,
It fell, bloodless, in a harmless loss.
After such fear, such a complaint, Regulus—
Who would deny that you are the care of the gods,
For whose sake the very ruin was innocent?
83. LXXXIII
Your little dog licks your mouth and lips, Manneia:
No wonder, if a dog enjoys eating filth.
84. LXXXIV
Quirinalis does not think he should take a wife,
Though he wants to have sons, and has found
A way to manage it: he beds his maidservants,
And fills his house and lands with home-bred knights.
Quirinalis is a true father of a family.
85. LXXXV
When the witty auctioneer was selling well-tended hills
And the lovely acres of suburban soil,
"He is wrong," he said, "who thinks Marius is forced
To sell: he owes nothing—rather, he is a lender."
"What is the reason, then?" "He lost all his slaves there,
And his cattle and crops; he does not like the place."
Who would set a price, except a man who wanted to lose
Everything? So the unlucky land clings to Marius.
86. LXXXVI
Novius is my neighbour, and from our windows
He can be touched by the hand.
Who would not envy me, and think me
Blessed at every hour,
For having a yoked companion to enjoy?
He is as far from me as Terentianus,
Who now governs Nilotic Syene.
I cannot dine with him, nor even see him,
Nor hear him, nor in the whole city
Is anyone so near to us and so far.
One of us must move further off.
Let a man be Novius's neighbour or lodger
If he does not wish to see Novius.

title: Epigrams
text:
87. LXXXVII
That you may not reek heavily, Fescennia, of yesterday's wine,
In your excess you devour the lozenges of Cosmus.
That breakfast coats your teeth, but stops nothing
When the belch comes back from the depths below.
What of it, that the poison, mixed with perfume, smells the worse,
And the doubled odour of your breath travels further?
So drop these tricks now too well known, these thefts found out,
And be simply, honestly drunk.
88. LXXXVIII
Alcimus, snatched from your master in your growing years,
Whom the Labican earth covers with light turf,
Receive no nodding weight of Parian marble,
Which empty toil gives the ashes, doomed to fall,
But pliant box and the dark shade of the vine
And meadows green and dewy with my tears
Receive, dear boy, as memorials of my grief:
Here for all time shall your honour live.
When Lachesis brings me to my final years,
No otherwise do I bid my own ashes lie.
89. LXXXIX
You always whisper in everyone's ear, Cinna,
Whispering even what may be said before a crowd of witnesses.
You laugh in the ear, complain, accuse, lament,
You sing in the ear, you judge, you are silent, you shout,
And so deep has this disease settled in you,
That often, Cinna, you praise Caesar in the ear.
90. XC
Because I never saw you, Bassa, joined to men,
And no story gave you a lover,
But a crowd of your own sex was always
Performing every service round you, with no man coming near,
You seemed to us, I admit, a Lucretia:
But you, Bassa—the shame of it—were a fornicator.
You dare to bring two female parts together,
And your monstrous lust counterfeits a man.
You have devised a marvel worthy of the Theban riddle:
Here, where there is no man, there is adultery.
91. XCI
Though you publish nothing of your own, you carp at my poems, Laelius.
Either stop carping at ours, or publish your own.

title: Epigrams
text:
92. XCII
Cestos often complains to me, with eyes not dry,
That he is touched by your finger, Mamurianus.
There is no need of a finger: have Cestos whole for yourself,
If that, Mamurianus, is the only thing you lack.
But if there is neither a hearth nor the frame of a bare cot,
Nor the chipped cup of Chione or Antiope,
If a threadbare and patched cloak hangs from your loins
And a Gallic kilt covers half your buttocks,
And you feed on the mere smell of a black kitchen
And drink filthy water, bent down beside the dog:
Then not your arse—for it is no arse that never shits—
But the one eye you have left, that I will gouge with my finger:
And do not call me jealous, or call me malicious.
In short, Mamurianus, bugger on a full belly.
93. XCIII
Aquinus rests, joined to faithful Fabricius,
Who rejoices to have reached the Elysian homes first.
A double altar attests the gifts of the first rank:
But there is more in what you read in the shorter line:
"Each joined in the sacred bond of a praised life,
And—what fame rarely knows—he was a friend."
94. XCIV
You sang badly, Aegle, while you were being had.
Now you sing well; but you are not to be kissed.
95. XCV
That you always shout, Aelius, that you bawl over the pleaders,
You do not do this for nothing: you are paid to keep quiet.
96. XCVI
If it is no trouble, and you do not mind, limping verse,
We ask you to say a few words to our Maternus,
Whispered in his ear, that he alone may hear.
That lover of gloomy cloaks,
Dressed in Baetic grey and dull dun,
Who thinks men in scarlet are no men
And calls amethyst-purple the garb of women,
May praise the natural and have, if he likes, forever
His dusky colours—his morals are pale green.
He will ask why I suspect a man is soft.
We bathe together: he looks at nothing above,
But watches the athletes with devouring eyes
And cannot keep his lips off the sight of their cocks.
You ask who this is? The name has slipped my mind.

title: Epigrams
text:
97. XCVII
When everyone is shouting, then alone do you speak, Naevolus,
And you think yourself an advocate and a pleader.
By that method no one could fail to be eloquent.
Look, all are silent now: Naevolus, say something.
98. XCVIII
Diodorus goes to law, Flaccus, and suffers from gout.
But he hands his counsel nothing: that is gout of the hand.
99. XCIX
Lately you had not a full two million,
But you were so lavish and so liberal
And so splendid, Calenus, that all
Your friends wished you ten million.
The god heard our vows and prayers,
And within, I think, seven months,
Four deaths gave you this.
But you, as if it had not been left
But snatched from you, your ten million, went off
Into such wretched starvation
That the more sumptuous dinners,
Which once a year you get up for the whole year,
You unfold with the dirt of black coin,
And we seven, your old companions,
Cost you half a pound of lead.
What worthy of such merits shall we pray for you?
We wish you a hundred million, Calenus.
If this should fall to you, you will die of hunger.
100. C
Afra has her "mammas" and "papas," but she herself
Can be called the greatest mamma of papas and mammas.
101. CI
That hand, once faithful to my studies,
And blessed in its master, and known to the Caesars—
Demetrius, in his green years, has forsaken the prime of life:
A fourth harvest was added to his three lustres.
Yet, that he might not go down a slave to the Stygian shades,
When the wicked plague was burning him in its grip,
I took thought, and remitted to the sick man all a master's rights:
He deserved by my gift to have recovered.
Failing, he felt his reward, and called me his patron,
Free, as he went to the infernal waters.
102. CII
The painter who painted your Venus, Lycoris,
Was flattering Minerva, I think.
103. CIII
"If the gods above should give me ten times a hundred thousand"—
So you used to say, Scaevola, when not yet a proper knight—
"How I would live, how lavishly and how blessedly!"
The easy-going gods laughed and granted it.
After this your toga is much dingier, your cloak worse,
Your shoe patched in its leather three and four times:
And of ten olives, more are always kept back,
One table unfolds two dinners,
And the thick dregs of red Veientan are drunk,
A penny buys warm chickpeas, and a penny a girl.
Let us go to law, you cheat and welsher:
Either live, Scaevola, or give the gods back their million.

title: Epigrams
text:
104. CIV
That the leopard bears the dainty yoke
On its painted neck, and the savage tigers
Submit patiently to the whip,
That the stags bite the golden bit,
That Libyan bears are tamed by reins,
And a boar as huge as Calydon is said to have borne
Obeys the purple halter,
That ugly bisons drag the chariots
And the beast, bidden to give soft dances,
Does not refuse its black master:
Who would not think these the shows of gods?
Yet a man passes all this by as lesser,
Whoever sees the humble huntings of lions,
Whom the swift fear of hares tires out.
They let go, they fetch back, they love their captives,
And the prey is safer in the mouth,
To which they delight to give loose, open jaws
And to hold their timid teeth,
Ashamed to crush so soft a spoil,
Just when they have come from slaughtered bullocks.
This clemency is not got by art,
But the lions know whom they serve.
105. CV
The wine that is born, Ovidius, in Nomentan fields,
As often as it has gained long years,
Strips off, in its aged old age, its character and its name:
And whatever it pleases, the old jar is called.
106. CVI
You keep adding water now and then, Rufus,
And if forced by a comrade, you drink a scant
Ounce of diluted Falernian.
Has Naevia promised you a blessed
Night, and do you prefer the sober
Naughtiness of a sure embrace?
You sigh, you keep silent, you groan: she has said no.
So you may drink your goblets thick and fast
And throttle the harsh grief in wine.
Why spare yourself, Rufus? You must sleep alone.
107. CVII
You often tell me, Lucius Julius, dearest of friends,
"Write something great: you are an idle fellow."
Give me leisure—such as Maecenas once made
For his Flaccus and his Virgil:
I would try to fashion works to live through the ages
And to snatch my name from the flames.
The oxen will not bear the yoke onto barren fields:
A rich soil tires, but the labour itself delights.

title: Epigrams
text:
108. CVIII
You have a house—and long may it stand and grow through the years, I pray—
Lovely, indeed, but across the Tiber:
But my garret looks out on the Vipsanian laurels,
And in this quarter I have grown old already.
I must move, to greet you at home in the morning, Gallus:
It is worth it, even if it were further off.
But it is no great thing to you if I furnish one client in a toga:
It is much, Gallus, if I deny you that one—my own self.
I myself will greet you, often, at the tenth hour:
In the morning my book shall say "good day" to you for me.
109. CIX
Issa is more naughty than Catullus's sparrow,
Issa is purer than a dove's kiss,
Issa is more winning than all girls,
Issa is dearer than Indian pearls,
Issa is the pet, the lapdog of Publius.
If she whimpers, you will think she is speaking;
She feels both sorrow and joy.
She lies leaning on his neck and takes her sleep,
So that no breathing can be heard;
And when forced by the need of her belly,
She has never stained the coverlet with a drop,
But with a coaxing paw rouses him and warns him
She must be set down from the couch, and asks to be lifted.
So great a modesty is in the chaste lapdog:
She knows nothing of love; nor have we found
A mate worthy of so tender a girl.
That the last day may not snatch her away entire,
Publius renders her in a painted tablet,
In which you will see an Issa so like
That she herself is not so like to herself.
In short, set Issa beside the picture:
Either you will think both are real,
Or you will think both are painted.
110. CX
You complain, Velox, that I write long epigrams.
You yourself write nothing: you make shorter ones.
111. CXI
Since your fame for wisdom equals your devotion to the gods,
And your piety is no less than your genius,
He knows nothing of giving gifts to merit, who wonders
That a book is given you, Regulus—or incense.

title: Epigrams
text:
112. CXII
When I did not know you, I called you lord and king:
Now I know you well: now you shall be plain Priscus to me.
113. CXIII
Whatever I trifled at, a young man and a boy once,
And our trifles, which now I myself no longer know,
If you wish to misspend good hours
And grudge your leisure, reader,
You may seek them from Quintus Pollius Valerianus,
Through whom my nothings are not allowed to perish.
114. CXIV
These gardens near you, Faustinus, Telesphorus
Faenius holds, and a small estate and watery meadows.
Here he buried the ashes of his daughter and consecrated the name
You read, Antulla's—though he himself were worthier to be read.
It had been just that the father should have gone to the Stygian shades:
But since that was not allowed, let him live, to tend her bones.
115. CXV
A certain girl desires me—envy me, Procillus!—
A girl whiter than the washed swan,
Than silver, snow, the lily, the privet.
But I want a certain girl blacker than night,
Than the ant, than pitch, the jackdaw, the cicada.
Already you were plotting a cruel hanging:
If I know you well, Procillus, you will live.
116. CXVI
This grove Faenius consecrated to the eternal honour of the ashes,
And the lovely acres of well-tilled soil.
In this tomb Antulla, snatched too soon from her own, is covered;
In this both parents shall be mingled with Antulla.
If anyone desires this little field, I warn him: let him not hope for it:
That land shall serve its own masters forever.
117. CXVII
Whenever you meet us, Lupercus,
"Shall I send my boy," you keep saying,
"To whom you may hand the little book of epigrams,
Which, once read, I will return to you at once?"
There is no need, Lupercus, to trouble your boy.
It is a long way, if he should want to come to the Pear-tree,
And I live up three flights of stairs—and high ones.
What you seek you may look for nearer.
You often go down, I suppose, to the Argiletum:
Opposite Caesar's forum there is a shop,
With its doorposts written over on this side and that,
So that you may quickly read through all the poets.
Seek me from there. You need not ask Atrectus—
That is the name the master of the shop bears:
From the first or second pigeon-hole he will give you
Martial, smoothed with pumice and adorned with purple,
For five denarii.
"You are not worth so much," you say? You are wise, Lupercus.

title: Epigrams
text:
118. CXVIII
The man for whom it is not enough to have read a hundred epigrams,
For him no amount of trouble is enough, Caedicianus.

title: Epigrams
text:
pr. Valerius Martial to his friend Decianus, greetings.
"What have we to do," you say, "with a preface? Are we not doing enough for you if we read your epigrams? Besides, what are you going to say here that you could not say in verse? I can see why tragedy or comedy should be given a preface, since they may not speak for themselves: epigrams have no need of a herald, and are content with their own tongue—that is, a wicked one: on whatever page it pleases them, they make a preface. Do not, then, if you please, do a ridiculous thing and bring on a character dancing in a toga. In short, consider whether it pleases you to face the net-fighter with a ferule. I sit among those who shout you down at once."
By Hercules, Decianus, I think you speak the truth. What if you knew with how long a letter, and what sort, you would have had to deal? So let it be done as you require. Whoever falls upon this book will owe it to you that they reach the first page not yet wearied.

title: Epigrams
text:
1. I
You could indeed have carried three hundred epigrams,
But who would carry you, and read you through, my book?
Now learn what merits a tight little volume has.
This is the first: that less paper is wasted on me;
Next, that the copyist will finish it in a single hour,
And will not be a slave only to my trifles;
The third point is this: that if by chance someone reads you,
Bad though you may be throughout, you will not be tiresome.
A guest will read you over his mixed five-measures, but
Before the cup, once set down, has had time to grow cool.
Do you think yourself made safe by such brevity?
Alas for me—to how many even so you will seem long!
2. II
Crete gave a great name, Africa a greater,
Which Scipio as victor holds, and Metellus too;
A nobler one Germany bestowed for the Rhine subdued,
And even as a boy, Caesar, you were worthy of this name.
Your brother earned the Idumaean triumphs with your father,
But the laurel that comes from the Chatti is all your own.
3. III
Sextus, you owe nothing, you owe nothing, Sextus—we admit it.
For a man owes, Sextus, only if he can pay.
4. IV
O how coaxing you are, Ammianus, to your mother!
How coaxing your mother is to you, Ammianus!
She calls you brother and is called sister.
Why do such naughty names attract you both?
Why does it not please you to be what you are?
Do you think this a game and a joke? It is not:
A mother who longs to be called a sister
Is happy to be neither mother nor sister.
5. V
May I lose my health, Decianus, if I would not be glad
To be with you all day and all night long.
But there are two miles that keep us apart:
These become four, when I go to come back again.
Often you are not at home, even when you are; often you are denied:
Often you have time only for your cases, or for yourself.
Still, to see you, I do not mind going the two miles:
Not to see you, I do mind going the four.

title: Epigrams
text:
6. VI
Go now, bid me publish my little books.
With scarcely two pages read, you,
Severus, look to the colophon at the end,
And draw out long yawns.
These are the very things which, when I read them over,
You used to snatch and copy down—but on Vitellian tablets;
These are the things you carried, one by one, in your bosom
Through all the dinners, through the theatres;
These are they, or anything better you may not know of.
What good is so lean a little book to me,
That it is no thicker than its boss,
If it takes you three days to read it whole?
Never was idleness more supine.
So soon, weary traveller, do you give out,
And when you ought to run to Bovillae,
Do you seek to change horses at the Camenae?
Go now, bid me publish my little books.
7. VII
You declaim prettily, Atticus, plead cases prettily,
Write pretty histories, pretty poems,
Compose mimes prettily, epigrams prettily,
A pretty grammarian, a pretty astrologer you are,
And you sing prettily and dance, Atticus, prettily,
You are pretty at the art of the lyre, pretty at the art of ball.
Since you do nothing well, yet do everything prettily,
Do you want me to say what you are? You are a great busybody.
8. VIII
If anything seems to you, reader, in these pages
Either too obscure or too poor in Latin,
The fault is not mine: the copyist spoiled them,
While he hurried to reckon up the verses for you.
But if you think it was not he but I who erred,
Then I shall believe you have no understanding at all.
"Yet these things are bad." As if we denied the obvious:
These things are bad, but you make nothing better.
9. IX
I wrote; Naevia wrote nothing back. She will not give, then.
But I suppose she had read what I wrote: she will give, then.
10. X
Because you give me kisses, Postumus, with half a lip,
I praise you: you may take away half of this too.
Do you wish to give a still greater and unspeakable gift?
Keep this half whole for yourself, Postumus.

title: Epigrams
text:
11. XI
That you see Selius with clouded brow, Rufus,
That, walking, he wears down the portico till late,
That his dull face keeps something mournfully silent,
That his ugly nose nearly touches the ground,
That he beats his breast with his right hand and tears his hair:
He is not mourning the death of friend or brother;
Both his sons are alive—and may they live, I pray—
His wife is safe, and his goods and his slaves,
His tenant and his bailiff have squandered nothing.
What, then, is the cause of his grief? He dines at home.
12. XII
What am I to call this, that your kisses smell of myrrh,
And that you never have a scent that is your own?
This makes me suspicious, Postumus, that you always smell good:
Postumus, he does not smell good who always smells good.
13. XIII
Both the judge demands his fee, and the advocate demands his.
I advise you, Sextus, to pay the creditor.
14. XIV
Selius leaves nothing untried, nothing unattempted,
Whenever he sees he must dine at home.
He runs to the Europa colonnade, and praises you,
Paulinus, and your Achillean feet—without end.
If Europa has done nothing, then the Saepta are sought,
To see if the son of Phillyra or of Aeson can do anything.
Cheated here too, he haunts the Memphitic temples,
And sits by your seats, you sorrowful heifer.
Thence he makes for the roofs hung on a hundred columns,
And thence the gifts of Pompey and the double grove.
He scorns neither the baths of Fortunatus nor of Faustus,
Nor the dark of Gryllus and the Aeolia of Lupus:
For he bathes in the hot baths again and again and again.
When he has done everything, but the god refusing,
Washed, he hurries back to the box-thickets of warm Europa,
In case some friend there is taking a late walk.
By you, you wanton bull, and by your girl,
Invite Selius to dinner, I beg you.

title: Epigrams
text:
15. XV
That you toast your cup to no one,
You do a kind thing, Hormus, not a proud one.
16. XVI
Zoilus is ill: it is his bedclothes that bring on this fever.
If he were well, what would his scarlet covers do?
What the couch from the Nile, what the cloth dyed with stinking Sidon?
What does sickness display but foolish wealth?
What have you to do with doctors? Dismiss all your Machaons.
Do you want to get well? Take my bedclothes.
17. XVII
A barber-woman sits at the first entrance of the Subura,
Where the bloody scourges of the torturers hang
And many a cobbler besets the Argiletum.
But that barber-woman, Ammianus, does not shave,
Does not shave, I say. What does she do, then? She fleeces.
18. XVIII
I angle for your dinner—shame on me, but I angle for it, Maximus—
You angle for another's: so now we are equals.
I come in the morning to pay my respects; you are said to have gone
To pay yours before me: so now we are equals.
I am your own attendant and walk before the swollen king;
You attend another: so now we are equals.
It is enough to be a slave; I will not be an underling's underling.
He who is a king, Maximus, should have no king.
19. XIX
Do you believe you make me happy, Zoilus, by a dinner?
Happy by a dinner, Zoilus—and then by yours?
The guest must recline on the Arician slope to beg,
Whom your dinner, Zoilus, makes happy.
20. XX
Paulus buys his poems; Paulus recites his own poems.
For what you buy you may rightly call your own.
21. XXI
You give kisses to some, to others, Postumus, you give your right hand.
You say, "Which do you prefer? Choose." I prefer the hand.
22. XXII
What have I to do with you, O Phoebus and you nine sisters?
See, the merry Muse harms her own poet.
Postumus used to give me half his kisses before;
Now he has begun to give them with both lips.
23. XXIII
I will not tell, though you keep asking me,
Who the Postumus in my little book is,
I will not tell: for what need is there
To offend these kissings,
Which can avenge themselves so well?

title: Epigrams
text:
24. XXIV
If unjust fortune should bring you a sad charge in court,
Pale, squalid, I will cling beside you, paler than the accused:
If she should bid you, condemned, leave your native land,
Over seas, over crags I will go, the exile's comrade.
She gives you riches: are these things shared between two?
Do you give me a part? Is it much? Candidus, do you give anything?
With me, then, you will be wretched: but if the god with serene face
Should nod assent, happy, Candidus, you will be alone.
25. XXV
You never give, Galla, you always promise to the man who asks.
If you always deceive, then now, Galla, I ask you—say no.
26. XXVI
That Naevia breathes a querulous, bitter cough,
And keeps spitting into your lap,
Do you now think, Bithynicus, that you have the matter settled?
You are wrong: Naevia is flattering you, not dying.
27. XXVII
When Selius, praising you, spreads his nets for a dinner,
Take him along, whether you read aloud or plead as advocate:
"Perfect! weighty! quick! cleverly! bravo! divine!"
"That is what I wanted! Now your dinner is earned—be quiet."
28. XXVIII
Laugh heartily at whoever calls you, Sextillus, a catamite,
And give him the middle finger.
But you are no sodomite, Sextillus, nor a fornicator,
Nor does the hot mouth of Vetustina please you.
You are none of these, I admit, Sextillus: what are you then?
I do not know, but you know there are two things left.
29. XXIX
Rufus, you see that man wearing down the front benches,
Whose hand even from here gleams with its sardonyx,
And whose cloaks have drained off Tyrian dye so many times,
And whose toga is bidden to outdo untouched snows,
Whose oiled hair reeks of all the Marcellan colonnade,
And whose smooth arms gleam with the hair plucked out,
On whose foot sits no day-old crescent-marked strap,
And scarlet leather paints his unblemished foot,
And many plasters cover his star-spangled brow.
You do not know what it is? Take off the plasters: you will read it.

title: Epigrams
text:
30. XXX
By chance I was asking for a loan of twenty thousand sesterces,
Which would have been no heavy gift even to a giver.
For the man I asked was a prosperous old comrade,
And one whose money-chest scourges its loose-flowing wealth.
He said to me, "You will be rich, if you plead cases."
Give me what I ask, Gaius: I do not ask for advice.
31. XXXI
Often I have had Chrestina. You ask how good she is?
There is nothing, Marianus, that can surpass it.
32. XXXII
I have a quarrel with Balbus; you do not want to offend Balbus,
Ponticus: I have one with Licinus—here too is a great man.
Patrobas, my neighbour, often harasses my little field;
You are afraid to go against a freedman of Caesar.
Laronia refuses and keeps back my slave;
You answer, "She is childless, rich, old, a widow."
A friend who is a slave, believe me, is poorly served:
Let him be free who wants to be my master.
33. XXXIII
Why do I not kiss you, Philaenis? You are bald.
Why do I not kiss you, Philaenis? You are red-haired.
Why do I not kiss you, Philaenis? You are one-eyed.
The man who kisses these, O Philaenis, sucks cocks.
34. XXXIV
Though Phileros pleases you, ransomed at the cost of your whole dowry,
You suffer your three sons, Galla, to die of hunger.
Such indulgence is shown to a grey cunt,
Which not even chaste Venus could now become.
May the gods make you the everlasting mistress of Phileros,
O mother, no worse than Pontia herself.
35. XXXV
Since your legs are like the horns of the moon,
You could, Phoebus, wash your feet in a drinking-horn.
36. XXXVI
I would not have you curl, but neither tousle, your hair;
I would not have your skin gleaming, nor would I have it dirty;
Let there be no beard of the mitred, nor the beard of the accused:
I want a man, Pannychus, neither too much so nor too little.
Now your legs are bristly with hairs, and your chest
With shaggy bristles, but your mind, Pannychus, is plucked smooth.

title: Epigrams
text:
37. XXXVII
Whatever is set down, you sweep up from here and there,
The teats of a sow's udder and a rib of pork
And a moor-hen meant to be shared by two,
Half a mullet and a whole bass
And the side of a lamprey and the thigh of a fowl
And a wood-pigeon dripping with its own gravy.
When these are stowed in your dripping napkin,
They are handed to a slave to be carried home:
We recline, an idle company.
If you have any shame, put back the dinner:
I did not invite you, Caecilianus, for tomorrow.
38. XXXVIII
You ask, Linus, what my Nomentan farm yields me?
This my farm yields me: that I do not see you, Linus.
39. XXXIX
You give scarlet and violet robes to a notorious whore:
Do you wish to give the gift she has earned? Send her a toga.
40. XL
Tongilius is said to be badly burned with semi-tertian fever.
I know the man's tricks: he is hungry and thirsty.
Now sly nets are spread for the fat thrushes,
And the hook is cast for mullet and bass.
Let the Caecuban be strained, and what the year of Opimius ripened,
Let dark Falernian be stored in a thrifty glass.
All the doctors have ordered Tongilius to bathe:
O fools, you believe it is a fever? It is gluttony.
41. XLI
"Laugh if you are wise, O girl, laugh,"
The Paelignian poet, I think, had said.
But he had not said it to all girls.
Yet, granted that he said it to all girls,
He did not say it to you: you are no girl,
And you have three teeth, Maximina,
And those plainly pitch-black and box-yellow.
So, if you trust your mirror and me,
You ought to dread laughter no otherwise
Than Spanius the wind, or Priscus a hand,
Than chalked Fabulla dreads the rain-cloud,
Than white-leaded Sabella dreads the sun.
Put on a look more severe
Than the wife of Priam or his elder daughter-in-law.
Avoid the mimes of comic Philistion
And livelier dinner-parties
And whatever, with witty impudence,
Loosens the lips in clear laughter.
It becomes you to sit beside a grieving mother
Or one mourning her husband or her loyal brother,
And to have time only for the tragic Muses.
But you, following our advice,
Weep, if you are wise, O girl, weep.

title: Epigrams
text:
42. XLII
Zoilus, why do you spoil the bath-water with your washed backside?
To make it filthier, Zoilus, plunge in your head.
43. XLIII
"Friends share all in common"—these things are yours, Candidus, "in common,"
Which you, grandiloquent, harp on night and day:
A toga washed in Spartan Galaesus clothes you,
Or one Parma gave from a choice flock:
But me a hide clothes that bore the rages and horns of the bull,
One the first ball would not have called its own.
The land of Cadmus sent you Agenorean cloaks:
You would not sell my scarlet for three coins.
You hang up Libyan disks on Indian tusks:
A table of beech is propped up with a potsherd for me.
Huge mullets adorn your gold-inlaid dishes:
Of one colour in my plate, you blush, my little crab.
Your troop could vie with the Trojan catamite:
But for a Ganymede my own hand comes to my aid.
Out of such wealth, to an old and faithful comrade
You give nothing, and you say, Candidus, "Friends share all in common"?
44. XLIV
If I have bought a boy, or a well-combed toga,
Or three, say, or four pounds of silver,
That Sextus, the moneylender at once,
Whom you know as my old comrade,
Fears and takes care that I may not chance to ask for something,
And whispers to himself, but so that I may hear:
"I owe seven thousand to Secundus,
Four to Phoebus, eleven to Phyletus,
And there is not a farthing in my chest."
O the great wit of my comrade!
It is hard, Sextus, to refuse when you are asked,
How much harder before you are asked!
45. XLV
The cock that would not stand for you has been cut off, Glyptus.
Madman, what had you to do with the knife? You were already a eunuch.
46. XLVI
As flowery Hybla is painted in various colours
When the bees plunder the brief Sicilian spring,
So your presses glow with the cloaks laid up beneath them,
So your chest sparkles with countless festal robes,
And your whites could clothe a whole tribe,
Which the Apulian land bore with more than one flock.
You watch, unmoved, the winter of your scantily clad friend
—what a crime!—and fear the worn cold of his side.
What would it have cost you, hard-hearted man, to defraud two rags
—what do you fear?—not yourself, Naevolus, but the moths?

title: Epigrams
text:
47. XLVII
I warn you, flee the sly nets of a notorious adulteress,
You who are smoother, Gallus, than the shells of Cythera.
Do you trust to your backside? The husband is no sodomite:
There are two things he does: he forces the mouth, or he forces the front.
48. XLVIII
A tavern-keeper and a butcher and a bath,
A barber and a board and gaming-pieces
And a few books—but for me to choose them:
One comrade not too unpolished,
And a tall slave-boy long kept smooth,
And a girl dear to my boy:
Grant me these, Rufus, even at Butunti,
And keep the Baths of Nero for yourself.
49. XLIX
I do not want to marry Telesina: why?
She is an adulteress. But Telesina gives to boys. I do.
50. L
That you suck cocks and drink water, Lesbia—you do no wrong.
You take water, Lesbia, where you have need of it.
51. LI
Though there is often but a single denarius in your whole chest,
And that, Hyllus, more worn than your own arse,
Still the baker will not take it from you, nor the tavern-keeper,
But anyone proud of an excessive prick.
Your unhappy belly watches the feastings of your backside,
And the one is forever starving, wretch, while the other gorges.
52. LII
Dasius knows how to count those about to bathe: he charged
Big-breasted Spatale for three: she paid.
53. LIII
Do you wish to become free? You lie, Maximus, you do not wish it:
But if you do wish to become so, this is the way you can.
You will be free, Maximus, if you refuse to dine out,
If the Veientan grape masters your thirst,
If you can laugh at the gold dishes of wretched Cinna,
If you can be content with a toga like mine,
If plebeian Venus is bought for you with a couple of asses,
If you cannot enter your own house without stooping.
If you have this strength, if such power of mind is yours,
You can live more free than the Parthian king.

title: Epigrams
text:
54. LIV
What your wife suspects about you, Linus,
And in what part she wants you more chaste,
She has proved well enough by sure tokens,
She who has given you a eunuch for a guard.
There is nothing keener than she, nor more malicious.
55. LV
You want to be courted, Sextus: I wanted to love.
I must obey you: as you command, you shall be courted:
But if I court you, Sextus, I shall not love.
56. LVI
Among the peoples of Libya, your wife, Gallus, is ill spoken of
On the foul charge of immoderate greed.
But these are sheer lies: she is not at all in the habit
Of taking. What is she in the habit of, then? Of giving.
57. LVII
This man you see strolling with idle steps,
Who in amethyst-purple cuts through the middle of the Saepta,
Whom my Publius does not surpass in cloaks,
Nor Cordus himself, the alpha of cloak-wearers,
Whom a toga-clad and long-haired troop follows,
And a fresh sedan with its linen and its straps:
Just now, just now he pawned at Cladus's counter
For scarcely eight coins a ring, to get himself a dinner.
58. LVIII
Sleekly combed, you laugh at my threadbare clothes, Zoilus.
They are threadbare indeed, Zoilus, but they are mine.
59. LIX
I am called Mica: you see what I am, a little dining-room:
From me, look, you behold the Caesarean dome.
Break the couches, call for wine, take roses, anoint yourself with nard:
The god himself bids you remember death.
60. LX
You bed the wife, boy Hyllus, of an armed tribune,
While you fear only a boy's punishment.
Woe to you—while you play, you will be gelded. Now you will tell me,
"That is not allowed." What? Is what you do, Hyllus, allowed?
61. LXI
When your cheeks bloomed with their first doubtful down,
Your shameless tongue licked men's middles.
Now that your foul head has earned the loathing of undertakers
And the disgust of the wretched hangman,
You use your mouth otherwise, and, seized by excessive spite,
You bark at every name there is.
Better that so harmful a tongue should cling to the groin:
For when it sucked cocks, it was cleaner.

title: Epigrams
text:
62. LXII
That you pluck your chest, your legs, your arms,
That your shaved prick is girt with short hairs:
This you do, Labienus—who does not know it?—for your mistress.
For whom do you do it, Labienus, that you depilate your arse?
63. LXIII
You had a hundred thousand sesterces, your sole fortune, Milichus,
Which you spent to buy Leda on the Sacred Way.
Milichus, it is extravagance, if you, a rich man, loved at such a price.
"I do not love," you will now say: this too is extravagance.
64. LXIV
While you fashion yourself now an advocate, now a rhetorician,
And cannot decide, Laurus, what you want to be,
The age of Peleus and Priam and Nestor has passed by,
And it would now be late for you even to stop.
Begin: three rhetoricians died in a single year,
If you have any spirit, if you have any worth in the art.
If the school is condemned, all the forums seethe with lawsuits,
Even Marsyas himself could become an advocate.
Come, away with you, break off delay: how long shall we go on hoping for you?
While you doubt what you are, you can already be nothing.
65. LXV
Why do we see Saleianus sadder than usual?
"Is it a slight cause?" you ask. "I have buried my wife."
O grievous crime of fate! O heavy blow!
Is she, is that rich Secundilla dead,
Who gave you a million for her dowry?
I would not have had this happen to you, Saleianus.
66. LXVI
Of the whole world of her hair, one curl alone had gone wrong,
Not well fixed with an unsteady pin.
This crime Lalage avenged with the mirror in which she had seen it,
And Plecusa fell, struck by the cruel curls.
Cease now, Lalage, to dress those sorry locks,
And let no girl touch that mad head.
Let a salamander brand it, or the savage razor lay it bare,
That your image may become worthy of the mirror.
67. LXVII
Wherever you meet me, Postumus, you shout out
At once, and your first word is this: "How are you doing?"
This, even if you meet me ten times in one hour,
You say: I think, Postumus, you have nothing to do.

title: Epigrams
text:
68. LXVIII
That I now greet you by your own name,
Whom before I used to call king and lord,
Do not say that I am insolent:
I bought back my freedman's cap with all my baggage.
A man must have kings and lords
Who has not himself and covets
What kings and lords covet.
If you can do without a slave, Olus,
You can also do without a king, Olus.
69. LXIX
You say, Classicus, that you dine out unwillingly:
If you are not lying, Classicus, may I perish.
Apicius himself was glad to go to dinner:
When he dined at home, he was gloomier.
Yet if you go unwillingly, why, Classicus, do you go?
"I am compelled," you say: true; Selius too is compelled.
See, Melior invites you, Classicus, to a proper dinner.
Where are your grand words? If you are a man, look—say no.
70. LXX
You do not want anyone to bathe in the tub before you,
Cotilus: what is the reason, unless it is this,
That you may not be soaked in befouled waters?
You may wash first: yet here, of necessity,
The prick is washed before the head.
71. LXXI
Nothing is more candid than you, Caecilianus. I have noticed:
Whenever I read a few couplets of mine,
You at once recite the writings of Marsus or of Catullus.
Do you do me this favour, as though you read worse stuff,
That mine may please more by comparison? I believe it:
Yet I would rather, Caecilianus, you recited your own.
72. LXXII
At yesterday's dinner, Postumus, a thing is said to have been done
That I should not wish—for who would approve such deeds?—
Your mouth was so battered that not even Latinus himself
Strikes the cheap face of Panniculus with such a sound:
And what is more wondrous, rumour through the whole city
Names Caecilius as the author of this crime.
You deny it was done: do you want me to believe this? I believe it.
But what of it, Postumus, that Caecilius has witnesses?

title: Epigrams
text:
73. LXXIII
Lyris wants to know what she does: what she does sober—she sucks cocks.
74. LXXIV
Saufeius girt about, before and behind, with a toga-clad crowd,
As great a throng as Regulus has when he returns,
When he sent his shaven client, acquitted, to the lofty temples—
Maternus, do you see him? Do not envy him.
May such an escort, I pray, never be yours.
These friends and these troops of toga-wearers
Fuficulenus and Faventinus furnish him.
75. LXXV
A lion, wont to bear unmoved the blows of its master
And to suffer, gently, a hand thrust into its mouth,
Suddenly unlearned its peace, its savagery returning,
As great as ought not to have been even on the slopes of Libya.
For two of the boyish band, of tender body,
Who were renewing the bloody sand with rakes,
The cruel beast destroyed, ill-starred, with its raging tooth:
The arena of Mars saw no greater outrage.
One wants to cry out: "Cruel, treacherous robber,
Learn from our she-wolf to spare children!"
76. LXXVI
Marius left you five pounds of silver,
You to whom he gave nothing himself: did he keep his word to you?
77. LXXVII
Cosconius, you who think our epigrams too long,
You might be useful for greasing axles.
By that reasoning you would think the colossus long,
And call the boy of Brutus short.
Learn what you do not know: of Marsus and learned Pedo
Often a double page treats a single subject.
Those are not long from which you can take nothing away,
But you, Cosconius, make even couplets long.
78. LXXVIII
You ask where, in summertime, you may keep your fish?
Keep it, Caecilianus, in your hot baths.
79. LXXIX
You invite me, Nasica, just when you know I have invited guests.
I beg you, hold me excused: I dine at home.
80. LXXX
While fleeing the foe, Fannius slew himself.
Is this not madness, I ask—to die that you may not die?

title: Epigrams
text:
81. LXXXI
Though your litter may be roomier than a six-bearer chair:
Yet, since it is yours, Zoilus, it is a pauper's bier.
82. LXXXII
Why, Ponticus, do you crucify your slave with his tongue cut out?
Do you not know that the people speak the very thing he keeps silent?
83. LXXXIII
You disfigured the wretched adulterer, husband,
And the maimed features, robbed of nose and ears,
Seek for what they were before.
Do you believe you are sufficiently avenged?
You are wrong: that man can still force the mouth.
84. LXXXIV
Soft and yielding to men was the Poeantian hero:
So Venus is said to have avenged the wounds of Paris.
Why Sicilian Sertorius licks the cunt, this is the reason:
. . . By him, Rufus, Eryx seems to have been slain.
85. LXXXV
A guard of snow-white cooled drink, enclosed in light wicker,
This shall be your gift at the season of Saturn.
Because I sent you the gifts of summer in the month of December,
If you complain, send me back a threadbare toga.
86. LXXXVI
That I do not glory in verse read backwards,
Nor read in reverse the catamite Sotades,
That no Greekish echo anywhere chimes back,
Nor does the brilliant Attis dictate to me
A galliambic soft with its enfeebling:
I am not, Classicus, so bad a poet for that.
What if you bade Ladas, against his will,
Take to the slender paths of the spring-board?
It is base to have trifles that are hard to make,
And foolish is the labour of silly things.
Let Palaemon write poems for the schoolboy rings;
It pleases me to please a few choice ears.
87. LXXXVII
You say, Sextus, that pretty girls burn with love of you,
You who have the face of a man swimming under water.
88. LXXXVIII
You recite nothing, and yet you wish, Mamercus, to seem a poet.
Be whatever you wish—provided you recite nothing.
89. LXXXIX
That you delight in drawing out the night with too much wine,
I pardon you: you have the vice, Gaurus, of Cato.
That you write poems with no Muse and no Apollo,
You ought to be praised: you have this from Cicero.
That you vomit, is Antony's vice; that you live in luxury, Apicius's.
But that you suck cocks—tell me, whose vice is that?

title: Epigrams
text:
90. XC
Quintilian, supreme guide of wandering youth,
Glory, Quintilian, of the Roman toga,
That I hasten to live, poor and not useless in my years,
Forgive me: no one hastens enough to live.
Let him put it off who longs to outdo his father's fortune
And crowds his halls with too many ancestral busts.
A hearth, and a roof that does not resent the black smoke,
Delight me, and a living spring and untouched grass.
Let me have a well-fed home-born slave, a wife not too learned,
A night with sleep, a day without litigation.
91. XCI
Sure salvation of all things, glory of the earth, Caesar,
By whose safety we believe the great gods exist,
If the poems of mine, so often read in hasty little books,
Have held your eyes a while,
Permit it to seem—what fortune forbids to be—
That I be thought the father of three children.
These shall be my consolation, if I have displeased you;
These shall be my reward, if I have pleased.
92. XCII
The right of three children, which I asked for,
He alone who could granted me,
As the reward of my Muses. Farewell, wife.
The gift of the master must not be wasted.
93. XCIII
"Where is the first," you say, "since this book is the second?"
What am I to do, if that one has more modesty?
Yet if you would rather, Regulus, that this become the first,
You can take one iota from the title.
1. I
This, whatever it is, is sent to you from a far-off shore
By the Gaul called by the name of the Roman toga.
You read this book, and perhaps you praise the earlier one:
Both that and this are mine—choose which you think the better.
Of course the one born in our mistress city should please more:
A home-bred book must surely surpass a Gallic one.
2. II
Whose gift do you wish to become, little book?
Make haste to provide yourself a protector,
Lest, snatched off quickly to a sooty kitchen,
You wrap young tunny-fish in your soggy paper,
Or be a wrapper for incense or pepper.
You flee into the bosom of Faustinus? You are wise.
Now you may walk anointed with cedar oil,
And, handsome with the twofold honour of your front,
Revel in your painted bosses,
And let delicate purple clothe you,
And your proud title blush with scarlet.
With him for protector, fear not even Probus.

title: Epigrams
text:
3. III
[You hide your lovely face with a black cosmetic,
But you spoil the water with your unlovely body.
Believe the goddess herself tells you in our words:
"Either uncover your face, or bathe in your tunic."]
4. IV
Go to Rome, my book: if anyone asks where you have come from,
Say from the region of the Aemilian Way.
If he asks in what land, in what city we are,
You may answer that I am at Cornelius's Forum.
He will ask why I am away: confess much briefly:
"He could not bear the tedium of the empty toga."
"When is he coming?" he will say: you answer: "A poet
He went out; he will come when he is a lyre-player."
5. V
Do you wish to be recommended, little book, since you will run
Into the city without me, to many, or will one suffice?
One will suffice, believe me, to whom you will be no stranger,
Julius, a name forever on my lips.
You will seek him at once at the threshold of the first Covered Way:
The home that Daphnis held, he now holds.
He has a wife, who will receive you in her hands and lap,
Though you come all dusty.
Whether you see them together, or her, or him first,
You will say this: "Marcus bids you good day,"
And that is enough: let a letter recommend others: he errs
Who thinks he must be recommended to his own friends.
6. VI
The third day after the Ides of May is counted to you,
Marcellinus, to be twice celebrated by your rites.
This day reckons up the heavenly birth of your father,
This day first sips your own blooming cheeks.
Though it gave great gifts of a pleasant life,
That day never granted more to a father.
7. VII
Farewell now, you wretched hundred farthings,
The dole of a weary client who walks before the patron,
Which the boiled bath-attendant used to share out.
What are you thinking, O hunger of friends?
The doles of the proud patron have been withdrawn.
"There are no more tricks: now a salary must be paid."

title: Epigrams
text:
8. VIII
"Quintus loves Thais." What Thais? "One-eyed Thais."
Thais lacks one eye, he both.
9. IX
Cinna is said to write little verses against me.
He does not write, whose poems no one reads.
10. X
Your father, Philomusus, settled two thousand a month on you,
And paid it out to you every day,
Since each tomorrow's want forever cramped your luxury,
And your daily allowance had to feed your vices.
The same man, dying, left you his sole heir.
He disinherited you, Philomusus, your father did.
11. XI
If your girl, Quintus, is neither Thais nor one-eyed,
Why do you think the couplet was aimed at you?
But is there some likeness? Did I say Thais for Lais?
Tell me, what is alike in Thais and Hermione?
Yet you are Quintus: let us change the lover's name:
If Quintus does not want her, let Sextus love Thais.
12. XII
You gave your guests good perfume yesterday,
I admit—but you carved nothing.
It is a fine joke, to smell sweet and go hungry.
The man who does not dine, Fabullus, but is anointed,
That man seems to me truly dead.
13. XIII
While you will not have the fish, will not carve the fowl,
And spare the boar, Naevia, that is more than rotten,
You accuse and storm at the cook, as if he had brought
Everything raw. I shall never be so raw as that.
14. XIV
Starving Tuccius was making for Rome,
Having set out from Spain.
The tale of the doles met him on the way:
He turned back from the Mulvian Bridge.
15. XV
No one in the whole city gives more credit than Cordus.
"Though he is so poor, how?" Blind, he loves.
16. XVI
You give a show of gladiators, Cerdo, you princeling of cobblers,
And what the awl bestows on you, the sword snatches away.
You are drunk: for never would you do this sober—
To wish to play, Cerdo, with your own hide.
You have played with hide: but, believe me, remember
Now to keep, Cerdo, within your own skin.

title: Epigrams
text:
17. XVII
A tart, long carried round at the second course,
Burned the hands cruelly with too much heat;
But Sabidius's gullet burned more: so at once
He puffed at it three and four times with his cheeks.
It did indeed grow cool, and seemed to let the fingers in,
But no one could touch it: it had become a turd.
18. XVIII
Your preface complained that your throat had caught a chill.
Since you have made your excuse, Maximus, why recite?
19. XIX
Near the Hundred Columns a she-bear is shown,
Where sculpted beasts adorn the plane-tree grove.
While, playing, the handsome Hylas tried its gaping jaws
And thrust his tender hand into its mouth,
But a wicked viper lurked in the dark bronze
And lived with a worse life than the beast.
The boy did not feel the trap, until the fang sank in,
While he died. O the crime, that the bear was false!
20. XX
Tell me, Muse, what my friend Canius Rufus is doing:
Is he committing to immortal pages
The deeds of Claudian times, to be read hereafter?
Or what a lying historian fastens on Nero?
Or does he rival the tales of wicked Phaedrus?
Is he wanton in elegy, or severe in epic?
Or grim in the buskins of Sophocles?
Or, at leisure in the school of poets,
Does he tell jokes dipped in Attic charm?
If he has left there, is he treading the portico of the temple,
Or strolling slowly through the spaces of the Argonauts?
Or in the sun of delicate Europa again,
Among the warm box-trees, after midday,
Does he sit or walk, free of biting cares?
Does he bathe in the baths of Titus or Agrippa,
Or in the bath of shameless Tigellinus?
Does he enjoy the country place of Tullus and Lucanus?
Does he run to Pollio's sweet fourth milestone?
Or, set out now for seething Baiae,
Does he sail, lazy, on the Lucrine pool?
"Do you want to know what your Canius is doing? He is laughing."

title: Epigrams
text:
21. XXI
A slave, his brow branded, saved his proscribed master.
This was not the master's life, but his disgrace.
22. XXII
You had given, Apicius, sixty million to your belly,
