And still there remained ten million loose to you.
Burdened by this, as if you could not bear hunger and thirst,
You drained off poison in a final draught.
Nothing you ever did, Apicius, was more gluttonous.
23. XXIII
Since you hand all the courses back to your slaves,
Why is the table not set for you at your feet?
24. XXIV
Harmful to the vine and the rose, a he-goat stood at the altar,
Ready to die, a welcome victim, Bacchus, for your hearth.
When a Tuscan soothsayer wished to slay him to the god,
He had told by chance a rough and uncouth man
To cut quickly the testicles with a sharp sickle,
That the foul stench of the unclean flesh might depart.
While, bending over the green altar, he cut with his knife
The struggling neck and pressed it down with his hand,
A huge rupture appeared at the angry rites.
The countryman seized it with the iron and cut it off,
Thinking that the ancient rites of sacrifice required this
And that the old gods were worshipped with such entrails.
So you, who lately were a Tuscan, now a Gallic soothsayer,
While you cut the goat's throat, became a gelding yourself.
25. XXV
If you wish, Faustinus, to cool a boiling bath
That Julianus himself would scarcely enter,
Ask the rhetorician Sabineius to bathe.
He chills the Neronian hot baths.
26. XXVI
You alone have estates, and you alone, Candidus, have cash,
You alone have gold plate, you alone the murrine ware,
You alone the Massic, you alone the Caecuban of Opimius,
And you alone have wit, you alone genius.
You alone have everything—imagine my wanting to deny it!—
But your wife, Candidus, you have in common with the public.
27. XXVII
You never invite me back, though you often come when invited:
I forgive you, Gallus, if only you invite no one.
But you invite others: the fault is on both sides. "What?" you ask.
I have no sense, and you, Gallus, have no shame.

title: Epigrams
text:
28. XXVIII
You marvel that Marius's little ear smells foul.
You do this, Nestor: you chatter into his little ear.
29. XXIX
These chains, with their twin fetter, Zoilus dedicates
To you, Saturn—the rings he wore before.
30. XXX
No dole is given; you recline as a guest for free:
Tell me, Gargilianus, what do you do at Rome?
Whence comes your shabby toga and the rent of your dark cell?
Whence the farthing? Whence the means to keep Chione?
Though you may say you live by the highest reason,
That you live at all you do with no reason at all.
31. XXXI
You have, I confess, acres of wide-spreading field,
And your town house holds many estates,
And many a debtor serves your money-chest's mistress,
And a mass of gold sustains your feasts.
Yet do not look down, Rufinus, on lesser men:
Didymus had more, Philomelus has more.
32. XXXII
I cannot do an old woman. You complain, Matrinia? I can
Do even an old woman, but you are dead, not old.
I can do Hecuba, I can do Niobe, Matrinia, but only
If the one is not yet a dog, the other not yet a stone.
33. XXXIII
I prefer a freeborn girl, but if she is denied me,
A freedwoman is my next condition:
A slave-girl comes last: but she will beat them both,
If, in face, she seems to me freeborn.
34. XXXIV
Why you both deserve and do not deserve your name, I will tell.
You are cold and you are black: you are not, and you are, Chione—Snow.
35. XXXV
You behold the fish, a famous masterpiece of Phidian art:
Add water, and they will swim.
36. XXXVI
What a new and lately made friend does for you,
This you bid me do for you, Fabianus:
That, unkempt, I should always greet you at first light,
And your sedan drag me through the middle of the mud,
That, weary, at the tenth hour or later,
I should follow you to Agrippa's baths, when I bathe at Titus's.
Have I earned this, Fabianus, through thirty Decembers,
That I be always a raw recruit to your friendship?
Have I earned this, Fabianus, with a toga worn and my own,
That you do not yet believe I have earned my discharge?

title: Epigrams
text:
37. XXXVII
You prosperous friends know only how to take offence.
You do not act prettily, but it pleases you: go on, do it.
38. XXXVIII
What cause draws you, or what confidence, to Rome,
Sextus? What do you hope or seek from it? Tell me.
"I will plead cases," you say, "more eloquent than Cicero himself,
And in the three forums none will be my equal."
Atestinus pleaded cases, and Civis—you knew them both—
But neither earned even his rent in full.
"If nothing comes of this, I will compose poems:
When you hear them, you will say they are the work of Maro."
You are mad: all who are there in chilly cloaks
You see are Nasos and Virgils.
"I will haunt the great halls." That trade has barely fed
Three or four; the rest of the crowd is pale with hunger.
"What shall I do? Advise me: for I am resolved to live at Rome."
If you are an honest man, Sextus, you can live—by chance.
39. XXXIX
A boy like the Trojan cup-bearer, Faustinus,
One-eyed Lycoris loves. How well the one-eyed girl sees!
40. XL
A lizard, drawn by the hand of Mentor, set into the bowl,
Lives, and the silver is feared.
41. XLI
Because you lent me thrice fifty thousand
Out of such great wealth as your heavy chest weighs down,
You think yourself, Telesinus, a great friend to me.
You great, because you give? No—I, because you get it back.
42. XLII
Because you try to bury the wrinkles of your belly with bean-meal,
Polla, you smear your stomach, not my lips.
Let the flaw, perhaps a trifling one, lie simply open:
What is concealed is believed to be a great evil.
43. XLIII
You counterfeit youth, Laetinus, with dyed hair,
So suddenly a raven, you who were lately a swan.
You do not fool everyone: Proserpina knows you are grey:
She will tear the mask from your head.
44. XLIV
That no one meets you gladly,
That, wherever you come, there is flight and a vast
Solitude around you, Ligurinus,
Do you wish to know what it is? You are too much a poet.
This is a fault exceedingly dangerous.
No tigress roused, her cubs torn from her,
No viper scorched by the noonday sun,
Nor the wicked scorpion is so feared.
For who, I ask, could bear such ordeals?
You read to me standing, you read to me sitting,
You read to me running, you read to me on the privy.
I flee to the hot baths: you buzz in my ear.
I seek the swimming-pool: I am not allowed to swim.
I hurry to dinner: you hold me as I go.
I come to dinner: you put me to flight as I sit.
Weary, I sleep: you rouse me as I lie.
Do you want to see how much harm you do?
A man just, upright, innocent—you are feared.

title: Epigrams
text:
45. XLV
Whether Phoebus fled the table and dinner of Thyestes,
I do not know: we, Ligurinus, flee yours.
That is indeed splendid and furnished with proud dishes,
But nothing at all pleases while you recite.
I do not want you to set before me turbot or a two-pound mullet,
Nor do I want mushrooms, nor oysters: be silent.
46. XLVI
You demand of me endless service in the toga:
I do not go, but I send you my freedman.
"It is not the same," you say. I will prove it is much more:
I should scarcely keep up with your litter; he will carry it.
If you fall into a crowd, he will thrust them all back with his shoulder:
My side is weak and freeborn.
Whatever you say in your case, I myself shall be silent:
But he will bellow you a triple "Bravo!"
There is a lawsuit: he will hurl abuse in a mighty voice:
Shame forbids me to use strong words.
"So you will do nothing for me as a friend?" you say.
Whatever, Candidus, my freedman cannot do.
47. XLVII
Where the Capene Gate drips with its great drops
And the Almo washes the Phrygian iron of the Mother,
Where the sacred field of the Horatii is green
And the little shrine of Hercules seethes with crowds,
Faustinus, Bassus was riding in a loaded wagon,
Hauling all the riches of a blessed countryside.
There you would see cabbages of noble stalk
And both kinds of leek and low-growing lettuce
And beets not useless to a sluggish belly,
There a wreath heavy with fat thrushes
And a hare mauled by a Gallic hound's tooth
And a milk-fed pig fed on beans not yet shelled.
Nor did the runner go idle before the carriage,
But the courier carried eggs safe in hay.
Was Bassus making for the city? No—he was going to the country.
48. XLVIII
Olus built a poor man's cell, but sold his
Estates: now Olus has a poor man's cell.
49. XLIX
You mix Veientan for me, while you drink Massic:
I would rather smell these cups than drink them.

title: Epigrams
text:
50. L
This, and no other, is your reason for inviting me to dinner,
That you may recite, Ligurinus, your little verses.
I have taken off my sandals; at once a huge book is brought
Among the lettuces and the fish-sauce:
A second is read through, while the first courses are delayed:
There is a third, and the second course has not yet come:
And you recite a fourth and a fifth book at last.
It is rank, if you serve me a boar so many times over.
But if you do not give your wicked poems to the mackerel,
You will dine alone now, Ligurinus, at home.
51. LI
When I praise your face, when I admire your legs and hands,
You are wont to say, Galla, "Naked, I shall please more,"
And you always avoid the baths we share.
Surely, Galla, you are not afraid I shall not please you?
52. LII
You had bought a house, Tongilianus, for two hundred thousand:
A mishap too frequent in the city carried it off.
Ten times that was collected. I ask: can you not seem yourself
To have set fire, Tongilianus, to your own house?
53. LIII
I could do without your face,
And your neck and hands and legs,
And your breasts and buttocks and hips,
And, not to labour through them one by one,
I could do without you whole, Chloe.
54. LIV
Since I cannot give what you demand, Galla, when you ask,
You could much more simply, Galla, say no.
55. LV
Because wherever you come, we think Cosmus is moving house
And cinnamon pours, spilled from a shaken bottle,
I would not have you please yourself, Gellia, with foreign trifles.
You know, I suppose, my dog could smell as sweet that way.
56. LVI
I would rather have a cistern than a vineyard at Ravenna,
Where I could sell water for so much more.
57. LVII
A cunning tavern-keeper cheated me lately at Ravenna:
When I asked for it mixed, he sold me wine neat.
58. LVIII
Our Faustinus's villa at Baiae, Bassus,
Is not laid out in idle myrtle-groves
And barren plane and clipped box,
holding the wide field's ungrateful spaces,
But rejoices in a real and rough countryside.
Here Ceres is crammed and pressed into every corner,
And many a jar is fragrant with the wine of old autumns;
Here, after November, with winter already at hand,
The rough pruner brings back the late grapes.
Fierce bulls bellow in the deep valley,
And the calf, with hornless brow, itches for a fight.
The whole flock of the dirty farmyard roams about,
The shrill goose and the jewelled peacocks
And the bird that owes its name to its reddening feathers,
The painted partridge and the spotted Numidian hens
And the pheasant of the impious Colchians;
Proud cocks tread the Rhodian hens;
The cotes resound with the clapping of doves,
Here moans the wood-pigeon, there the waxen turtle-dove.
The greedy pigs follow the bailiff's wife's lap,
And the soft lamb awaits its full-uddered mother.
The milk-white home-born slaves ring the bright hearth,
And the festive household gods are lit by a great heap of wood.
No idle tavern-keeper grows pale with white leisure,
Nor does the slippery wrestling-master waste his oil,
But he sets a sly net for the greedy thrushes
Or draws up the caught fish on a quivering line
Or brings back a doe entangled in the toils;
The kindly garden gives the cheerful townsmen exercise,
And, with no schoolmaster bidding them, the long-haired
Wanton boys gladly obey the bailiff,
And the dainty eunuch enjoys the work.
Nor does the rustic caller come empty-handed:
One brings pale honey with its own combs
And a cone of cheese from the Sassinate wood;
One offers up drowsy dormice,
This one a bleating kid from its bristly mother,
Another capons forced to be chaste.
And the strapping daughters of honest tenants
Offer their mothers' gifts in woven wicker.
When the work is done, the glad neighbour is invited;
Nor does a greedy table keep back tomorrow's feast,
All eat, and the well-fed servant does not know
How to envy the drunken guest.
But you, near the city, possess an elegant famine,
And from a high tower you survey nothing but laurels,
Secure, with Priapus fearing no thief;
And you feed your vine-dresser on town-bought grain
And, at your leisure, carry to your painted villa
Greens, eggs, fowl, fruit, cheese, new wine.
Ought this to be called a country place, or a town house far off?

title: Epigrams
text:
59. LIX
The cobbler Cerdo gave you a show, well-dressed Bologna,
The fuller gave one at Modena: now where will the tavern-keeper give one?
60. LX
Since I am invited to dinner, no longer for sale as before,
Why is not the same dinner given me as is given you?
You take oysters fattened in the Lucrine pool,
I suck a mussel through a slit shell:
You have mushrooms, I take pig-fungus:
You deal with turbot, but I with a bream:
A golden turtle-dove fills you with its huge rump,
A magpie dead in its cage is set before me.
Why do I dine without you, Ponticus, when I dine with you?
Let it profit me that the dole is gone: let us eat the same.
61. LXI
You say whatever you ask is nothing, you shameless Cinna:
If you ask nothing, Cinna, I refuse you nothing, Cinna.
62. LXII
Because you buy boys for a hundred thousand, often two hundred,
Because you drink wines laid up under King Numa,
Because not very spacious furniture costs you a million,
Because a pound of wrought silver carries off five thousand,
Because a golden carriage is got for the price of a farm,
Because your mule cost more than the house you bought:
Do you believe, Quintus, you provide all this with a great soul?
You are wrong: a petty soul, Quintus, buys these things.
63. LXIII
Cotilus, you are a fine fellow: many say this, Cotilus.
I hear it: but what is a fine fellow? Tell me.
"A fine fellow is one who arranges his curled locks in order,
Who always smells of balsam, always of cinnamon;
Who hums the songs of the Nile, the songs of Gades,
Who waves his smooth-plucked arms to various measures;
Who lounges all day long among the women's chairs
And always whispers something in someone's ear,
Who reads notes sent from here and there and writes them;
Who shrinks from the cloak of his neighbour's elbow;
Who knows who loves whom, who flits through the dinner-parties,
Who knows well the old pedigrees of Hirpinus the horse."
What are you saying? Is this, is this a fine fellow, Cotilus?
A fine fellow, Cotilus, is a very fiddling thing.

title: Epigrams
text:
64. LXIV
The Sirens, the merry bane of sailors,
The coaxing deaths and the cruel joy,
Whom once no man left, once he had heard them,
Wily Ulysses is said to have left behind.
I do not wonder: this, Cassianus, I would wonder at,
If he had left Canius in mid-story.
65. LXV
The fragrance an apple breathes, bitten by a tender girl,
The breeze that comes from Corycian saffron;
The scent of the grey vine when it flowers with its first clusters,
Of the grass that the sheep has just cropped;
Of myrtle, of the Arab harvester, of rubbed amber,
The smell of a pale fire of eastern incense;
Of the clod when it is lightly sprinkled with a summer shower,
Of the garland that has rested on hair dripping with nard:
Of all these your kisses smell, cruel boy Diadumenus.
What if you gave them whole, without grudging?
66. LXVI
Antony committed an equal crime with the swords of Egypt:
Each sword cut off sacred faces.
That one, Rome, was your head, when, joyful,
You drove your laurelled triumphs; this one, when you spoke.
Yet Antony's cause is worse than that of Pothinus:
The latter did the deed for his master, the former for himself.
67. LXVII
You idle, boys, and you know nothing,
Lazier than the Vaternus and the Rasina,
Through whose sluggish shallows sailing
You dip your slow oars to the time-call.
Already, as Phaethon sinks, Aethon sweats
And the day blazes, and the noonday hour
Unyokes the wearied horses.
But you, wandering over such peaceful waves,
Idly play at leisure in your safe boat.
I think you no sailors—but Argo-nauts.
68. LXVIII
Thus far the book is written for you, matron.
For whom are the inner pages written, you ask? For me.
The gymnasium, the baths, the racetrack are in this part: withdraw.
We are stripping: spare to see naked men.
From here, with modesty laid aside after the wine and roses,
Tipsy Terpsichore knows not what she says:
With no doubtful figure, but openly she names that thing
Which proud Venus receives in the sixth month,
Which the bailiff sets as guard in the middle of the garden,
Which the chaste maiden looks at with her hand held against it.
If I know you well, you were laying down the long book,
Wearied; now, eager, you will read it whole.

title: Epigrams
text:
69. LXIX
Because you write all your epigrams in chaste words
And in your poems there is no prick,
I marvel, I praise: there is nothing more saintly than you alone:
But no page of mine is free of wantonness.
So let naughty youths and easy girls read these,
And let the older man read them too, if a mistress torments him.
But your venerable and saintly words, Cosconius,
Ought to be read by boys and virgins.
70. LXX
You are the lover of Aufidia, Scaevinus, whose husband you once were;
He who was your rival is now her husband.
Why does another's wife please you, when your own did not?
Can you not get it up unless you feel insecure?
71. LXXI
When the boy's prick hurts and yours, Naevolus, your arse,
I am no prophet, but I know what you do.
72. LXXII
You want to be had, but you will not bathe with me, Saufeia.
I suspect some great defect.
Either your flabby breasts hang from your chest,
Or, naked, you fear to betray the furrows of your belly,
Or your torn groin gapes with an endless cleft,
Or something of your cunt juts out at its mouth.
But none of these is so, I believe; naked, you are most beautiful.
If that is true, you have a worse fault: you are a fool.
73. LXXIII
You sleep with well-endowed boys,
And what stands for them, Gallus, does not stand for you.
What, I ask you, Phoebus, do you want me to suspect?
I wanted to believe you a soft man,
But rumour denies that you are a catamite.
74. LXXIV
You smooth your face with depilatory and your bald head with pitch-paste.
Are you afraid, Gargilianus, of the barber?
What will you do about your nails? For surely you cannot
Pare them with resin or with Venetian clay.
Stop, if you have any shame, parading your wretched baldness:
This, Gargilianus, is usually done to a cunt.
75. LXXV
Your prick, Lupercus, long ago ceased to stand,
Yet, madman, you struggle to get it up.
But rocket and lecherous bulbs do nothing,
And shameless savory now profits you nothing.
You have begun to corrupt pure mouths with bribes:
Even so, your Venus, urged on, does not come alive.
Could anyone marvel enough at this, or believe it—
That what does not stand stands you, Lupercus, at a great price?

title: Epigrams
text:
76. LXXVI
You get it up for old women, Bassus, you spurn girls,
And not the beautiful, but the dying, please you.
Is this not madness, I ask, is this not a crazed prick?
When you could have Hecuba, you cannot do Andromache!
77. LXXVII
Neither mullet nor thrush delights you, Baeticus,
Nor is hare ever, nor boar, agreeable to you,
Nor do cakes please you, nor a slice of cut pastry,
Nor does Libya send, nor Phasis, birds to you:
You devour capers and onions swimming in rotten fish-sauce
And the flesh of a doubtful gammon,
And gurnards delight you and tunny-chunks with grey skin,
You drink resined wines, you flee Falernian.
I suspect there is some more secret fault of the stomach:
For why else, Baeticus, do you eat putrid things?
78. LXXVIII
You pissed once with the keel running, Paulinus.
Do you want to piss again? Then you will be a Palinurus.
79. LXXIX
Sertorius finishes nothing, begins everything.
This man, when he has a woman, I do not think he completes the act.
80. LXXX
You speak ill of no one, you slander no one, Apicius:
Yet rumour says that your tongue is a foul one.
81. LXXXI
What have you to do, Baeticus the Gaul, with a woman's pit?
That tongue of yours ought to lick men's middles.
Why was your prick cut off with a Samian sherd,
If a cunt, Baeticus, was so welcome to you?
Your head must be gelded: for though you are a eunuch in the groin,
Yet you cheat the rites of Cybele: in the mouth you are a man.
82. LXXXII
Whoever can be a guest of Zoilus,
Let him dine among the whores of Summemmius
And drink sober from the chipped jar of Leda:
This, I maintain, is lighter and cleaner.
He lies, dressed in pale green, on a couch he fills,
And shoves his guests aside with his elbows on either hand,
Propped on purple and silken cushions.
A worn-out catamite stands by and supplies him, as he belches,
Red feathers and toothpicks of mastic,
And, as he sweats, a reclining concubine fans
A faint coolness with a green fan,
And a boy drives off the flies with a myrtle branch.
A masseuse runs over his body with nimble art
And spreads her skilled hand on all his limbs;
A eunuch knows the signal of his snapping finger
And, the inquirer into his dainty bladder,
Guides the drunken member of his drinking master.
But he himself, turned back to the crowd at his feet,
Among the lapdogs licking the entrails of geese,
Divides the boar's sweetbreads among the wrestlers
And gives the turtle-doves' rumps to his catbamite;
And while Ligurian rock-wine is served to us
Or must boiled in Massilian smoke,
He toasts his fools with Opimian nectar
In crystal and in murrine cups.
And himself, dark with Cosmus's flasks,
He does not blush to share out among us, in golden-purple flagons,
A poor adulteress's pomade.
Then, undone by many a half-pint, he snores:
We recline, and, bidden to keep silence for his snorts,
We pledge each other with nods.
Such insolence of shameless Malchio we endure,
Nor can we be avenged, Rufus: he sucks cocks.

title: Epigrams
text:
83. LXXXIII
You advise me, Cordus, to make my epigrams shorter.
"Do for me what Chione does": I could not be briefer.
84. LXXXIV
What does your adulteress say? I did not say a girl,
Gongylion. What then? Your tongue.
85. LXXXV
Who persuaded you to cut off the adulterer's nose?
It was not with this part, husband, that you were wronged.
Fool, what have you done? Your wife has lost nothing here,
Since the prick of your Deiphobus is safe.
86. LXXXVI
That you should not, chaste lady, read the wanton part of the book,
I foretold and warned you: yet, look, you are reading it.
But if you watch Panniculus and Latinus, chaste lady,—
These things are no more shameless than the mimes—read on.
87. LXXXVII
Rumour reports, Chione, that you have never been had
And that nothing is purer than your cunt.
Yet you bathe covered, not in the part you should:
If you have any shame, move your loincloth to your face.
88. LXXXVIII
They are twin brothers, but lick different parts.
Tell me, are they more unlike, or more alike?
89. LXXXIX
Eat lettuce and eat soft mallows:
For you have the face, Phoebus, of a man straining at stool.
90. XC
Galla wants, does not want, to give to me, and I cannot say,
Since she wants and does not want, what Galla wants for herself.
91. XCI
When a discharged soldier was seeking the fields of his native Ravenna,
He joined his journey with the half-man troop of Cybele.
A boy clung to him as companion, Achillas, runaway from his master,
Remarkable for his beauty and his wantonness.
The barren men perceived this: they ask in what part
He would sleep. But he too perceived their silent treachery:
He lies; they believe. After the wine, sleep is sought:
At once the wicked crew seize the iron
And geld the old man, who lay on the edge of the couch;
For the boy was safe, guarded by the bedstead.
There is a story that once a hind was substituted for a virgin,
But now a prick was substituted for a hind.

title: Epigrams
text:
92. XCII
My wife asks me to allow her an adulterer, Gallus—but one.
Shall I not gouge out, Gallus, this fellow's two eyes?
93. XCIII
Since you have outlived three hundred consuls, Vetustilla,
And have three hairs and four teeth,
The breast of a grasshopper, the leg and colour of an ant;
Since you wear a brow more wrinkled than your gown
And breasts like the webs of spiders;
Since, compared with your jaws,
The Nile crocodile has a narrow gape,
And the frogs of Ravenna croak more sweetly,
And the gnat of Adria sings more tunefully,
And you see about as much as owls see at morning,
And you smell like a billy-goat,
And you have the rump of a scrawny duck,
And your bony cunt outdoes a Cynic graybeard;
Since the bath-keeper admits you, with the lamp put out,
Only among the whores of the graveyard;
Since for you winter falls in the month of August,
And not even the plague can thaw you out:
You dare, after two hundred deaths, to want to marry
And, mad, you seek a man to itch for your ashes.
What if Sattia's tombstone wanted to wed?
Who will call you spouse, who wife,
You whom Philomelus lately called grandmother?
But if you demand that your corpse be tickled,
Let a couch be spread from Acorus's funeral parlour—
The only one that suits your wedding,
And let the corpse-burner carry torches before the new bride:
Only a funeral brand can enter that cunt.
94. XCIV
You say the hare is not cooked and call for the whip.
You would rather, Rufus, carve up the cook than the hare.
95. XCV
You never say "good day," but always return it, Naevolus,
A thing the raven too often is wont to say first.
Why, I ask you, Naevolus, do you expect me to say it:
For I think, Naevolus, you are neither my better nor my elder.
Each Caesar bestowed rewards on me, the praised,
And gave the paternal rights of three children.
I am read by many a mouth, and fame, without waiting for the pyre,
Gives my name, known throughout the towns.
There is something in this too: Rome has seen me a tribune,
And I sit where Oceanus rouses you.
As many as have been made citizens by Caesar's gift to me,
I do not think you have so many slaves.
But you are buggered, and prettily, Naevolus, you wag your rump.
Now, now you are the better, Naevolus, you win: good day.

title: Epigrams
text:
96. XCVI
You lick my girl, you do not have her,
And you boast like an adulterer and a fornicator.
If I catch you, Gargilius, you will hold your tongue.
97. XCVII
Lest Chione read this book, I commission you, Rufus.
She was hurt by my poem, and she can hurt back.
98. XCVIII
You ask how scrawny your arse is?
You can sodomize, Sabellus, with your arse.
99. XCIX
You ought not to be angry, Cerdo, at my little book.
It is your trade, not your life, that my poem has wounded.
Allow my harmless wit. Why should I not be allowed
To jest, if you were allowed to cut throats?
100. C
I sent the courier back to you, Rufus, at the sixth hour,
And I think he carried my poems soaked through:
For by chance the sky was crashing down with measureless rains.
No otherwise ought that book to have been sent.
1. I
Caesar's life-giving day, more sacred than that light
which Ida shared, when she bore Cretan Jove,
come long, I pray, and richer in years than Pylian Nestor,
and shine forever with this face, or one still finer.
Let him long honour Pallas in Alban gold,
and let the great oak-crown pass through such mighty hands;
let him keep the ages that return in the vast cycle
and the rites that Romulean Tarentos holds.
Great things, you gods, we ask—but owed to the earth:
for so great a god, what prayers could be too bold?
2. II
Lately Horatius alone, among them all,
watched the show in a black cloak,
while the commons, the lesser ranks and the greatest,
sat in white beside their sacred prince.
Suddenly snow fell from the whole sky:
now Horatius watches in a white cloak.
3. III
Look how thick a fleece of silent waters
streams down on Caesar's face and into his lap.
Yet he indulges Jove, and with head unmoved
laughs at the waters thickened by sluggish frost,
he who is used to tiring the star of northern Bootes
and ignoring Helice with his dripping hair.
Who plays with dry waters and sports from the sky?
I suspect these snows belong to Caesar's boy.

title: Epigrams
text:
4. IV
What a dried marsh of a stagnant pool stinks of,
what the raw fumes of the Albulan springs,
what the stale reek of a saltwater fish-tank,
what a lazy he-goat pressing on a she-goat,
what an old soldier's worn-out marching boot,
what a fleece twice steeped in purple dye,
what the fasts of women keeping the Sabbath,
what the panting breath of sad defendants,
what filthy Leda's dying lamp,
what wrestlers' grease made from Sabine lees,
what a fox in flight, a viper's den—
all that, Bassa, I would rather smell than smell of you.
5. V
An honest man and poor, true in tongue and heart,
what do you want, Fabianus, making for Rome?
You cannot pass for a pimp or a party-reveller,
nor summon trembling defendants with a grim voice,
nor seduce the wife of a dear friend,
nor get it up for frigid old women,
nor peddle empty smoke around the Palatine,
nor clap for Canus, nor clap for Glaphyrus:
how, poor wretch, will you live? "A reliable man, a loyal friend—"
That's nothing: you'll never make a Philomelus that way.
6. VI
You want to be thought chaster than a modest virgin
and seem of tender innocence, Malisianus,
when you are filthier than the man
who recites poems made in Tibullus's metre
in Stella's house.
7. VII
Why, boy Hyllus, do you refuse today what you gave yesterday,
turned harsh so suddenly, who were just now so soft?
But already you plead your beard, your years, your hairs.
O night, how long you are, that make a man old in one go!
Why mock us? Yesterday, Hyllus, you were a boy—
tell us, by what reasoning are you a man today?
8. VIII
The first and second hours wear out the morning callers,
the third sets the hoarse pleaders to work,
into the fifth Rome stretches her varied labours,
the sixth is rest for the weary, the seventh will be the end,
the eighth till the ninth suffices for the gleaming wrestling-grounds,
the ninth bids us crush the piled-up couches:
the tenth is the hour for my little books, Euphemus,
when your care prepares the ambrosial feast
and good Caesar relaxes with heavenly nectar
and holds in his great hand a modest cup.
Then let my jokes in: with timid step my Thalia
fears to go in loose stride to Jove at morning.

title: Epigrams
text:
9. IX
Daughter of Sotas the doctor, Labulla,
you leave your husband and chase after Clytus,
you give and you love: you are going to ruin.
10. X
While my little book is new, its brow not yet shaved smooth,
while the page, not quite dry, fears to be touched,
go, boy, and carry the light gift to a dear friend
who has earned to be the first to hold my trifles.
Run, but well equipped: let a Punic sponge
go with the book—it suits my kind of gifts.
Many erasures, Faustinus, cannot
mend my jokes: one erasure can.
11. XI
While you swell, puffed up with an empty name,
and are ashamed, poor wretch, to be a Saturninus,
you stirred up unholy wars beneath the Arcadian Bear,
like the man who bore the arms of his Egyptian wife.
Had the fate of this name so slipped your mind,
that the heavy wrath of the Actian sea once buried?
Or did the Rhine promise you what the Nile
did not give him, and grant you more than the northern waters?
That Antonius too fell by our arms,
who set beside you, traitor, had been a Caesar.
12. XII
You refuse no one, Thais; but if that does not shame you,
let this at least shame you, Thais—to refuse nothing.
13. XIII
Claudia Peregrina weds my Pudens, Rufus:
joy to your torches, O Hymenaeus, joy.
So well does rare cinnamon blend with its nard,
so well Massic wine with Attic honeycombs;
no better are elms joined to tender vines,
no more does the lotus love the water, the myrtle the shore.
Fair Concord, dwell forever on that bed,
and let Venus be always kind to so matched a yoke:
let her love him grown old one day, and let her,
even when old, not seem old to her husband.
14. XIV
Silius, glory of the Castalian sisters,
who with mighty voice crush the perjuries
of barbarian rage and the treacherous
wiles of Hannibal, and force the fickle Carthaginians
to yield to the great Africani:
set your sternness a little aside,
while wandering December, with coaxing dice,
rattles its uncertain dice-boxes here and there
and plays at heads-or-tails with the wickeder die,
and grant some leisure to my Muses;
read with no grim brow, but relaxed,
my little books, soaked in playful jests.
So perhaps tender Catullus dared
to send his Sparrow to great Maro.

title: Epigrams
text:
15. XV
When yesterday you asked me for a thousand sesterces
for six or seven days, Caecilianus,
I said "I haven't got it"; but you, pleading a friend's
arrival, ask me for a dish and a few vessels.
Are you a fool? Or do you think me one, my friend? I refused
you a thousand sesterces—shall I give you five thousand?
16. XVI
That you were no stepson to your stepmother, Gallus,
was the rumour, while she was your father's wife.
Yet while your father lived, it could not be proved.
Now your father is nowhere, Gallus; the stepmother is at home.
Let great Tullius be called back from the shades below
and Regulus himself defend you—still
you cannot be acquitted: for she who does not cease to be
a stepmother after the father, Gallus, never was one.
17. XVII
You bid me write verses against Lycisca, Paulus,
such that, reading them, she may blush and be enraged.
O Paulus, you are wicked: you want to have her all to yourself.
18. XVIII
Where the gate near the Vipsanian columns drips
and the slick stone is soaked with constant rain,
into a boy's throat, as he passed beneath the dripping roof,
a mass of water fell, heavy with winter ice:
and when it had finished the poor boy's cruel fate,
the tender blade melted in the warm wound.
What has savage Fortune not claimed as her right?
Or where is death not, if water cuts our throats?
19. XIX
This thick weave, nursling of a Sequanian weaver,
which, though foreign, bears a Spartan name—
coarse, but in icy December not to be scorned—
I send you as a gift, an outlandish endromis:
whether you rub the sluggish wrestling-grease or the warm trigon,
or snatch the dusty handballs in your grip,
or share out the feathery weight of the loose ball,
or seek to outrun swift Athas in the race—
so that the piercing cold not enter your dripping limbs,
nor a sudden rainbow weigh you down with rain.
Wrapped in this gift, you will laugh at winds and showers:
not even in Tyrian linen would you be so safe.

title: Epigrams
text:
20. XX
Caerellia calls herself an old woman, though she's a doll;
Gellia calls herself a doll, though she's a hag.
You could bear neither one, Collinus, nor the other:
one is absurd, the other sickening.
21. XXI
That there are no gods, that heaven is empty,
Segius declares: and his proof is that he sees himself
made rich while he denies all this.
22. XXII
Having endured her first bridal night, still to be soothed toward her husband,
Cleopatra had plunged herself into the gleaming pool,
fleeing his embrace. But the water betrayed her hiding:
she shone, though covered wholly by the water.
So lilies hidden are counted through clear glass,
so thin crystal forbids roses to lie concealed.
I leaped in, and diving through the shallows snatched
struggling kisses: the clear water, you forbade more.
23. XXIII
While you dawdle too long and slowly debate
who should be first for you and who second
among those the Greek epigram has matched:
Callimachus himself, Thalia, has yielded the palm
of his own will to eloquent Bruttianus.
And if he, sated with Attic wit,
should sport with the salt of Roman Minerva,
make me, I pray, second after him.
24. XXIV
Every woman she had as a friend, Fabianus, Lycoris
has carried out to burial: let her be my wife's friend.
25. XXV
Shores of Altinum that rival the villas of Baiae,
and you, wood that witnessed Phaethon's pyre,
and you, fairest of the Dryads, who wed Antenor's Faunus,
Sola, the maiden, by the Euganean lakes,
and you, Aquileia, blessed by the Ledaean Timavus,
where Cyllarus drank the seven streams:
you shall be the rest and harbour of my old age,
if my leisure should ever be my own.
26. XXVI
That all year I have not seen you at home in the morning,
shall I tell you, Postumus, how much I have lost?
Sixty sesterces, I think, twice; thrice twenty, I think.
Forgive me: I buy my little toga for more, Postumus.

title: Epigrams
text:
27. XXVII
You often praise my little books, Augustus.
Look, the envious man denies it: do you praise them the less?
What of this—that you gave me not only honouring words,
but gifts no other man could give?
Look, again the spiteful one gnaws his blackened nails.
Give all the more, Caesar, that he may suffer.
28. XXVIII
You gave tender Lupercus, Chloe,
cloaks Spanish, Tyrian, and scarlet,
a toga washed in warm Galaesus,
Indian sardonyx, Scythian emeralds,
and a hundred lords of fresh-struck coin:
and whatever he keeps asking you keep giving.
Alas, poor sleek plucked thing, alas for you:
your Lupercus will leave you stripped bare.
29. XXIX
Their own great number stands against my little books, dear Pudens,
and the crowded work wearies and gluts the reader.
Rare things please: so the first fruits hold more favour,
so winter roses earn their price;
so a grasping mistress's scorn commends her,
nor does an ever-open door keep the young man.
Persius is counted more often in his one book
than trifling Marsus in his whole Amazonis.
You too, whatever of my little books you reread,
think it the only one: so it will be worth more to you.
30. XXX
Far from the Baian lake, we warn you,
fisherman, flee, lest you go off guilty.
These waters are swum by sacred fish
that know their master and lick that hand
than which nothing in the world is greater.
What's more, they have names, and at their master's
voice each comes when called.
Once an impious Libyan, in this deep,
while drawing his prey with trembling rod,
suddenly, his eyes snatched away, went blind,
and could not see the fish he'd caught,
and now, hating the sacrilegious hooks,
he sits by the Baian lake, a beggar.
But you, while you may, withdraw guiltless,
casting only honest food into the waves,
and revere the delicate fish.
31. XXXI
That you wish to be named and read in my little books,
and think that some honour comes to you in this,
may I die if it is not most welcome to me,
and I want to have set you among my pages.
But you bear a name imposed against the sisters' spring,
which your hard mother gave you;
one that neither Melpomene nor Polyhymnia could utter,
nor pious Calliope with Phoebus.
So adopt some name the Muses can welcome:
"Hippodame" is not always nicely said.

title: Epigrams
text:
32. XXXII
It both hides and shines, sealed in a Phaethontian drop,
so the bee seems shut in its own nectar.
A worthy reward she won for all her toils:
one may believe she herself chose to die so.
33. XXXIII
Though you have chests full of laboured books,
why, Sosibianus, do you publish nothing?
"My heirs," you say, "will bring out my poems." When?
It was high time, Sosibianus, that you were read.
34. XXXIV
Though your toga is dirty, still he speaks the truth, Attalus,
whoever says you have a snow-white toga.
35. XXXV
With facing brows we saw soft does
charge together and fall by an equal lot of fate.
The dogs watched the prey, and the proud hunter stood amazed
that nothing was left for his knife.
Whence did such light spirits burn with such fury?
So bulls fight, so heroes fall.
36. XXXVI
Your beard is grey, your hair is black: you cannot
dye your beard—that's the reason—but you can, Olus, dye your hair.
37. XXXVII
"Coranus owes a hundred, Mancinus two hundred,
Titius three hundred, Albinus twice that,
Sabinus a million and another, Serranus the same;
from his apartment-blocks and estates, three million clear,
from his Parman flocks come twice three hundred a year":
all day long, Afer, you tell me this,
and I know it better than my own name.
You must pay out something, that I may bear it:
ease my daily nausea with cash—
I cannot listen to all that for free, Afer.
38. XXXVIII
Galla, say no: love sates itself, unless its joys are torment.
But don't, Galla, say no too long.
39. XXXIX
You have collected silver of every kind,
and you alone have Myron's old craft,
you alone the hand of Praxiteles and Scopas,
you alone the chasing of Phidias's tool,
you alone the labours of Mentor.
Nor do you lack genuine Gratian pieces,
nor what is overlaid with Galician gold,
nor embossed plate from ancestral tables.
Yet among all your silver I wonder
why you have none, Charinus, that is pure.

title: Epigrams
text:
40. XL
While the halls of the Pisos stood with all their lineage
and learned Seneca's house, three times to be reckoned;
above such great realms I preferred you alone, Postumus:
you were poor and a knight, but to me you were a consul.
With you, Postumus, I counted thirty winters:
we had a couch in common, one and shared.
Now you can give, now lose, full of honours,
lavish with wealth: I wait, Postumus, to see what you do.
You do nothing, and it's too late to seek another patron.—
Does this please you, Fortune? "Postumus has cheated."
41. XLI
Why, about to recite, do you wrap wool round your neck?
That would suit our ears better.
42. XLII
If anyone could grant me what I ask,
hear, Flaccus, what sort of boy I'd want to ask for.
First, let the boy be born on Nile's shores:
no land knows better how to give naughtiness.
Let him be whiter than snow: for in dusky Mareotis
that colour is the fairer, the rarer it is.
Let his eyes vie with the stars, and soft locks
lash his neck: I don't like curled hair, Flaccus.
A small brow, a nose slightly and lightly hooked,
lips that redden, rivals of Paestan roses.
Let him often force me unwilling, and be unwilling when I'm willing,
let him often be freer than his master;
let him fear the boys, and often shut out the girls:
a man to the rest, let him be a boy to me alone.
"Now I know, and you don't fool me: for in my judgement too it's true.
Such," you'll say, "was my Amazonicus."
43. XLIII
I did not call you a pervert, Coracinus:
I am not so rash or bold,
nor one to tell lies gladly.
If I called you a pervert, Coracinus,
may Pontia's flask be angry with me,
may Metilus's cup be angry with me:
I swear by the Syrian tumours,
I swear by the Berecyntian frenzies.
What did I say, then? This light, trifling thing,
which is well known, which you yourself won't deny—
I said, Coracinus, you go down on women.

title: Epigrams
text:
44. XLIV
Here is Vesuvius, lately green with shady vines,
here the noble grape had pressed its dripping vats:
these ridges Bacchus loved more than the hills of Nysa,
on this mount the Satyrs lately led their dances.
This was Venus's seat, dearer to her than Sparta,
this place was famous for the name of Hercules.
All lies sunk in flames and dismal ash:
the gods themselves would not have wished this allowed them.
45. XLV
These offerings, Phoebus, for his son the Palatine
Parthenius joyfully gives from a full incense-box,
that Burrus, who marks his first five years with a new cycle,
may fill out countless Olympiads.
Make the father's vows come true: so may your own tree love you,
and your sister rejoice in her sure virginity,
so may you shine in perpetual bloom, so may Bacchus's locks
at last be not so long, Phoebus, as yours.
46. XLVI
The Saturnalia made Sabellus rich:
deservedly Sabellus swells with pride,
and thinks and proclaims that no one
among the pleaders is more blessed.
These airs and high spirits are given Sabellus
by half a peck of grain and crushed beans,
and three half-pounds of incense and pepper,
and a Lucanian sausage with a Faliscan paunch,
and a Syrian flask of black boiled wine,
and figs frozen in a Libyan jar
with onions and snails and cheese.
From a Picene client too there came
a little box that holds but scant olives,
and, polished with the potter's coarse tool,
a seven-piece dinner-set of Saguntum,
the yellow earthenware of a Spanish wheel,
and a napkin striped with a broad purple band.
More fruitful Saturnalia than these
Sabellus has not had in ten years.
47. XLVII
Phaethon is painted for you on this panel in encaustic.
What do you mean, making Phaethon twice-burned?
48. XLVIII
You love to be buggered; once buggered, Papylus, you weep.
Why, Papylus, grieve at the deed you wish done?
Do you repent the obscene itch? Or do you weep more
at this, Papylus—that you have stopped being buggered?

title: Epigrams
text:
49. XLIX
He does not know, believe me, what epigrams are, Flaccus,
who calls them only sport and jokes.
He plays more who writes the breakfast of savage
Tereus, or your dinner, indigestible Thyestes,
or Daedalus fitting liquid wings to his boy,
or Polyphemus pasturing Sicilian sheep.
All windy bombast is far from my little books,
nor does my Muse swell in a madman's tragic robe.
"Yet everyone praises, admires, adores those works."
I admit it: they praise those—but they read these.
50. L
Why, Thais, do you keep calling me old?
No one, Thais, is too old to be sucked off.
51. LI
When you didn't have six thousand, Caecilianus,
you rode about widely in a huge six-bearer litter:
after blind fortune gave you two million and the coins
burst your purse, look—you've become a footman.
What should I wish you for your merits and such great praises?
May the gods give you back your sedan, Caecilianus.
52. LII
If you don't stop riding behind your team of goats, Hedylus,
you who were just now a fig will soon be a wild fig.
53. LIII
This man whom you often see within the inner shrine
of our Pallas and the threshold of the new temple,
Cosmus, an old man with staff and wallet, whose hair
stands grey and rotting, and a filthy beard falls on his chest,
whom a coarse cloak covers, wife of his bare pallet,
to whom the crowd he meets gives food he's barked for—
you think him a Cynic, deceived by the false image:
he's no Cynic, Cosmus. What then? A Dog.
54. LIV
O you who have been allowed to touch the Tarpeian oaks
and crown your deserving locks with the first wreath,
if you are wise, Collinus, make use of all your days
and always think the last is at hand for you.
No one has won by prayer from the three wool-spinning girls
a respite: they keep the day they have fixed.
Be richer than Crispus, steadier than Thrasea himself,
more elegant than splendid Melior though you may—
Lachesis adds nothing to the wool, unwinds the sisters'
spindles, and one of the three always says no.

title: Epigrams
text:
55. LV
Lucius, glory of your times,
who do not let old Caius and our Tagus
yield to eloquent Arpi:
let the man born among Argive cities
sing in song of Thebes or Mycenae,
or famous Rhodes, or the Ledaean
wrestling-grounds of lustful Sparta:
let us, sprung from Celts and Iberians,
not be ashamed in grateful verse
to name the harsher names of our land:
Bilbilis, supreme in its fierce metal,
which beats the Chalybes and Norici,
and Platea ringing with its own iron,
which, with a slender but restless current,
Salo, temperer of arms, surrounds,
and the guardianship and dances of Rixamae,
and the festive banquets of Carduae,
and Peteris red with woven roses,
and the ancient theatres of our fathers, Rigae,
and the Silai, sure with the light javelin,
and the lakes of Turgontum and Turasia,
and the pure shallows of little Tvetonissa,
and the holy oak-grove of Burado,
through which even the lazy traveller strolls,
and the fields of curving Vativesca
that Manlius works with sturdy young oxen.
At these so rustic names, dainty reader,
do you laugh? Laugh you may—
these so rustic I prefer to Butunti.
56. LVI
Because you send huge gifts to old men and widows,
do you want me to call you generous, Gargilianus?
Nothing is fouler, nothing more vile than you alone,
who can call your snares gifts:
so the deceitful hook indulges greedy fish,
so the cunning bait deceives the foolish beasts.
What it is to be lavish, what it is to give, I'll teach you,
if you don't know: give, Gargilianus, to me.
57. LVII
While the alluring pools of wanton Lucrinus hold me
and the caves that steam with their pumice springs,
you dwell in the realm of the Argive settler, Faustinus,
where the twentieth milestone leads you from the city.
But the bristling breast of the Nemean monster burns,
and it is not enough that Baiae glow with their own fire.
So, sacred springs and pleasant shores, farewell,
home alike of Nymphs and of Nereids.
In icy winter outdo the Herculean hills,
but now yield to the cool of Tibur.

title: Epigrams
text:
58. LVIII
In the dark you mourn your lost husband, Galla.
By now, I think, you're ashamed to weep for a husband, Galla.
59. LIX
While a viper crept among the weeping Heliads' boughs,
an amber drop flowed onto the beast in its path:
and while it marvels to be held in the rich dew,
it stiffened, suddenly bound by the congealed ice.
Don't be proud of your royal tomb, Cleopatra,
if a viper lies in a nobler sepulchre.
60. LX
Let men make for Ardea and the Castran fields at midsummer
and the land that burns under the Cleonaean star,
since Curiatius condemned the airs of Tibur,
sent to the Styx among its praised waters.
You can shut out fate in no place: when death
has come, in the midst of Tibur there is Sardinia.
61. LXI
That a friend gave you two hundred thousand, Mancinus,
you lately boasted with proud lips, delighted.
Four days ago, in the poets' school,
while we chatted, you said cloaks bought
for ten thousand were a gift from Pompulla,
and a true sardonyx ringed three times with veins,
and two gems like the waves of the sea,
you swore Bassa and Caelia had given.
Yesterday at the theatre, while Pollio sang,
when you suddenly left, in flight you babbled
that three hundred thousand had come to you in legacy,
and a hundred in the morning, and a hundred after noon.
What such great wrong have we, your friends, done you?
Have pity now, cruel man, and be silent at last.
Or, if that tongue of yours cannot keep still,
tell us, some time, what we'd like to hear.
62. LXII
Black Lycoris has moved to Hercules' Tibur,
believing all things turn white there.
63. LXIII
While mother Caerellia made for Baiae from Bauli,
she perished, sunk by the crime of the mad strait.
What glory you have lost! These monstrous deeds, waters,
you never showed Nero once, even when bidden.
64. LXIV
Julius Martialis's few acres,
more blessed than the gardens of the Hesperides,
recline on the long ridge of the Janiculum:
broad retreats jut out over the hills,
and the level top, with its modest swell,
enjoys a clearer sky,
and when mist covers the curving valleys
it alone shines with its own peculiar light;
the dainty rooftops of the lofty villa
are gently raised toward the clear stars.
From here you may see the seven sovereign hills
and take the measure of all Rome,
the Alban and Tusculan hills too
and every cool spot that lies near the city,
old Fidenae and little Rubrae,
and Anna Perenna's fruitful grove
that delights in virgin blood.
On that side, on the Flaminian and Salarian roads,
the traveller is in view, his carriage silent,
lest the wheel be a nuisance to sweet sleep,
which neither the sailors' chant
nor the shout of bargemen can break,
though the Mulvian bridge is so near
and keels glide swift down the sacred Tiber.
This country place, or rather house to be called,
its master commends: you'll think it your own,
so unenvious and so generous,
so kindly open in its hospitality:
you'd believe it the pious home of Alcinous
or of Molorchus just made rich.
You who now think all things small,
tame icy Tibur with a hundred hoes
or Praeneste, and hand over hanging Setia
to a single tenant—
so long as, in my judgement, to all these
are preferred Julius Martialis's few acres.

title: Epigrams
text:
65. LXV
Philaenis always weeps from one eye.
You ask how that comes about? She's one-eyed.
66. LXVI
You have always lived a small-town life, Linus,
than which nothing at all can be cheaper.
On the Ides and on rare Kalends the little toga was shaken out,
and one dinner-suit lasted ten summers.
The forest sent you boar, the field hare, unbought,
the beaten woods gave heavy thrushes,
the caught fish came from the river's depth,
the red jar poured wine not foreign.
No tender page sent from Argive stock,
but a rustic crowd stood by the rough hearth.
The bailiff's wife, or the hard tenant's bride, was tumbled
whenever the wounded vein grew hot with wine.
Fire did no harm to your roofs, nor the Dog-star to your fields,
no ship was sunk at sea, for you had none.
The gambling-die was never slipped you for the coaxing knuckle-bone,
but nuts alone were the play of your thrift.
Tell me, where is the million your greedy mother left?
Nowhere: you've done, Linus, a difficult thing.
67. LXVII
Poor Gaurus begged the praetor for a hundred thousand sesterces,
known to him by an old friendship,
and said this alone was lacking to his three hundred thousand,
that he might be able, as a proper knight, to applaud his lord.
The praetor said, "You know I'll give to Scorpus and Thallus,
and would that I gave a hundred thousand only."
Ah, shame on the ungrateful, shame on the ill-gotten chest.
What you won't give a knight, praetor, will you give a horse?
68. LXVIII
You invite me on a hundred farthings and dine well.
Am I invited to dine, Sextus, or to envy?
69. LXIX
You always set out Setine or Massic, Papylus,
but rumour denies wines so good:
you're said to have been four times widowed by this flask.
I neither think it nor believe it, Papylus, nor am I thirsty.
70. LXX
Nothing but a dry rope did his father leave Ammianus,
dying, in his last will.
Who could have thought it possible, Marullinus,
that Ammianus would not want his father dead?

title: Epigrams
text:
71. LXXI
Long I search the whole city, Safronius Rufus,
to find a girl who says no: no girl says no.
As though it weren't allowed, as though it were shameful to refuse,
as though it weren't permitted: no girl says no.
Is none then chaste? A thousand are chaste: what, then,
does a chaste one do? She doesn't give, yet she doesn't say no.
72. LXXII
You demand, Quintus, that I give you my little books.
I haven't got them, but the bookseller Tryphon has.
"Shall I pay money for trifles and buy your poems, sane?
No," you say, "I won't do anything so foolish." Nor will I.
73. LXXIII
When grievous Vestinus was drawing his last hours
and was now about to pass through the Stygian waters,
he begged the sisters spinning his final threads
to draw the dark strands a little while longer,
already dead to himself, while he lived on for his dear friends.
Such pious prayers moved the grim goddesses.
Then, having divided his great wealth, he withdrew from the light
and after this believed he died an old man.
74. LXXIV
You see how brave the battles unwarlike does attempt?
How great the anger in such timid beasts?
With small brows they burn to charge to the death.
Do you wish, Caesar, to spare the does? Send dogs.
75. LXXV
O happy in your heart, Nigrina, happy in your husband,
and first glory among Latin brides:
it delights you to share your inherited wealth with your spouse,
rejoicing in a partner who is your fellow.
Let Evadne be burned, flung onto her husband's flames,
nor let lesser fame bear Alcestis to the stars:
you do better: by a sure pledge of life you've earned
that your love need not be proved by death.
76. LXXVI
You sent me six thousand when I asked twelve:
to get twice six, I'll ask twice twelve.
77. LXXVII
Never have I asked the gods for riches,
content with little and happy with my own:
Poverty—forgive me—be gone.
What is the cause of this sudden, novel prayer?
I want to see Zoilus hanged.

title: Epigrams
text:
78. LXXVIII
Though your sixtieth harvest is already stored away
and your white face shines with much grey hair,
you dash about, wandering the whole city, nor is there any chair
to which you don't carry an unwearied "Good morning" each dawn;
without you no tribune may rightly go forth,
nor does either consul lack your attendance;
ten times you climb back up the sacred Palatine slope
and sound nothing but Sigeri and Partheni.
Let young men do this: nothing, Afer,
is more unseemly than a busybody grown old.
79. LXXIX
You were always a guest at my Tibur place, Matho.
Now you buy it. I've tricked you: I'm selling you your own land.
80. LXXX
You declaim in a fever, Maro: that this is madness,
if you don't know, you're not sane, friend Maro.
You declaim while sick, you declaim in a semi-tertian fever:
if you can't sweat otherwise, there's a method in it.
"Yet it's a great thing." You're wrong; when fever burns
your guts, the great thing, Maro, is to keep quiet.
81. LXXXI
When Fabulla had read my epigram
in which I complain that no girl says no,
asked once and twice and three times, she ignored
a lover's prayers. Now, Fabulla, promise:
I told you to refuse, I did not tell you to refuse forever.
82. LXXXII
Commend these little books too to Venuleius, Rufus,
and ask him to charge a little leisure to me,
and, forgetting a while his cares and his own works,
not to weigh my trifles with a sour ear.
But let him read them neither after the first cup nor the last,
but when Bacchus in the middle loves his battles.
If it's too much to have read both books, let one roll
be folded back: so the work, divided, will be brief.
83. LXXXIII
Nothing is worse than you, Naevolus, when carefree; the same man
when anxious, nothing is better than you, Naevolus.
Carefree, you return no greeting, you despise everyone,
no man is free in your eyes, no man born:
anxious, you give gifts, you greet your lord and king,
you invite to dinner. Be anxious, Naevolus.

title: Epigrams
text:
84. LXXXIV
There is no one in the people or the whole city
who can prove by his own account that Thais has gone to bed with him,
though many desire and many ask.
Is Thais so chaste, I ask? No—she sucks.
85. LXXXV
We drink from glass, you from myrrhine ware, Ponticus. Why?
So that a clear cup won't betray your two kinds of wine.
86. LXXXVI
If you wish to win approval from Attic ears,
I urge and advise you, little book,
to please learned Apollinaris.
Nothing is more exacting and erudite,
but nothing more candid and kind:
if he holds you in his heart, on his lips,
you need fear no sneers from the spiteful,
nor will you give the mackerel troublesome coats.
If he condemns you, you may at once
run to the fishmongers' shelves,
fit paper for boys to scribble on the back.
87. LXXXVII
Your Bassa, Fabullus, always keeps an infant by her,
calls it her sport and her darling,
and—what you'd wonder at more—she's no fond of children.
What's the reason, then? Bassa is in the habit of farting.
88. LXXXVIII
You sent back no gift for my small present,
and now five days of Saturn have already passed.
So not even six scruples of Septician silver
were sent, nor a napkin from a grumbling client,
nor a jar reddened with the blood of an Antipolitan
tunny, nor one bearing small Syrian figs,
nor a little basket of wrinkled Picene olives—
so that you could say you remembered me?
You'll deceive others with kind words and looks,
for to me you'll now be a known dissembler.
89. LXXXIX
Stop now, enough now, little book,
we've already reached the very end-knobs.
Yet you want to go further on and on,
nor can you be held back at the last sheet,
as if your work were not yet done,
which was done at the first page too.
Now the reader grumbles and grows faint,
now the copyist himself says it too:
"Stop now, enough now, little book."

title: Epigrams
text:
1. I
This I send you, Caesar—whether you enjoy the hills of Palladian Alba
and look from there toward Trivia, from there toward Thetis,
or whether the truth-telling sisters learn your responses
where the smooth wave of the suburban strait lies still,
or whether Aeneas's nurse pleases you, or the Sun's daughter,
or white Anxur with its health-giving waters—
this I send, O happy guardian and safety of the world,
while you are safe we believe Jove is kind.
Only accept it: I'll think that you have read it
and indulge, swollen with Gallic credulity.
2. II
Matrons and boys and maidens,
to you our page is dedicated.
You, whom too-saucy naughtiness
and naked wit delight too much,
read the four wanton little books:
the fifth book jokes with our lord;
which Germanicus may read, his cheek unblushing,
before the Cecropian maiden.
3. III
Degis, now a dweller on our bank, Germanicus,
who came to you from the servant waters of the Hister,
glad and amazed at having just seen the world's protector,
is said to have spoken thus to his companions:
"How much better is my lot than my brother's, who is allowed
so near to behold the god whom from afar he worships."
4. IV
Myrtale tends to reek of much wine,
but to fool us she gobbles laurel leaves
and, careful, mixes her neat wine with foliage, not water.
Whenever you see her coming toward you, Paulus,
flushed, with bulging veins,
you may well say, "Myrtale has been drinking laurel."
5. V
Sextus, eloquent attendant of Palatine Minerva,
who enjoy the nearer genius of the god—
for you are allowed to know our lord's nascent cares
and the leader's secret heart—:
let there be a place, even in some corner, for my little books too,
where Pedo, where Marsus, where Catullus will be.
Beside the heavenly songs of the Capitoline war
set the great work of buskined Maro.

title: Epigrams
text:
6. VI
If it is not too burdensome or too troublesome,
Muses, ask your Parthenius:
so may a later and once-blessed old age
end your days with Caesar safe,
and may you be happy with envy in your favour,
so may Burrus soon feel himself a parent:
admit my timid and brief page
within the threshold of the holier court.
You know the times of Jove serene,
when he shines with his own calm face,
with which he is wont to deny suppliants nothing.
There's no cause to fear unjust prayers:
my page never asks for great or troublesome things,
which, adorned with cedar oil and purple,
has grown up with black end-knobs.
Don't hold it out, but keep it
as if you offered and did nothing.
If I know the lord of the nine sisters,
he'll ask of his own accord for the purple little book.
7. VII
As fires renew the Assyrian nests
each time the one bird has lived ten generations,
so new Rome has shed her old age
and herself taken on the face of her protector.
Now, I pray, forgetting the well-known complaint, Vulcan,
spare us: we are the throng of Mars, but of Venus too:
spare us, father: so may your wanton wife forgive
the Lemnian chains and patiently love.
8. VIII
The edict of our lord and god,
by which the seating is made more certain
and the knight has recovered his unmixed rows,
while Phasis just now was praising it in the theatre,
Phasis, red in his purple cloak,
and boasting, proud, with swollen mouth:
"At last one may sit more comfortably,
now the equestrian dignity is restored,
we're not crowded by the mob nor soiled":
while he reclined and reported such things,
Leitus ordered those purple and arrogant
cloaks to get up.
9. IX
I was ill: but you came at once to me,
Symmachus, attended by a hundred students.
A hundred hands chilled by the north wind touched me:
I had no fever, Symmachus—now I have.

title: Epigrams
text:
10. X
"What shall I call this—that fame is denied the living,
and that rare is the reader who loves his own age?"
These, no doubt, Regulus, are the ways of envy,
that it should always prefer the old to the new.
So, ungrateful, we seek out old Pompey's shade,
so old men praise Catulus's paltry temples;
Ennius was read while you, Rome, still had Maro,
and his own age laughed at the Maeonian,
the seldom-crowded theatre applauded crowned Menander,
only Corinna knew her Naso.
Yet you, O my little books, do not be in haste:
if glory comes after death, I'm in no hurry.
11. XI
Sardonyxes, emeralds, diamonds, jaspers—my Stella
turns them all, Severus, on one knuckle.
Many gems on his fingers, more in his verse
you'll find: hence, I think, this cultured hand.
12. XII
That proud Masclion bears nodding weights
on his brow with the pole that props them,
or that great Ninus lifts with all his muscles
seven boys or eight,
seems no hard feat to me,
when my Stella with one finger, this one or that,
carries ten girls.
13. XIII
I am, I confess, and always was, Callistratus, poor,
but no obscure or ill-known knight;
I'm read throughout the world and people say "That's the man",
and what death gives to few, life has given me.
But your roofs rest on a hundred columns,
your strongbox lashes freedman's wealth,
the great soil of Nile's Syene serves you,
and Gallic Parma shears your countless flocks.
This is what I and you are: but what I am, you cannot be;
what you are, anyone from the crowd can be.
14. XIV
Nanneius, used always to sit in the front row,
back when one could grab a seat,
twice and three times moved on, shifted his camp,
and almost as a third party, among the very chairs,
sat down behind a Gaius and a Lucius.
From there, his head covered with a hood, he peers out
and watches the games, unseemly, with one eye.
And from there, poor wretch, thrown out, he passes into the gangway,
and half-propped on the edge of a back bench,
and ill-received, on one knee, he pretends
to a knight that he's sitting, to Leitus that he's standing.

title: Epigrams
text:
15. XV
This is the fifth book of my jokes, Augustus,
and no one complains of being hurt by my verse,
but many a reader rejoices at an honoured name,
to whom by my gift lasting fame is given.
"Yet what do these things profit, though they honour many?"
Granted they profit not—still they delight me.
16. XVI
That I prefer to write what pleases, though I could write
serious things—you are the cause, friendly reader,
you who read and sing all my songs throughout Rome:
but you don't know how much such love costs me.
For if I chose to defend the temple of the scythe-bearing Thunderer
and sell words to anxious defendants,
many a sailor would send me Spanish casks
and my pocket would grow grimy with varied coin.
But now my little book is a guest and a reveller,
and my page pleases only for free.
Yet the ancients were not content with praise alone,
when the least gift to a poet was an Alexis.
"Nicely said," you say; "it delights me and we'll praise it always."
You play dumb? You'll make me a pleader, I think.
17. XVII
While you recount grandfathers and ancestors and great names,
while a knight like me is to you a sordid match,
while you say you cannot marry, Gellia, anyone but a man
of the broad stripe—you've married, Gellia, a chest-bearer.
18. XVIII
That in December, the month when napkins fly
and slender ladles and wax tapers and papers
and the sharp jar of Damascus plums goes to old men,
I sent you nothing but home-born little books,
perhaps I may seem stingy or unkind—
I hate the crafty and wicked arts of gifts:
gifts mimic hooks: for who does not know
that the greedy scarus is caught by the swallowed fly?
Whenever a poor man gives nothing to a rich friend,
O Quintianus, he is generous.
19. XIX
If there's any faith in truth, O greatest Caesar,
no ages can be preferred to your times.
When was it allowed to see worthier triumphs?
When did the Palatine gods deserve more?
Under what leader was warlike Rome fairer and greater?
Under what prince was liberty so great?
Yet there is this fault—and no slight one, though it's the only one—
that the poor man cultivates ungrateful friendships.
Who lavishes wealth on an old and faithful comrade,
or whom does a knight, not unrelated, attend?
To have sent a ladle of a half-pound at the Saturnalia,
or ten full scruples of a flame-coloured toga,
is luxury, and the swollen patrons call these gifts:
one who might jingle gold pieces will perhaps be the only one.
Since these patrons don't exist, be you, Caesar, our friend:
no virtue of a leader can be sweeter.
Long since you've been laughing, Germanicus, with silent nose,
that I give you advice useful to me.

title: Epigrams
text:
20. XX
If with you, dear Martialis, I were allowed
to enjoy carefree days,
to dispose of leisured time
and alike be free for true life:
we'd know neither the halls nor the houses of the powerful,
nor grim lawsuits and the gloomy forum,
nor proud ancestral busts;
but riding, talk, little books,
the Field, the colonnade, shade, the Virgin's water, the baths—
these would always be our haunts, these our labours.
Now neither of us lives for himself, and feels the good
suns flee and pass away,
which perish for us and are charged to our account.
Does any man, who knows how to live, delay?
21. XXI
Quintus instead of Decimus, Macer instead of Crassus, Regulus,
the rhetor Apollodotus used to greet.
Now he returns each man's greeting by his own name. How much
care and toil can do! He wrote it down and learned it by heart.
22. XXII
If I did not wish and deserve to see you at home in the morning,
let your Esquiline, Paulus, be farther off for me.
But I'm a near neighbour to the Tiburtine pillar,
where rustic Flora looks on ancient Jove:
the steep path of the Suburan slope must be climbed,
and the filthy stones, with a step never dry,
and one can scarcely break through the long mule-trains
and the marble you see dragged with much rope.
Worse still is this: that after a thousand labours
the doorkeeper tells me, Paulus, you're not at home, exhausted.
This is the end of my vain effort and my soaked little toga:
it was scarcely worth so much to see Paulus in the morning.
The dutiful man always has unkind friends:
unless you sleep in, you cannot be my patron.
23. XXIII
You had clothed yourself in grass-green colours, Bassus,
while the laws of the theatre seats were silent.
But after the gentle censor's care bade them
be reborn, and the knight, made surer, obeys Oceanus,
you shine in no clothing but what is soaked with scarlet
or dyed with purple, and think thus to fool him.
There are no four-hundred-thousand cloaks, Bassus,
or my Cordus would have a horse before all others.

title: Epigrams
text:
24. XXIV
Hermes, the warlike delight of the age,
Hermes, skilled in all weapons,
Hermes both gladiator and trainer,
Hermes, the throng and terror of his own school,
Hermes, whom Helius fears, but him alone,
Hermes, to whom Advolans falls, but to him alone,
Hermes, taught to conquer and not to wound,
Hermes, his own understudy,
Hermes, the riches of the seat-sellers,
Hermes, the care and toil of the gladiators' women,
Hermes, proud with the warlike spear,
Hermes, menacing with the sea-god's trident,
Hermes, fearsome with the drooping helmet,
Hermes, the glory of universal Mars,
Hermes, all things in one and three times one.
25. XXV
"You don't have four hundred thousand, Chaerestratus: get up,
look, Leitus is coming: stand, flee, run, hide."
Is there anyone, ah, who calls him back and leads the departing in?
Is there any friend, ah, who opens his ample wealth?
Whom shall we give to our pages and to fame and to the talk of nations?
Who would not wish to go down whole to the Stygian lakes?
Is not this, I ask, better than to spatter the stage with a red shower
and be drenched with lavished saffron?
Than to give four hundred thousand to a horse that won't feel it,
so that Scorpus's golden nose may gleam everywhere?
O rich man in vain, O dissembler of your friend,
do you read this and praise it? What fame you're losing!
26. XXVI
That I called you the alpha of the cloaked men, Cordus,
lately, when I was joking on some page,
if perchance this verse stirred your bile,
you may call me the beta of the toga-wearers.
27. XXVII
Talent and study and manners and birth
you have of a knight, I admit: the rest you have of the plebs.
Don't let your fourteen rows of benches be worth so much
that you sit pale at the sight of Oceanus.
28. XXVIII
That Mamercus should speak and think well,
you could bring about by no manners, Aulus:
though you outdo the Curvian brothers in piety,
the Nervas in calm, the Rusos in courtesy,
the Macers in honesty, the Mauricuses in fairness,
the Reguli in oratory, the Pauli in jests:
he gnaws everything with rusty teeth.
You might believe him perhaps a spiteful man:
I believe him a wretched one, whom no one pleases.

title: Epigrams
text:
29. XXIX
Whenever you send me a hare, Gellia, you say:
"You'll be handsome, Marcus, for seven days."
If you don't mock, if you tell the truth, my light,
you've never eaten a hare, Gellia.
30. XXX
Varro, not to be disowned by the Sophoclean buskin,
nor less to be admired in the Calabrian lyre,
put off your work, let neither eloquent Catullus's stage
detain you, nor elegy with her dressed hair;
but in smoky December read these poems,
not to be scorned, sent you in their own month:
unless perhaps it seems to you handier and better
to lose, Varro, the Saturnalian nuts.
31. XXXI
See how the troop leaps over the gentle bullocks
and how the easy-natured bull loves its own burden.
This one hangs from the very tips of the horns, that one, ranging,
runs along the shoulders and brandishes his weapons all over the ox.
But the savage beast stays rigid, unmoved: the sand
would be no safer, and the level ground could deceive them more.
Their gestures don't tremble; but for the prize at stake
the boy is unconcerned, the herd anxious.
32. XXXII
Crispus, Faustinus, in his last will did not leave
his wife a farthing. "To whom did he leave it, then?" To himself.
33. XXXIII
A pleader is said to carp at my poems: who he is,
I don't know: if I find out, woe to you, pleader.
34. XXXIV
To you, father Fronto, mother Flaccilla, I commend
this girl, my kisses and my darling,
that little Erotion may not shudder at the dark shades
and the monstrous jaws of the hound of Tartarus.
She would have completed the cold of her sixth winter,
had she not lived just so many days too few.
Among such aged patrons let her play, wanton,
and chatter my name with lisping mouth.
Let no hard turf cover her soft bones, and you,
earth, do not be heavy on her: she was not heavy on you.
35. XXXV
While scarlet-clad Euclides was shouting
that he gets two hundred thousand back from his Patran estates
and more from his suburban land near Corinth,
and traced his long pedigree from fair Leda,
and resisted Leitus, who was making him get up:
from the proud, noble, wealthy knight's
bosom a great key suddenly fell.
Never, Fabullus, was there a more good-for-nothing key.

title: Epigrams
text:
36. XXXVI
A certain man, praised in my little book, Faustinus,
pretends, as if he owed nothing: he's cheated me.
37. XXXVII
A girl sweeter to me than the aged swans,
softer than the lamb of Phalantine Galaesus,
daintier than the shell of the Lucrine pool,
to whom you'd prefer neither Erythraean pearls,
nor the just-polished tooth of the Indian beast,
nor virgin snows nor the untouched lily;
who outdid in hair the fleece of the Baetic flock
and the knots of the Rhine and the golden dormouse;
whose breath was fragrant as the rose-gardens of Paestum,
as the first honey of Attic combs,
as a lump of amber snatched from the hand;
compared to whom the peacock was unlovely,
the squirrel unpleasing, and the phoenix common:
Erotion is still warm on her fresh pyre,
whom the bitter law of cruellest fates
finished in her sixth winter, and not even all of it,
my love and joy and play—
and yet my Paetus forbids me to be sad,
beating his breast and tearing his hair the same:
"Aren't you ashamed to weep at a little slave-girl's death?
I," he says, "have buried a wife, and yet I live,
a famous, proud, noble, wealthy wife."
What can be braver than our Paetus?
He inherited twenty million, and yet he lives.
38. XXXVIII
Calliodorus has an equestrian fortune—who doesn't know it?—
Sextus, but Calliodorus also has a brother.
He who says "Split the four hundred thousand" is dividing a fig:
do you think two can sit on one horse?
What have you to do with your brother, with troublesome Pollux?
If you had no Pollux, you'd be Castor.
Since you are one, will you, Calliodorus, sit as two?
Get up: you're committing a solecism, Calliodorus.
Or imitate Leda's brood—if you can't sit with your brother—:
take turns, Calliodorus, in sitting.
39. XXXIX
Thirty times in a year, Charinus, when you sealed
your last will, I sent you cakes
soaked in Hyblaean thyme.
I'm worn out: have pity now, Charinus:
seal less often, or do once for all
what your cough keeps falsely promising.
I've emptied my money-boxes and my purse:
though I'd been richer than Croesus,
I'd be poorer than Irus, Charinus,
if you so often ate up my bean-soup.

title: Epigrams
text:
40. XL
You painted Venus, Artemidorus, and you worship Minerva:
and you wonder your work has displeased?
41. XLI
Though you are more unmanned than a flabby eunuch,
and softer than the catamite of Celaenae,
whom the gelded Gallus of the frenzied mother bewails,
you talk of theatres and rows and edicts,
and of robes and the Ides and brooches and fortunes,
and point out the poor with your pumiced hand.
Whether you may sit on the knights' benches,
I'll see, Didymus: you may not sit on the husbands'.
42. XLII
A cunning thief will carry off your coins with the chest broken open,
impious flame will lay your ancestral home in ruins:
a debtor will deny alike the interest and the principal,
the barren field won't return the seed cast in:
a deceitful mistress will rob your steward,
the wave will overwhelm your ships piled with merchandise.
Beyond fortune's reach is whatever is given to friends:
the wealth you give away is the only wealth you'll always have.
43. XLIII
Thais has black teeth, Laecania snow-white.
What's the reason? This one has bought hers, that one has her own.
44. XLIV
What has happened, I ask, what suddenly has happened,
that when I invited you to dinner, Dento—
who would believe it?—you dared four times to refuse?
And you don't look back and you flee me when I follow,
whom you used just now to seek at the baths and theatres
and in every gathering-room.
So it is—you've been caught by a richer table,
and a bigger kitchen has snatched the dog.
Soon, but quickly, recognized and dropped,
when the rich cookshop has grown tired of you,
you'll come back to the bones of your old dinner.
45. XLV
You call yourself beautiful, Bassa, you call yourself a girl.
That's what she who is neither tends to say, Bassa.
46. XLVI
Since I want no kisses but those I've snatched in struggle,
and your anger pleases me more than your face,
to ask you often, Diadumenus, I often beat you:
and I achieve this—that you neither fear nor love me.

title: Epigrams
text:
47. XLVII
Philo swears he's never dined at home, and it's true:
he doesn't dine, whenever no one has invited him.
48. XLVIII
What does love not compel? Encolpos cut his hair
against his master's wish—though not forbidden—
Pudens allowed it and wept: so the father gave up the reins,
complaining of bold Phaethon:
so Hylas was carried off, so Achilles, discovered,
laid down his hair gladly, his mother grieving.
But you, don't hurry—don't trust to short hair—
and come slowly, beard, in return for so great a gift.
49. XLIX
When just now I happened to see you sitting
alone, Labienus, I thought you three.
The number of your bald head deceived me:
you have hairs on this side, you have them on that,
such as might even suit a boy;
the head's bare in the middle, and not one
hair is marked on the long expanse.
This mistake profited you in December,
then, when the Emperor sent out the dinners:
you came back with three little bread-baskets.
Such, I believe, was Geryon.
You should avoid, I advise, Philip's colonnade:
if Hercules sees you, you're done for.
50. L
Whenever I dine at home, unless I've invited you, Charopinus,
at once there are huge hostilities,
and you could run me through the middle with drawn sword,
if you learn my hearth grew warm without you.
So I'm not allowed even once to steal a meal?
Nothing is more shameless than this gullet of yours, Charopinus.
Stop now, I beg, watching my kitchen,
and let my cook for once put one over on you.
51. LI
This man, who carries a left hand weighed down with books,
whom a light chorus of clerks crowds round,
who, with notebooks brought out from this side and that
and with letters, lends a grave countenance,
