like Cato and Tullius and Brutus,
though the racks should force him, Rufus, cannot
manage a Latin "Greetings," nor a Greek "Chaire."
If you think I'm making this up, let's greet him.

title: Epigrams
text:
52. LII
What you've done for me I remember and will always keep in mind.
Why then am I silent, Postumus? Because you talk.
Whenever I begin to recount your gifts to someone,
at once he cries, "He told me himself."
Some things two don't do nicely: one is enough
for this task: if you want me to speak, be silent yourself.
Believe me, Postumus, gifts, however huge,
are spoiled by the chattering of their giver.
53. LIII
Why write of Medea, why, friend, write of Thyestes?
What use to you, Bassus, are Niobe or Andromache?
The fittest subject for your pages, believe me,
is Deucalion, or, if he doesn't please, Phaethon.
54. LIV
My rhetor has become an improviser:
he didn't write down "Calpurnius," and he greeted him.
55. LV
Tell me, whom do you carry, queen of the birds? "The Thunderer."
Why does he hold no thunderbolts in his hand? "He's in love."
With what fire does the god burn? "A boy's." Why do you look back
gently at Jove, with open beak? "I'm speaking of Ganymede."
56. LVI
To what schoolmaster you should hand your son, Lupus,
you ask, anxious, and inquire a long time.
Avoid, I advise, all the grammarians and rhetors:
let him have nothing to do
with the books of Cicero or Maro,
let him leave Tutilius to his own fame;
if he makes verses, disown the poet.
Does he want to learn the money-making arts?
See that he learns lyre-playing or flute-playing;
if the boy seems of dull wit,
make him an auctioneer or an architect.
57. LVII
When I call you "lord," Cinna, don't be pleased with yourself:
I often return your slave's greeting that way too.
58. LVIII
Tomorrow you'll live, tomorrow, you keep saying, Postumus.
Tell me, that "tomorrow," Postumus—when does it come?
How far off is that "tomorrow," where is it? Or where is it to be sought?
Surely it doesn't hide among the Parthians and Armenians?
That "tomorrow" already has the years of Priam or Nestor.
That "tomorrow"—tell me—for how much could it be bought?
You'll live tomorrow? Today it's already too late to live, Postumus:
he is wise, whoever, Postumus, lived yesterday.

title: Epigrams
text:
59. LIX
That I send you no silver, that I send you no gold,
this I do, eloquent Stella, for your own sake.
Whoever has given great things wished great things sent back to him;
by my earthenware you'll be relieved of that.
60. LX
Though you bark at us on and on
and provoke us with your shameless yelping,
I'm resolved to deny you outright this fame,
which you've long sought, that in my little books,
such as they are, you should be read throughout the world.
For why should anyone know you existed?
You must perish unknown, poor wretch.
Yet perhaps there'll be no lack, in this city,
of one or two or three or four
willing to gnaw the dog's hide:
but I keep my nails from this scab.
61. LXI
Who is that curly-haired fellow, Marianus, always
clinging to your wife? Who is that curly-haired fellow?
Who whispers I-don't-know-what into your lady's tender ear
and presses her chair with his right elbow?
On all of whose fingers a slim ring runs,
whose legs bear not a hair to mar them?
You give me no answer? "He manages my wife's
affairs," you say. To be sure, he's a steadfast, hard man,
who shows the agent in his very face:
Aufidius of Chios won't be sharper than this.
O how you deserved, Marianus, the slaps of Latinus:
you'll be the successor, I believe, to Panniculus.
He manages your wife's affairs? That curly fellow, any affairs?
Not your wife's affairs—your affairs he manages.
62. LXII
By your own right you may stay in my gardens, guest,
if you can lay your limbs on the bare ground,
or if a great supply of furnishings is carried with you:
for mine has already given up the ghost for guests.
No mattress—not even an empty one—covers the broken couches,
the rotten webbing lies with its cord snapped.
Yet let the lodging be shared between us two:
I bought the gardens; that's the greater part: you furnish them; that's the less.

title: Epigrams
text:
63. LXIII
"What do you think," you say, "Marcus, of my little books?"
So you often ask me, Ponticus, anxious.
I admire, I'm astonished: nothing is more perfect than they,
Regulus himself will yield to your genius.
"You think so?" you say. "So may Caesar be good to you,
so may Capitoline Jupiter." No—to you.
64. LXIV
Pour me two measures of Falernian, Callistus,
and you, Alcimus, melt summer snows over them,
let my dripping hair grow rich with abundant balsam
and my temples be wearied with sewn rose-garlands.
The Mausoleum so near bids us live,
since it teaches that the gods themselves can perish.
65. LXV
Stars and heaven were given—though his stepmother opposed—
to Alcides by the terror of Nemea and the Arcadian boar
and the chastised wrestling-grease of the Libyan ring
and Eryx, laid low heavily in Sicilian dust,
and the woods' terror, who by silent fraud was wont
to lead off cattle, walking backward, into his cave—Cacus.
Of your arena, Caesar, what small fraction is this seen?
The new day brings greater battles in the morning.
How many heavier weights fall than the Nemean monster!
How many Maenalian boars your spear lays low!
Were the Iberian shepherd's triple fight renewed,
you have one who could conquer Geryon.
Though the Greek Lerna's beast be counted often,
what does the wicked Hydra do beside the Nile's beasts?
For such great merits, Augustus, the gods gave heaven
to Alcides quickly, but to you they'll give it late.
66. LXVI
Often greeted, you never greet first yourself:
so you'll have, Pontilianus, your "Eternal farewell."
67. LXVII
When the Attic birds were seeking their winter retreats
in the usual way, one bird stayed behind in the nests.
The others caught the crime when they returned in spring-time,
and her own kind tore the deserter to pieces.
Late she paid the penalty: the guilty mother should have been
torn apart, but then, when she mangled Itys.

title: Epigrams
text:
68. LXVIII
From a northern race I've sent you hair, Lesbia,
that you might know how much more golden yours is.
69. LXIX
Antonius, who'll reproach Pharian Pothinus with nothing,
and more lightly guilty by the proscription-list than by Cicero:
why, madman, do you draw a sword against Roman lips?
Not even Catiline would have allowed this crime.
The impious soldier is bribed with unspeakable gold,
and for such great wealth one voice falls silent for you.
What use is the precious silence of that sacred tongue?
All men will begin to speak for Cicero.
70. LXX
A hundred thousand just poured into him by his patron,
in full, Maximus—Syriscus,
wandering through the cookshops with their stools
around the four baths, ran through it.
O what a gullet, to eat up a hundred thousand!
And greater still—and not even reclining!
71. LXXI
Where moist Trebula sends down her chill valleys
and the green field is cold in the months of the Crab,
country never violated by the Cleonaean lion
and a house always friendly to the Aeolian South wind,
they call you, Faustinus: pass your long harvests
on these hills; Tibur will be your winter now.
72. LXXII
He who could call the Thunderer Bacchus's mother
could call Semele, Rufus, his father.
73. LXXIII
Why I don't give you my little books,
when you beg and demand them so often,
do you wonder, Theodorus? There's a great reason:
that you may not give me your little books.
74. LXXIV
The young Pompeys Asia and Europe cover, but the father himself
the land of Libya covers, if indeed any land covers him.
What wonder if he's scattered over the whole world? In one
place so great a ruin could not lie.
75. LXXV
She who married you to obey the law, Laelia, Quintus,
you may call your lawful wife.
76. LXXVI
Mithridates profited by often drinking poison,
so that savage toxins could not harm him.
You too have taken precautions, dining always so badly,
that you could never, Cinna, die of hunger.

title: Epigrams
text:
77. LXXVII
A certain man is said, Marullus, to have wittily said
that you carry oil in your ear.
78. LXXVIII
If you suffer from a dismal dinner alone at home,
Toranius, you can go hungry with me.
You won't lack, if you're used to an aperitif,
cheap Cappadocian lettuce and pungent leeks,
a slice of tuna will lie hidden in halved eggs.
There'll be set out, to be held in scorched fingers
on a black dish, green sprouts,
which just now left the chilly garden,
and a little sausage pressing snowy porridge,
and pale beans with reddish bacon.
If you'll have the gifts of the second course,
shrivelled grapes will be offered you
and pears that bear the name of the Syrians,
and chestnuts that learned Naples produced,
roasted in slow heat:
the wine you'll make good by drinking it.
After all this, if by chance Bacchus stirs
the hunger he usually does,
noble olives will come to your aid,
such as the Picene branches lately bore,
and hot chickpeas and warm lupins.
The little dinner is small—who can deny it?—
but you'll feign nothing nor hear feigned talk,
and you'll recline at ease with your own face;
nor will the host read out a fat scroll,
nor will girls from wicked Gades
keep quivering, lustful, without end,
their wanton loins with practised trembling;
but the pipe of little Condylus will sound
something neither heavy nor coarse.
This is the little dinner. You'll follow Claudia.
What girl do you want me to put before you?
79. LXXIX
Eleven times you got up at one dinner, Zoilus,
and your dinner-suit was changed eleven times,
lest the sweat, retained, should cling to your damp clothes
and a thin breeze chafe your loosened skin.
Why don't I sweat, who dine with you, Zoilus?
Because one dinner-suit makes great cold.
80. LXXX
You may give me, Severus, not a whole hour,
if you have time—and you may charge it to me—
while you read and assess my trifles.
"It's hard to lose a holiday": I ask
that you bear and endure this loss.
But if you read these with eloquent
—but surely we're not shameless?—Secundus,
this little book will owe you much more
than it owes its own author.
For it will be carefree, nor will it see
the restless marbles of weary Sisyphus,
once the censorial file of learned Secundus,
with my Severus, has nibbled it.

title: Epigrams
text:
81. LXXXI
You'll always be poor, if you're poor, Aemilianus.
Wealth is now given to none but the rich.
82. LXXXII
Why did you promise me two hundred thousand, Gaurus,
if you couldn't give me ten thousand, Gaurus?
Or can you and won't? I ask, isn't that more shameful?
Go, may you perish, Gaurus: you're a paltry man.
83. LXXXIII
You pursue, I flee; you flee, I pursue; this is my disposition:
I don't want what you want, Dindymus, and I want what you don't.
84. LXXXIV
Now the gloomy boy, his nuts abandoned,
is called back by his bawling schoolmaster,
and, badly betrayed by the coaxing dice-box,
just dragged from his secret cookshop,
the soaked gambler begs the aedile off.
The Saturnalia have all gone by,
and you've sent me no little gifts, not even smaller ones,
Galla, than you used to.
Well, let my December pass like that:
you know surely, I think, that your own
Saturnalia are coming now, the Kalends of March;
then I'll give you back, Galla, what you gave.
1. I
This sixth little book is sent you here,
Martialis, dear to me above all others:
if you polish it with attentive ear,
it will dare, less anxious and trembling,
to come into Caesar's great hands.
2. II
It was sport to betray the bonds of sacred wedlock,
sport too to cut the undeserving males.
Both you forbid, Caesar, and to the peoples to come
you bring relief, bidding them be born without violation.
Now no man will be eunuch or adulterer with you as guardian:
but before—O the morals!—even a eunuch was an adulterer.
3. III
Be born, name promised to Dardanian Iulus,
true offspring of the gods; be born, great boy:
to whom your father may hand the eternal reins after the ages,
and may you rule the world, old, with one older still.
Julia herself with snowy thumb will spin you golden threads
and weave the whole fleece of Phrixus.

title: Epigrams
text:
4. IV
Greatest censor and prince of princes,
though Rome already owes you so many triumphs,
so many temples newly born, so many reborn,
so many spectacles, so many gods, so many cities:
Rome owes you more—that she is chaste.
5. V
I've bought a country estate for much money:
lend me a hundred thousand, Caecilianus, I ask.
You give me no answer? I believe you say in silence
"You won't repay": that, Caecilianus, is why I ask.
6. VI
There are three actors, but your Paula, Lupercus,
loves four: and Paula loves even the mute role.
7. VII
Since the Julian law was reborn for the peoples, Faustinus,
and Chastity was ordered to enter our homes,
it's less than, or surely not more than, thirty days,
and already Telesilla is marrying her tenth husband.
She who marries so often does not marry: by the law she's an adulteress.
I'm less offended by a more straightforward harlot.
8. VIII
Two praetors, four tribunes,
seven pleaders, ten poets
were lately seeking a certain girl's hand
from a certain old man. He, without delay,
gave the girl to Eulogus the auctioneer.
Tell me, Severus—did he act foolishly?
9. IX
You sleep in Pompey's theatre, Laevinus:
and you complain if Oceanus wakes you?
10. X
When I lately happened to ask Jove for a few thousand,
"He will give it," he said, "who gave me my temples."
Temples indeed he gave to Jove, but to me no
thousands did he give: I'm ashamed, ah, to have asked Jove for so little.
But how unfrowning, how clouded by no anger,
with how calm a face he had read my prayers!
Such is he when he grants diadems to suppliant Dacians
and goes and comes along the Capitoline ways.
Tell me, I pray, O maiden who shares our Thunderer's secrets,
if he refuses with that face, with what face does he grant?
So I; and so to me, briefly, with her Gorgon laid aside, Pallas:
"What has not yet been given, fool, do you count as refused?"

title: Epigrams
text:
11. XI
That there's no Pylades in this age, no Orestes,
you wonder? Pylades, Marcus, drank the same wine,
nor was better bread or thrush given to Orestes,
but the dinner was equal and the same for both.
You devour Lucrine oysters, watery clams feed me:
my palate is no less wellborn than yours, Marcus.
Cadmean Tyre clothes you, rich Gaul clothes me:
do you want me, dressed in coarse wool, to love you in purple?
For me to be your Pylades, let someone be my Orestes.
This is not done by words, Marcus: to be loved, love.
12. XII
Fabulla swears the hair she bought is her own:
does she, Paulus, perjure herself?
13. XIII
Who would not think you, Julia, shaped by Phidias's chisel,
or the work of Pallas's art?
The white marble answers with no silent image,
and living grace gleams in your calm face.
Your hand—not rough—plays with the Acidalian knot
that it snatched, little Cupid, from your neck.
To call back the love of Mars and the supreme Thunderer,
let Juno ask the girdle of you, and Venus herself.
14. XIV
You declare you can write eloquent verses,
Laberius: why then won't you?
Whoever can write eloquent verses,
let him not write, Laberius: I'll think him a man.
15. XV
While an ant was wandering in Phaethon's shade,
an amber drop entangled the slender creature.
So she, who lately had been despised while life remained,
has now been made precious by her own death.
16. XVI
You who terrify men with your member and perverts with your sickle,
guard these few acres of secluded soil.
So may no aged thieves enter your orchards,
but a boy and a fair girl with long hair.
17. XVII
You bid yourself be called Cinna, Cinnamus.
Isn't this, I ask, Cinna, a barbarism?
If you'd been called Furius before,
by that reasoning you'd be called Fur—Thief.
18. XVIII
Saloninus rests in the Spanish lands,
where no better shade sees the Stygian halls.
But to mourn is wrong: for he who left you, Priscus,
lives on in the better part by which he wished to live.

title: Epigrams
text:
19. XIX
Not of violence nor murder nor poison,
but my lawsuit is about three she-goats:
I complain that my neighbour stole them.
This the judge demands be proved to him:
you thunder of Cannae and the Mithridatic war
and the perjuries of Punic frenzy
and the Sullas and Mariuses and Muciuses
with great voice and your whole hand.
Now speak, Postumus, about the three she-goats.
20. XX
I asked you, Phoebus, to lend me a hundred thousand sesterces,
when you'd said to me, "You ask nothing, then?"
You inquire, you hesitate, you delay, and for ten days
you torment me and yourself: now, Phoebus, I ask—refuse.
21. XXI
While glad Venus joined the everlasting Ianthis to Stella the poet,
she said, "I could give no more."
This before the lady; but more wickedly that into his ear:
"See you commit no fault, you ruinous man.
Often, in fury, I have beaten wanton Mars,
when he was straying before lawful beds.
But since he's mine, no rival has wronged me:
Juno would wish to have so well-behaved a husband."
She spoke, and struck his breast with her secret thong.
The blow pleases: but you now, goddess, beat the gods.
22. XXII
That you marry your bedfellow, Proculina,
and make him now a husband whom you lately made a lover,
so that the Julian law cannot brand you:
you don't marry, Proculina—you confess.
23. XXIII
You bid my member always stand for you, Lesbia:
believe me, what's a finger isn't a prick.
Though you press me with coaxing hands and words,
your face is commanding against you.
24. XXIV
Nothing is more wanton than Charisianus:
at the Saturnalia he walks about in a toga.
25. XXV
Marcellinus, true offspring of a good father,
whom the bristling Bear covers under the Arcadian ridge,
hear what your old, ancestral friend would wish for you,
and keep these prayers in a mindful heart:
let your valour be cautious, nor let rash ardour
bear you into the midst of swords and savage weapons.
Let the irrational want wars and fierce Mars;
you can be both your father's soldier and your leader's.

title: Epigrams
text:
26. XXVI
Our Sotades stands in peril of his head.
You think Sotades is a defendant? He isn't.
Sotades has lost the power to get it up: he licks.
27. XXVII
Twice my neighbour, Nepos—for you too dwell near Flora
and you too dwell in old Ficeliae—
you have a girl whose face is sealed with her father's likeness,
a witness born to her mother's chastity.
Yet don't be too sparing of your aged Falernian,
and rather leave the jars full of money.
Let her be dutiful, let her be rich, but let your daughter drink new wine:
the amphora, now new, will grow old along with its mistress.
Let the Caecuban vintage nourish not only the childless:
fathers too can live, believe me.
28. XXVIII
That famous freedman of Melior,
who fell with all Rome grieving,
the brief darling of his dear patron,
Glaucias, buried beneath this marble,
lies in a tomb joined to the Flaminian way:
pure in morals, untouched in modesty,
quick of wit, blessed with beauty.
The boy had just completed twice six harvests
and was barely adding one more year.
You who weep at such things, traveller, weep at nothing.
29. XXIX
Not of the household's commons, nor a slave of the greedy auction-block,
but a boy worthy of his master's holy love,
when he could not yet feel his patron's gifts,
Glaucias was already Melior's freedman.
This was granted to his character and his beauty: who was more charming than he?
Or who was fairer with Apollo's face?
For the extraordinary, life is brief and old age rare.
Whatever you love, pray it not please too much.
30. XXX
Had you given me six thousand sesterces at once,
when you said to me, "Take it, take it up, it's a gift,"
I'd owe you, Paetus, as if for two hundred thousand.
But now, since you gave it after long delay,
after seven, I think, or nine Kalends,
do you want me to tell you something truer than truth?
You've wasted six thousand sesterces, Paetus.

title: Epigrams
text:
31. XXXI
You yourself know and allow, Charidemus, that your wife
is laid by the doctor: you want to die without a fever.
32. XXXII
While the war-goddess of civil strife still wavered
and soft Otho could perhaps have won,
he condemned a Mars that would cost much blood
and pierced his whole breast with a sure hand.
Let Cato, while he lives, be even greater than Caesar:
but in dying—was he greater than Otho?
33. XXXIII
Nothing more pitiable, Matho, than Sabellus the sodomite
have you seen, than whom nothing was happier before.
Thefts, runaways, deaths of slaves, fires, mourning
afflict the man, and now, wretched, he even goes with women.
34. XXXIV
Give me kisses, Diadumenus, pressed close. "How many?" you ask.
You bid me number the waves of Ocean
and the shells scattered along the Aegean shores
and the bees that wander on the Cecropian mount,
and the voices and hands that sound in the full theatre
when the people suddenly see Caesar's face.
I don't want as many as Lesbia, won over, gave to clever Catullus:
he wants few who can count them.
35. XXXV
Seven water-clocks, demanded by you in a loud voice,
the unwilling judge, Caecilianus, granted.
But you speak much and long, and half-reclining
drink lukewarm water from glass flasks.
That you may at last sate both voice and thirst, we ask
that you now drink, Caecilianus, from the water-clock.
36. XXXVI
Your member is as big, Papylus, as your nose,
so that you can smell it whenever you get it up.
37. XXXVII
Charinus has, of his split backside, right up to the navel,
no remnant left,
and yet he itches right up to the navel.
O with what an itch the wretch suffers!
He has no arse, yet he's a pervert.
38. XXXVIII
You see how little Regulus, not yet three full years old,
listens and praises his father himself?
And how, at the sight of his sire, he leaves his mother's lap
and feels his father's praises to be his own?
Already the shouting and the Hundred Men and the dense
crowd of the ring and the Julian hall please the infant.
So the spirited horse's offspring delights in the great dust,
so the calf longs for battles with its soft brow.
Gods, preserve, I pray, the mother's vows for her, the father's for him,
that Regulus may hear his son, and she hear two.

title: Epigrams
text:
39. XXXIX
You've been made the father of seven, Cinna, by Marulla—
not of children: for none is yours,
nor a friend's son nor a neighbour's,
but, conceived on cots and mats,
they betray their mother's thefts by their own heads.
This one, who walks as a Moor with curled hair,
admits he's the offspring of Santra the cook.
But that one, with snub nose and swollen lips,
is the very image of Pannychus the wrestler.
Who doesn't know the third is the baker's,
whoever knows and sees blear-eyed Dama?
The fourth, with a pervert's brow and fair face,
was born to you from your bedfellow Lygdus:
bugger your son, if you like: it's no crime.
But this one, with pointed head and long ears,
which twitch the way donkeys' usually do,
who can deny is the son of Cyrta the fool?
The two sisters, that one dark and this one red,
are the children of Crotus the flute-player and Carpus the bailiff.
Already you'd have a full flock of Niobids,
if Coresus and Dindymus weren't eunuchs.
40. XL
No woman could be preferred to you, Lycoris:
no woman can be preferred to Glycera.
She will become what you are: you can't be what she is.
What time does! Her I want, you I wanted.
41. XLI
He who recites with throat and neck wrapped in wool,
denies that he can speak or can keep silent.
42. XLII
Unless you bathe at Etruscus's little baths,
you'll die unwashed, Oppianus.
No waters will so caress you,
not the springs of Aponus, untried by girls,
not soft Sinuessa and the scalding
floods of Passer or proud Anxur,
not Phoebus's shallows and royal Baiae.
Nowhere is so bright a clear sky at leisure:
the very light is longer there, and the day
withdraws from no place more slowly.
There the quarries of Taygetus gleam green
and stones vie in varied beauty,
which the Phrygian and the Libyan cut deep.
Rich onyx breathes out dry heat
and the serpentine stones glow with a thin flame:
if Spartan customs please you,
content with the dry vapour,
you may plunge in raw Virgin or Marcian water;
which shines so bright, so clear,
that you'd suspect no water there
and believe empty marble gleams.
You're not attending, and with idle ear
you've long heard me as if carelessly.
You'll die unwashed, Oppianus.

title: Epigrams
text:
43. XLIII
While happy Baiae indulges you, Castricus,
and the white nymph swims in the sulphurous waters,
the leisure of my Nomentan farm restores me
and a cottage not burdened by its own acres.
This is my Baian sunshine and soft Lucrine,
this, Castricus, is your wealth to me.
Once I would run to the praised waters wherever I pleased
and not dread long journeys,
now I delight in the neighbourhood of the city and easy retreats,
and it's enough, if I'm allowed to be lazy.
44. XLIV
You believe, Calliodorus, that you joke wittily
and that you alone are steeped in much salt.
You grin at everyone, you sling gibes at everyone;
so you think you can please as a dinner-guest.
But if I should say something not nicely, but truly,
no one will toast you, Calliodorus.
45. XLV
You've had your sport, it's enough: marry, you wanton cunts:
no Venus is allowed you but the chaste.
Is this chaste Venus? Laetoria marries Lygdus:
she'll be a fouler wife than she was lately a harlot.
46. XLVI
The Blue team's four-horse chariot is whipped constantly,
yet doesn't run: it's doing a great thing, Catianus.
47. XLVII
Nymph, who, household to my Stella, glide from the pure spring
and pass beneath your master's jewelled roof,
whether Numa's wife sent you from Trivia's caves,
or you come ninth from the troop of the Camenae:
Marcus pays his vows to you with this sow,
because, sick, he drank your water on the sly.
You, content now with my offence, grant me safely
the joys of your spring: let my thirst be healthy.
48. XLVIII
That the toga-clad crowd shouts so loud a "Bravo!" for you,
it's not you, Pomponius—your dinner is eloquent.
49. XLIX
I'm not carved from brittle elm,
nor is this column, that stands stiff and erect,
made of any chance wood,
but begotten from living cypress:
which fears neither the ages run a hundred times
nor the rot of long old age.
You, whoever you are, O wicked man, fear this.
For if with greedy hand you harm
even the smallest grapes of this vine,
there will grow—though you may wish to deny it—
a fig grafted on you from the cypress.

title: Epigrams
text:
50. L
When poor Telesinus cultivated honest friends,
he wandered shabby in his chilly little toga:
since he began to court obscene perverts,
he alone buys silver, tables, estates.
Do you want to grow rich, Bithynicus? Be an accomplice:
pure kisses will give you nothing, not even the least.
51. LI
That you dine without me so often, Lupercus,
I've found out how to do you harm.
I'm angry: you may keep calling and sending and asking—
"What will you do?" you say. What will I do? I'll come.
52. LII
In this tomb lies, carried off in his boyhood years,
Pantagathus, his master's care and grief,
skilled with barely-touching blade to trim the straying hair
and dress the shaggy cheeks.
Though you be, as you should, kind and light, earth,
you cannot be lighter than the craftsman's hand.
53. LIII
He bathed with us, dined merrily, and the same man
was found dead in the morning—Andragoras.
You ask the cause of so sudden a death, Faustinus?
In his sleep he'd seen the doctor Hermocrates.
54. LIV
If you forbade Sextilianus, Aulus, to say
"so many men" and "so many women," he'd scarcely string three words together, poor man.
"What does he mean by it?" you ask. I'll tell you what I suspect:
Sextilianus loves so many men and so many women.
55. LV
That you always reek black with cassia and cinnamon
and the nest of the proud bird,
fragrant with Niceros's leaden boxes,
you laugh at us, Coracinus, who smell of nothing:
I'd rather smell of nothing than smell good.
56. LVI
That your legs are stiff with bristles and your chest with shaggy hair,
do you think, Charidemus, you fool report?
Pluck out, believe me, the hairs from your whole body
and testify that you depilate your buttocks.
"What's the reason?" you say. You know many say many things:
make them think, Charidemus, that you get buggered.
57. LVII
You feign fake hair with ointment, Phoebus,
and your dirty bald head is covered with painted locks.
There's no need to bring a barber to your head:
a sponge, Phoebus, can shave you better.

title: Epigrams
text:
58. LVIII
While it delights you, Aulus, to behold the Arcadian
Bear close at hand and bear the stars of the Getic sky,
O how nearly was I, snatched to the Stygian waters,
made to see the dark clouds of the Elysian realm!
Though weary, my eyes were seeking your face,
and "Pudens" was forever on my cold lips.
If the wool-spinning sisters draw me threads not black
and that voice has no deaf gods,
safe yourself, with me safe, you'll be carried back to the Latin cities
and return, a famous knight, with the rewards of your service.
59. LIX
Baccara both grieves and complains that the cold doesn't reach him,
because of his six hundred shaggy cloaks,
he longs for dark days and winds and snows,
and hates the winter days, if they've turned warm.
What harm have my cloaks done you, cruel man,
which a light breeze can lift from one's shoulders?
How much simpler, how much more humane it would be
to put on your shaggy cloaks even in the month of August!
60. LX
My Rome praises, loves, recites my little books,
and every pocket holds me, every hand holds me.
Look—a certain man reddens, pales, gapes, yawns, hates.
This I want: now my songs please me.
61. LXI
Pompullus has done a great thing, Faustinus: he'll be read
and scatter his name throughout the whole world.
"So may the light race of the fair-haired Usipi fare well,
and whoever does not love the Ausonian empire."
Yet Pompullus's writings are said to be ingenious.
"But for fame that's not enough, believe me:
how many eloquent men feed bookworms and moths,
and only cooks buy up learned poems!
There's something more, something that grants the ages to pages:
a book that will live must have a genius."
62. LXII
Salanus has lost his only son, a father:
do you delay to send gifts, Oppianus?
Alas, cruel crime and the wicked Fates!
Whose vulture will this corpse be?

title: Epigrams
text:
63. LXIII
You know you're being courted, you know this courtier is greedy,
and you know, Marianus, what the one who courts you wants.
Yet you, fool, write him heir in your last will
and want him, madman, to take your place.
"Still, he sent great gifts." But he sent them on a hook;
and can a fish love the fisherman?
Will this man weep for your fate with real grief?
If you want him to weep, Marianus, leave him nothing.
64. LXIV
Though you're not born of the rigid Fabian stock,
nor such as a ruddy wife bore to Curius beneath the shaggy oak
while she brought lunch to her ploughing husband,
but the son of a father shaved at the mirror and a toga-wearing mother,
and your bride could call you her bride:
yet you presume to correct my little books, which fame knows,
and to carp at the trifles of a happy man—
these trifles, I say, to which the leaders of city and forum
do not scorn to turn their whole ear,
which the bookcases of eternal Silius deem worthy
and which Regulus so often repeats with eloquent voice,
and which Sura, neighbour of Aventine Diana,
who watches the great Circus's contests more closely, praises,
which Caesar himself, the lord, under so great a weight of affairs,
does not disdain to unroll two and three times.
But you have more sense, your heart with sharpening Minerva
is keener, and refined Athens shaped your breast.
May I perish if that isn't far wiser
which, with slack paunch and great foot
and red lung, old and fearsome with its nostrils,
the cruel butcher carries about through all the crossroads.
Besides, you dare to write against me little verses
that no one would know, and waste your miserable papers.
But if the heat of my bile should scorch you with anything,
it will live and stick and be read throughout the world,
nor will Cinnamus erase the brand-marks with his cunning art.
But have pity on yourself, and don't, lost in rabid madness,
provoke the smoking nostril of a living bear.
Though he be gentle and lick your fingers and hands,
if grief and bile, if just anger compel him,
he'll be a bear: weary your teeth on an empty hide
and seek some silent flesh that you can gnaw.

title: Epigrams
text:
65. LXV
"You make an epigram in hexameters"—I know Tucca says it.
Tucca, it's customary; in short, Tucca, it's allowed.
"But still, this is long." That too is customary, Tucca, and allowed:
if you approve shorter ones, read only the couplets.
Let us agree that it's fair for you to skip
long epigrams, Tucca, and for me to write them.
66. LXVI
A girl of not too good a name,
such as sit in the middle of the Subura,
the crier Gellianus was lately auctioning.
When the price stayed low a long time,
wishing to prove her pure to all,
he drew her toward him, resisting, with his hand
and kissed her twice and thrice and four times.
What did he gain by the kiss, you ask?
The man who'd just bid six hundred withdrew it.
67. LXVII
Why does your Caelia have only eunuchs, you ask,
Pannychus? Caelia wants to be laid and not to bear.
68. LXVIII
Weep for your sin, but weep with all Lucrinus,
Naiads, and let Thetis herself feel the grief.
Among the Baian waves, snatched away, a boy has died,
that Eutychos, your sweet companion, Castricus.
This was your partner in cares and your coaxing solace,
this was your love, this was our poet's Alexis.
Did some wanton nymph see you naked beneath the glassy waves
and send back Hylas to Alcides?
Or does the goddess now neglect womanish Hermaphroditus,
stirred by the embrace of a tender man?
Whatever it is, whatever the cause of the sudden seizure,
may both earth and water, I pray, be gentle to you.
69. LXIX
I don't wonder that your Bassa drinks water, Catullus:
I wonder that Bassus's daughter drinks water.
70. LXX
The sixtieth harvest, Marcianus,
is past, and now, I think, the second of Cotta,
nor does he recall having felt the weariness of a fevered bed
even for a single day.
He shows his finger—but the indecent one—
to Alcon and Dasius and Symmachus.
But if our years be well reckoned,
and whatever the grim fevers
or heavy languor or evil pains took away
be separated from the better life:
we are infants, and we seem old men.
He who thinks the age of Priam and Nestor
long, Marcianus,
is much deceived and mistaken.
To live is not life, but to be well.

title: Epigrams
text:
71. LXXI
She who is skilled to perform wanton gestures to Baetic music
and to play in the Gaditanian style,
who could rouse trembling Pelias and Hecuba's husband
to Hector's pyre,
Telethusa burns and torments her former master:
he sold her as a slave-girl, now he buys her back as mistress.
72. LXXII
A thief of all-too-noted rapacity,
Cilix, wished to plunder a garden,
but in the huge garden, Fabullus, there was
nothing but a marble Priapus.
Not wanting to return empty-handed,
Cilix stole Priapus himself.
73. LXXIII
No rude settler made me with unskilled blade:
you see the noble work of a steward.
For the richest cultivator of the Caeretan land,
Hilarus, holds these hills and joyful ridges.
See how I seem not wooden, with sure face,
nor bear the weapons of my groin devoted to the hearth-fire,
but for me, of everlasting, never-dying cypress,
stands stiff a member worthy of Phidias's hand.
Neighbours, I warn you, honour holy Priapus
and spare these twice seven acres.
74. LXXIV
He who reclines lowest on the middle couch,
his three-haired bald head streaked with ointment,
and picks his loose mouth with clipped mastic-twigs,
is lying, Aefulanus: he has no teeth.
75. LXXV
When you send me a thrush or a slice of cake,
or a hare's thigh, or something like these,
you say, Pontia, that you've sent me your tidbits.
These, Pontia, I'll neither send on nor eat.
76. LXXVI
That guardian of the sacred side and of Mars in the toga,
to whom the camp of the supreme leader was entrusted,
here lies Fuscus. This, Fortune, we may confess:
this stone now fears no enemy threats;
the Dacian has taken the great yoke on his subdued neck,
and the victorious shade possesses the grove as its slave.
77. LXXVII
Though you're as poor as wretched Irus is not,
as young as Parthenopaeus was not,
as strong as Artemidorus was not, even when he won,
why do you delight to be the burden of six Cappadocians?
You're laughed at and much more disgraced, Afer,
than if you walked naked in the middle of the forum.
Just so Atlas is pointed at, with his matched mule,
and the black beast that carries a Libyan like itself.
You ask how hateful your litter is?
You shouldn't be carried dead in a six-bearer.

title: Epigrams
text:
78. LXXVIII
The famous drinker, Aulus, Phryx,
was blind in one eye and bleary in the other.
To him Heras the doctor said, "Beware of drinking:
if you drink wine, you'll see nothing."
Laughing, Phryx said to his eye, "Farewell."
He at once orders measures mixed for himself,
but frequent ones. You ask the outcome?
Phryx drank wine, his eye drank poison.
79. LXXIX
You're sad and fortunate. Beware lest Fortune know it:
she'll call you ungrateful, Lupus, if she knows.
80. LXXX
That she might send you new gifts, Caesar, the land of Nile
in her eagerness had sent you winter roses.
The Memphian sailor laughed at the Pharian gardens
as soon as he entered the first thresholds of your city:
so great was the glory of spring and the grace of fragrant Flora,
so great the splendour of the Paestan countryside;
wherever, wandering, he bore his step and his eyes,
every path was red with clipped garlands.
But you, now bidden to yield to the Roman winter,
send us your harvests, Nile, and accept our roses.
81. LXXXI
You bathe as if enraged at the people, Charidemus:
so you wash your groin all over in the tub.
Nor would I have you wash even your head here, Charidemus.
And look, you do wash your head: I'd rather you washed your groin.
82. LXXXII
A certain man, Rufus, having lately inspected me
carefully, like a buyer or a trainer,
when he'd marked me with face and finger,
"Are you," he said, "are you that famous Martial,
whose naughtiness and jokes are known
to everyone who hasn't a Batavian ear?"
I smiled modestly, and with a slight nod
didn't deny I was who he'd said.
"Why then," he said, "do you have a bad cloak?"
I replied, "Because I'm a bad poet."
That this may not happen too often to the poet,
send me, Rufus, good cloaks.
83. LXXXIII
As much as anxious Etruscus's father's fortune,
so much, highest of leaders, do they both owe you.
For with your right hand you recalled the thunderbolts you'd hurled:
I'd wish such conduct were in the fires of Jove;
if your nature, Caesar, belonged to the supreme Thunderer,
a hand would rarely use the whole thunderbolt.
Etruscus attests to both gifts of yours,
that it fell to him both as companion and as returnee.

title: Epigrams
text:
84. LXXXIV
Philippus is carried, in good health, by eight bearers, Avitus.
If you think him in health, Avitus, you're mad.
85. LXXXV
See, the sixth book is published for me without you, Rufus Camonius,
nor does the book hope for you as reader, friend:
the impious land of the Cappadocians, seen by you under an ill star,
returns ashes and bones to your father.
Pour out tears, Bononia, bereft of your Rufus,
and let the lament resound through all Aemilia:
alas, what piety, alas how brief an age has perished!
He had just seen the fifth rewards of the Alphean games.
You, who used to unroll our sport in a mindful breast,
you, Rufus, used to hold all my jokes by heart,
receive, with weeping, the brief poem of your grieving friend,
and consider these to have been the incense for one absent.
86. LXXXVI
Setine wine and the master's snows and thick goblets.
When shall I drink you with the doctor not forbidding?
Foolish and ungrateful and unworthy of so great a gift
is he who would rather be the heir of rich Midas.
Let him possess Libyan harvests and the Hermus and the Tagus,
and let him drink warm water, who envies me.
87. LXXXVII
May the gods give you, and you, Caesar, whatever you deserve:
may the gods give me, and you, what I want, if I've deserved it.
88. LXXXVIII
This morning I greeted you by your real name, by chance,
and didn't call you my lord, Caecilianus.
You ask how much such great freedom costs me?
It cost me a hundred farthings.
89. LXXXIX
When, now at midnight, Panaretus, drunk,
sought the late chamber-pot with snapping thumb,
a Spoletine flask was given him, but one he'd emptied himself,
nor had the whole jar been enough for him alone.
He, with utmost faith of the vessel, measured back his wine
and gave back the full weight of his wine-jar.
You wonder the flask held as much as he'd drunk?
Stop wondering, Rufus: he'd drunk it neat.

title: Epigrams
text:
90. XC
Gellia has only one lover.
This is fouler still: she's the wife of two.
91. XCI
The holy censure of the supreme leader forbids and bans
adultery. Rejoice, Zoilus: you don't go with women.
92. XCII
Though there's chased for you, Annianus,
a serpent on your bowl by Myron's art,
you drink Vatican wine: you drink poison.
93. XCIII
Thais smells as foul as not the old jar of a greedy fuller,
just now broken in the middle of the road,
not a he-goat fresh from love, not a lion's mouth,
not the Transtiberine hide stripped from a dog,
not a chick rotting in an aborted egg,
not an amphora spoiled with tainted fish-sauce.
That she may shrewdly swap this stench for another scent,
whenever she lays her clothes aside and seeks the baths,
she's green with depilatory or hides smeared with sour chalk
or is covered three and four times with rich bean-paste.
When she's thought herself well safe by a thousand tricks,
when she's done it all, Thais smells of Thais.
94. XCIV
Gold-inlaid dishes are always set before Calpetanus,
whether he dines out or at home in the city.
So he dines always, even in an inn, so in the country.
Has he nothing else, then? No—and not even his own.
1. I
Receive the rough breastplate of warlike Minerva,
the very thing the wrath of Medusa's snaky hair dreads.
While unused, Caesar, it may be called a cuirass:
once it rests on your sacred breast, it will be the aegis.
2. II
A breastplate for our lord, proof against Sarmatian arrows
and surer than the Getic hide of Mars,
woven from the smooth hooves of countless boars,
safe even against the thrust of an Aetolian spear:
happy in your lot, for it will be granted you to touch
that sacred breast and grow warm with our god's spirit.
Go, his companion, and earn great triumphs unscathed,
and lead the way to the palm-embroidered robe — but quickly, give him back.

title: Epigrams
text:
3. III
Why do I not send you my little books, Pontilianus?
So that you, Pontilianus, may not send me yours.
4. IV
Since Oppianus, Castricus, was sickly in complexion,
he took to writing verses.
5. V
If you regard the longing of the people and the senators,
Caesar, and the true joys of the Latin toga,
give back our god to the prayers that beg for him. Rome
envies her own foe, though many a laurel come his way:
that foe sees the lord of the earth at closer range,
and the barbarian is terrified by your face — and enjoys it.
6. VI
Has Caesar, turned toward us at last from the Hyperborean shores,
already made ready to take the Ausonian roads?
The sure informant is missing, yet every voice proclaims it:
I believe you, Rumour — you are wont to speak the truth.
The public dispatches of victory attest the general joy;
the spears of Mars grow green with laurelled point.
Once more, hurrah, Rome cries great triumphs for you,
and unconquered, Caesar, you resound within your city.
But now, that our gladness may rest on firmer ground,
come yourself, the messenger of the Sarmatian laurel.
7. VII
Though the wintry Bear and rude Peuce
and the Hister, hot with the beat of hooves,
and the Rhine, now three times broken in his unruly horn,
hold you taming the realms of a treacherous race,
O supreme ruler of the world and parent of the globe:
still you cannot be absent from our prayers.
There we are with you, in eyes and hearts, Caesar,
and you alone so possess the minds of all,
that the very crowd of the great Circus does not know
whether Passerinus or Tigris is running.
8. VIII
Now be merry, Muses — if ever for me, be merry now and play:
the god comes back victor from the Odrysian world.
You first, December, make the people's prayers sure:
now we may cry aloud, 'He comes!'
Happy in your lot! You could refuse to yield to Janus,
if you gave us the joys that he will give.
The garlanded soldier shall play at festal taunts,
when he walks as comrade among the laurelled horses.
It is right to hear jests and lighter songs, Caesar,
for you too — if the very triumph loves a game.

title: Epigrams
text:
9. IX
Though Cascellius counts sixty years,
he is a clever man: when will he be eloquent?
10. X
Eros is sodomized, Linus sucks: Olus, what is it to you
what either of them does with his own skin?
Matho fucks for a hundred thousand: Olus, what is it to you?
You will not be the poorer for it — only Matho.
Sertorius dines till dawn: Olus, what is it to you,
when you are free to snore the whole night through?
Lupus owes Titus seven hundred thousand: Olus, what is it to you?
Don't you give Lupus a penny, or trust him with one.
The thing you ignore is the one that concerns you, Olus,
the one that ought to be more your care.
You owe for your shabby toga: this concerns you, Olus.
No one now will trust you for a farthing: this too.
Your wife is an adulteress: this concerns you, Olus.
Your grown-up daughter now demands a dowry: this too.
I could name fifteen things that concern you:
but what you do, Olus, is nothing whatever to me.
11. XI
You force me, Pudens, with my own pen and hand,
to correct my little books.
Oh, how excessively you approve of me and love me,
you who want to own my trifles in the original!
12. XII
So may my lord read me, Faustinus, with serene brow,
and take in my jests with the ear he is used to,
as truly my page has never injured even those it justly hates,
and no fame that comes by a blush can please me.
What good is it, when certain men want my work to seem theirs,
if any darts of mine drip with the blood of Lycambes,
and someone spews viper's venom under my name —
one who cannot bear the rays of Phoebus and the day?
I play harmlessly: you know this well. I swear by the genius
of mighty Fame, and by the Castalian band,
and by your ears, which are like a great divinity to me,
reader free of every inhuman spite.
13. XIII
When dusky Lycoris heard that the ivory of an old tusk
turns white under the suns of Tibur,
she went up to the Herculean hills. What power the air
of lofty Tibur has! In a short while she came back black.

title: Epigrams
text:
14. XIV
An unspeakable disaster has befallen my girl, Aulus;
she has lost her plaything and her darling:
not such as Catullus' tender mistress Lesbia mourned,
robbed of the naughtiness of her sparrow,
nor such as the Ianthis my Stella sang of wept for,
whose black dove flies in Elysium:
my light is not caught by such trifles or such fancies,
nor do such losses move my mistress's heart:
she has lost a boy who was counting twice ten years,
whose cock was not yet a foot and a half long.
15. XV
What boy is this who keeps off from the bright waters of Ianthis?
Is it Hylas, fleeing his mistress the Naiad?
How well it is that the Tirynthian is worshipped in this grove
and guards these amorous waters so close at hand!
You may tend these springs in safety, Argynnus:
the Nymphs will do nothing — but beware lest he himself should wish it.
16. XVI
There is no cash at home, Regulus; the only thing left
is to sell the gifts you gave me: will you buy them?
17. XVII
Library of a charming country house,
from which the reader sees the neighbouring city,
if among holier songs there be any place
for wanton Thalia,
you may set on even the lowest shelf
these seven little books I have sent you,
marked by their author's own pen:
this erasure makes their value.
But you, dedicated by my small gift,
who will be sung, famed through the whole world,
guard this pledge of my heart,
library of Julius Martialis.
18. XVIII
Though your face is such that no woman could
fault it, though no blemish marks your body,
why so rarely does a lover want you and come back for more?
Do you wonder? The fault is no light one, Galla:
every time I set to work and we are moved
with mingled loins, your cunt is not silent — while you yourself are.
Would to the gods you spoke and it kept quiet:
I am offended by your cunt's chatter.
I would rather you broke wind: for that, says Symmachus,
is not without use, and the thing raises a laugh as well.
But who can laugh at the silly noises of a cunt?
When it sounds off, whose cock and whose mind does not collapse?
Say something at least, drown out that clamorous cunt,
and if you are so dumb, learn to talk at least from that quarter.

title: Epigrams
text:
19. XIX
This fragment, which you think cheap and useless wood,
was the first keel of an unknown sea.
The crashing Cyaneae of old could not break her,
nor the grimmer wrath of the Scythian strait:
the ages have conquered her — but though she has yielded to the years,
the little plank, saved, is holier than the whole ship was.
20. XX
Nothing is more wretched or more gluttonous than Santra.
Invited at last to a proper dinner,
which for so many days and nights he had angled for,
three times he asks for boar's sweetbreads, four for loin,
and for both haunches of a hare and its two shoulders,
nor does he blush to perjure himself over a thrush
and to snatch the dingy fibres of oysters.
He smears his filthy napkin with gobs of cake;
in it too are stowed away preserved grapes
and a few seeds of pomegranates
and the unsightly skin of a hollowed-out sow's womb,
and a runny fig and a flabby mushroom.
But when the napkin already bursts with a thousand thefts,
he hides in his warm bosom gnawed vertebrae
and a headless turtledove with its head devoured.
Nor does he think it shameful to gather with a long arm
whatever the crumb-collectors and the dogs have left.
And the edible loot is not enough for his gullet:
he fills his flask at his feet with mixed wine.
When he has carried all this home up two hundred stairs
and shut himself, anxious, in his bolted room,
that glutton — the next day he sells it.
21. XXI
This is that day, conscious of a mighty birth,
which gave Lucan to the nations and to you, Polla.
Alas, cruel Nero, no shade more hateful than yours,
this at least ought not to have been permitted you.
22. XXII
The day of the Apollonian bard, memorable for his great birth,
returns: throng of the Muses, favour the rites.
This day deserved, when it gave you, Lucan, to the earth,
that Baetis should be mingled with Castalia's water.

title: Epigrams
text:
23. XXIII
Come, Phoebus, but as great as you were when you yourself
gave the second plectrum to the Latin lyre as it thundered war.
What shall I pray for, on so great a day? You, Polla,
cherish your husband often, and let him feel himself cherished.
24. XXIV
You who try to set me at odds with my Juvenal,
what will you not dare to say, treacherous tongue?
With you inventing crimes, Orestes would have hated Pylades,
the love of Pirithous would have abandoned Theseus,
you could have parted the Sicilian brothers, and the Atridae —
a greater name — and the offspring of Leda.
This I call down on you for such deserts and such ventures:
that you do, my tongue, the thing I think you do.
25. XXV
Though you only ever write sweet epigrams,
whiter than white-leaded skin,
and there is in them no grain of salt nor any drop
of bitter gall — yet, you fool, you want them read!
Even food does not please when robbed of the bite of vinegar,
nor is a face charming that lacks a dimple.
Give honey-apples and insipid figs to a baby:
for me, the Chian fig that knows how to sting has flavour.
26. XXVI
Go find my friend Apollinaris, Scazon;
and if he has leisure — don't come at him as a bother —
give him this, such as it is, of which he himself is some part:
let his ears take in this witty song.
If you see yourself received with a fully open brow,
ask him to support it with his well-known favour.
You know with what love of my trifles he burns:
not even I can love you more.
If you want to be safe against the spiteful,
go find my friend Apollinaris, Scazon.
27. XXVII
A boar, ravager of Tuscan acorns and now sluggish
from much oak, second in fame to the Aetolian beast,
which my Dexter pierced with shining point,
lies as prey, the envy of my hearth:
let my house-gods grow fat, glad in the dripping savour,
and let the festive kitchen blaze with a felled ridge of wood.
But the cook will use up a huge heap of pepper
and add Falernian mixed with secret fish-sauce:
go back to your owner, my fire cannot hold you,
ruinous boar: I go hungry more cheaply.

title: Epigrams
text:
28. XXVIII
So may the wood of Tiburtine Diana grow for you
and the often-felled grove make haste to come back,
nor may your olives, Fuscus, yield to Tartessian presses,
and may the vats give the good must of an ample crop;
so may the forums admire you, the palaces praise you,
and many a palm adorn your twin doors:
while mid-December gives you a little leisure,
weigh — but with a sure ear — the jests you read.
'You wish to know the truth? That is a hard task.' But you,
Fuscus, can say what you want said to you.
29. XXIX
Thestylus, sweet torment of Voconius Victor,
than whom no boy is better known in all the world,
so may you be lovely even when your curls are laid aside,
and may no girl please your poet:
set aside your master's learned little books awhile,
while I read small verses to your Victor.
And Maecenas, when Maro sang of Alexis,
still knew the dusky Melaenis of Marsus.
30. XXX
You give yourself to Parthians, to Germans, to Dacians, Caelia,
nor do you spurn the beds of Cilicians and Cappadocians;
to you sails a Memphitic fornicator from the Pharian city,
and a black Indian from the Red Sea waters;
nor do you flee the circumcised loins of Jews,
nor does the Alan pass you by on his Sarmatian horse.
What is your reason, since you are a Roman girl,
that no Roman cock pleases you?
31. XXXI
The birds of the noisy farmyard and the mothers' eggs,
and the yellow Chian figs ripened by gentle heat,
and the rough young of the bleating she-goat,
and olives no longer able to bear the cold,
and greens beneath the chilly frosts —
do you believe these were sent you from my farm?
Oh, how diligently you err, Regulus!
My little fields bear nothing but me.
Whatever your Umbrian bailiff or your tenant
or the country marked at the third milestone
or the Tuscans send you, or the men of Tusculum,
all that is born for me in the whole Subura.

title: Epigrams
text:
32. XXXII
Atticus, you who revive the name of an eloquent line
and do not let a mighty house fall silent,
the pious throng of Cecropian Minerva attends you,
quiet seclusion loves you, every sage loves you.
But other youths a trainer with a battered ear cultivates,
and the grimy masseur snatches their undeserving wealth.
No ball, no bladder, no rustic football at the baths
prepares you, nor the dull blow of a bare stump,
nor do you stretch crooked arms in the sticky wrestler's grease,
nor, roaming, do you snatch the dusty handballs,
but you only run near the snowy waters of the Virgin,
or where the bull glows with Sidonian love.
To play, through the various arts that every field serves,
when one is free to run, is sloth.
33. XXXIII
Though your toga is filthier than mud, Cinna,
while your shoe is whiter than the first snow,
why, fool, do you drench your feet with your dragging cloak?
Gather up your toga, Cinna — look, your shoe is ruined.
34. XXXIV
By what means, Severus, you ask,
could the worst man of all, Charinus,
have done one thing well?
I'll tell you, but quickly. What is worse than Nero?
What is better than the Neronian baths?
At once, behold, one of the spiteful is not lacking,
who speaks thus with rancid mouth:
'What? Do you prefer this to all the gifts
of our lord and god?' I prefer the Neronian
baths — to the bathing-place of a catamite.
35. XXXV
A slave with his black loins girt in leather
stands by, whenever you bathe in warm water all over.
But my slave, Laecania — to say nothing of myself —
has a Jewish weight under his bare skin,
and young men and old bathe naked with you.
Or is your slave's cock the only real one?
Do you, married woman, seek out the women's recesses,
and bathe apart, you cunt, in your own water?
36. XXXVI
When my unfinished farmhouse refused to bear the rains
and dripping Jupiter, and swam in winter waters,
many a tile to pour off the sudden showers
came, sent by your gifts.
Behold, rough December roars with Boreas' shriek:
Stella, you roof the house — you do not roof the farmer.

title: Epigrams
text:
37. XXXVII
You know the quaestor's deadly sign, Castricus?
It is worth your while to learn a new mark of death:
whenever he wiped his nose, running with cold,
he had ordered that to be the fatal sign for the throat.
A foul icicle was hanging from his loathsome nose,
when fierce December blew from his dripping jaw:
his colleagues held his hands — what more do you ask?
The poor wretch, Castricus, was not allowed to blow his nose.
38. XXXVIII
So vast you are, and such, our Severus' Polyphemus,
that even the Cyclops himself could marvel at you.
But Scylla is no smaller. If you should join the two
wild monsters, each would become the other's terror.
39. XXXIX
When Caelius could no longer endure or suffer
the various rushing about, the wandering mornings,
the haughtiness and the 'good morning' of the powerful,
he began to feign the gout.
And while he wants too much to prove it real,
and smears and binds his healthy soles
and walks with a laboured step
— such is the power of care and the art of pain! —
Caelius stopped feigning the gout.
40. XL
Here lies that old man, known in the imperial court,
who bore both gods with no humble breast;
whom his children's piety mingled with the holy shade
of his wife: both possess the Elysian grove.
She fell first, cheated of her green youth:
he lived nearly thrice six Olympiads.
But whoever saw your tears, Etruscus, believed him
snatched from you in years cut short.
41. XLI
You seem to yourself, Sempronius Tucca, to be a man of the world:
the world's ways, Sempronius, are as bad as they are good.
42. XLII
If anyone should wish to vie with you in gifts,
let him also dare, Castricus, in verses.
We are slight in both, and ready to be beaten:
hence sleep is ours, and deep quiet pleases us.
You ask, then, why I gave you such bad verses?
Do you think no one gave apples to Alcinous?

title: Epigrams
text:
43. XLIII
The first thing, Cinna, is to grant whatever I ask of you;
the next thing after, Cinna, is to refuse quickly.
I love the man who grants; I do not hate, Cinna, the one who refuses:
but you neither grant, Cinna, nor quickly refuse.
44. XLIV
That great Caesonius of yours, Ovidius, is the man here,
whose face the living wax still keeps.
Nero condemned him; but you dared to condemn
Nero, and to follow the fate of the exile, not your own:
a noble comrade you went across Scylla's seas with the banished man,
you who had lately refused to go as comrade of a consul.
If names entrusted to my pages are to live,
and it is granted me to survive my own ashes:
the crowd now present and to come shall hear that you were
to him what he was to his own Seneca.
45. XLV
Mighty friend of eloquent Seneca,
next to dear Serenus, or before him,
this is that Maximus, whom on many a page
the lucky letter greets in close array.
Him you followed through the Sicilian waves,
O Ovidius, not to be passed over by any tongue,
and you scorned the rage of a raving lord.
Let antiquity admire its Pylades,
who clung as comrade to the exile of his parent:
who would compare the dangers of the two?
You clung, a comrade, to the exile of Nero.
46. XLVI
While you want to commend your gift to me in song
and long to speak more learnedly than Maeonian lips,
you torment both me and yourself alike for many days,
and your Thalia, Priscus, says nothing of mine.
You can send the rich your Muses and your sounding elegies:
but to the poor give gifts in prose.
47. XLVII
Licinius Sura, most renowned of learned men,
whose grave and ancient tongue brought back our forefathers,
you are given back to us — heavens, by what gift of the fates! —
all but released, having tasted of Lethe's water.
Our prayers had already lost their fear, and untroubled
sorrow wept, and you were as good as done with our tears:
but the ruler of silent Avernus would not bear the spite,
and himself gave back the snatched distaff to the Fates.
You know, then, what great laments a false report of death
has stirred among men, and you enjoy your own posterity.
Live as one whose life is snatched, and pluck fugitive joys:
let your returned life lose not a single day.

title: Epigrams
text:
48. XLVIII
Though he has nearly three hundred tables,
Annius has servants instead of tables:
the dishes run past, the platters fly.
Keep these feasts to yourselves, you elegant folk:
I am put off by a dinner that walks about.
49. XLIX
I send you small gifts from my suburban garden:
eggs for your throat, Severus, apples for your appetite.
50. L
Fountain of the mistress, queen of the place that Ianthis delights in,
glory and darling of a famous house,
since your bank is adorned with so many snow-white attendants
and your water gleams with a Ganymede-like band:
what is the Alcides doing, hallowed in that grove?
Why does the god keep a cave so near to you?
Does he, perhaps, watch over the known loves of the Nymphs,
lest so many Hylases be carried off at once?
51. LI
If it irks you, Urbicus, to buy my trifles,
yet you would like to know my wanton songs,
seek out Pompeius Auctus — perhaps you know him;
he sits at the front of the temple of Mars the Avenger:
steeped in law and polished by the varied wear of the toga,
he is not my reader, Urbicus, but my book.
So he holds my absent verses by heart and recites them,
that not a letter perishes from my pages:
in short, if he wished, he could seem to have written them;
but he prefers to favour my fame.
You may pester him from the tenth hour — for he will not
be free enough before — a little supper will hold the two of you;
he will read, you drink; though you don't wish it, he will sound off;
and when you have said 'That's enough now,' he will read.
52. LII
It is gratifying, Auctus, that you read my little books to Celer,
if, that is, what you read, Auctus, pleases Celer too.
He governed my own people and the Celtic Iberians,
and there was no surer good faith in all our world.
A greater reverence the more disturbs me, and I think
my ears are those not of a hearer, but of a judge.

title: Epigrams
text:
53. LIII
You sent me everything at the Saturnalia, Umber —
all the gifts the five days had brought you:
twelve three-leaved tablets and seven toothpicks;
with these came a sponge, a napkin, a cup,
a half-peck of beans with a basket of Picentine olives,
and a black flask of Laletanian must;
small Syrian figs came with wrinkled prunes
and a jar heavy with the weight of Libyan figs.
I reckon the whole gift was scarcely worth thirty
sesterces — and eight strapping Syrians brought it.
How much more conveniently, with no labour at all,
a single boy could have carried me five pounds of silver!
54. LIV
Every morning you tell me sheer dreams about myself,
to stir and trouble my mind.
The last vintage has gone to the dregs, and this one too,
while the witch wears out my nights to placate you;
I have used up the salted meal and the heaps of incense;
my flocks have dwindled, while lamb after lamb falls;
no pig, no farmyard birds, no eggs are left.
Either keep watch, Nasidianus, or dream for yourself.
55. LV
If you send back gifts to no one, Chrestus,
then don't give to us or send any back:
I will believe you generous enough.
But if you make returns to Apicius and Lupus,
to Gallus and Titius and Caesius,
you shall lick — not mine, for it is honest and small —
but the one that comes from burnt Jerusalem,
the cock lately condemned to tribute.
56. LVI
You have grasped the stars and the sky with pious mind, Rabirius,
who with wondrous art build the Parrhasian palace.
If Pisa prepares to give temples worthy of Phidian Jove,
she will seek these hands of yours from our Thunderer.
57. LVII
Gabinia made an Achilles out of Castor — out of a Pollux:
he had been a good boxer; now he will be a horse-tamer.
58. LVIII
You have married six or seven catamites by now, Galla,
while their combed hair and dressed beards please you too much.
Then, having tried their flanks and loins like a soaked thong,
and parts that no tired hand could force to stand,
you desert the unwarlike marriage-beds and the soft husband;
and again and again you fall back into beds of the same kind.
Look for some man forever talking of Curii and Fabii,
shaggy and grim with harsh rusticity:
you'll find one — but that grim crowd has its catamites too.
It is hard, Galla, to marry a real man.

title: Epigrams
text:
59. LIX
Our friend Caecilianus, Titus, never dines without a boar.
A fine dinner-guest Caecilianus keeps!
60. LX
Reverend ruler of the Tarpeian court,
whom, while our chief is safe, we believe the Thunderer,
since each man wearies you with prayers for himself
and begs you to grant what you gods are able:
do not be angry, Jupiter, as at a proud man,
that I ask nothing for myself.
For Caesar I must pray to you;
for myself I must pray to Caesar.
61. LXI
The reckless huckster had stolen the whole city,
and no man's threshold was his own at his own door.
You ordered the narrow alleys to grow, Germanicus,
and what had lately been a footpath became a road.
No pillar now is girt with chained flasks,
nor is the praetor forced to walk through the mud,
nor is a razor blindly drawn in the thick crowd,
nor does the black cookshop seize whole streets.
Barber, taverner, cook, butcher keep to their own thresholds.
Now it is Rome; lately it was one big shop.
62. LXII
Behind open doors you bugger grown men, Amillus,
and you want to be caught while you do it,
so that no freedman or your father's slaves may tattle,
nor a dark client with sidelong gossip.
The man who calls others to witness he is not sodomized,
Amillus, often does the thing he does without a witness.
63. LXIII
You who read the never-dying volumes of eternal Silius,
poems worthy of the Latin toga,
do you suppose only the Pierian retreats pleased the bard,
and the Bacchic garlands on his Aonian hair?
He did not touch the rites of buskined Maro
before he had filled the work of great Cicero:
him the grave spear of the Hundred Men still admires,
him many a client speaks of with grateful mouth.
After he had ruled the mighty year with its twelve fasces —
the year that was hallowed when the world was set free —
he handed over his earned years to the Muses and to Phoebus,
and now keeps Helicon as his forum.

title: Epigrams
text:
64. LXIV
You who were the most famous barber in all the city,
and afterward, by your mistress's gift, were made a knight,
you sought out the Sicilian cities and Aetna's realms,
Cinnamus, when you fled the grim laws of the forum.
By what art will you now bear, useless, your burdensome years?
What does an unhappy, fugitive leisure do?
You cannot be a rhetor, a grammarian, or a schoolmaster,
nor a Cynic, nor a Stoic,
nor sell your voice and applause to Sicilian theatres:
what is left, Cinnamus, is to be a barber again.
65. LXV
A lawsuit, while you count the frosts of twice ten winters,
wears you down, Gargilianus — one suit in three courts.
Ah, wretched and mad! Does anyone litigate for twenty years,
Gargilianus, when he is free to lose?
66. LXVI
Fabius left Labienus heir to the whole estate:
yet Labienus says he deserved more.
67. LXVII
Philaenis the tribade buggers boys,
and, fiercer than a husband in her lust,
ploughs eleven girls a day.
Tucked up, she plays at handball too,
grows yellow with sand, and whirls with easy arm
the weights heavy for athletes;
and, muddied from the crumbling wrestling-ground,
she is whipped by the oiled trainer's lash.
Nor does she dine or recline before
she has vomited up seven measures of neat wine;
to which she thinks it right to return
when she has eaten sixteen rissoles.
After all this, when she lusts,
she does not suck — she thinks that too unmanly —
but plainly devours the middles of girls.
May the gods give you your own mind, Philaenis,
you who think it manly to lick a cunt.
68. LXVIII
Forbear, I beg, to commend my Muses, Instantius Rufus,
to your father-in-law: perhaps he likes serious things.
But if he too admits wanton little books,
these I would read even to a Curius or a Fabricius.
69. LXIX
This is that Theophila promised to you, Canius,
whose breast is steeped in Cecropian endowment:
the garden of the great old man might justly claim her for its own,
nor would the Stoic throng less wish her theirs.
Whatever work you send out through these ears will live:
so unwomanly, so uncommon is her taste.
Let not your Pantaenis prefer herself too much to her,
though she is well known to the Pierian choir.
Sappho the lover praised her as she fashioned songs:
Theophila was chaster, and Sappho no more learned.

title: Epigrams
text:
70. LXX
Tribade of the very tribades, Philaenis,
you rightly call the woman you fuck your 'girlfriend.'
71. LXXI
The wife is poxed with figs, the husband poxed himself,
the daughter poxed, and the son-in-law and grandson;
neither steward nor bailiff lacks the foul sore,
nor the sturdy digger, nor even the ploughman.
Since young and old alike are poxed,
it is a marvel: one single field has no figs.
72. LXXII
So may December be welcome to you, Paulus,
nor may there come empty three-leaved tablets and skimpy napkins
nor light half-pounds of incense,
but may a great defendant or a powerful friend
bring you platters and your grandsires' goblets,
or whatever rather pleases and takes you;
so may you beat Novius and Publius
shut in by their stockades and glass robber-pieces;
so may the favour of the umpire of the oiled ring
give you the palm at bare ball-play,
and praise no more the left-handed strokes of Polybius:
if any spiteful man says that the songs
which drip with black venom are mine,
lend me your voice as advocate
and cry, as loud and as long as you can:
'My Martial did not write that.'
73. LXXIII
You have a house on the Esquiline, a house on Diana's hill,
and the patrician quarter holds your rooftops;
from here you look on widowed Cybele's shrines, from there on Vesta's,
on the new Jupiter from this side, the old from that.
Tell me where I may meet you, tell me where to find you:
the man who lives everywhere, Maximus, lives nowhere.
74. LXXIV
Glory of Cyllene and the sky, eloquent minister,
whose golden wand grows green with a twisted serpent:
so may you never lack a store of wanton intrigue,
whether you long for Paphos or grow warm for Ganymede,
and may your mother's Ides be decked with sacred leaves,
and your aged grandfather be pressed with a light burden:
this day may Norbana ever keep with her husband Carpus,
glad — the day they came together to their first bed.
Here this pious priest of wisdom offers you his gifts,
here he calls you with incense, himself faithful to Jove too.

title: Epigrams
text:
75. LXXV
You want to be fucked for free, though you are ugly and old.
A most ridiculous thing: you want to give, yet won't pay.
76. LXXVI
That more powerful men tear you to pieces
at banquets, porticoes, theatres,
and it delights them, whenever you've fallen in their way,
to be carried and to bathe with you:
do not be too pleased with yourself.
You amuse, Philomusus; you are not loved.
77. LXXVII
You demand, Tucca, that I make you a gift of my little books.
I won't: for you want to sell them, not read them.
78. LXXVIII
Since a tail of Saxetan mackerel is served you,
and beans dressed for you, if you dine well:
yet you send out sow's udder, boar, hare, mushrooms, oysters, mullet —
you have, Papylus, neither heart nor taste.
79. LXXIX
I lately drank a consular wine.
You ask how old and how generous?
Laid down under Priscus' consulship: but the very man
who set it before me, Severus, was the consul.
80. LXXX
Since now the Roman peace tempers the Odrysian North
and the grim trumpets have fallen silent,
you may send this little book to Marcellinus, Faustinus:
now he is free for pages, now for jests.
But if you wish to commend the small gifts of your friend,
let a boy carry my songs —
not the kind who, gorged on the milk of a Getic heifer,
plays on the stiff Sarmatian stream with a hoop,
but the rosy youth of a Mitylenean dealer,
or a Laconian not yet flogged at his mother's bidding.
But to you a captive servant shall be sent from the Hister,
one able to pasture your Tiburtine sheep.
81. LXXXI
'Thirty epigrams in the whole book are bad.'
If as many are good, Lausus, the book is good.
82. LXXXII
So large a sheath clothes Menophilus' penis
that it alone would be enough for all the comic actors.
I had believed — for we often bathe together —
that he was anxious, Flaccus, to spare his voice:
but while he played in the middle of the wrestling-ground, with the crowd looking on,
the sheath slipped off the poor man: he was circumcised.

title: Epigrams
text:
83. LXXXIII
While the barber Eutrapelus goes round Lupercus' face
and paints his cheeks, a second beard comes up.
84. LXXXIV
While my likeness is being shaped for Caecilius Secundus
and the painted panel breathes from a skilful hand,
go, book, to Getic Peuce and the recumbent Hister:
he holds those places, the peoples thoroughly tamed.
You will give small, but sweet, gifts to a dear comrade:
my face will be surer in my song;
proof against any chances, blottable by no years,
it will live, when the work of Apelles dies.
85. LXXXV
That you write certain quatrains not without wit,
and a few couplets prettily, Sabellus,
I praise, but do not marvel. It is easy to write epigrams
prettily; but to write a book is hard.
86. LXXXVI
I used to be invited to your birthday feasts,
back when I was not your friend, Sextus:
what has happened, I ask, what has suddenly happened,
after so many pledges between us, after so many years,
that I, an old comrade, am passed over?
But I know the reason: no pound of refined
Spanish silver came to you from me,
no light toga, no fresh cloaks.
A dole that drives a bargain is no dole;
you feed gifts, Sextus, not friends.
Now you'll say to me, 'Let the summoner be flogged.'
87. LXXXVII
If my Flaccus delights in a long-eared fox-ape,
if Canius enjoys a grim Ethiopian;
if Publius burns with love for a tiny lapdog,
if Cronius loves a monkey like himself;
if a destructive ichneumon pleases Marius,
if a chattering magpie pleases you, Lausus;
if Cadilla winds a cold serpent round her neck,
if Telesilla gave a tomb to a nightingale:
why should not the man who sees such monsters please their owners
love the charming face of Cupid-like Labyrtas?
88. LXXXVIII
It is said, if the report is true, that lovely Vienna
holds my little books among her delights:
there every old man and youth and boy reads me,
and the chaste girl before her grim husband.
This I would rather than that my songs were sung
by those who drink the Nile straight from its very mouth;
than that my Tagus should fill me with Spanish gold,
and Hybla and Hymettus feed my bees.
So I am something, then, nor am I deceived
by the gift of a flattering tongue: now, Lausus, I think I'll believe you.

title: Epigrams
text:
89. LXXXIX
Go, happy rose, and with your soft garlands
crown the hair of my Apollinaris.
And remember to bind them, white — but only in time to come,
so may Venus love you always — when his hair is grey.
90. XC
Matho boasts that I have made an uneven little book:
if it is true, Matho praises my poems.
Calvinus and Umber write even books:
an even book, Creticus, is the one that is bad throughout.
91. XCI
From my little farm, eloquent Juvenal,
I send you, look, some Saturnalia nuts.
The rest of the fruit the lustful cock of the guardian god
gave away to wanton girls.
92. XCII
'If you need anything, you know you've only to ask me' —
this you say twice and three times a day, Baccara, in one breath.
Grim Secundus duns me in a harsh voice:
you hear, and don't know, Baccara, what I need.
The rent is demanded of me in your presence, loud and open:
you hear, and don't know, Baccara, what I need.
I complain my cloaks are cold and threadbare:
you hear, and don't know, Baccara, what I need.
What I need is this: that you suddenly be struck dumb by some star,
so you can't say, Baccara, 'If you need anything.'
93. XCIII
Narnia, whom the river, white with its sulphurous current,
girdles, scarcely to be reached by a double ridge,
why does it please you so often to steal my Quintus from us
and detain him with sluggish delay?
Why do you ruin for me the worth of my Nomentan farm,
which was precious because of its neighbour?
But now spare me, Narnia, do not abuse my Quintus:
so may you enjoy your bridge forever.
94. XCIV
What the small onyx jar lately held was perfume:
after Papylus smelled it — behold, it is fish-sauce.
95. XCV
It is winter, and rough December is stiff with cold,
yet you dare, with a snowy kiss,
to stop everyone you meet on this side and that,
and to kiss all Rome, Linus.
What heavier, what crueller thing could you do
if you were struck and flogged?
In this cold let no wife kiss me,
nor my young daughter with her coaxing lips.
But you are sweeter and more refined,
you from whose dog's nostrils
hangs a livid icicle, and whose beard is stiff,
such as the Cilician barber reaps with upturned shears
from a Cinyphian goatherd.
I'd rather meet a hundred cunt-lickers,
and I fear a fresh-castrated priest of Cybele less.
So if you have any sense and shame,
your winter kissings, Linus,
I beg you put off till the month of April.

title: Epigrams
text:
96. XCVI
Here I am buried, Bassus' grief, the infant Urbicus,
to whom greatest Rome gave birth and name.
Six months were lacking to me of my first three years,
when the grim goddesses cut short my thread of life.
What good to me was beauty, speech, or age?
Give tears to my tomb, you who read this:
so may the one you wish to outlive you not go down
to Lethe's waters, unless later than Nestor.
97. XCVII
If you know Caesius Sabinus well, my little book,
glory of mountainous Umbria,
the townsman of my Aulus Pudens,
you will give him these, even when he is busy:
though a thousand cares press and weigh on him,
he will still have time for my songs:
for he loves me, and reads me next
to the noble little books of Turnus.
Oh, what a name is being won for you!
Oh, what glory! how frequent a lover!
You will sound at banquets, at the forum,
at mansions, crossroads, porticoes, taverns.
You are sent to one, you are read by all.
98. XCVIII
You buy everything, Castor: so it will come about that you sell everything.
99. XCIX
So may you ever see the Thunderer calm, Crispinus,
nor may Rome love you less than your own Memphis:
if my songs are read in the Parrhasian court
— for they are wont to enjoy Caesar's sacred ear —
dare to say of me, like a candid reader:
'This man brings no little credit to your times,
and is not too far beneath Marsus and learned Catullus.'
This is enough: the rest I entrust to the god himself.

title: Epigrams
text:
pr. To the Emperor Domitian Caesar Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, Valerius Martialis sends greeting.
All my little books, my lord, to which you have given fame — that is, life — make their supplication to you; and on that account, I think, they will be read. This one, however, which is inscribed as the eighth of my work, enjoys the occasion of devotion more often.
