So there was less need to labour with my wit, since subject-matter had taken its place: this I have tried now and then to vary with some mixture of jests, lest every verse should heap up on your heavenly modesty its own praises, which might more easily weary you than satisfy me. Yet, although epigrams have been written even by the gravest men of the highest rank in such a way that they seem to have aimed at the verbal license of the mime, I have not allowed mine to speak as wantonly as they are wont. Since the part of the book that is both the larger and the better is bound to the majesty of your sacred name, let it remember that none should approach the temples unless cleansed by religious purification. That my readers may know I shall observe this, I have decided to declare it on the very threshold of this little book in a very brief epigram.

title: Epigrams
text:
1. I
Book, about to enter the laurelled household of our lord,
learn to speak more holily, with modest lips.
Withdraw, naked Venus; this little book is not yours:
come to me, you, Caesar's own Pallas, come.
2. II
Janus, begetter and father of the calendar,
when he lately saw the conqueror of the Hister,
thought all his faces not enough for himself,
and wished he had more eyes:
and, speaking at once with every tongue,
he promised to the lord of the earth and god of all things
the Pylian old age of Nestor, four times over.
Add, father Janus, your own, we pray.
3. III
'Five would have been enough: for six or seven little books
is too much: what pleasure is it still to play, Muse?
Let there be shame and an end: now Fame can add
nothing more to me — my book is thumbed everywhere;
and when Messala's stones lie shattered by decay
and Licinus' tall marbles are dust,
still mouths will read me, and many a stranger
will carry my songs home to his native land.'
I had finished, when the ninth of the sisters answered thus,
her hair and dress dirty with perfume:
'Can you, ingrate, abandon your sweet trifles?
Tell me, what better will you do in your idleness?
Or does it please you to change the slipper for the tragic buskin,
or to thunder harsh wars in even measures,
so that a swollen schoolmaster may declaim you in a raucous voice
and the grown girl and the good boy may hate you?
Let the over-grave and over-severe write such things,
the wretches whom the lamp sees at midnight.
But you, dip your charming little books in Roman salt:
let life recognize and read its own ways.
Though you may seem to sing on a narrow reed,
let your reed outdo the trumpets of many.'
4. IV
What a great gathering of the world, hurrah, at the Latin altars
takes up and pays vows for its leader!
These are not the joys of men alone, Germanicus,
but the very gods, I think, are now performing rites.

title: Epigrams
text:
5. V
While you give rings to girls, Macer,
you have ceased, Macer, to have any rings.
6. VI
Nothing is more tiresome than old Euctus' antiques
— I'd sooner have crockery shaped from Saguntine clay —
when he tells the mad pedigree of his silver
and, garrulous, turns wine musty with his words.
'These cups belonged to Laomedon's table:
to win them, Apollo built the walls with his lyre.
With this mixing-bowl fierce Rhoetus joined battle
with the Lapiths: you see a piece weakened by the fight.
These two bowls are reckoned of long-lived Nestor:
a dove, polished by a Pylian thumb, gleams there.
Here is the cup in which Aeacus' grandson bade
neat wine be mixed more freely and stronger for his friends.
In this dish most lovely Dido toasted Bitias
when the banquet was given to the Phrygian man.'
When you have marvelled much at the ancient embossings,
you'll drink Astyanax from Priam's cups.
7. VII
Is this pleading causes, is this speaking eloquently, Cinna —
in ten hours, Cinna, to say nine words?
But just now, in a mighty voice, you demanded
four water-clocks. Oh, Cinna, how long you can keep silent!
8. VIII
Though you give the swift years their beginning, Janus,
and renew long ages with your face,
though pious incense beg of you first, vows greet you,
the lucky purple honour you, every dignity court you:
yet you prefer this — that it fell to the Latin city
in your month, Janus, to see its god come home.
9. IX
Bleary-eyed Hylas lately wished to pay you, Quintus,
three-quarters of the debt; now, one-eyed, he wants to give half.
Take it as soon as you can; the chance of gain is brief:
if Hylas goes blind, he'll pay you nothing at all.
10. X
Bassus bought Tyrian cloaks of the finest dye
for ten thousand. He made a profit.
'Did he buy so cheaply?' you say. No — he won't pay.
11. XI
The Rhine already knows you have reached your city;
for it too hears the voices of your people:
the Sarmatian tribes also, and the Hister and the Getae,
the very shout of strange rejoicing has terrified.
While long-drawn joys revere you in the sacred Circus,
no one noticed the horses run, though sent forth four times.
Rome has loved no leader, nor you, Caesar, so much:
even she could not love you more, much as she'd wish.

title: Epigrams
text:
12. XII
Why I would not wish to marry a rich wife,
you ask? I do not want to be the bride to my wife.
Let the matron be beneath her husband, Priscus:
not otherwise do woman and man become equals.
13. XIII
He was called a fool: I bought him for twenty thousand.
Give me back my money, Gargilianus: he has his wits.
14. XIV
That his pale Cilician orchards may not fear the winter,
and a too-strong breeze nip the tender grove,
window-panes set against the wintry south-winds
admit the clear suns and the cloudless day.
But to me is given a cell, not wholly closed by a window,
in which not even Boreas himself would care to stay.
So you bid an old friend lodge, cruel man —
better, then, that I be the guest of your tree.
15. XV
While the new glory of the Pannonian war is recounted,
and every altar makes offering to Jupiter the home-bringer,
the people give, the grateful knights give, the senate gives incense,
and a third gift enriches the Latin tribes:
these secret triumphs too Rome has recorded,
nor was that laurel of your peace any less,
in that you trust to the holy devotion of your own.
A prince's greatest virtue is to know his own.
16. XVI
You who were long a baker, Cyperus,
now plead causes and seek two hundred thousand:
but you spend, and you keep on borrowing.
You do not retreat from the baker's trade, Cyperus:
you make bread, and you make flour-dust of your fortune.
17. XVII
I pleaded your case, Sextus, agreed on two thousand:
that you sent me a thousand coins — what is this?
'You told nothing,' you say, 'and the case was lost by you.'
You owe so much the more, Sextus, because I blushed.
18. XVIII
If you brought out your epigrams, Cerrinius, before the public,
you could be read either alongside me or even ahead of me:
but so great is your regard for an old friend,
that my fame is dearer to you than your own.
So Maro did not attempt the songs of Calabrian Flaccus,
though he knew how to surpass the Pindaric measures,
and yielded to Varius the glory of the Roman buskin,
though he could speak more powerfully in the tragic voice.
Gold and wealth and lands a friend will often give:
he who is willing to yield in talent will be rare.

title: Epigrams
text:
19. XIX
Cinna wishes to seem poor; and he is poor.
20. XX
Though you make two hundred verses every single day,
Varus, you recite nothing. You have no sense — and you have sense.
21. XXI
Phosphor, give back the day: why do you delay our joys?
With Caesar coming, Phosphor, give back the day.
Rome asks it. Do the sluggish wains of placid Boötes
carry you, that you come on too slow an axle?
You could have led off Cyllarus from the Ledaean star:
Castor himself will now yield you his own horse.
Why do you hold back the eager Titan? Already Xanthus and Aethon
want the reins; Memnon's kindly mother is awake.
Yet the slow stars do not yield to the shining light,
and the moon longs to see the Ausonian leader.
Now, Caesar, come even by night: though the stars stand still,
the day will not fail the people when you come.
22. XXII
You invite me to boar, Gallicus, you set pork before me.
I'm a half-breed, Gallicus, if you fool me.
23. XXIII
I seem to you savage and too much a glutton,
Rusticus, because over a dinner I flog the cook.
If that seems to you a trivial cause for the lash,
then for what cause would you have the cook beaten?
24. XXIV
If by chance I ask anything in a timid, slender little book,
grant it, if my page has not been shameless.
And if you will not grant it, Caesar, allow it to be asked:
incense and prayers never offend Jupiter.
He who shapes sacred faces in gold or marble
does not make gods: the man who prays does.
25. XXV
You saw me ill just once, Oppianus,
hardly at all; I'll see you often.
26. XXVI
The Gangetic ravisher feared not so many tigers
in the Eastern fields, fleeing white on his Hyrcanian horse,
as your Rome has seen, Germanicus, new tigers:
it could not even count its own delights.
Your arena, Caesar, surpasses the Erythraean triumphs
and the wealth and riches of the conquering god:
for when he drove captive Indians beneath his chariot,
Bacchus was content with a pair of tigers.

title: Epigrams
text:
27. XXVII
The man who gives gifts to you, Gaurus, rich and old,
if you have wit and sense, says this to you: 'Die.'
28. XXVIII
Tell me, toga, welcome gift of an eloquent friend,
of what flock do you wish to be the fame and pride?
Did the Apulian grass of Ledaean Phalanthus bloom for you,
where Galaesus waters the tilled fields with Calabrian streams?
Or did Baetis, the Tartessian nurse of the Spanish fold,
also wash you in a Hesperian sheep?
Or did your wool number among many-branched Timavus,
which pious Cyllarus drank with his star-bearing mouth?
It became you not to be stained with Amyclaean dye,
nor was Miletus worthy of your fleece.
You outdo the lilies and the privet not yet fallen,
and the ivory that chills on the Tiburtine hill;
the Spartan swan will yield to you, and the Paphian doves,
the gem dug from the Erythraean shallows will yield:
but though these gifts rival the first snows,
they are not whiter than their Parthenius.
I would not prefer the embroidered weavings of proud Babylon,
which the Semiramian needle makes various;
nor would I admire myself more in Athamantian gold,
should you give me, Phrixus, the Aeolian sheep.
Oh, what laughter will my cloak stir up, when seen
together with my Palatine toga!
29. XXIX
He who writes couplets, I think, wants to please by brevity.
But what good is brevity, tell me, if it makes a book?
30. XXX
The show now watched in Caesar's arena
was the highest glory in the days of Brutus.
You see how the brave hand holds the flames and delights in its punishment
and reigns over the astonished fire!
He stands as his own spectator, and loves
the noble death of his right hand: it feeds on the whole sacrifice;
and had the punishment not been snatched from the unwilling man,
the fiercer left hand was getting ready to go into the failing flames.
After such a glorious deed, it irks me to know what it did before:
it is enough for me to know the hand I saw.

title: Epigrams
text:
31. XXXI
You confess something not very pretty about yourself, Dento,
you who, having taken a wife, seek the rights of a father.
But now stop wearying our lord with begging little books,
and return at last from the city to your homeland:
for while you are far off, your wife long deserted,
and you seek three sons, you'll find four.
32. XXXII
Gliding down through the silent air, a coaxing dove
flowed into the very lap of seated Aretulla.
Chance would have made sport of this, but the bird stayed unwatched
and, though free to fly, would not go off.
If a pious sister may hope for better things,
and if prayers avail to bend the lord of the world,
this bird perhaps comes to you from the Sardinian shores of the exile
as a messenger that your brother will return.
33. XXXIII
From your praetorian crown you send me a leaf, Paulus,
and bid it bear the name of a saucer.
With this gauze your stage-platform was lately smeared,
which the wave of red saffron washed pale.
Or is it gold-leaf scraped off by the nail of a crafty servant,
which I think comes from the foot of your couch?
That leaf can feel a gnat flying far off
and be stirred by the wing of the tiniest butterfly;
it flutters, suspended on the heat of a small lamp,
and breaks at the light touch of poured wine.
With this spit are smeared the date-palms of January's Kalends,
which the shabby client brings with his stingy penny.
Less limp grow the colocasia on their slender stalk,
more fully the lilies fall in too much sun;
nor does the wandering spider run on so thin a web,
nor does the hanging silkworm press out so light a work.
Thicker stands the chalk on old Fabulla's face,
thicker the bubble swells on struck water;
stronger is the bladder that keeps curled hair,
and the Batavian foam that changes Latin locks.
With such a skin the chick is clothed in the Ledaean egg,
such patches sit on the crescent-marked brow.
What have you to do with a saucer, when you could send a spoon,
when you could send me even a little ladle —
I speak too grandly — when you could send a snail-shell,
in short, when you could send, Paulus, nothing?

title: Epigrams
text:
34. XXXIV
You say you own the original silver of Mys.
A thing made without you — is that the more original?
35. XXXV
Since you are alike and matched in life,
a wretched wife, a wretched husband,
I wonder you don't get on well together.
36. XXXVI
Laugh, Caesar, at the royal wonder of the pyramids;
now barbaric Memphis is silent about her Eastern work:
how small a part is the Mareotic labour beside the Parrhasian hall?
The day sees nothing brighter in the whole world.
You'd think the seven hills rise together;
Thessalian Pelion bore a lower Ossa;
it so enters the air that, hidden among the bright stars,
its serene peak thunders below the cloud
and is filled with the secret godhead of Phoebus
before Circe sees the face of her rising father.
Yet this house, Augustus, which strikes the stars with its summit,
is the equal of heaven — but less than its lord.
37. XXXVII
That you give back the bills to Caietanus, Polycharmus,
do you suppose you have made him a gift of a hundred thousand?
'He owed it,' you say. Keep the bills to yourself, Polycharmus,
and lend Caietanus another two thousand.
38. XXXVIII
He who excels in stubborn devotion
toward one who will feel the good of his generosity
may perhaps be angling, or claiming a return:
but he who keeps on giving to a name left behind,
after the shade and the tomb,
what does he seek, except to grieve more sparingly?
It matters whether you are good or wish to seem so.
This you do, Melior, with Fame for witness,
you who, careful of the rites of the buried,
do not let the name of Blaesus perish,
and, lavish from your bountiful coffer,
to honour his birthday,
what you give to the mindful and pious band of scribes
you make a thing of Blaesus.
This will be your tribute long, while life remains,
this too after your ashes.
39. XXXIX
There was no place before to hold the banquets of the Palatine table
and its ambrosial feasts:
here it is fitting to drink the sacred nectar, Germanicus,
and the cups mixed by a Ganymede-hand.
Be willing, I beg, to be a late guest of the Thunderer:
but if you are in a hurry, Jupiter, come yourself.

title: Epigrams
text:
40. XL
Not of a garden nor of a happy vine,
but of a thin grove, Priapus, are you guardian,
from which you were born and can be born again;
I warn you, keep off thieving hands
and save the wood for your master's hearths:
if this fails, you too are firewood.
41. XLI
'Gloomy Athenagoras has not sent us the gifts
he is wont to send in mid-winter's month.'
Whether Athenagoras is gloomy, Faustinus, I shall see:
certainly Athenagoras has made me gloomy.
42. XLII
If a bigger dole among the rich
has not corrupted you, as it does, then,
Matho, you may bathe a hundred times at my expense.
43. XLIII
Fabius buries his wives, Chrestilla her husbands,
and each shakes a funeral torch over the marriage-bed.
Match the victors, Venus: the end that waits these two
is that one Libitina carry the pair away together.
44. XLIV
Titullus, I warn you, live: it is always too late;
even were you to begin under your tutor, it is too late.
But you, poor Titullus, do not live even as an old man,
but wear down every threshold as a caller,
and in the morning sweat, wet with the kisses of the city,
and, splashed before all the horses in the triple forum
and the temple of Mars and the colossus of Augustus,
you run through them all, at the third hour and the fifth.
Snatch, heap up, carry off, possess: it must be left behind.
Though your proud strongbox grow pale with packed coins,
though a hundred pages of account-books be unrolled,
your heir will swear you left nothing,
and over your bier, while you lie there — a board or a stone —
while your couch, stuffed with paper, swells for you,
he will proudly kiss your weeping eunuchs;
and your sorrowing son, whether you will or no,
the first night will sleep with your catamite.
45. XLV
Priscus Terentius is given back to me, Flaccus, from the shores of Etna:
let a milk-white gem mark this day;
let the cloudy amphora drip and grow bright through the slow strainer,
the jar made smaller under its hundredth consul.
When will so fair a night fall to my table?
When shall I be allowed to grow warm with so deserved a wine?
When Cytherean Cyprus gives you back to me, Flaccus,
there will be so good a cause for my excess.

title: Epigrams
text:
46. XLVI
As great as your honesty, so great is the innocence of your beauty,
boy Cestus, chaster than chaste Hippolytus!
Diana would wish you with her and teach you to swim,
Cybele would rather have you whole, a Phrygian;
you could succeed to Ganymede's couch,
but, hard, you'd give your lord kisses only.
Happy the bride who will vex her tender husband,
and the girl who will first make a man of you!
47. XLVII
Part of your jaws is clipped, part of you is shaved,
part is plucked. Who would think it is one head?
48. XLVIII
Crispinus does not know to whom he gave his Tyrian mantle,
while he changes his dress and puts on the toga.
Whoever has it, give the cloak back to its shoulders, we beg:
it is not Crispinus who asks you this, but the mantle.
Not just anyone is fit for garments steeped in purple,
nor does that colour suit any but the elegant.
If loot delights you and the madness of foul gain,
take the toga — with it you can cheat better.
49. XLIX
As great as the table of the Giants' triumph is recounted,
and as great a night as that was for all the gods above,
when the good father reclined with the common folk of the gods
and the Fauns were allowed to ask Jupiter for wine:
so great are the banquets that celebrate your laurels, Caesar;
our joys gladden the very gods.
Every knight feasts with you, and the people and the fathers,
and Rome takes ambrosial fare with her leader.
Having promised great things, how much greater you have given!
A dole was promised us; a full dinner was served.
50. L
What labour is in this dish? Learned Mys' work, or Myron's?
Is this the hand of Mentor, or, Polyclitus, yours?
It is not dulled by any dark tarnish, nor does the cloudy mass
hate the fires that test it;
true amber gleams less than this yellow metal,
and the lucky boss outshines snowy ivory.
The work does not yield to its material: so it rings the disc round,
as the full moon shines with all its lamp.
A goat stands, decked with the Aeolian fleece of Theban Phrixus:
his sister might have wished to be carried by this one;
not even the Cinyphian shearer would harm him, and you,
Lyaeus, would yourself wish him fed on your vine.
On the beast's back rides a golden Cupid with twin wings,
and the Pallas-lotus sounds from his tender mouth:
so the dolphin, delighting in Methymnaean Arion,
bore the languid burden, not silent, through the seas.
Let your hand, Cestus, steep this fine gift for me with worthy nectar —
not one of the master's herd, but your own;
Cestus, glory of the table, mix Setine wine: the boy himself,
the goat himself, seem to us to thirst.
Let the letter of Instantius Rufus give the number of cyathi:
for he is the author to me of so great a gift:
if Telethusa comes and brings the promised joys,
I'll be kept for my mistress, Rufus, by your four measures;
if she's doubtful, I'll be dragged on through seven; if she fails her lover,
to cut my cares' throat I'll drink both names.

title: Epigrams
text:
51. LI
A truly beautiful woman — but Asper loves her blind.
So Asper, as the case stands, loves more than he sees.
52. LII
A boy barber, but of such skill
as not even Nero's Thalamus had,
to whom the beards of the Drusi fell,
I lent to Rufus, Caedicianus,
when asked for once, to even out his cheeks.
While, as bidden, he goes over the same hairs,
his judgement guided by the mirror in his hand,
and paints the skin and makes a long second going-over
of the close-cut hairs,
my barber came back to me with a beard.
53. LIII
As loud a roar as is heard through the Massylian wilds,
whenever the wood rages with countless lions,
when the pale shepherd calls back to the Punic huts
his frightened bulls and his witless flock:
so great a terror lately growled in the Ausonian sand.
Who would not have thought it a herd? It was one,
but one whose laws even the lions themselves would tremble at,
to whom the marble-painted Nomad would give a diadem.
Oh, what glory round his neck, what honour the golden shadow
of his crescent mane scattered, when he stood!
How the great hunting-spears became his broad breast,
and what joys he took from a noble death!
Whence, Libya, came so happy a glory to your forests?
Had he come, perhaps, from the yoke of Cybele?
Or rather, Germanicus, did your brother or father himself
send this beast to you from the Herculean star?
54. LIV
Of women most beautiful, who have been or are,
but most worthless, who have been or are,
oh, how I would wish you to become, Catulla,
either less beautiful or more chaste!
55. LV
Since the age of our grandfathers yields to our times,
and Rome has grown greater with her leader,
you wonder that the genius of sacred Maro is wanting,
and that no one sounds wars with so great a trumpet.
Let there be Maecenases, Flaccus, and Marones will not be lacking;
even your own farm will give you a Virgil.
Tityrus had lost the acres next to wretched Cremona,
and grieved, sick at heart, for his sheep driven away:
the Tuscan knight laughed, and pushed back grudging poverty
and bade it depart in swift flight.
'Take riches,' he said, 'and be the greatest of bards;
you may even love our Alexis.'
That loveliest boy stood by his master's table,
pouring dark Falernian with a marble hand,
and gave the sipped cups from rosy lips,
cups that could have tempted Jupiter himself.
The astonished poet forgot plump Galatea
and Thestylis, her red cheeks burnt at harvest;
at once he conceived Italy and 'arms and the man,'
he who lately had barely wept the Gnat with rude lips.
Why speak of the Varii and Marsi and the enriched names
of bards whom it would be great labour to count?
So I'll be a Virgil, if you give me Maecenas' gifts?
A Virgil I'll not be: I'll be a Marsus.

title: Epigrams
text:
56. LVI
Though you bestow great gifts so often, about to give greater,
conqueror of leaders, conqueror even of yourself,
you are loved by the people not for your rewards, Caesar;
for you the people love your rewards, Caesar.
57. LVII
He had three teeth, all of which he spat out together
while Picens himself sat at his own tomb;
and he gathered in his lap the last fragments of his
loose mouth, and buried them in heaped-up earth.
Though some day his heir need not gather the dead man's bones,
Picens has already done himself this office.
58. LVIII
Since your cloaks are so thick, Artemidorus,
I could rightly call you Sagaris.
59. LIX
Do you see this man content with one eye, beneath whose
worn brow a bleary socket gapes?
Don't despise the fellow: nothing is more thievish than he;
not even Autolycus' hand was so peppered.
Take care to keep a wary eye on this dinner-guest:
then he rages, and one-eyed sees with both eyes;
the anxious servants lose their cups and spoons,
and many a napkin hides in his warm bosom;
nor does he fail to filch a cloak slipped from an elbow,
and often goes off covered with two mantles;
nor was the cheat ashamed to cheat a drowsing slave
of the lamp, though it be burning.
If he has seized nothing, then with crafty art
he goes round a boy and steals his own slippers.
60. LX
You could equal the summit of the Palatine colossus,
Claudia, if you became a foot and a half shorter.
61. LXI
Charinus is livid, he bursts, he rages, he weeps,
and seeks high branches to hang himself from:
not now because I am sung and read throughout the world,
nor because, smart with bosses and cedar-oil,
I am scattered through all the nations Rome holds:
but because I have a summer place in the country near the city,
and ride on mules not, as before, hired.
What shall I call down, O Severus, on the livid man?
This I pray: may he have mules and a suburban farm.

title: Epigrams
text:
62. LXII
Picens writes epigrams on the back of the paper,
and grieves that he does it with the god turned away.
63. LXIII
Aulus loves Thestylus, but burns no less for Alexis,
and perhaps now loves my Hyacinthus too.
Go now and doubt whether he loves the bards themselves,
when my Aulus loves the bards' darlings.
64. LXIV
That you may beg a gift and exact it, Clytus,
you are born eight times in one year,
and you have only, I think, three or four
Kalends that are not your birthday.
Though your face be smoother
than the worn pebbles of a dry shore,
though your hair be blacker than the falling mulberry,
though you outdo trembling feathers in softness,
or a lump of curdled milk just now,
and such a swelling rouse your nipples
as an unripe girl keeps for a man,
you seem to us, Clytus, already an old man:
for who would believe that even Priam or Nestor
had so many birthdays?
Let there be at last some shame and limit to your robberies.
But if you keep playing, and to be born once
in one year is not now enough for you,
I'll think, Clytus, you were not born even once.
65. LXV
Here, where the temples of Fortune the Home-Bringer
gleam wide and bright, was lately a happy open space:
here stood Caesar, handsome with the dust of Northern war,
pouring a purple radiance from his face;
here Rome, her hair wreathed with laurel and bright in dress,
greeted her leader with voice and hand.
Other gifts attest the great merit of the place:
a sacred arch stands and exults over conquered nations;
here twin chariots count many an elephant,
the golden figure himself suffices for the huge teams.
This gate is worthy of your triumphs, Germanicus;
such entrances befit the city of Mars to have.
66. LXVI
Pious incense and victims for Augustus,
Camenae, give on behalf of your Silius.
Lo, he bids twice six fasces return,
his son made consul, and with noble rod
he bids the Castalian house of the bard resound —
Caesar, the first and only safety of the world.
There remains still for the rejoicing man to wish for:
the lucky purple and a third consul.
Though the senate and Caesar may have given
sacred honours to Pompey and his son-in-law,
whose names peace-making Janus thrice enlarged:
Silius prefers thus to count frequent consulships.

title: Epigrams
text:
67. LXVII
The boy has not yet announced the fifth hour to you, and already
you come as my dinner-guest, Caecilianus,
though the courts of the hoarse fourth have just put off their sureties
and the arena still tires the Floralian beasts.
Run, come, Callistus, call back the unwashed servants;
let the couches be spread: Caecilianus, sit down.
You ask for hot water: cold has not yet come to me;
the kitchen is shut and chills still with bare hearth.
Come in the morning rather; for why should the fifth hour keep you?
To breakfast, Caecilianus, you come late.
68. LXVIII
He who has seen the orchards of the Corcyraean king
will prefer, Entellus, the country of your house.
That envious winter may not scorch the purple clusters
and cold frost devour the gifts of Bacchus,
the vintage lives shut in transparent glass,
and the happy grape is covered, yet not hidden:
so a woman's body shines through silk,
so a pebble is counted in clear water.
What did Nature not wish to allow to genius?
Barren winter is bidden to bear an autumn.
69. LXIX
You admire only the ancients, Vacerra,
and praise no poets but the dead.
We beg your pardon, Vacerra: it is not worth
dying, just to please you.
70. LXX
As great as gentle Nerva's calm, so great his eloquence,
but modesty restrains his powers and his genius.
Though he could drain the sacred Permessis with a full
mouth, he chose rather to keep his thirst modest,
content to wreathe his Pierian brow with a slender crown,
and not to spread sail to his own fame.
Yet whoever knows the famous songs of learned Nero
knows that this man is the Tibullus of our age.
71. LXXI
Four pounds of silver you sent me at winter time,
Postumianus, ten years ago,
to one expecting more — for gifts ought to stand or grow —
two came, more or less;
the third and fourth brought much less;
in the fifth it was a Septician pound indeed;
in the sixth year we came down to an eight-ounce dish;
after this a half-pound, scraped, in a small cup, was given;
the eighth sent a spoon weighing less than two ounces;
the ninth scarcely brought a little ladle lighter than a needle.
Now the tenth year has nothing left to send us:
go back, Postumianus, to your four pounds.

title: Epigrams
text:
72. LXXII
Not yet decked with purple, nor smoothed
by the rough bite of dry pumice,
you hurry to follow Arcanus, little book,
whom most lovely Narbo bids return —
Narbo, the home of learned Votienus Paternus —
to her laws and her yearly fasces:
what with equal vows you must wish for,
that place and this friend will be granted you.
How I'd wish to become my own little book!
73. LXXIII
Instantius, than whom no other is held more sincere
in heart, nor first in snow-white candour,
if you wish to give strength and spirit to my Thalia
and seek songs that will live, give me something to love.
Cynthia made you a bard, wanton Propertius;
fair Lycoris was the genius of Gallus;
lovely Nemesis is the fame of smart Tibullus;
Lesbia dictated to you, learned Catullus:
neither the Paeligni nor Mantua will scorn me as a bard,
if I have some Corinna, some Alexis.
74. LXXIV
A gladiator now, you were an eye-doctor before.
You did as a doctor what you do as a gladiator.
75. LXXV
While the Lingonian, fresh from the Tecta and the Flaminian Way,
sought his hired lodgings late at night,
he struck his thumb and dislocated his injured ankle
and lay stretched full-length upon the ground.
What was the Gaul to do, by what means move himself?
The huge master had but one little slave,
so thin he could scarcely carry the smallest lamp:
chance came to the wretch's aid and brought him help.
Four branded slaves were carrying a cheap corpse,
such as the poor man's pyre receives by the thousand;
the feeble companion begs them in a lowered voice
to carry the empty body wherever they wish:
the load is exchanged, and the great bundle, crammed,
is lifted high on the narrow bier.
This man of many, Lucanus, seems to me one
to whom 'dead Gaul' can rightly be said.
76. LXXVI
'Tell me the truth, Marcus, tell me, please;
there is nothing I would hear more gladly.'
So both when you recite your little books,
and whenever you plead a client's case,
you beg me, Gallicus, and always ask.
It is hard for me to deny you what you ask.
So hear what is truer than truth:
the truth, Gallicus, you do not gladly hear.

title: Epigrams
text:
77. LXXVII
Liber, sweetest care of your friends,
Liber, worthy to live in eternal roses,
if you are wise, let your hair forever gleam
with Assyrian balm, and flowery garlands ring your head;
let bright crystal grow dark with old Falernian,
and the soft couch grow warm with charming love.
He who has so lived, though cut off even in mid-course,
has made his life longer than the life that was given him.
78. LXXVIII
Such games as Phlegraean victory would wish its own,
such, Lyaeus, as the Indian procession would wish yours,
Stella, celebrant of the Hyperborean triumph, has staged —
O modesty! O devotion! — and thinks it too little.
Not enough for him is Hermus, dirty with churned gold,
and Tagus, which sounds in the Hesperian world.
Every day has its gifts: nor does the rich line of prizes
cease, and much plunder falls upon the crowd;
now wanton tokens come in sudden showers,
now the lavish ticket gives the beasts on show,
now the bird rejoices to fill safe bosoms and, absent,
chooses its owners by lot, that it not be torn apart.
Why count the chariots and the thirty prizes of the palm,
which not even both consuls are always wont to give?
But all is surpassed, Caesar, by so great an honour,
that your laurel has you for its spectator.
79. LXXIX
All your women friends are either old hags
or ugly and fouler than old hags.
These you lead as companions and drag with you
through banquets, porticoes, theatres.
So you are beautiful, Fabulla, so you are a girl.
80. LXXX
You give us back the wonders of our holy forefathers,
nor do you let the hoary ages die, Caesar,
when the old rites of the Latin sand are renewed
and valour fights with a simpler hand.
So with you as guardian, honour is kept for ancient temples,
and the hut has its godhead under so cultured a Jupiter;
so, while you found new things, you call back the old, Augustus —
both what is owed to you and what once was.

title: Epigrams
text:
81. LXXXI
Not by the mystic rites of Dindymene,
nor by the bull of the Nile's heifer,
nor, in short, by any gods or goddesses
does Gellia swear, but by her pearls.
These she embraces, these she covers with kisses,
these she calls brothers, these she calls sisters,
these she loves more fiercely than her two children.
If by some chance the poor wretch should lose them,
she says she would not live a single hour.
Alas, how well now, Papirianus,
the hand of Annaeus Serenus would do its work!
82. LXXXII
Since the crowd gives you their querulous little books, Augustus,
and we too give our small songs to our lord,
we know that a god can find leisure alike for affairs and the Muses,
and that these garlands too please you.
Bear with your bards, Augustus: we are your sweet glory,
we are your earlier care and your delight.
Not the oak alone becomes you, nor Phoebus' laurel:
let our civic crown of ivy be made for you too.

title: Epigrams
text: pr. Greetings, my Toranius, dearest brother. The epigram that stands outside the order of the pages I wrote to Stertinius, a most distinguished man, who wished to set up my likeness in his library. About this I thought I should write to you, lest you not know who this Avitus is who is addressed. Farewell, and prepare a lodging.

title: Epigrams
text:
Bard renowned, whether you wish it or not, with a lofty heart,
to whom your late ashes shall bring worthy rewards,
let this brief poem live for you beneath my likeness,
which, Avitus, you join with men of no obscure name:
'I am that man, second to none in the praise of trifles,
whom you, reader, do not admire, but, I think, love.
Let greater men sound greater things: for me, who speak of small matters,
it suffices to come often back into your hands.'
1. I
While Janus lends the years their winters, Domitian his autumns,
and Augustus his summers,
while the great light of the German Kalends
claims the mighty title of the subdued Rhine,
while the Tarpeian rocks of the highest Father stand,
while the suppliant matron with voice and incense
appeases the sweet godhead of divine Julia:
the lofty glory of the Flavian line shall remain
with the sun and the stars and with the Roman light.
Whatever the unconquered hand has founded belongs to heaven.
2. II
Though you are poor toward friendship, Lupus, you are not so toward your mistress,
and your cock alone has no complaint of you.
That adulteress grows fat on wheaten cunts,
while black flour feeds your dinner-guest;
Setine wine, that would inflame the snows, is strained for your mistress,
while we drink the dark poisons of a Corsican jar;
a night is bought from you with no small part of your father's lands,
while your deserted comrade ploughs fields not his own;
your mistress shines, translucent with Erythraean pearls,
while your client is led off, made over to debt, as you fuck;
a litter borne up by eight Syrians is given to the girl,
while your friend will be the naked weight of a pauper's bier.
Go now, Cybele, and cut off the wretched catamites:
this, this was the cock worthy of your knives.
3. III
How much you have already given to the gods above, Caesar, and to heaven,
if you should call it back and choose to be the creditor,
though a great auction be held on aethereal Olympus
and the gods be forced to sell whatever they have,
Atlas will go bankrupt, and there will not be a whole ounce
on which the very father of the gods could settle with you:
for what can he pay you for the Capitoline temples,
what for the honour of the Tarpeian foliage?
What can the Thunderer's matron pay for her twin roofs?
Pallas I pass over: she manages your affairs.
Why speak of Alcides, and Phoebus, and the pious Laconians?
What of the Flavian temple added to the Latian sky?
You must wait and endure, Augustus, of necessity:
for Jupiter's coffer has nothing to pay you with.

title: Epigrams
text:
4. IV
Though Galla can be fucked for two gold pieces,
and for more than fucked, if you add as many again:
why does Galla get ten gold pieces from you, Aeschylus?
Galla does not suck for so much. What, then? She keeps quiet.
5. V
To you, supreme tamer of the Rhine and parent of the world,
chaste prince, the cities give thanks:
they will have peoples; now it is no crime to bear children.
No longer does the boy, cut by the greedy dealer's art,
mourn the losses of his stolen manhood,
nor does the wretched mother give to her prostituted infant
the petty fee that the haughty pander would count.
What modesty did not exist even in the bedchamber before your day
has begun, thanks to you, even in the brothel.
6. VI
I wished to say 'Good morning' to you, Afer, on your return
from the Libyan tribes, for five days running:
'He's not free' or 'He's asleep' was said, twice and three times, as I came back.
That's enough now: you don't want to be greeted, Afer; farewell.
7. VII
As though it were a small injury to our sex
to have prostituted males for the people's filthy use,
the cradle had already become the pander's, so that, snatched from the breast,
the boy demanded sordid coins with his wailing:
immature bodies paid unspeakable penalties.
The Ausonian father did not bear such monstrosities,
the same who lately came to the aid of tender youths,
that savage lust might not make men barren.
Before, boys and young men and old men loved you,
but now infants too love you, Caesar.
8. VIII
Fabius left you nothing, Bithynicus, you to whom
you used to give, if I remember, six thousand a year.
He gave more to no one: don't complain, Bithynicus:
he has left you six thousand a year.
9. IX
Though you dine abroad gladly, Cantharus,
you shout and slander and threaten.
Lay aside your fierce spirit, we warn you:
you cannot be both a free-spoken man and a glutton.

title: Epigrams
text:
10. X
You want to marry Priscus: I'm not surprised, Paula; you're wise.
Priscus doesn't want to marry you: and he too is wise.
11. XI
A name born with violets and roses,
by which the best part of the year is named,
which tastes of Hybla and Attic flowers,
which smells of the proud bird's nest;
a name sweeter than blessed nectar,
by which Cybele's boy would rather be called,
and he who mixes the Thunderer's cups;
which, if you sound it in the Parrhasian hall,
the Venuses and Cupids answer;
a noble name, soft, delicate,
I wished to speak in no rough verse:
but you, stubborn syllable, rebel.
Yet poets say 'Eiarinos' —
but Greek ones, to whom nothing is denied
and whom it befits to sound 'Ares, Ares':
we are not allowed to be so eloquent,
we who cultivate the sterner Muses.
12. XII
You have a name that names the season of the tender year,
when the Cecropian bees plunder the brief spring;
a name that deserved to be painted with Acidalia's reed,
that Cytherea delights to write with her own needle;
a name that, made a letter with Erythraean pearls,
a gem polished by the Heliads' thumb might mark;
that the cranes might raise to the stars with writing wing;
that befits being only in Caesar's house.
13. XIII
If autumn gave me my name, I'd be Oporinos;
if the harsh stars of winter, Chimerinos;
named from the summer month, I'd be called Therinos by you:
but he to whom the spring season gave his name — who is he?
14. XIV
This friend whom your table, whom your dinner has won you —
do you think his is a heart of faithful friendship?
He loves the boar and the mullets and the udder and the oysters, not you.
If I dined as well, he would be my friend.
15. XV
The wicked Chloe inscribed on the tombs of her seven
husbands that she had made them. What could be plainer?
16. XVI
The counsellor of his beauty, the mirror, and his sweet hair
that boy, most pleasing of all the court to his master,
who marks the spring season with his name,
set up as hallowed gifts to the Pergamene god.
Happy the land esteemed with such a gift!
Nor would it wish to have Ganymede's locks.

title: Epigrams
text:
17. XVII
Venerable grandson of Latona, who with gentle herbs
prevail upon the Parcae's threads and their short distaffs,
this hair, praised by his master, a granted vow,
that boy of yours sent from the Latian city;
he added too a shining disc to the hallowed locks,
by whose verdict his happy face was kept safe.
Preserve his youthful charm, that he be no fairer
in long hair than in shorter.
18. XVIII
I have — and may I have it long with you as guardian, Caesar —
a tiny country place, and small are my household gods in the city too.
But from a low valley, to give what it can to the thirsty gardens,
the curved pump raises laboured-up waters:
my dry house complains that no dew refreshes it,
though the Marcian water sounds in a fountain near me.
The water you give to my household, Augustus,
will be for me Castalia's spring or Jove's own rain.
19. XIX
You praise the baths of Ponticus, who dines well,
in three hundred verses, Sabellus.
You want to dine, Sabellus, not to bathe.
20. XX
This ground, which lies all open and is covered with marble and gold,
was conscious of our infant lord,
happy, oh, with what wailings it rang, and what
crawling hands it saw and held up:
here had stood the venerable house that gave the world
what Rhodes gave the starry sky, what pious Crete.
The Curetes shielded Jove with clashing arms,
such as the half-male Phrygians could bear:
but you the father of the gods protected, and for you, Caesar,
the thunderbolt and aegis served as javelin and shield.
21. XXI
Artemidorus has a boy, but he sold his farm;
Calliodorus has a farm in exchange for a boy.
Tell me, Auctus, which of these has done the better business:
Artemidorus loves, Calliodorus ploughs.
22. XXII
You believe, perhaps, Pastor, that I beg for wealth on the same grounds
as the common, thick-witted crowd begs,
that Setine soil may wear out my hoes
and a Tuscan field clank with countless fetters of slaves;
that a hundred Moorish round tables stand on Libyan tusks
and golden plate rattle on my couches,
that no crystal but the great be worn by my lips
and my Falernian make black snows;
that a Canusian-cloaked Syrian sweat under my chair-pole
and my chair be thronged with well-dressed clients;
that a guest grow hot, drenched, at the hands of my servant,
whom you'd not exchange even for Ganymede;
that a muddy mule daub my Tyrian cloaks
and a Massylian wand steer my horse.
None of these is the reason: I call the gods and stars to witness.
What then? That I may give, Pastor, and build.

title: Epigrams
text:
23. XXIII
O you to whom it has fallen to grow golden with the virgin's gold,
tell me, Carus, where is your Palladian honour?
'You see, look, my master's face gleaming in marble?
My crown came of itself to those locks.'
The pious oak of the Alban olive may well be livid,
that the oak first crowned the unconquered head.
24. XXIV
Who, having imitated the Palatine features in his likeness,
outdid Phidian ivory with Latian marble?
This is the face of the world, these the lips of serene Jove:
so that god thunders, when he thunders without a cloud.
Not the crown alone did Pallas grant you, Carus;
she gave the master's image, which you worship.
25. XXV
Whenever we have looked at your Hyllus giving the wine,
you mark us, Afer, with a more troubled eye.
What, I ask, what crime is it to watch a soft servant?
We look at the sun, the stars, the temples, the gods.
Shall I turn away my face, as if a Gorgon
held out the cups to me and sought my eyes and face?
Alcides was grim, and one could look at Hylas;
one may play with Mercury and Ganymede.
If you don't want a guest to watch your tender servants,
invite, Afer, men like Phineus and the Oedipuses.
26. XXVI
He who dares to send poems to eloquent Nerva
will give pale woad-perfume to you, Cosmus,
violets and white privet to the Paestan gardener,
Corsican honey to the bees of Hybla:
but yet even a small Muse has some grace;
the cheap olive is sought after when the boar is set aside.
Nor let it be a wonder to you that my Thalia,
aware of her modest bard, fears your judgement:
even Nero himself is said to have feared your ears,
when as a young man he played a wanton work for you.
27. XXVII
Though you carry depilated balls, Chrestus,
and a cock like a vulture's neck,
and a head smoother than prostitutes' arses,
and not a hair lives on your leg,
and savage tweezers cleanse your white lips:
yet you talk and thunder, menacing, with grand words
of Curii, Camilli, Quintii, Numas, Ancuses,
and whatever hairy worthies we ever read of,
and you brawl with the theatre and the age.
If meanwhile some strongman crosses your path,
just freed from his tutor and whose
swollen penis the smith has unbuckled:
you call him with a nod and lead him off, and I am ashamed to say,
Chrestus, what you do with your Cato-like tongue.

title: Epigrams
text:
28. XXVIII
Sweet glory of the stage, fame of the games, I am
that Latinus, your applause and your delight,
who could have made a spectator of Cato,
who could relax the grave Curii and Fabricii.
But my life took nothing from our theatre,
and I am called an actor by my art alone;
nor could I be pleasing to our lord without good character;
that god looks more deeply into men's minds.
Call me the parasite of laurelled Phoebus,
so long as Rome knows me the servant of her own Jove.
29. XXIX
Philaenis, who had measured out the ages of Nestor's old age,
have you been snatched so soon to the infernal waters of Dis?
You did not yet count the long years of the Euboean
Sibyl: she was greater by three months.
Ah, what a tongue is silent! A thousand auction-blocks
could not outdo it, nor the throng that loves Sarapis,
nor the curled-haired band of the morning schoolmaster,
nor the bank that sounds with the Strymonian flock.
Who now will know how to draw down the moon with the Thessalian wheel,
who, as a bawd, to sell this man's bed or that?
May the earth lie light on you and soft sand cover you,
that the dogs may not be unable to dig up your bones.
30. XXX
Antistius Rusticus died on the savage shores of the Cappadocians.
O land guilty of a grievous crime!
Nigrina brought back in her bosom the bones of her dear husband
and complained the long roads were not enough;
and when she gave the holy urn to the tomb she envies,
she felt herself twice widowed of her snatched husband.
31. XXXI
When Velius clung as comrade to Caesar's Northern arms,
he vowed this bird to Mars on behalf of his leader;
the moon had not yet finished twice four circuits,
and already the god demanded the vows owed him:
of itself the goose hastened gladly to its altar
and fell, a small victim, on the holy hearth.
You see eight coins hanging from the bird's open beak?
These were lately hidden in the entrails:
the victim that makes offering for you, Caesar, with silver, not blood,
teaches that there is now no need of the knife.

title: Epigrams
text:
32. XXXII
I want her who is easy, who roams in a little cloak,
I want her who has already given herself to my boy,
I want her whom a single denarius buys outright,
I want her who, one alone, suffices three at once.
Let the cock of thick-witted Bordeaux possess
the woman who demands money and sounds off grand words.
33. XXXIII
If you hear applause in any bath, Flaccus,
know that Maro's cock is there.
34. XXXIV
Jupiter laughed at the lies of his Idaean tomb,
while he saw the Flavian temple of Augustus' sky,
and amid the tables, now flowing with abundant nectar,
as he himself handed the cups to his own Mars,
looking on Phoebus and Phoebus' sister alike,
with whom were Alcides and the pious Arcadian:
'You gave me,' he said, 'monuments in Cnossos:
see how much better it is to be Caesar's father.'
35. XXXV
By these arts, Philomusus, you always earn your dinner,
inventing much, but reporting it as if true.
You know what Pacorus deliberates in the Arsacid court,
you count the Rhenish and Sarmatian forces,
you unseal the words of the Dacian leader committed to paper,
you see the victor's laurel before it comes,
you know how often dark Syene is drenched by the Pharian Jove,
you know how many ships go from the Libyan shore,
on whose head the Julian olives are born,
to whom the aethereal father destines his own garlands.
Away with your arts; today you'll dine at my house
on this condition, Philomusus: that you tell nothing new.
36. XXXVI
The Phrygian boy, the known joy of the other Jove,
had seen the Ausonian servant just now with his hair laid aside:
'What your Caesar, look, has allowed his own youth,
allow yours, greatest ruler,' he said;
'Already my first down hides in long hair,
already your Juno laughs at me and calls me a man.'
To him the aethereal father said, 'O sweetest boy,
it is not I, but the thing itself, that denies you what you ask:
our Caesar has a thousand servants like you,
and that great hall scarcely holds his star-like males;
but if shorn hair gives you a manly look,
who else will there be to mix me nectar?'

title: Epigrams
text:
37. XXXVII
Though you are yourself at home and dress in the middle of the Subura,
your hair, Galla, is made for you in your absence,
and you lay aside your teeth at night as you do your silks,
and you lie stowed in a hundred boxes,
nor does your face sleep with you, and you wink with that
eyebrow that was brought out for you in the morning,
and no reverence for your grey cunt moves you,
which you can now number among your forebears.
Yet you promise six hundred delights; but the cock is deaf,
and though it be one-eyed, it nonetheless sees you.
38. XXXVIII
Though you play, Agathinus, at the highest perils with speed,
yet you cannot make your shield fall.
It follows you against your will, and, turned back through the thin air,
sits on your foot or your back, your hair or your nail;
though the boards be slippery with Corycian saffron-spray
and swift south-winds snatch the denied sails,
the neglected shield walks over the boy's untroubled limbs,
and wind and water harm the artist not at all.
Though you wish to err, when you have done everything, you cannot
be foiled: it takes art to make your shield fall.
39. XXXIX
This first light dawned for the Palatine Thunderer,
on which Cybele would have wished to have borne Jove;
on this too holy Caesonia, my Rufus' wife, was born:
no girl owes more to her mother.
The husband rejoices in the double lot of his prayers,
that it has fallen to him to love this day for both.
40. XL
When Diodorus sought Rome from the Pharos he had left,
for the Tarpeian crowns,
Philaenis vowed, for her husband's return,
that, as a simple girl, she would lick the part
that even chaste Sabine women cherish.
His ship scattered by grim storms,
sunk in the waves and overwhelmed by the sea,
Diodorus swam to fulfil the vow.
O too slow and sluggish husband!
Had my girl made this vow on the shore,
I would have come back at once.

title: Epigrams
text:
41. XLI
Ponticus, that you never fuck, but use your left hand
as a concubine, and your hand serves Venus as a mistress —
do you think this is nothing? It is a crime, believe me, and a great one,
greater than you yourself can conceive in your mind.
Horace, surely, fucked but once to beget three;
Mars once, that chaste Ilia might give twins:
all would have been lost, had each of them, masturbating,
entrusted his foul pleasures to his own hands.
Believe that Nature herself says this to you:
'That which you waste with your fingers, Ponticus, is a man.'
42. XLII
So, Apollo, may you enjoy the rich Myrine plains,
so may you ever delight in your aged swans,
so may the learned sisters serve you,
nor let your Delphi lie to anyone,
so may the Palatine court you and love you:
quickly, at your asking, may good Caesar grant Stella
twice six fasces and nod assent.
Then happy I, and bound by a vow,
will lead to your rustic altars a bullock
with gilded horns, to fall for you.
The victim is born, Phoebus; why do you delay?
43. XLIII
This god who, seated, softens the hard rocks with his outstretched
lion-skin, great in a little bronze,
and gazes with upturned face at the stars he bore,
whose left hand is warm with his club, his right with wine:
this is no recent fame, no glory of our chisel;
you see the noble gift and work of Lysippus.
This godhead the table of the Pellaean tyrant possessed,
who, conqueror, lies in a world soon subdued;
to this Hannibal as a boy swore at the Libyan altars;
this bade grim Sulla lay down his power.
Offended by the swollen terrors of varied courts,
he now rejoices to dwell in private households,
and as he was once the guest of gentle Molorchus,
so the god wished to be learned Vindex's.
44. XLIV
Just now I was asking Vindex's Alcides
whose work and happy labour he was.
He laughed — for so he is wont — and with a slight nod
said, 'Poet, do you not know Greek?
The base is inscribed and gives the name.'
I read 'Lysippus' work'; I had thought it Phidias'.

title: Epigrams
text:
45. XLV
A soldier, Marcellinus, you lately bore the Hyperborean Bears
and the sluggish stars of the Getic sky:
behold, the rocks of Prometheus and the fabled mountain,
how near to your eyes they now are to be approached!
When you see the rocks that rang with the old man's
boundless laments, you'll say, 'He himself was harder.'
And you may add this: 'He who could bear such things
had deserved to fashion the human race.'
46. XLVI
Gellius is always building: now he sets thresholds,
now he fits keys to doors and buys locks,
now these, now those windows he remakes and changes;
so long as he builds at all, he does anything —
that he may say to a friend begging for money
that one word, Gellius: 'I'm building.'
47. XLVII
Democrituses, Zenos, and tangled Platos,
and whatever moulders in shaggy busts,
you talk of, as though the successor and heir of Pythagoras.
Your beard, indeed, hangs no shorter than theirs:
but what is shameful in goatish, foul in hairy men,
you gladly take a stiff one in your soft buttocks.
You, who know the principles and weight of the sects,
tell me, Pannychus, what doctrine is it to be buggered?
48. XLVIII
When you swore I was heir to a fourth part of your estate, Garricus,
by your sacred rites and your own head,
I believed it — for who readily condemns his own hopes? —
and kept fostering the hope with gifts I gave.
Among them I sent a Laurentine boar of rare weight:
you'd think it from Aetolian Calydon.
But you at once invited the people and the senate,
and pale Rome still belches up my boar:
I myself — who would believe it? — was a guest, and not the lowest,
yet no rib was given me, no tail sent my way.
What can I hope for from your quarter-share, Garricus? Not
one ounce of my own boar came to me.
49. XLIX
This is that toga, much sung in my little books,
which my reader has learned by heart and loves.
It was once Parthenius', a memorable gift to the bard:
in it I went, a knight to be admired,
while it shone, splendid, with new and glossy wool,
and while it was worthy of the name of its giver:
now an old thing, scarcely fit for a shivering pauper,
which you could rightly call snow-white.
What does long time, what do the years not consume?
This toga is no longer Parthenius'; it is mine.

title: Epigrams
text:
50. L
You prove to me, Gaurus, that my talent is so small,
because I make poems that please by their brevity.
I confess it. But you, who write in twice six books
the grand battles of Priam — are you a great man?
We make a living Brutus' boy, we make a living Langon:
you, Gaurus, make a great Giant of clay.
51. LI
What you always begged of the gods against your brother's wish,
this, Lucanus, has fallen to you — to die first.
He envies you; for Tullus wished, though he is younger,
to go first to the Stygian shades.
You dwell in Elysium, and now, an inhabitant of the lovely grove,
you long to be without your brother for the first time;
and if he comes by turns from the bright stars,
in Pollux's place you warn Castor not to return.
52. LII
If you believe me, Quintus, what you deserve,
I love your birthday, Ovidius, the Kalends of April,
as I love my own Kalends of March.
Happy each light and day for us,
to be marked with the better pebbles!
This gave me life, but that gave me a friend.
Your Kalends, Quintus, give me more.
53. LIII
On your birthday, Quintus, I wished to give you small
gifts; you forbid it: you're an imperious man.
I must obey your warnings; let it be done as we both wish
and as pleases us both: you, Quintus, give to me.
54. LIV
If a thrush were ripening for me on a Picene olive,
or a Sabine wood were stretching my nets,
or light prey were drawn in by the growing reed
and the limed twig held the entangled birds:
my dear kinship would give you its customary gift,
nor would a brother or grandfather come before you.
Now the field hears poor starlings and the chaffinches' complaints
and grows green in spring with the chattering sparrow;
hence the ploughman, greeted, answers the magpie,
hence the rapacious kite flies near the topmost stars.
So I send you the little gifts of a small farmyard:
if you accept such things, you'll often be a kinsman.

title: Epigrams
text:
55. LV
On the day of kinsmen, when birds are sent in plenty,
while I prepare thrushes for Stella, and for you, Flaccus,
a huge and burdensome crowd comes to mind,
in which each man counts himself first and mine.
To oblige two is my wish; to offend more
is hardly safe; to send gifts to many is grievous.
By the only means I can, I'll win pardon:
I'll give thrushes neither to Stella nor to you, Flaccus.
56. LVI
Spendophorus, the master's armour-bearer, seeks the Libyan cities:
prepare, Cupid, the darts you would give the boy,
those with which you pierce young men and soft girls:
but let the spear too be smooth in his tender hand.
Breastplate, shield, and helmet I give back to you;
that he may safely enter battles, let him go naked:
neither javelin, sword, nor arrow harmed Parthenopaeus
while he was free of the helmet.
Whoever is pierced by this boy will die of love.
O happy, if such a good fate awaits anyone!
While you are a boy, come back; while your face is smooth, and let
not Libya make you a man, but your own Rome.
57. LVII
Nothing is more worn than Hedylus' cloaks:
not the handles of old Corinthian bronzes,
nor the leg made slippery by a ten-year fetter,
nor the chafed neck of a broken-down mule,
nor the ruts that cut the Flaminian Way,
nor the pebbles that shine on the shore,
nor the hoe polished by a Tuscan vineyard,
nor the pale toga of a dead clansman,
nor the cracked wheel of a lazy muleteer,
nor the side of a bison shaved by its cage,
nor the now-aged tusk of a fierce boar.
There is one thing, though — he himself won't deny it:
Hedylus' arsehole is more worn than his cloaks.
58. LVIII
Nymph, queen of the sacred lake, to whom welcome Sabinus
gave temples that will endure, a pious gift,
so may mountain Umbria forever tend your springs,
nor may your Sassina prefer the waters of Baiae:
receive kindly my anxious gifts, these little books;
be the Pegasean spring to my Muses. —
'Whoever gives his own songs to the temples of the Nymphs,
shows himself what ought to be done with such books.'

title: Epigrams
text:
59. LIX
Mamurra, having wandered long and much in the Saepta,
here where golden Rome torments its own wealth,
inspected the soft boys and devoured them with his eyes,
not those whom the front stalls prostitute,
but those whom the boards of the secret platform keep
and whom neither the public nor my sort sees.
Then, sated, he stripped the covers from tables and round tops
and asked for the rich ivory displayed up high,
and, measuring four times the tortoiseshell six-couch table,
groaned that it was not big enough for his citrus-wood top.
He consulted his nose, whether the bronzes smelled of Corinth,
he found fault even with your statues, Polyclitus,
and, complaining that some crystal was spoiled by bits of glass,
he marked ten murrine cups and set them aside.
He weighed old goblets, and any cups
ennobled by Mentor's hand,
and counted green gems in painted gold,
and whatever, larger, rings from a snow-white ear.
Sardonyxes, indeed, he sought at every table
and set a price on great jaspers.
When at last, wearied, he was leaving at the eleventh hour,
he bought two cups for a penny and carried them himself.
60. LX
Whether you were born in Paestan or in Tiburtine fields,
or whether the soil of Tusculum blushed with your bloom,
or whether the bailiff's wife gathered you in a Praenestine garden,
or whether you were lately the glory of Campanian country:
that you may seem a fairer garland to my Sabinus,
let him think you come from my Nomentan farm.
61. LXI
In the Tartessian lands there is a most famous house,
where rich Corduba loves the placid Baetis,
where the tawny fleeces grow pale with native metal
and living gold-leaf coats the Hesperian flock.
In the midst of the house, embracing the whole household,
stands a Caesarian plane-tree with thick foliage,
which the happy right hand of the unconquered guest set,
and from that hand the shoot began to grow.
The grove seems to feel its planter and master:
so it is green and seeks the high stars with its branches.
Often beneath this tree the drunken Fauns have played,
and a late pipe has frightened the silent house;
and while nocturnal Pan fled through the lonely fields,
often beneath this leafage a rustic Dryad hid.
And the household gods smelled of Lyaeus the reveller,
and the shade grew gladder for the spilled wine;
the grass was reddened, strewn with yesterday's garlands,
and no one could call the roses his own.
O tree beloved of the gods, O tree of great Caesar,
fear not the iron and the sacrilegious hearths.
You may hope for the perpetual honours of your leaves:
no Pompeian hands planted you.

title: Epigrams
text:
62. LXII
That Philaenis wears garments dyed with purple
both night and day,
she is not ostentatious nor haughty:
she delights in the smell, not the colour.
63. LXIII
All the catamites invite you to dinner, Phoebus.
The man whom a cock feeds is not, I think, a clean man.
64. LXIV
Caesar, having deigned to come down into the features of great Hercules,
gives new temples to the Latin way,
where the traveller, as he seeks Trivia's wooded realms,
reads the eighth milestone from the mistress city.
Before, he was worshipped with vows and abundant blood;
now the lesser Alcides himself worships the greater.
This man asks him for great wealth, that one for honours;
to him this one, untroubled, makes his lesser vows.
65. LXV
Alcides, now to be recognized by the Latian Thunderer,
since you bear the fair face of the god Caesar,
if you had then had these features and this bearing,
when the wild monsters yielded to your hands:
the nations would not have seen you serve as slave
to the Argive tyrant and suffer his savage rule,
but you would have given orders to Eurystheus; nor would treacherous
Lichas have brought you the perfidious gifts of Nessus,
without the law of the Oetaean pyre, untroubled, you would have approached
the stars of your highest father, which your punishment gave you;
nor would you have drawn out Lydian wool for a haughty mistress,
nor seen the Styx and the Tartarean dog.
Now Juno favours you, now your Hebe loves you;
now, if a nymph saw you, she would send back Hylas.
66. LXVI
Since you have a wife, beautiful, chaste, a young girl,
what need have you, Fabullus, of the rights of three children?
What you beg as a suppliant from our lord and god,
you will give to yourself, if you can get it up.
67. LXVII
I possessed all night a wanton girl,
whose naughtinesses no one can outdo.
Tired of a thousand ways, I asked for that boyish thing:
she granted it before all my prayers and first words.
Laughing and blushing, I asked something more shameless:
the lustful girl promised it with no delay.
But for me she was pure; for you she won't be, Aeschylus, if you wish
to receive this favour on a bad condition.

title: Epigrams
text:
68. LXVIII
What have you to do with us, accursed schoolmaster,
head hateful to boys and girls?
The crested cocks have not yet broken the silence:
already you thunder with savage muttering and lashings.
As loudly does the bronze ring from struck anvils,
when the smith fits a lawyer to a horse in the middle;
gentler the shouting rages in the great amphitheatre,
when its crowd cheers the winning shield.
We neighbours ask for sleep — not all night long:
for to lie awake is light, to lie awake all night is grievous.
Dismiss your pupils. Will you take, chatterbox, as much
to keep quiet as you take to shout?
69. LXIX
When you fuck, Polycharmus, you usually shit at the end.
When you are buggered, Polycharmus, what do you do?
70. LXX
'O the times! O the manners!' Tullius once cried,
when Catiline was contriving his sacrilegious crime,
when son-in-law and father-in-law clashed in dreadful arms
and the mournful earth was soaked with civil slaughter.
Why do you now say 'O the manners!', why now 'O the times!'?
What is there, Caecilianus, that displeases you?
There is no savagery of leaders, no madness of the sword;
we may enjoy a sure peace and gladness.
It is not our times that make your age sordid to you,
but your own manners, Caecilianus.
71. LXXI
A lion, the fame of the Massylian ridge, and a husband of the woolly flock
joined together in wondrous loyalty.
You may see it yourself: they are stabled in one cage
and each crops the shared feast alike:
they delight neither in the woods' offspring nor in mild herbs,
but a tender lamb sates their harmonious hunger.
What did the terror of Nemea earn, what the bearer of Helle,
that they should gleam as bright signs of the high sky?
If beasts of flock and field could earn the stars,
this ram was worthy of the stars, this lion.
72. LXXII
Liber, your brow bound with the Amyclaean crown,
who shake Greek lashes with Ausonian hand,
since you send me lunches shut in woven wicker,
why does no flask come to accompany the feast?
Yet if you brought gifts worthy of your name,
you know, I think, what gifts ought to have been given me.

title: Epigrams
text:
73. LXXIII
You who used to draw out old hides with your teeth
and bite the rotten, ancient sole with mud,
now hold the Praenestine realms of your deceived patron,
in which I am indignant if you ever had a cell;
and, drunk, you break the crystal with burning Falernian,
and you lust with your master's Ganymede.
But my foolish parents taught me my letters:
what have I to do with grammarians and rhetors?
Break the light reeds and tear up the books, Thalia,
if a shoe can give such things to a cobbler.
74. LXXIV
Only the likeness of the boy Camonius does the painting keep,
and the small image of the infant remains.
No portrait marked his face in its flowering,
since the pious father feared to see the mute features.
75. LXXV
Not of hard flint or built-up rubble,
nor of baked brick, with which Semiramis girt
long Babylon, did Tucca make his bath:
but of slaughtered groves and pinewood frame,
so that Tucca could sail in his bath.
The same man, elegant, builds rich warm-baths
of every marble that Carystos found,
that Phrygian Synnas, that African Nomas sent,
and that Eurotas washed with its green stream.
But wood is wanting: put the bath under the warm-baths to burn.
76. LXXVI
These are those features of my Camonius you behold,
this was the boy's face and first form.
This face had grown stronger in twice ten years,
and the beard rejoiced to paint his cheeks,
and the bloom, sipped but once, had just sprinkled
the topmost razors: of three, one sister envied
and cut the threads with hastened spinning,
and the urn brought back to the father the pyre of his absent son.
But lest the painting alone speak of the boy,
this greater image will be in my pages.
77. LXXVII
What is the best banquet, the eloquent page
of Priscus disputes,
and reports much sweetly, much sublimely,
but all with learned heart.
You ask what is the best banquet?
One at which there will be no flute-player.

title: Epigrams
text:
78. LXXVIII
After the funerals of seven husbands, Galla married you,
Picentinus: Galla wants, I think, to follow her husbands.
79. LXXIX
Rome hated before the leaders' servants and the former throng
and the Palatine arrogance:
but now so great is the love of all for your people, Augustus,
that each cares for his own house second.
So peaceful are their minds, so great their reverence for us,
so calm their quiet, so much modesty in their faces.
No one — this is the nature of a powerful court —
but the master's manners does a Caesarian have.
80. LXXX
A poor, hungry man married a rich old woman:
Gellius both feeds his wife and fucks her.
81. LXXXI
Reader and listener approve my little books, Aulus,
but a certain poet says they are not polished.
I don't much care: for I'd rather the courses of my dinner
pleased the guests than the cooks.
82. LXXXII
The astrologer had said you would soon perish, Munna,
nor, I think, had he lied to you when he said it.
For while you feared to leave anything behind after death,
you devoured your father's wealth in luxury,
and your two million melted in less than a year:
tell me, Munna, is this not to perish soon?
83. LXXXIII
Among the great wonders of your arena, Caesar,
which surpass the famous shows of leaders of old,
the eyes confess they owe much, but the ears more,
to you, because those who used to recite now watch.
84. LXXXIV
When your sacred loyalty stood, Norbanus, for our lord Caesar
against sacrilegious frenzies,
I was playing these things, safe in the Pierian shade,
a known cultivator of your friendship.
The Raetian told of me to you on the Vindelician shores,
nor was the North unaware of my name:
oh, how often, not denying an old friend,
you said, 'That poet is mine, mine!'
All my work, which for twice three years now joined
my reader gave you before, the author will now give.

title: Epigrams
text:
85. LXXXV
Whenever our Paulus is rather indisposed, Atilius,
he keeps not himself but his guests from food.
You, indeed, suffer a sudden and feigned indisposition,
but my dole, Paulus, has stretched out its feet.
86. LXXXVI
That Silius, more than once mighty in Ausonian speech,
groaned at the hastened fate of his Severus,
I sadly complained with the Pierian band and Phoebus.
'I myself wept my own Linus,' said Apollo:
and he looked back at his Calliope, who stood
nearest his brother, and said: 'You too have a wound.
Look at the Tarpeian and the Palatine Thunderer:
Lachesis, daring the unspeakable, wounded both Joves.
When you see godheads subject to harsh fates,
you may free the gods of the charge of envy.'
87. LXXXVII
After seven cups of Opimian wine,
when I lie thick-tongued with deep draughts,
you bring me some tablets or other
and say, 'I have just ordered Nasta to be freed —
he's a slave inherited from my father —:
sign.' Tomorrow it will go better, Lupercus:
just now my ring seals the wine-flask.
88. LXXXVIII
While you were angling for me, you sent me gifts:
now that you've caught me, Rufus, you give me nothing.
To keep what you've caught, send the caught one gifts too,
lest the ill-fed boar flee from the cage.
89. LXXXIX
By too hard a law you force a guest to write verses,
Stella. 'One may, of course, write bad ones.'
90. XC
So, reclining on the flowery grass,
where here and there the curving wave with gem-like streams
stirs the pebble,
all troubles shut far off,
may you pierce the ice with a dark draught,
your brow red with stitched garlands;
so may you have for yourself alone a catamite boy
and a most chaste girl lust for you:
the ill-famed Cyprus, in too great a heat,
beware of, I warn and beg you, Flaccus,
when the threshing-floor wears the crackling harvest
and the burning mane of the lion rages.
But you, goddess of Paphos, send back, send back
to my prayers the young man unharmed:
so may the Kalends of March serve you,
and with incense and wine and victim
may there be poured for you at your white altars
many a cut square of cake.

title: Epigrams
text:
91. XCI
If to dinner amid opposite stars there summoned me,
on this side Caesar's inviter, on that Jove's,
though the stars were nearer, the Palatine farther off,
these answers to the gods above I would give to bring back:
'Seek one who would rather become the Thunderer's guest:
my Jupiter, look, keeps me on earth.'
92. XCII
What are a master's ills, what a slave's advantages, you do not know,
Condylus, who groan that you have long been a slave.
A cheap little mat gives you untroubled sleep,
while Gaius, look, lies sleepless on feathers.
Gaius from first light, trembling, greets
so many masters, but you, Condylus, not even a master.
'Pay what you owe, Gaius,' says Phoebus, and from over there
Cinnamus: this, Condylus, no one says to you.
Do you fear the torturer? Gout in foot and hand racks
Gaius, and he would rather suffer a thousand lashes.
Because you neither vomit in the morning nor lick cunt, Condylus,
would you not rather be yourself three times over than Gaius?
93. XCIII
Why do you delay, boy, to add the immortal Falernian?
Double my quarter-measure from the older jar.
Now tell me, Catacissus, to which of the gods do I bid you
pour six cups? 'It will be Caesar.'
Let a stitched rose be fitted ten times to our hair, that there be
one who set up the noble work of the sacred line.
Now give me twice five kisses, that that name be made
which the god bore from the Odrysian world.
94. XCIV
With a Santonican herb-drugged drink Hippocrates gave me a cup:
the cheek of the man! Now he asks me for honey-wine.
Never were you so stupid even, I think, Glaucus,
who gave golden gifts to one who gave you bronze.
Does anyone ask for a sweet gift in return for a bitter one?
Let him have it — but only if he drinks it in hellebore.
95. XCV
He was Alfius before; now he has begun to be Olfius,
since Athenagoras took a wife.

title: Epigrams
text:
95b. XCVb
You believe, Callistratus, that 'Athenagoras' is a real name.
May I die if I know who Athenagoras is.
But suppose I do speak a real name, Callistratus:
it is not I, but your Athenagoras, who errs.
96. XCVI
The physician Herodes had filched a ladle from a sick man:
caught, he said, 'Fool, why then do you drink?'
97. XCVII
A certain man bursts with envy, dearest Julius,
because Rome reads me, he bursts with envy.
He bursts with envy, because in every crowd
I am always pointed at with a finger, he bursts with envy.
He bursts with envy, because both Caesars granted me
the right of children, he bursts with envy.
He bursts with envy, because I have a sweet country place near the city
and a small house in the city, he bursts with envy.
He bursts with envy, because I am dear to my friends,
because I am a frequent guest, he bursts with envy.
He bursts with envy, because I am loved and approved:
let him burst, whoever bursts with envy.
98. XCVIII
The yield of the vintage did not everywhere fail,
Ovidius; the great rain helped.
Coranus made a hundred amphoras — of water.
99. XCIX
Marcus Antonius loves my Muses, Atticus,
if the saluting paper now reports truly:
Marcus, the not-to-be-denied glory of Palladian Toulouse,
whom Quiet, the nursling of Peace, begot.
You who can bear the long expense of the roads,
go, book, a pledge of absent friendship.
You were cheap, I confess, if a buyer now sent you;
the author will be the great price of your gift:
it matters much, believe me, whether water be drunk
that flows from the source, or that stagnates in a sluggish pool.
100. C
For three denarii you invite me, and bid me in the morning,
gowned, attend your halls, Bassus,
then cling to your side, walk before your chair,
go with you to ten widows, more or less.
My little toga, indeed, is worn and cheap and old:
yet for three denarii, Bassus, I do not buy it.

title: Epigrams
text:
101. CI
Appian Way, whom venerable Caesar, in the likeness of Hercules,
hallows, greatest fame of the Ausonian road,
if you wish to know the deeds of the earlier Alcides,
learn: he tamed the Libyan, carried off the golden apples,
unbelted the shield-bearing Amazon of her Scythian knot,
added to the Arcadian boar the lion's hide,
took the bronze-footed stag from the woods, the Stymphalian birds
from the stars, came back from the Stygian water with the dog,
forbade the fruitful hydra to be renewed by deaths,
washed the Hesperian cattle in the Tuscan stream.
These the lesser Alcides did: hear what the greater has done,
whom the sixth milestone from the Alban citadel worships.
He claimed the Palatine, possessed by evil rule,
and as a boy waged his first wars for his own Jove;
when he alone now held the Julian reins,
he handed them over and was third in his own world;
thrice he crushed the treacherous horns of the Sarmatian Hister,
thrice he washed his sweating horse in Getic snow;
sparing, often refusing to lead triumphs,
he, victor, won a name from the Hyperborean world;
he gave temples to the gods, manners to peoples, rest from the sword,
stars to his own, constellations to heaven, garlands to Jove.
The godhead of Hercules is not enough for such deeds:
let this god lend his face to the Tarpeian father.
102. CII
You hand me back, Phoebus, the tablets for four hundred thousand:
rather lend me, Phoebus, a hundred thousand.
Seek another to whom you may boast of so empty a gift:
what I cannot pay you, Phoebus, is mine.
103. CIII
What new Leda bore servants so like you?
What Spartan woman was taken naked by another swan?
Pollux gives his face to Hierus, Castor to Asylus,
and in each face the Tyndarian sister shines.
Had that beauty been at Therapnaean Amyclae,
when lesser gifts overcame the two goddesses,
you would have stayed, Helen, and Dardanian Paris
would have returned to Phrygian Ida with a twin Ganymede.

title: Epigrams
text:
1. I
If I seem too much a book, too long, my final flourish late,
read just a little: I'll be a slim small thing for you.
Three and four times over my page is finished off with a tiny poem:
make me as short as you yourself desire.
2. II
Rushed out before its time, the work of my tenth little book,
that slipped from my hands, I've now called back again.
Some pieces you'll know, but planed smooth by a recent file;
the larger part is new: reader, be kind to both,
reader, my wealth: when Rome had given you to me,
"I've nothing greater to give you," she said.
"Through this you'll flee the sluggish streams of thankless Lethe,
and survive in the better part of yourself.
The wild fig splits Messalla's marble, and the bold
muleteer laughs at Crispus' half-broken horses:
but theft does pages no harm, and the ages serve them,
and these monuments alone know nothing of dying."
3. III
The quips of home-bred slaves, the foul tooth,
and the vile abuse of a hawker's gutter tongue,
