stuff a peddler of cracked Vatinian cups
wouldn't take if bought with a brimstone match,
some sneaking poet scatters about
and wants them taken for mine. Do you believe it, Priscus?
That a parrot should speak in a quail's voice,
and Canus long to be a bagpiper?
Far from my little books be black repute;
a gem-bright rumour bears them on a snow-white wing:
why should I labour to be known so vilely,
when silence can be had for free?
4. IV
You who read of Oedipus and murky Thyestes,
of Colchian witches and Scyllas—what but monsters do you read?
What good to you is the rape of Hylas, what Parthenopaeus and Attis,
what good the sleeper Endymion?
Or the boy stripped of his slipping wings? Or he
who hates the waters that love him, Hermaphroditus?
What pleasure in the empty mockeries of a wretched page?
Read this, of which life can say, "It's mine."
Here you'll find no Centaurs, no Gorgons or Harpies:
my page tastes of a human being.
But you don't wish, Mamurra, to know your own habits,
nor to know yourself: read the Origins of Callimachus.

title: Epigrams
text:
5. V
Whoever, scorning the matron's robe and the purple,
has wronged with impious verse those he ought to honour,
let him wander the city, an exile from bridge and slope,
and last among the hoarse-voiced beggars
beg for the dog's mouthfuls of vile bread;
let a long December and a dripping winter
and the closed archway prolong his bitter cold:
let him call blessed and shout out the good fortune
of those borne by on the bier of death.
And when the threads of his last hour have come,
and the slow day, let him feel the snarling of dogs,
and beat off the harmful birds with a flapping rag.
Nor let his punishment end with death,
but now flayed by the lash of stern Aeacus,
now crushed beneath restless Sisyphus' mountain,
now parched amid the waters of the babbling old man,
let him wear out all the fables of the poets:
and when the Fury bids him confess the truth,
let his conscience, betraying him, cry out, "I wrote it."
6. VI
Happy are they whose lot it was to see the leader
flashing among Arctic suns and stars.
When will that day come, when field and tree and every
trim window will be bright with a Latian bride?
When the sweet delays, the long dust raised by Caesar,
and all Rome to be seen along the Flaminian Way?
When will you ride forth, knights and Moors in painted
Nilotic tunics, and the people's voice be one: "He comes"?
7. VII
Father of nymphs and streams, Rhine,
and all who drink the Odrysian frosts,
so may you ever enjoy your flowing waters,
nor may the barbarian wheel of an insolent
oxherd grind you trodden underfoot;
so may you go with your golden horns restored
and Roman now on either bank:
the Tiber, your master, begs you give back
Trajan to his own peoples and to the City.
8. VIII
Paula wants to marry me; I'm unwilling to marry Paula:
she's an old woman. I'd be willing, were she older still.

title: Epigrams
text:
9. IX
By elevens of feet and syllables
and with much salt yet nothing crude,
that Martial known to the nations
and known to the peoples—why do you envy?—
I'm no better known than Andraemon the racehorse.
10. X
While you, who enter the year with laurel-wreathed rods,
wear down a thousand thresholds at the morning round,
what am I to do here? What do you leave for us, Paulus,
who are of Numa's common crowd and the packed throng?
Shall I, who sees me, call him lord and king?
This you yourself do—but how much more smoothly!
Shall I follow litter or chair? You don't refuse to carry it,
you fight to go ahead through the middle of the mud.
Shall I rise more often to one reciting verse? You stand
and stretch both hands together toward his face.
What shall the poor man do, who isn't allowed to be a client?
Your purple has dismissed our togas.
11. XI
You talk of nothing but Theseus and Pirithous,
and you think yourself, Calliodorus, a match for Pylades.
May I die, if you deserve to hand Pylades his chamber-pot
or to feed the swine of Pirithous.
"And yet," you say, "I gave my friend five thousand
and a toga washed, at most, three or four times."
What of it, since Orestes never gave Pylades anything?
He who gives, however much, refuses more.
12. XII
You who make for the Aemilian peoples and Apollo's Vercellae
and the fields of the Phaethontean Po,
may I not live, Domitius, if I don't let you go gladly,
though without you no day is pleasing to me:
but the longing is worth this, that even by one summer's reaping
you ease your neck, scorched by the City's yoke.
Go, I pray, and drink in whole suns with greedy skin—
oh, how handsome you'll be, while you're abroad!
And you'll come back unrecognized by your pale-faced friends,
and the wan crowd will be jealous of your cheeks.
But the colour the road gives you, Rome will swiftly snatch away,
though you come back black as a Nile-bred face.

title: Epigrams
text:
13. XIII
That the Celtiberian Salo leads me to gold-bearing shores,
that I long to visit my homeland's hanging roofs,
you bring this about, Manius, dear to me from my simple years
and cherished in friendship since boyhood's days;
in the Iberian lands there is no other man
sweeter, more worthy of true love than you.
With you I could have loved, as a guest, the Gaetulian huts
of the parched African and the Scythian cabins.
If your mind is the same, if our care is mutual,
in whatever place, Rome will belong to us two.
14. XIV
Though the cushioned carriage carry your smooth-skinned servants for you,
and the Libyan rider sweat in the long dust,
though spread couches ring more than one Baiae for you
and Thetis grow pale, smeared with your perfume,
though Setine wine break the bright crystal cups,
nor Venus sleep on softer down than yours:
you lie at the night-time threshold of a haughty whore,
and the deaf door, alas, is wet with your tears,
nor do sighs cease to scorch your wretched breast.
Shall I tell you why things go badly with you, Cotta? They go well.
15. XV
You say you yield to none of our friends.
But, granting this is true, what, I ask, Crispus, do you do?
When I begged five thousand sesterces as a loan, you refused,
though your heavy strongbox couldn't hold your cash.
When did you give me a peck of beans or grain,
though a Nile-bred tenant farms your acres?
When was a short toga sent in the cold of winter's time?
When did half a pound of silver come to me?
I see nothing else by which we might believe you a friend,
than that you tend to fart in my presence, Crispus.
16. XVI
He pierced his dowried wife's heart with a sharp reed,
but while Aper was at play: Aper knows how to play.
17. XVII
If you call promising and not giving a gift, Gaius,
I'll outdo you in my gifts and presents.
Take whatever the Asturian digs in Galician fields,
whatever the golden flood of rich Tagus holds,
whatever the black Indian finds in Red Sea weed,
whatever the lone bird guards in its nest,
whatever shameless Tyre boils up in Agenor's cauldron:
take whatever everyone has—the way you give.

title: Epigrams
text:
18. XVIII
To cheat Macer of his Saturnalian tribute
you long in vain, my Muse: it's not allowed: he asks for it himself,
and demands the customary jokes, not gloomy verse,
and complains that my trifles have gone silent.
But now he has time only for the surveyors' long account-books.
Appian Way, what will you do, if Macer reads these?
19. XIX
Marius neither invites to dinner nor sends gifts,
nor stands surety, nor will lend, nor even has anything to lend.
Yet a crowd's not lacking that courts the barren friend.
Alas! how foolish are your togas, Rome!
20. XX
Take a little book not learned enough and too little grave,
yet not quite rustic either,
to eloquent Pliny for me, my Thalia—
go, carry it: the labour's brief, once done,
to climb the steep path of the Subura.
There you'll see at once the Orpheus
slick on the summit of his dripping theatre,
and the wondering beasts, and the king's own bird
that bore off the ravished Phrygian to the Thunderer;
there is the small house of your Pedo,
engraved with an eagle's lesser wing.
But take care not to knock, drunk and at the wrong hour,
on his eloquent door:
he gives whole days to austere Minerva,
while he toils for the ears of the hundred men
at what the ages and posterity might be able
to set even beside the pages of Arpinum.
You'll go more safely to the late lamps:
this is your hour, when Lyaeus rages,
when the rose reigns, when the hair is drenched:
then let even rigid Catos read me.
21. XXI
To write what Modestus himself can scarcely understand
and Claranus scarcely—what good is it, I ask, Sextus?
Your books need no reader, but Apollo:
in your judgment, Cinna was greater than Maro.
So let yours be praised, by all means: but my poems, Sextus,
may they please the grammarians, so long as they please without them.
22. XXII
Why do I often come out with a plastered chin,
or my sound lips painted with white lead,
Philaenis, you ask? I don't want to kiss you.

title: Epigrams
text:
23. XXIII
Happy Antonius Primus now counts off
in tranquil age his fifteen Olympiads gone by,
and looks back on days that are past and on years made safe,
nor does he now fear the waters of Lethe drawing near.
No day, as he recalls them, is unwelcome or hard;
there was none he wouldn't wish to remember.
A good man enlarges for himself the span of his life: this is
to live twice—to be able to enjoy a former life.
24. XXIV
The Kalends of March, my birthday,
a day lovelier than all the Kalends,
on which the girls send me a gift,
to your hearths I add this fiftieth
and seventh cake and this casket of incense.
If it suits you to grant a petitioner, on these
years add, I pray, twice nine more,
so that, not yet sluggish with excessive age,
but with the three stages of life completed,
I may seek the groves of the Elysian girl.
After such a Nestor's span I'll ask for not one more day.
25. XXV
That Mucius lately seen in the morning arena,
who laid his own limb upon the fire—
if he seems to you patient and hard and brave,
you've the wits of the people of Abdera.
For when, with the torturing shirt set before him, he's told
"Burn your hand," it's more to say "I won't do it."
26. XXVI
Varus, lately noble through the Latian vine
in the Paraetonian towns, leader to be remembered by a hundred men,
but now, promised in vain to Ausonian Quirinus,
you lie, a stranger's shade, on the shore of the Nile.
It wasn't granted to sprinkle your cold face with tears,
nor add rich incense to the mournful pyres.
But it's given you—a name to live by eternal song:
can you deny even this, deceitful Nile?
27. XXVII
On your birthday, Diodorus, the senate as your guests
reclines, and a rare knight is not left out,
and your dole hands out thirty coins apiece.
Yet no one, Diodorus, thinks you were ever born.
28. XXVIII
Loveliest sire of the years and of the shining world,
whom the public vows and prayers first invoke,
once you dwelt in cramped quarters as a thoroughfare,
where teeming Rome wore down the middle of the road:
now your thresholds are ringed with Caesar's gifts,
and you count as many forums, Janus, as you bear faces.
But you, holy father, grateful for so great a gift,
keep watch over the iron bars with their bolt forever fastened.

title: Epigrams
text:
29. XXIX
The dish you used to send me at Saturn's season,
you've sent, Sextilianus, to your mistress;
and the gown you'd give on the Kalends named for Mars,
out of my green toga is the dinner-suit bought.
Now the girls have begun to cost you nothing:
you screw, Sextilianus, with my gifts.
30. XXX
O sweet shore of temperate Formiae,
you, when he flees the town of stern Mars
and wearied sheds his restless cares,
Apollinaris prefers above all places.
Not the sweet Tibur of his pious wife,
nor his Tusculan or Algidan retreats,
does he so admire, nor Praeneste and Antium;
no charming Circe nor Dardanian Caieta
is missed, nor Marica nor the Liris,
nor Salmacis bathed in the Lucrine spring.
Here the surface of Thetis is brushed by a gentle wind;
the sea doesn't languish, but a living stillness of the deep
bears the painted skiff with a helping breeze,
just as, from a girl who has no love of summer's heat,
a healthful coolness comes from the waved purple fan.
Nor does the line seek its prey in the long sea,
but the fish, hooked from couch and little bed,
is watched as it draws the line from high above.
If ever Nereus feels the reign of Aeolus,
the table laughs at the storms, safe in its own supply:
the fishpond feeds the turbot and home-bred bass,
the dainty lamprey swims to its keeper,
the namer of names calls the well-known mullet,
and the old red mullets, bidden, come forth at the summons.
But when does Rome allow the enjoyment of these things?
How many days at Formiae does the year reckon
to one held fast by the City's pressing affairs?
O happy doorkeepers and bailiffs!
These things are prepared for the masters; they serve you.
31. XXXI
You sold a slave yesterday for twelve hundred coins,
Calliodorus, so you might dine well—once.
And you didn't dine well: a mullet bought at four
pounds was the show and headpiece of the meal.
One wants to cry out: "This is no fish, you scoundrel, no fish:
it's a man; a man, Calliodorus, you're eating."

title: Epigrams
text:
32. XXXII
This picture, tended with violets and roses,
whose features it recalls, Caedicianus, you ask?
Such was Marcus Antonius Primus in his middle years:
in this face the old man sees his younger self.
Would that art could shape the character and the soul!
No tablet on earth would be more beautiful.
33. XXXIII
Simpler than the old Sabines, Munatius Gallus,
who surpass the Cecropian sage in goodness,
so may chaste Venus grant you to keep your daughter's husband's
bright house with her wedding-torch unbroken:
that you, if perchance ill-will calls verses dipped
in green verdigris to be mine,
do as you do—drive them from me, and don't insist
that anyone who is read writes such poems.
My little books have learned to keep this rule:
to spare persons, to speak of vices.
34. XXXIV
May the gods grant you, Caesar Trajan, whatever you deserve,
and ratify forever what they've been willing to bestow:
you who restore his rights to the patron stripped of them
—he'll be no exile to his own freedmen—,
you deserve the power to keep the whole client safe:
which—if only one may prove the truth—you can.
35. XXXV
Let all girls read Sulpicia,
who wish to please one man alone;
let all husbands read Sulpicia,
who wish to please one bride alone.
She doesn't recount the frenzy of the Colchian
nor tell of dire Thyestes' banquet;
nor does she believe there was a Scylla or a Byblis:
but she teaches chaste and honest loves,
games, delights, and pleasantries.
Whoever judges her poems rightly
would say none is more mischievous,
would say none is more pure.
Such, I'd believe, were Egeria's jests
in dewy Numa's grotto.
With her as fellow-pupil or as teacher,
you'd have been more learned and chaste, Sappho:
but had hard Phaon seen Sulpicia
beside you and at once, he'd have loved her.
In vain: for neither as the Thunderer's wife
nor as the girl of Bacchus or Apollo
would she live, with her Calenus torn away.

title: Epigrams
text:
36. XXXVI
Whatever the wicked smokehouses of Massilia ripen,
each cask that takes its age from the fire,
comes from you, Munna: to your wretched friends you send
across the straits, down the long roads, your savage poisons;
and at no easy price, but one that would content
a jar of Falernian or Setine dear to its own cellars.
Why you don't come to Rome in so long a time,
this, I think, is the reason: that you'd not drink your own wines.
37. XXXVII
Most holy worshipper of justice and even-handed laws,
who rule the Latian forum with truth-telling lips,
to your townsman, Maternus, your old comrade,
if you're sending anything to the Galician Ocean—.
Or do you think it better to drag ugly frogs
and slender needle-fish on the Laurentian shore
than to send the captive mullet back to its own rocks,
since it would seem to weigh less than three pounds?
And to dine on an insipid clam at the head of the table,
and on what a small thin-shelled mussel covers,
rather than oysters not envious of Baian shells,
which the slave-boys gulp, their master not forbidding?
Here you'll noisily drive the reeking fox into the nets,
and the filthy prey will bite your dogs:
there the wet lines, lately scarce drawn up from the fishy
deep, will entangle my hares.
While I speak, look—the fisherman returns with empty basket,
the hunter stands by, proud of a captured badger:
every dinner comes from the city market to the sea.
If you're sending anything to the Galician Ocean—.
38. XXXVIII
O the soft fifteen years, Calenus,
which the god granted and brought to completion
in wedlock with your Sulpicia!
O every night and hour that was marked
with the precious pebbles of the Indian shore!
O what battles, what struggles on both sides
the happy little bed and the lamp beheld,
drunk with Nicerotian perfumes!
You've lived three lustres, Calenus:
this whole age is reckoned to you,
and you count only the days of a husband.
If, long besought, Atropos would give you back
from those one single day—but one—
you'd rather have it than four times Nestor's age.

title: Epigrams
text:
39. XXXIX
That you swear you were born when Brutus was consul, Lesbia,
you lie. Were you born when Numa was king, Lesbia?
There too you lie. For, as your centuries report,
you're said to be moulded from Prometheus' clay.
40. XL
Since I was always being told
that my Polla was secretly with a lover,
I burst in, Lupus. It was no lover.
41. XLI
In the new month of Janus, Proculeia, you abandon
your old husband and bid him keep his goods to himself.
What, I ask, what's happened? What's the cause of this sudden grief?
You give me no answer? I'll tell you: he was made praetor.
The purple for the Megalensian games would have cost a hundred
thousand, even if you gave the shows too sparingly,
and the people's festival would have carried off twice ten thousand.
This is no divorce, Proculeia: it's profit.
42. XLII
Your down is so faint, so soft, that breath
and the suns and a light breeze wear it away.
A coming quince hides itself in similar fuzz,
which gleams when stripped by a maiden's thumb.
Whenever I've pressed five firmer kisses on you,
I become bearded, Dindymus, from your lips.
43. XLIII
Now, Phileros, your seventh wife is buried in your field.
No man's field, Phileros, yields more than yours.
44. XLIV
Quintus Ovidius, soon to see the Caledonian Britons
and green Tethys and Father Ocean,
so you leave Numa's hills and the Nomentan
leisure, and neither country nor hearth holds the old man back?
You put off your joys, but Atropos doesn't put off
her threads, and every hour is charged to you.
You'll have proved to a dear friend—who wouldn't praise it?—
that sacred loyalty is worth more to you than life;
but be at last returned, to remain among your Sabines,
and count yourself among your own friendships.
45. XLV
If my little books say anything gentle and sweet,
if a flattering page sounds anything that honours you,
you think this fat and would rather gnaw the rib,
when I serve you the flank of a Laurentian boar.
Drink Vatican wine, if you delight in vinegar:
my flagon doesn't suit your stomach.

title: Epigrams
Epigrams
text:
49. XLIX
Though you drink your amethyst-coloured measures
and are soaked in dark Opimian,
you toast me with a Sabine just now broached
and say to me, Cotta, "Will you have it in gold?"
Does anyone want leaden wine in a golden cup?
50. L
Let mournful Victory break her Idumaean palms,
beat, Favour, your bare breast with a savage hand;
let Honour change his garb, and you, sad Glory,
fling your garlanded hair to the cruel flames as an offering.
Alas, the crime! cheated of your first youth, Scorpus,
you fall and so soon yoke the black horses.
That goal, always too swiftly hastened and brief
for your chariots—why was it so near to your life too?
51. LI
Now Tyrian Taurus looks back on the stars of Phrixus' ram,
and winter flees the alternating Castor;
the field laughs, the ground is clothed, the tree is clothed,
the Attic mistress weeps for Ismarian Itys.
What days, Faustinus, what a Ravenna has Rome
stolen from you! O suns, O tunic-clad repose!
O grove, O springs, and the firm shore of the moist
sand, and Anxur splendid with its sea-waters,
and the couch that watches more than one stretch of water,
which sees from here the river's boats, from there the sea's!
But there is no Theatre of Marcellus or Pompey, nor there
the triple baths, nor the fora joined four times,
nor the topmost shrine of Capitoline Thunderer,
nor the temples that shine next to their own heaven.
How often, weary, I think you say to Quirinus:
"What's yours, keep for yourself: what's mine, give back to me."
52. LII
Numa had seen the eunuch Thelys in a toga,
and said he was a convicted adulteress.
53. LIII
I am that Scorpus, glory of the clamorous Circus,
your applause, Rome, and your brief delight,
whom envious Lachesis snatched in his ninth third-year,
and, counting my palms, believed to be an old man.
54. LIV
You set out good dishes, Olus, but you set them covered.
It's ridiculous: I can have good ones that way too.

title: Epigrams
text:
55. LV
Whenever Marulla has weighed in her fingers
an erect member and long taken its measure,
she names the pounds, the scruples, the half-ounces;
the same one, after the work and its exercises,
when it lies slack like a loosened thong,
Marulla says by how much it's lighter.
So that's no hand of hers, but a balance-scale.
56. LVI
You bid me, Gallus, serve you all day long
and run three, four times through your Aventine.
Cascellius pulls out or repairs the aching tooth,
you, Hyginus, burn off the lashes hostile to the eyes;
Fannius cuts not, but removes the dripping uvula,
Eros erases the grim brands of stone;
Hermes is called the Podalirius of ruptures:
who heals the broken, tell me, Gallus, who is it?
57. LVII
You used to send a pound of silver; it's become a half-pound,
but of pepper. I don't buy pepper that dear, Sextus.
58. LVIII
While I tended the calm retreats of sea-girt Anxur,
Frontinus, and Baiae nearer still and the shore-house,
and the grove that the inhuman cicadas, when the Crab
seethes, never knew, and the river-fed lakes,
I had leisure to honour with you the learned
Pierians: now the greatest Rome wears me down.
When is a day my own here? I'm tossed on the deep
of the City, and life perishes in barren toil,
while I feed the harsh acres of a suburban farm
and the household gods near you, holy Quirinus.
But not only he loves who, night and day, frequents
your thresholds, nor do such losses befit a poet.
By the venerable rites of the Muses, by all
the gods I swear: even unattentive, I love you.
59. LIX
If a page is used up on a single subject, you skip it,
and the shorter, not the better, pleases you.
A rich dinner is set out, furnished from every market
for you, but only the tidbit delights you.
I've no need of too dainty a reader;
I want one who isn't satisfied without bread.

title: Epigrams
text:
60. LX
Munna asked Caesar for the privilege of three pupils,
though he's always been used to teaching two.
61. LXI
Here rests Erotion, a too-hasty shade,
whom her sixth winter slew by the crime of fate.
Whoever you'll be, after me the ruler of my little field,
to her slight shade pay each year its due:
so may your hearth endure, your household be unharmed,
and this stone be the only thing to mourn on your land.
62. LXII
Schoolmaster, spare the simple throng:
so may the long-haired boys flock to hear you
and the chorus love your dainty desk,
nor any reckoner or swift clerk
be ringed by a larger circle.
The white days glow with the flaming Lion
and seething July cooks the parched harvest.
Let the Scythian hide, fringed with rough thongs,
with which Marsyas of Celaenae was flogged,
and the grim canes, the sceptres of pedagogues,
rest and sleep until the Ides of October:
in summer, if boys keep well, they learn enough.
63. LXIII
Marble small indeed, but not to yield, traveller,
to the stones of Mausolus and the pyramids, you read.
Twice was my life seen at the Roman Tarentine games,
and it lost nothing before the final pyres:
Juno gave me five boys, as many girls,
and the hands of all closed my eyes.
A rare glory of the marriage-bed fell to me too:
one member alone was known to my chastity.
64. LXIV
If you should touch my little books, queen Polla,
receive my jests with no stern brow.
That bard of yours, the glory of our Helicon,
when he sang of fierce wars on the Pierian trumpet,
did not yet blush to say in wanton verse:
"If I'm not even buggered, Cotta, what am I doing here?"
65. LXV
Though you boast yourself a citizen of the Corinthians,
Charmenion, with no one denying it,
why am I called your brother, I, born of Iberians
and Celts, a citizen of the Tagus?
Or do we seem alike in face?
You wander sleek with curled hair,
I unruly with Spanish locks;
you smooth with daily depilatory,
I with shaggy legs and cheeks;
your speech lisps and your tongue is feeble,
my little daughter would speak more forcefully:
the dove is not so unlike the eagle,
nor the timid gazelle the stiff-maned lion.
So stop calling me brother,
lest I, Charmenion, call you sister.

title: Epigrams
text:
66. LXVI
Who, I ask, was so hard, who so haughty,
as to order you, Theopompus, made a cook?
Does anyone bear to defile this face with the black kitchen,
to pollute these locks with greasy fire?
Who'll rather hold the wine-cups or the crystal?
By what hand will Falernian be better mixed?
If such an end awaits star-bright servants,
let Jupiter now use Ganymede as a cook.
67. LXVII
Daughter of Pyrrha, stepmother of Nestor,
whom Niobe saw white-haired as a girl,
whom old Laertes called grandmother,
Priam nurse, Thyestes mother-in-law,
now outliving all the crows,
at last laid in this tomb still itches,
bald Plutia, with Melanthion.
68. LXVIII
Though you have neither Ephesus nor Rhodes nor Mytilene,
but a house, Laelia, in a patrician quarter,
and a mother never tanned, born of swarthy Etruscans,
a stern father from the Arician region;
"My lord, my honey, my soul"—you keep heaping it up,
—for shame!—you, a citizen of Hersilia and Egeria.
Let the little bed hear these words, not every bed,
but the one a mistress has spread for her wanton man.
Do you want to know how you, a chaste matron, talk?
Can you, even when you writhe, be more seductive?
Though you learn by heart and recite the whole of Corinth,
you still won't, Laelia, be wholly a Lais.
69. LXIX
You give your husband watchmen, Polla, but take none yourself.
This, Polla, is to wed a man as a wife yourself.
70. LXX
That scarcely one book a year comes out from me,
I stand charged of sloth before you, learned Potitus.
But how much more justly might you marvel that one comes out,
when whole days often slip away from me.
At night I visit friends who don't return the greeting,
I congratulate many, no one congratulates me, Potitus.
Now my gem seals letters to light-bringing Diana,
now the first hour snatches me, now the fifth.
Now a consul or praetor holds me, and the returning dances,
often a poet is heard the whole day through.
But you can't safely refuse the pleading lawyer,
nor if a rhetor or a grammarian should ask you.
After the tenth hour the baths are sought, weary, and a hundred
quadrantes. When, Potitus, will the book be done?

title: Epigrams
text:
71. LXXI
Whoever you are who wish glad and late
fates for your parents, love the brief inscription of this marble.
Here Rabirius has buried dear shades in the earth;
no old folk lie under a brighter lot:
a gentle and last night closed twice six lustres of their wedlock,
two funerals burned on a single pyre.
Yet he mourns them as snatched in their earliest years.
Nothing can be more outrageous than these tears.
72. LXXII
In vain you come to me, Flatteries,
pitiful with your worn-down little lips:
I'm not going to call anyone lord and god.
There's no longer a place for you in this city;
go far off, to the felt-capped Parthians,
and, foul and grovelling and suppliant,
kiss the soles of painted kings.
There's no lord here, but an emperor,
but the most just senator of all,
through whom from the Stygian home there's brought back
rustic Truth, with dry hair.
Under this prince, if you're wise, beware,
Rome, of speaking in your former words.
73. LXXIII
A letter brought me the welcome pledge of an eloquent
friend, the austere gift of an Ausonian toga,
which not Fabricius, but Apicius would wish to wear,
which Maecenas, Caesar's knight, would wish.
This would have been cheaper to me, sent by another;
not by whatever hand the victim is slain does it appease:
sent by you it comes: could I not love your gift,
Marcus, I could love my own name.
But more than the gift and more welcome than the name itself
is the kind service and judgment of a learned man.
74. LXXIV
Now spare your weary congratulator, Rome,
your weary client. How long, as a morning caller
among forerunners and little toga'd men,
shall I earn a hundred leaden coins the whole day,
when Scorpus in a single hour carries off, victorious,
fifteen heavy sacks of glowing gold?
I'd not want, as the prize for my little books
—for what do they earn?—the Apulian fields:
neither Hybla nor the corn-bearing Nile takes me,
nor the dainty grape that from the citadel of the Setine slope
looks out on the Pomptine marshes.
You ask, then, what I long for? To sleep.

title: Epigrams
text:
75. LXXV
Once Galla demanded twenty thousand from me,
and, I confess, she wasn't too dear at the price.
A year went by: "You'll give twice five thousand," she said.
She seemed to me to ask more than before.
Now, six months later, when she asked two thousand,
I offered a thousand coins. She wouldn't take them.
Two or perhaps three Kalends had passed:
of her own accord she asked four gold pieces.
I didn't give them. She bade me send a hundred coins:
but even this sum seemed to me too heavy.
A meagre dole of a hundred quadrantes joined us;
this she wanted: I said it had been given to my boy.
Could she go any lower? She did.
Galla gives for free, gives of her own accord: I say no.
76. LXXVI
Does this, Fortune, seem fair to you?
A citizen not of Syria or Parthia,
nor a knight from a Cappadocian platform,
but a home-bred slave of the people of Remus and Numa,
pleasant, honest, harmless—a friend,
learned in both tongues, whose one fault,
but a great one, is that he's a poet,
Mevius shivers in a drab cowl,
while the muleteer Incitatus shines in scarlet.
77. LXXVII
Nothing was ever more wickedly done by Carus, Maximus,
than that he died of a fever: it too committed a crime.
The savage, harmful fever should at least have been a quartan!
He ought to have been kept for his own doctor.
78. LXXVIII
You'll go, Macer, to shore-set Salonae,
and there will go rare loyalty and love of right
and that office which, when it drags modesty along as companion,
always returns the poorer:
happy farmer of the gold-bearing land,
you'll send your governor back with an empty purse
and wish for delays, and as he departs
the Dalmatian will follow him with wet-eyed joy.
We'll make for the Celts, Macer, and the fierce Iberians
with longing for you.
But whatever page is brought from there,
marked by the reed of the fishy Tagus,
my page will name Macer:
so let me be read among the old poets,
and don't prefer to me many earlier ones,
but let me be lesser to you than Catullus alone.

title: Epigrams
text:
79. LXXIX
Torquatus has a mansion at the fourth milestone;
at the fourth milestone Otacilius bought a little farm.
Torquatus built baths gleaming with varied marble;
Otacilius made a cooking-pot.
Torquatus laid out a laurel-grove on his land;
Otacilius planted a hundred chestnut-trees.
When Torquatus was consul, that one was a ward-master,
and thought himself no less in so great an honour.
As once a great ox burst a tiny frog,
so, I think, will Torquatus burst Otacilius.
80. LXXX
Eros weeps, whenever he eyes the cups of spotted murra
or the slave-boys or the nobler citron-wood,
and draws his groans from deep in his breast, because
he can't, poor wretch, buy up the whole Saepta and carry it home.
How many do what Eros does, but with dry eye!
The greater part laughs at his tears and holds the same within.
81. LXXXI
When two had come one morning to fuck Phyllis
and each desired to take her naked first,
Phyllis promised to give herself to both at once,
and did: one lifted her foot, the other her tunic.
82. LXXXII
If my distress adds anything to your affairs,
in the morning or at midnight I'll wear the toga
and bear the shrieking blasts of the unkind north wind
and endure the storms and take the snow.
But if you grow no richer by a single quadrans
through my groans and freeborn torments,
spare me, I pray, worn out, and let go these vain labours
that profit you nothing and harm me, Gallus.
83. LXXXIII
You gather your sparse hairs from here and there
and cover the broad field of your gleaming bald head, Marinus,
with the hair from your temples;
but at the wind's bidding the disturbed locks return
and restore themselves, and ring your bare head
with great curls on this side and that:
between Spendophorus and Telesphorus
you'd think Cyda's Hermeros was standing.
Won't you confess yourself an old man more simply,
so you may at last seem to be a single person!
Nothing is uglier than a bald man with hair.

title: Epigrams
text:
84. LXXXIV
You wonder why Afer doesn't go off to bed?
You see, Caedicianus, the one he reclines with.
85. LXXXV
Old Ladon now, a boatman of a Tiber barge,
bought a farm near the waters he loved.
And since wandering Tiber often pressed it with rushing waves
and broke up the fields with its wintry flood,
he filled with stones his discharged boat, which stood
on the high bank, and set it against the shallows.
So he turned aside the excessive waters. Who could believe it?
The sunken boat brought aid to its master.
86. LXXXVI
No one ever burned so inflamed with a new mistress
as Laurus blazed with love of the ball.
But he who was the prime player while his prime years flowered,
now that he's ceased to play, is the prime ball.
87. LXXXVII
Come, let pious Rome feel the October Kalends
of eloquent Restitutus:
with all your tongues favour him, and with your prayers;
we keep his birthday—be silent, lawsuits.
Away with the wax candle of the dried-up client,
and let the empty triple tablets and brief napkins
wait for the jests of icy December.
Let the richer compete in gifts:
Agrippa's swollen trader
should bring cloaks made by Cadmus' townsmen;
the man charged with brawls and a drunken night
should send dinner-clothes to his advocate;
the girl who has bested her slandered man
should present true sardonyx, but herself hand it over;
the old man who admires our forefathers
should give an embossed work of Phidian chasing;
the hunter a hare, the farmer a kid,
the fisherman should bring the sea's spoils.
If each sends what is his own, what do you think
the poet will send you, Restitutus?
88. LXXXVIII
You chase after all the praetors' little books, Cotta;
you receive their wax tablets too. You're a dutiful man.
89. LXXXIX
This Juno, Polyclitus, your labour and happy glory,
which Phidian hands would long to have earned,
shines with so great a face that on Ida she'd have surpassed
the goddesses convicted with the judge in no doubt.
Did not her brother love his own Juno, Polyclitus,
the brother could love your Juno.

title: Epigrams
text:
90. XC
Why do you pluck your old cunt, Ligeia?
Why stir up the ashes of your own tomb?
Such elegance befits girls
—for you can no longer even seem an old woman—;
that, believe me, Ligeia, is a charming thing
not for Hector's mother, but his wife.
You're wrong, if you think this a cunt
to which a cock has ceased to belong.
So if you've any shame, Ligeia, don't
pluck the beard of a dead lion.
91. XCI
Almo has all eunuchs and can't get it up himself:
and he complains that his Polla bears him nothing.
92. XCII
Marrius, cultivator and companion of a quiet life,
by whom old Atina boasts as her citizen,
to you I commend these twin pines, the glory of the wild grove,
and the holm-oaks of the Fauns,
and the altars of the Thunderer and rough Silvanus
raised by the half-skilled hand of the bailiff,
which the blood of lamb or kid has often stained,
and the maiden goddess, mistress of the holy shrine,
and him you see as guest of his chaste sister,
Mars, the patron of my Kalends,
and the laurel grove of dainty Flora,
into which she fled when Priapus pursued her.
All this gentle divinity of my little farm,
whether you appease it with blood or incense:
"Wherever your Martial is," you'll say,
"behold, with this right hand he sacrifices to you with me,
an absent priest; count him present,
and grant to both whatever either shall ask."
93. XCIII
If you should first see, Clemens, the Euganean shores of Helicaon
and the fields painted with vine-clad ridges,
carry to Sabina of Ateste my poems, not yet
made public, but lately dressed in the purple toga.
As a rose delights, plucked by the first thumb,
so a fresh page, not soiled by the chin, pleases.
94. XCIV
No Massylian serpent guards my orchards,
nor does the royal land of Alcinous serve me,
but my Nomentan garden buds in safety
with its tree, nor do the leaden apples fear a thief.
So these apples, just now born in the middle Subura,
I send—the waxen fruits of my autumn.

title: Epigrams
text:
95. XCV
Your husband sent back an infant to you, Galla, your lover too.
These two, I think, plainly deny they've fucked you.
96. XCVI
That I often speak too much of remote nations, Avitus,
you wonder, made old in the Latian city,
and that I thirst for gold-bearing Tagus and my native Salo
and seek again the humble fields of a well-stocked cottage.
That land pleases me, in which a small estate makes me
blessed and slender means run to luxury:
here the field is fed, there it feeds; here the hearth
warms with a grudging fire, there it gleams with a mighty blaze;
here hunger is costly and the market a bankrupter,
there the table is laid with the riches of its own country;
here four togas or more are worn through in a summer,
there one covers me for four autumns.
Go now, court patrons, when a place can provide you
whatever a friend does not, Avitus.
97. XCVII
While the light pyre is built of papyrus soon to burn,
while my weeping wife buys myrrh and cassia,
the grave now ready, now the bier, now the embalmer,
Numa wrote me his heir: he got well.
98. XCVIII
Though a servant adds my Caecuban,
looser than an Idaean catamite,
than whom no daughter reclines more elegant, no wife,
no mother of yours, no sister,
do you want me rather to gaze at your lamps
or your old citron-wood and Indian tusks?
But so you won't suspect me as I recline,
provide from the herd and the squalid farmstead
shaven, shaggy, raw, puny
sons of a stinking swineherd for me.
This jealousy will destroy you: you can't, Publius,
have these manners and these servants both.
99. XCIX
If these were the Roman features of Socrates, they'd have been
such as Julius Rufus has in his Satires.
100. C
Why, fool, do you mix your verses with mine?
What have you to do, wretch, with a book that's at war with you?
Why do you seek to herd foxes with lions
and make owls like to eagles?
Though you had one of Ladas' feet,
you'd run in vain, idiot, with a wooden leg.

title: Epigrams
text:
101. CI
If perchance old Gabba, released and sent back
from the Elysian field, happy in his own Caesar,
who'd have heard Capitolinus and Gabba jesting together,
will return and say: "Hold your tongue, country Gabba."
102. CII
By what method, you ask, was Philinus made
a father, who never fucked?
Let Gaditanus tell you that, Avitus,
who writes nothing and yet is a poet.
103. CIII
Townsmen, whom Augustan Bilbilis on its steep
mountain bore me, girt by Salo's rushing waters,
does the glad glory of your bard please you at all?
For I am your honour and name and fame,
nor does Verona owe more to its slender Catullus,
and she'd be willing for me to be called no less her own.
A thirtieth summer has been added to four harvests,
since without me you give country cakes to Ceres,
while I dwell in the loveliest walls of mistress Rome:
the Italian realms have changed my hair.
If you welcome my return with a calm mind, I come;
if you bear harsh hearts, I'm free to go back.
104. CIV
Go, my little book, go as companion to our Flavus
on the long sea—but of a favouring wave—,
and with easy course and your own winds
make for the citadels of Spanish Tarraco:
from there a wheel will lift you, and swiftly carried
you'll see, perhaps in the fifth carriage,
high Bilbilis and your own Salo.
What do I charge you with, you ask? That you greet
my few comrades, but old ones, and seen by me
before thirty and four winters,
at once, straight from the road,
and remind our Flavus now and then
to procure me a pleasant, not laborious
retreat at a wholesome price,
to make your parent lazy.
That's all. Now the swollen master calls
and chides the delays, and a better breeze
has opened the harbour: farewell, little book:
a ship, you know, I think, waits for no single passenger.
1. I
Where are you headed, where, my idle book,
dressed in no everyday Sidonian dye?
Surely not to see Parthenius? No doubt:
you'll go and return unrolled, unread:
he reads no books, only petitions;
nor has he time for the Muses—else he'd have time for his own.
Do you reckon yourself blessed enough,
if lesser hands take hold of you?
Make for the portico of neighbouring Quirinus:
no idler crowd is to be had at
Pompey's, or by Agenor's daughter's,
or at the fickle owner of the first ship's.
There are two or three there who'd unroll
the bookworms of my trifles,
but only when the wagers and stale gossip
about Scorpus and Incitatus are done.

title: Epigrams
text:
2. II
The grim eyebrow, the stern brow of hard Cato,
the daughter of Fabricius the ploughman,
the masked airs and the rule of morals,
and whatever we aren't, in the dark—out you go.
Look, my verses cry "Hurrah, Saturnalia!":
under your reign, Nerva, it's both allowed and a pleasure.
Sour readers, go memorize knotty Santra:
I've nothing to do with you: this book is mine.
3. III
Not only urban leisure delights in my Pimpleian Muse,
nor do I give these things to empty ears,
but my book is thumbed by a stiff centurion
amid Getic frosts, at the Martian standards,
and Britain is said to chant my verses.
What good is it? My purse knows nothing of this.
Yet what enduring pages we could compose,
what battles blast on the Pierian trumpet,
when the kindly gods have given an Augustus back to earth,
and a Maecenas too, if they gave you one, Rome!
4. IV
The rites and household gods of the Phrygians, which Troy's heir
chose to snatch rather than Laomedon's wealth about to burn,
and Jupiter, now inscribed for the first time in eternal gold,
and his sister and the perfect daughter of the supreme father,
and you, Janus, who now enter a third name in the purple
calendar for Nerva; I beg you with reverent voice:
preserve, all of you, this leader, preserve the senate;
let the one live by the prince's morals, the other by his own.
5. V
So great is your reverence for the right and the just, Caesar,
as was Numa's: but Numa was poor.
A hard thing it is, not to surrender morals to wealth,
and, when you've outdone so many Croesuses, to be a Numa.
If the old fathers, those mighty names, should return,
if one might empty the Elysian grove:
unconquered Camillus will court you, for freedom's sake,
Fabricius, while you give it, will want gold;
Brutus will rejoice with you as leader, to you bloody Sulla
will hand over command, when he's about to lay it down;
Magnus will love you, with Caesar a private man,
and Crassus will give you all his wealth.
Even Cato himself, recalled from the infernal shades
of Dis, if he were restored, would be a Caesarian.

title: Epigrams
text:
6. VI
In the festive days of the scythe-bearing old man,
over which the ruling dice-box holds sway,
you permit me, I think, felt-capped Rome,
to play in unlaborious verse.
You've smiled; so it's allowed, we're not forbidden.
Pale cares, depart far from here;
whatever comes to hand, let me speak it
without peevish forethought.
Mix the half-measures, boy,
such as Pythagoras gave to Nero,
mix them, Dindymus, but more frequent ones:
I can do nothing sober; drinking,
fifteen poets will come to my aid.
Now give kisses, but Catullan ones:
which if they prove as many as he named,
I'll give you the Sparrow of Catullus.
7. VII
Now at last, Paula, you won't say to your stupid husband,
whenever you want to go far off to your lover,
"Caesar bade me come to the Alban estate at dawn,
Caesar to Circeii." That trick is gone now.
You may be a Penelope under prince Nerva:
but the itch and your old nature forbid it.
Unhappy one, what will you do? Pretend a sick friend?
Your husband himself will cling, the companion of his lady,
and go with you to brother and mother and father.
What frauds, then, do you plot, so ingenious?
Another adulteress might perhaps say she was hysterical
and wanted to take the waters at the lake of Sinuessa.
How much better you manage it, whenever it pleases you to go and screw,
you who'd rather tell your husband the truth, Paula!
8. VIII
The scent of yesterday's balsam-resin that lingers faintly,
the last whiff that falls from curling saffron;
fruit ripening in a winter chest,
a field luxuriant with springtime trees;
silk from the empress's Palatine presses,
amber rewarmed by a maiden's hand;
a jar of dark Falernian, broken far off,
a garden that keeps Sicilian bees;
the perfume-jars of Cosmus and the altars of the gods,
a garland just now slipped from rich locks:
why name them one by one? They're not enough; mix them all:
this is how my boy's kisses smell in the morning.
You want to know his name? If for the sake of the kisses, I'll tell.
You've sworn: you want to know too much, Sabinus.

title: Epigrams
text:
9. IX
Bright with Jove's foliage, fame of the Roman buskin,
Memor breathes again, restored by Apelles' art.
10. X
Turnus turned his mighty genius to satire.
Why not to the songs of Memor? He was his brother.
11. XI
Take away, boy, the cups and the embossed work of the tepid Nile,
and hand me goblets with a careless hand,
worn by the lips of our fathers, clean from an unshorn servant;
let the ancient honour be restored to our tables.
A gem-cup befits you to drink from, who break Mentor's work
into a chamber-pot for your whore, Sardanapalus.
12. XII
Let the right of seven children be granted you, Zoilus,
so long as no one gives you a mother, no one a father.
13. XIII
Whoever you are who tread the Flaminian Way, traveller,
do not pass by this noble marble.
The delight of the city, the wit of the Nile,
art and grace, sport and pleasure,
the glory and grief of the Roman theatre,
and all the Venuses and Cupids
are buried in this tomb, with Paris.
14. XIV
Heirs, do not bury the short farmer:
for to him earth, however little, is heavy.
15. XV
I have pages that Cato's wife
and the dreadful Sabine women might read:
this whole little book I want to laugh
and be more wanton than all little books.
Let it be drenched with wine and not blush
to be dirty with rich Cosmian pomade,
let it play with boys, love girls,
and not speak in roundabout phrases of that
from which we're born, the parent of us all,
which holy Numa called a cock.
Yet remember that these verses are
of the Saturnalia, Apollinaris:
this little book does not have my morals.
16. XVI
You who are too solemn, reader, can leave now
wherever you like: I wrote these for the city's toga;
now my page grows wanton with Lampsacene verse
and clashes the cymbals with a Tartessian hand.
O how often you'll strike your cloak with stiffened member,
though you be graver than Curius and Fabricius!
You too, girl, will read the naughtiness and the games
of my little book, moist with desire, though you be from Patavium.
Lucretia blushed and put down my book,
but in Brutus' presence; Brutus, withdraw: she'll read.

title: Epigrams
text:
17. XVII
Not every page of my book is for the night:
you'll find, Sabinus, something to read in the morning too.
18. XVIII
You gave me, Lupus, a farm near the city;
but I've a bigger farm in my window.
Can you call this a farm, name this a farm?
In which a rue-sprig makes Diana's grove,
which the wing of a chirping cicada covers,
which an ant eats up in a single day,
for which a closed rose-petal is a garland;
in which no more grass is found
than a leaf of Cosmus or raw pepper;
in which neither a cucumber can lie straight
nor a whole snake make its home.
The garden scarcely feeds a single caterpillar,
the gnat dies once the willow-bed's consumed,
and a mole is my digger and ploughman.
The mushroom can't gape open, the fig
can't smile, the violets can't spread out.
A mouse ravages the borders, and by the farmer
is feared like a Calydonian boar,
and the crop, snatched by flying Procne's claw,
lies in a swallow's nest;
and though he stand there without sickle or member,
there's no room for half a Priapus.
The finished harvest scarcely fills a snail-shell,
and we store the new wine in a pitch-sealed nut.
You made a mistake, Lupus, but by a single letter:
for at the time you gave me a praedium, a farm,
I'd have preferred you'd given me a prandium, a lunch.
19. XIX
You ask why I won't marry you, Galla? You're eloquent.
My cock often commits a solecism.
20. XX
You who, being sour, read sour Latin words,
read six wanton verses of Caesar Augustus, you envious one:
"Because Antony fucks Glaphyra, Fulvia has decreed
this penalty for me, that I fuck her too.
That I should fuck Fulvia? What if Manius begged me
to bugger him, would I do it? I think not, if I were sane.
'Either fuck or let's fight,' she says. But what, since my prick
is dearer to me than life itself? Let the trumpets sound!"
You absolve, no doubt, my witty little books, Augustus,
you who know how to speak with Roman frankness.

title: Epigrams
text:
21. XXI
Lydia is as loose as the arse of a bronze horseman,
as the swift hoop that rings with shrill bronze,
as the wheel struck so often by the leaping vaulter,
as an old shoe soaked in muddy water,
as the wide-meshed nets that wait for wandering thrushes,
as the awnings denied to Pompey's south wind,
as the bracelet slipped from a consumptive catamite,
as a mattress widowed of its Leuconian stuffing,
as the old breeches of a poor Briton, and as
the foul gullet of a Ravenna pelican.
They say I fucked her in a sea-water pool.
I don't know; I think I fucked the pool.
22. XXII
That you wear away the soft kisses of snowy Galaesus
with your hard mouth, that you lie with naked Ganymede,
(who denies it?) that's too much. But let it be enough; at least

title: Epigrams
text:
24. XXIV
While I escort you and walk you home,

Does it not seem a loss to you,
if what Rome reads, the visitor seeks out,

25. XXV

title: Epigrams
text:

32. XXXII

title: Epigrams
text:
33. XXXIII
Time and again the Green has reached the palm

35. XXXV

36. XXXVI
Gaius Julius marks this day for me with a white gem—

Hypnus, why do you dally, lazy one? Pour out immortal

title: Epigrams
text:
40. XL

and the bending wood, and fell himself, chasing the shaken wealth.

and condemned the guilty timber to the pyres.

42. XLII

title: Epigrams
text:

title: Epigrams
text:

title: Epigrams
text:

69. LXIX
Reared among the trainers of the amphitheatre,

70. LXX
Can you sell, Tucca, boys bought for a hundred thousand each?
Can you sell, Tucca, weeping masters?

title: Epigrams
text:
80. LXXX
The golden shore of blessed Venus, Baiae,

82. LXXXII
The guest Philostratus, returning from the waters of Sinuessa
to his hired lodging at the bidding of night,

No one, Sosibianus, lets a house for more.

when the god-frenzied crowd raves to Phrygian measures;

and dresses broken bones with a workman's hand.
Let this man shear the destitute Cynics and Stoic chins
and strip the horse's neck of its dusty mane.
Let him scrape wretched Prometheus beneath the Scythian crag,

only let the barbarous weapons of Antiochus sound.
These scars, however many you count on my chin,

title: Epigrams
text:
85. LXXXV

90. XC
You approve no poems that run on a smooth path,
but those that fall through ruts and over deep rocks,
and you reckon a thing greater than Maeonian verse:
"Here lies Metrophanes, little pillar of Lucilius;"

and whatever Accius and Pacuvius vomit up.

Canace, daughter of Aeolis, lies entombed in this sepulchre,

took her face and settled on her tender mouth,
and the cruel disease itself devoured her kisses,
nor were her whole lips given to the black pyres.

title: Epigrams
text:
92. XCII

Whenever you fall in with the kisses of cocksuckers,
think you're plunging your head, Flaccus, into a bath-tub.
96. XCVI
Marcia, not the Rhine, leaps here, German: why do you stand in the way
and forbid the boy the bounty of the rich pool?
Barbarian, the conquering water ought not, with a citizen pushed aside,
relieve a captive servant's thirst.
97. XCVII
In one night I can do it four times: but if I can do you
once, Telesilla, in four years, may I die.
98. XCVIII
There's no escaping the kissers, Flaccus.
They press in, delay you, pursue, run to meet you,
from this side and that, everywhere, on every road.
No sharp ulcer or gleaming pustules,
no grim chin or filthy scabs,
no lips smeared with greasy salve,
no drop from a frozen nose will help you.
They kiss you sweating and they kiss you freezing,
and they kiss you saving up your bridal kiss.
It won't save you to have your head covered with cowls,
nor your litter shut safe with leather and curtain,
nor will a chair, however often closed, protect you:
the kisser will get in through every crack.
Not the consulship itself, not the tribunate
nor the six rods, nor the proud staff of a bawling
lictor will drive off the kisser:
though you sit on a high tribunal
and from the curule chair dispense justice to the nations,
the kisser will climb up here and there.
He'll kiss you fevered and weeping,
he'll give a kiss to you yawning and swimming,
he'll give one to you shitting. The sole remedy for the evil is
to make a friend of someone you'd not want to kiss you.

title: Epigrams
text:
99. XCIX
Whenever you rise from your chair—I've often noticed it—
your wretched tunics bugger you, Lesbia.
When you've tried with your right hand, tried with your left,
to pluck them out, you extract them with tears and groaning:
so they're gripped by the twin Symplegades of your arse
and enter your over-large, dark-blue buttocks.
You want to mend the unsightly fault? I'll teach you:
Lesbia, I advise you neither to rise nor to sit.
100. C
I don't want a girlfriend, Flaccus, so thin
that my rings would circle her arms,
who'd scrape me with a bare hip and prick me with her knee,
whose loins jut out like a saw, whose arse like a spear-point.
But I also don't want a girlfriend of a thousand pounds.
I'm a lover of flesh, not a lover of fat.
101. CI
Could you, Flaccus, even see Thais, she's so thin?
You, I think, can see, Flaccus, what isn't there.
102. CII
He didn't lie who told me you have
a beautiful body, Lydia, not a beautiful face.
It's so, if you keep silent and recline as mute
as a face is silent in wax or on a painted board.
But whenever you speak, Lydia, you ruin your body too,
and no one's tongue harms anyone more than yours does you.
Take care the aedile neither hears nor sees you:
it's a portent, whenever a statue begins to speak.
103. CIII
So great, Safronius, is the goodness of your spirit and face,
that I wonder you could have become a father.
104. CIV
Wife, out the door, or fall in with my ways:
I'm no Curius nor Numa nor Tatius.
Pleasant nights drawn out over cups delight me:
you, having drunk water, hurry sourly to rise.
You take joy in darkness: but I take joy in playing with the lamp as witness
and in bursting my flank with the light let in.
A band and tunics and dark cloaks hide you:
but no girl lies naked enough for me.
Kisses that mimic the coaxing doves win me:
you give me such as you give your grandmother in the morning.
You deign to help the work with neither motion nor voice
nor fingers, as though you were preparing incense and wine:
the Phrygian slaves used to masturbate behind the door
whenever Hector's wife sat on the steed,
and though the Ithacan snored, chaste Penelope
was always used to keep her hand busy there.
You refuse to be buggered: Cornelia gave this to Gracchus,
Julia to Pompey, Porcia, Brutus, to you;
before the Dardanian servant mixed his sweet
cups, Juno was Ganymede to Jove.
If gravity delights you, you may be a Lucretia
all day long: at night I want a Lais.

title: Epigrams
text:
105. CV
You used to send a pound, Garricus; you send a quarter now.
At least pay me half, Garricus.
106. CVI
Vibius Maximus, if you've leisure to be greeted,
read only this: for you're both busy
and not too fond of labour.
You skip these four lines too? You've shown sense.
107. CVII
You hand me back a book unrolled clear to its very horns
and as if read through, Septicianus.
You've read it all. I believe it, I know it, I'm glad, it's true.
I read through your five books the same way.
108. CVIII
Though you might be sated with so long a little book,
reader, you still ask a few more couplets from me.
But Lupus demands his interest and the boys their rations.
Reader, pay up. You're silent and pretend not to hear? Farewell.

title: Epigrams
text:
pr. Valerius Martialis to his friend Priscus, greetings.
I know I owe a defence for three years of most obstinate idleness; for which idleness there would be no excuse even amid those urban occupations by which we more easily achieve the look of being a nuisance rather than dutiful—much less in this provincial solitude, where, unless we even study to excess, I have withdrawn both without solace and without excuse. So receive my account. In which this is the chief and first point, that I miss the ears of the city, to which I had grown accustomed, and seem to myself to be pleading in a foreign court; for if there is anything that pleases in my little books, it was the audience that dictated it: that subtlety of judgment, that genius for subject-matter, the libraries, the theatres, the gatherings, in which pleasure does not feel itself to be study—in short, all those things which, grown soft, I left behind, I now miss as though abandoned. To this is added the rust of small-town teeth, and ill-will in the seat of judgment, and one or two malicious men—in a tiny place, a great many; against which it is hard to keep a good temper day by day: so do not wonder that what used to be done by an eager spirit is now cast off by an indignant one. Yet, lest I deny anything to you, both arriving from the city and demanding it—to whom I am ungrateful if I render only what I can—I have commanded myself to do what I used to indulge in, and have studied for very few days, so that I might receive your most intimate ears with their welcoming-gift. I should like you not to grudge the trouble of carefully weighing and sifting these things, which are at risk only with you; and—what is most difficult for you—of judging my trifles with elegance set aside, lest, if you so decide, we send to Rome not a Spanish-style book, but a Spaniard.

title: Epigrams
text:
1. I
While the nets are idle and the baying Molossian hounds,
and the wood is quiet, no boar found,
you can give your leisure, Priscus, to a brief little book.
The hour is not a summer one, nor is the whole of it lost on you.
2. II
You who lately used to be sent from the City to the nations,
now, hurrah, you'll go a foreigner to Rome, my book,
from the race of gold-bearing Tagus and grim Salo,
the native rivers which my mighty land gives me.
Yet you'll be no stranger, nor can you now be called a newcomer,
you, whose brothers the high house of Remus holds in such number.
By your own right, seek the venerable threshold of the new temple,
where the halls are given back to the Pierian choir.
Or, if you prefer, you'll walk to the head of the Subura;
there are the high halls of my consul:
eloquent Stella dwells in his laurel-crowned home,
bright Stella, thirster after the Hyantean water;
there a Castalian spring is proud with its glassy torrent,
whence the nine mistresses are said often to have drunk:
he will give you to people and senators and knights to read,
and will read you through himself with not too dry cheeks.
Why ask for a title? Let two or three verses be read,
and all, my book, will cry that you are mine.
3. III
What Maecenas, a knight sprung from royal forefathers,
was to Flaccus and Varius and supreme Maro,
that, Priscus Terentius, garrulous fame and the aged page
will say you were to me among the nations and the peoples.
You make my genius, you, if I seem to have any power;
you give me the right to a freeborn idleness.
Bravo for your spirit, which few have, and for your character,
such as Numa, such as a cheerful Cato might have.
To be generous, to bestow, to enlarge a slender estate,
and to give what the easy gods scarcely granted,
is now allowed and lawful. But you under a harsh prince
and in evil times dared to be good.

title: Epigrams
text:
4. IV
The longer labour of my eleventh and tenth little book
has been compressed and pared into a short work.
Let the idle read more, those to whom you gave safe leisure:
read these, Caesar; perhaps you'll read those too.
5. V
You poems, who lately were going to shore-set Pyrgi,
go now by the sacred way—no longer dusty.
The mildest of the nobles of the Ausonian court has come,
Nerva: now one may enjoy all of Helicon:
upright honour, cheerful clemency, cautious power
return now; the long fears have turned their backs.
This, pious Rome, your peoples and nations pray:
may such a leader always be yours, and this one for long.
7. VII
As many hairs as she bears on the whole of her head,
if Ligeia has so many years, she's three years old.
8. VIII
Rome, goddess of lands and nations,
to whom nothing is equal and nothing second,
when, lately glad, she was counting up the years to come
of Trajan over so many ages,
and saw in so great a leader a soldier
brave and young and warlike,
she said, glorious in such a guardian:
"Nobles of the Parthians and leaders of the Seres,
Thracians, Sauromatae, Getae, Britons,
I can show you a Caesar; come."
9. IX
Palma governs our Iberians, mildest Caesar,
and a foreign peace enjoys the gentle yoke.
So we render glad thanks for so great a gift:
you have sent your own ways into our regions.
10. X
Africanus has a hundred million, yet he hunts legacies.
Fortune gives too much to many, enough to none.
11. XI
Give greetings, Muse, to your Parthenius and mine:
for who drinks more freely from the Aonian stream?
Whose lyre comes brighter from the Pimpleian cave?
Whom does Phoebus love more of the Pierian flock?
And if perhaps—but this is scarcely to be hoped—he has leisure,
ask him to hand our poems to the leader himself,
and only to commend the timid and brief little book
with four words: "Your Rome reads this man."

title: Epigrams
text:
12. XII
You promise everything when you've drunk all night;
in the morning you provide nothing. Pollio, drink in the morning.
13. XIII
The rich have a kind of profit, Auctus, in their anger:
to hate costs less than to give.
14. XIV
Use the runaway horse more sparingly, I warn you,
Priscus, and don't go so violently after hares.
Often the hunter has paid the price to his quarry, and fallen
shaken from his fierce horse, never to return.
The plain too has its traps: though there be neither ditch nor mound
nor rocks, level ground is wont to deceive.
There'll be no lack of one to give you such spectacles,
but let him fall by a less envied fate.
If spirited dangers delight you, let's lie in wait for Tuscan
boars—that valour is safer.
What good to you are reckless reins? More often, Priscus,
it's been given to them to break a rider than a hare.
15. XV
Whatever was gleaming in the Parrhasian hall
has been given to our eyes and our gods.
Jupiter marvels at the Scythian
flames of green gold, and is amazed at the proud
king's luxuries and weighty playthings:
these are the cups that befit the Thunderer,
these are they that befit the Phrygian servant.
We are all now blessed, together with Jove;
but lately—it shames me, ah, it shames me to confess—
we were all poor, together with Jove.
16. XVI
You sold, Labienus, three little fields;
you bought, Labienus, three catamites:
you bugger, Labienus, three little fields.
17. XVII
Why your fever won't leave you, Laetinus,
for so many days, you ask, and keep groaning.
It's carried about with you and bathes with you alike;
it dines on mushrooms, oysters, sow's udder, boar;
it often gets drunk on Setine and often on Falernian,
and drinks no Caecuban except through snow-cooled water;
it reclines wreathed in roses and dark with balsam,
it sleeps on down and a purple couch.
Since it reclines so handsomely, since it lives so well at your house,
do you want your fever to go to Dama instead?

title: Epigrams
text:
18. XVIII
While you, Juvenal, perhaps wander restless
in the clamorous Subura,
or tread the hill of mistress Diana;
while across the thresholds of the more powerful
your sweat-soaked toga fans you, and the greater
and lesser Caelian wear you out as you roam:
me, after many Decembers come round again,
my Bilbilis, proud of its gold and iron,
has received and made a countryman.
Here lazily I cultivate, by sweet labour,
Boterdum and Platea—these are
the rougher names of Celtiberian lands—:
I enjoy a vast and shameless sleep,
which often not even the third hour breaks,
and now I pay myself back in full for whatever
I had stayed awake through three times ten years.
The toga is unknown, but at my request
the nearest garment from a broken chair is given.
When I rise, the hearth receives me, proud
with a heap from the neighbouring oak-wood,
which the bailiff's wife crowns with many a pot.
The hunter follows, but the kind
you'd wish to have with you in a secret wood;
the smooth bailiff doles out tasks to the boys
and asks to lay aside his long hair.
So I love to live, so I love to die.
19. XIX
In the baths Aemilius takes lettuce, eggs, mackerel,
and denies that he dines at home.
20. XX
Why Themison hasn't a wife, Fabullus,
you ask? He has a sister.
21. XXI
Who would think you, Marcella, a townswoman of grim Salo
and born in our regions?
So rare, so sweet is your wit. The Palatine will say,
if it has heard you even once, that you're its own;
no girl born in the heart of the Subura will rival you,
nor a nursling of the Capitoline hill;
nor will the glory of a foreign-born child soon arise
more fit to be a Roman bride.
You bid my longing for the mistress city
be gentler: you alone make Rome for me.
22. XXII
How unbecomingly one-eyed Philaenis is,
do you want me to tell you briefly, Fabullus?
Philaenis would be more becoming blind.

title: Epigrams
text:
23. XXIII
Teeth and hair—and you're not ashamed—you use, all bought.
What will you do for an eye, Laelia? That's not for sale.
24. XXIV
O pleasant solitude of my carriage,
a gift more welcome to me than coach
or chariot, gift of eloquent Aelianus!
Here you may, here, Iuvatus, speak
whatever comes to your mouth:
no black driver of a Libyan horse,
no girt-up runner goes ahead;
nowhere is there a muleteer: the ponies will keep silent.
O if Avitus were here to share it,
I'd not fear a third ear.
How well the whole day would pass like this!
25. XXV
When I ask you for money without a pledge, "I have none," you say;
yet, if my little field stands surety for me, you have it:
what you won't trust me with, Telesinus, your old comrade,
you trust to my cabbages and trees.
Look, Carus has charged you as defendant: let my little field attend.
You seek a companion for exile: let my little field go.
26. XXVI
You say you've been fucked by robbers,
Saenia: but the robbers deny it.
27. XXVII
I drink two ounces, you drink eleven, Cinna:
and you complain that we don't drink the same, Cinna?
28. XXVIII
Hermogenes is as great a thief of napkins
as Massa, I think, scarcely was of money;
though you watch his right hand and hold his left,
he'll find a way to make off with your napkin:
so the stag's breath sucks up the cold snake,
so Iris draws up the waters that will fall from on high.
Lately when discharge was sought for wounded Myrinus,
Hermogenes filched four napkins;
when the praetor wished to drop the chalk-white napkin,
Hermogenes stole the praetor's napkin.
No one had brought a napkin, while thefts were feared:
Hermogenes stole the cloth from the table.
And if even this is lacking, Hermogenes is not afraid
to strip the middle of the couches and the feet of the tables.
Though the spectacles glow with no small sun,
the awnings are drawn back when Hermogenes comes.
The anxious sailors hasten to furl their canvas,
whenever Hermogenes appears at the harbour.
The bald linen-clad priests flee, and the rattle-bearing throng,
when Hermogenes has stood among the worshippers.
Hermogenes never brought a napkin to dinner,
from dinner Hermogenes always carried one home.

title: Epigrams
text:
29. XXIX
Since you, a senator, tread sixty thresholds in the morning,
I seem to you an idle knight,
because I don't run about the city from first light
and carry home, weary, a thousand kisses.
But you do it to give new names to the purple calendar
or to seek the lands of the Nomads or the Cappadocians:
but for me, whom you force to break off my sleep in the middle
and to bear and endure the morning mud,
what's to be gained? When my straying foot comes out of broken leather
and a sudden shower of thick water falls,
and the home-born slave, called for, doesn't come with my stolen cloak,
a servant comes up to my chilled ear
and says, "Laetorius asks you to dine with him."
For twenty coins? Not I: I'd rather go hungry,
than that dinner be my wages while a province is yours,
and we do the same and not earn the same.
30. XXX
Aper is dry, sober; what's that to me?
That's how I praise a slave, not a friend.
31. XXXI
This grove, these springs, this woven shade of trailing
vine-shoots, this channelled stream of running water,
and the meadows and the rose-beds not to yield to twice-bearing Paestum,
and the herb that's green in January's month and doesn't freeze,
and the tame eel that swims in enclosed waters,
and the white tower that holds birds of the same hue,
are the gifts of my mistress: when I returned after seven lustres,
Marcella gave me this home and these little realms.
If Nausicaa would grant me her father's gardens,
I could say to Alcinous, "I prefer my own."
32. XXXII
O disgrace of the Julian Kalends,
I saw, Vacerra, your baggage, I saw it;
which, not held back for two years' rent,
your red-haired wife carried, with her seven locks,
and your white-haired mother with your huge sister.
I thought they were Furies risen from the night of Dis.
You followed these ahead, dry with cold and hunger,
and paler than aged boxwood,
the Irus of your times.
You'd think the Arician slope was on the move.
A three-legged cot went along and a two-legged table,
and with a lantern and an earthenware bowl
a chamber-pot was pissing through its broken side;
the neck of an amphora lay under a greening brazier;
that there'd been sprats or worthless mackerel
the shameless smell of the jar confessed,
such as scarce comes from a sea-water tank.
Nor was a square of Toulouse cheese lacking,
nor a four-year-old wreath of black pennyroyal
and bald ropes with garlic and onions,
nor your mother's pot full of vile resin,
with which the Summemmian wives are stripped of hair.
Why do you seek a house and mock the bailiffs,
when you could, Vacerra, live free of charge?
This parade of baggage belongs on the bridge.

title: Epigrams
text:
33. XXXIII
To buy boys Labienus sold his gardens.
Now Labienus has nothing but a fig-grove.
34. XXXIV
Thirty-four harvests I have spent
with you, Julius, if I remember rightly.
Of these the sweets are mixed with the bitter,
but still the pleasant were the more;
and if every pebble, this way and that,
distinct and two-coloured, were sorted out,
the white throng would beat the blacker.
If you'd avoid certain bitter things
and guard against sad bites of the heart,
make yourself too close a comrade to no one:
you'll rejoice less and you'll grieve less.
35. XXXV
As though you lived openly with me, Callistratus,
you're often used to tell me you've been buggered.
You're not so candid, Callistratus, as you want to be believed.
For whoever tells such things keeps more untold.
36. XXXVI
Four pounds of silver, or two, to a friend,
and a toga for the cold and a short cloak,
and now and then gold pieces clinking in the hand,
enough to last two Kalends—
because no one but you, Labullus, gives these,
you're not, believe me, a good man. What then?
To speak the truth, you're the best of the bad.
Give me back the Pisos and Senecas and Memmiuses
and Crispuses, but the earlier ones:
you'll become at once the last of the good.
Do you want to glory in running, in your feet?
Beat Tigris and swift Passerinus:
there's no glory in outrunning little donkeys.
37. XXXVII
You long too much to seem a man of sharp nose.
I want a man of nose, not one all polyps.
38. XXXVIII
This man, who paces day and night among the women's chairs,
too well known in the whole city,
gleaming of hair, dark with ointment, glistening with purple,
soft of face, broad of chest, smooth of leg,
who, a shameless companion, often clings to your wife—
there's no reason to fear him, Candidus: he doesn't fuck.
39. XXXIX
I hate you, Sabellus, because you're pretty.
A pretty fellow is a rancid thing—and a Sabellus.
In short, I'd rather have a war than a Sabellus.
May you waste away, pretty Sabellus!

title: Epigrams
text:
40. XL
You lie, I believe it: you recite bad poems, I praise them:
you sing, I sing: you drink, Pontilianus, I drink:
you fart, I pretend not to notice: you want to play at dice, I'm beaten:
there's one thing you do without me, and I keep silent.
Yet you provide me nothing at all. "When I'm dead," you say,
"I'll treat you well." I want nothing: but die.
41. XLI
It's not enough, Tucca, that you're a glutton:
you want both to be called one and to seem one.
42. XLII
Bearded Callistratus was married to rugged Afer,
on the same terms a virgin is wont to wed a man.
Torches blazed before them, bridal veils covered their faces,
nor were your words, Talassus, lacking to you.
A dowry too was named. Does this not yet seem to you,
Rome, enough? Are you waiting for him to give birth as well?
43. XLIII
You read me eloquent verses
on lewd matters, Sabellus, all too many,
such as neither the girls of Didymus know
nor the wanton little books of Elephantis.
There are in them new figures of love,
such as a desperate fornicator might dare,
what the catamites perform and keep silent,
in what entanglement five are coupled,
by what chain more are held together,
what is allowed when the lamp is put out.
It wasn't worth so much, your being eloquent.
44. XLIV
Unicus, you who bear a name joined to me by kindred
blood, and whose heart is near to mine in pursuits;
since you make poems yielding only to your brother,
you're no less in talent, but first in family love.
Lesbia could love you, with witty Catullus,
coaxing Corinna could follow you, after Naso.
Nor would the west winds fail, if it pleased you to set sail;
but you love the shore. This too you have of your brother's.
45. XLV
You who cover with a goatskin
the temples and crown of your bare, bald head,
he spoke wittily to you, Phoebus,
who said your skull was shod.

title: Epigrams
text:
46. XLVI
Difficult and easy, pleasant and bitter, you're the same:
I can't live with you, nor without you.
47. XLVII
Gallus and Lupercus sell their poems.
Now deny, Classicus, that poets are sane.
48. XLVIII
If you set out mushrooms and boar as though they were cheap things
and you think these aren't what I pray for, I'm willing:
but if you believe I'm made fortunate by them and want
me written down as heir for five Lucrine oysters, farewell.
The dinner's elegant, I admit, most elegant, but tomorrow
it'll be nothing—nay, today, nay, at once—nothing,
which the wretched sponge of a condemned mop may know,
or any dog and the broken pot beside the road:
this is the end of mullets and hares and sow's udder,
the sulphurous colour and the executioner feet.
Not the Alban revel would be worth so much to me,
nor the Capitoline banquets and those of the pontiffs;
let a god himself charge me with nectar, it'll turn to vinegar
and the treacherous flat wine of a Vatican cask.
Seek other guests, master of banquets,
whom the proud realms of your table may take:
let my own friend invite me to hasty cutlets:
this dinner, which I can return, pleases me.
49. XLIX
Linus, tutor of the long-haired throng,
whom rich Postumilla calls the master of her affairs
and to whom she entrusts
her gems, her gold, her wines, her concubines:
so may your patroness, proved by your unending loyalty,
prefer you to all others:
come, I pray, to the aid of my wretched madness
and guard now and then carelessly
those who badly scorch my heart,
whom both by night and by day I long,
in my desire, to see in my embrace,
the lovely, snow-white, matched, twin,
big ones—not boys, but pearls.
50. L
You have laurel-groves and plane-groves and airy pine-groves
and baths for more than one, all to yourself,
and a high portico stands for you on a hundred columns,
and the onyx gleams, trodden under your foot,
and the fleeing hoof claps the dusty hippodrome,
and the splash of falling water sounds everywhere;
long halls stand open. But there's nowhere a place
for diners or for sleep. How well you don't live!

title: Epigrams
text:
51. LI
That our Fabullinus is so often deceived,
do you wonder, Aulus? A good man is always a novice.
52. LII
Wont to wreathe his brows with the Pierian garland,
no less a voice celebrated by trembling defendants,
here he lies, here that Rufus of yours, Sempronia,
whose very ash burns with love of you.
You're told as a sweet tale in the Elysian field,
and Tyndareus' daughter herself is amazed at your abduction:
you're the better, who came back when your ravisher was deserted,
while she refused to follow her husband even when sought back.
Menelaus laughs and hears of the Trojan loves:
your abduction absolves Phrygian Paris.
When one day the glad places of the pious receive you,
no shade in the Stygian home will be better known:
Proserpina does not see the abducted as strangers, but loves them:
that love will win you the favour of the mistress.
53. LIII
Though you have so much money and wealth, Paternus,
as a rare citizen has,
you give away nothing and brood over your hoard,
like the great serpent the poets sing
was the guardian of the Scythian grove.
But the cause, as you yourself recall and boast,
is that you're the son of dire rapacity.
Do you really seek out fools and simpletons,
to mock and to rob of their wits?
To this vice you have always been a father.
54. LIV
Red of hair, black of face, short of foot, weak of eye,
you do a great thing, Zoilus, if you're good.
55. LV
Whoever bids you give yourselves for free, girls,
is the most tasteless and most shameless of men.
Don't give for free, but kiss for free.
This Aegle refuses, this, greedy, she sells.
But let her sell: to kiss well, how great a thing it is!
Yet she sells this too, and at no light plunder:
either she demands a pound of Cosmian perfume,
or eight new pieces from the fresh mint,
so the kisses won't be mute, won't be stingy,
won't deny entry with closed lips.
Yet she does one thing kindly, just one:
she who refuses to give a kiss for free
doesn't refuse to lick for free, Aegle.

title: Epigrams
text:
56. LVI
You fall ill ten times a year or oftener,
and this harms not you but us, Polycharmus:
for every time you get up, you ask your friends for recovery-gifts.
Have some shame: now, Polycharmus, fall ill just once.
57. LVII
Why I often make for the little fields of dry Nomentum
and the squalid home of my villa, you ask?
There's no place, Sparsus, for a poor man to think
