or to rest in the city. The schoolmasters deny him life
in the morning, the bakers at night,
the coppersmiths' hammers all day long;
here the idle money-changer rattles his dirty table
with a heap of Nero's coin,
there the beater of Spanish gold-dust
beats the worn stone with his gleaming club;
nor does the god-frenzied throng of Bellona cease,
nor the babbling shipwrecked man with his bandaged stump,
nor the Jew taught by his mother to beg,
nor the bleary-eyed hawker of sulphur-wares.
Who can count up the losses of lazy sleep?
He'll tell how many bronze pans the hands of the city beat,
when the cut Moon is flogged by the Colchian wheel.
You, Sparsus, know nothing of this, nor can you know,
luxurious in your Petilian realms,
where your level house looks down on the mountain-tops,
and there's countryside in the city, and a Roman vine-dresser,
and no greater vintage on the Falernian hill,
and within your boundary a wide drive for the chariot,
and sleep in the depths, and quiet broken by no
tongues, and no daylight unless let in.
Us the laughter of the passing crowd wakes,
and Rome is at our bedside. When, worn out with weariness,
it pleases us to sleep, we go to the villa.
58. LVIII
Your wife calls you a chaser of maids, and she herself
is a chaser of litter-bearers: you're a matched pair, Alauda.
59. LIX
Rome gives you so many kisses,
returned just now after fifteen years,
as Lesbia did not give Catullus.
The whole neighbourhood presses you, the hairy
farmer with his goatish kiss;
here the weaver besets you, there the fuller,
here the cobbler who's just kissed his leather,
here the master of a dangerous chin,
here the lame man on his right side, there the bleary-eyed,
and the cocksucker and the fresh cunt-licker.
Now it wasn't worth so much for you to return.

title: Epigrams
text:
60. LX
Day, child of Mars, on which we first saw
the rosy lamp and the great face of the starry god,
if you'll be ashamed to be honoured in the country and at green altars,
you who used to be honoured by me in the Latian city:
forgive me that I don't want to be a slave on my own Kalends,
and that I want to live on the day I was born.
To grow pale on one's own birthday, lest the hot water fail
for Sabellus; and that Alauda may drink clear unmixed wine,
to strain the muddy Caecuban through an anxious bag;
and to go to and fro among one's own tables;
to receive these and those, and rise the whole dinner long,
treading marble colder than ice:
what sense is it to endure and suffer of one's own accord
what you'd refuse if a king and master bade you do it?
61. LXI
That I'd make verses and a brief, lively poem
against you, you fear, Ligurra,
and you long to seem worthy of this fear.
But you fear in vain and long in vain.
Libyan lions rush upon bulls,
they're no trouble to butterflies.
I'd advise you to seek, if you toil to be read,
some drunken poet of a dark archway,
who writes with rough charcoal and crumbling chalk
poems that men read while shitting.
This brow of yours is not to be branded with my mark.
62. LXII
Great king of the ancient pole and of the former world,
under whom there was sluggish rest and no toil at all,
no lightning too regal nor men worthy of the lightning,
no earth split open to the Shades, but rich for itself:
glad and gracious, come to these solemn joys
of Priscus: it befits you to be present at your own rites.
You, best father, give back to his homeland, in the sixth winter,
peace-making Numa, returned from the Latian city.
Do you see how, like an Ausonian market, the procession
hangs for you, and how great an honour runs riot?
How no stinting hand and the coins of a lavish table,
what wealth, Saturn, is counted out for you?
And that there may be a reward for these deserts and greater thanks,
both a father and a frugal man thus honours your rites.
But you, holy one—so may you ever be loved in your December—
bid these days often return for him.

title: Epigrams
text:
63. LXIII
Corduba, richer than oil-rich Venafrum,
no less perfect than the Istrian jar,
you who surpass the sheep of white Galaesus,
false by no purple dye nor blood,
but with your flocks tinted in living colour:
tell your poet, I beg, to have some shame,
and not recite my little books for free.
I'd bear it, if a good poet did it,
to whom I could give pains in return.
A celibate corrupts without retaliation,
a blind man can't lose what he carries off:
nothing is worse than a naked robber:
nothing is safer than a bad poet.
64. LXIV
A cook who outdid his servants in face and hair,
Cinna made him. Cinna, you're a gluttonous man.
65. LXV
When beautiful Phyllis had given herself to me all night,
lavish in every way,
and in the morning I was thinking what gift to give,
whether a pound of Cosmus or of Niceros,
or a sharp weight of Baetic wool,
or ten yellow pieces from Caesar's mint:
embracing my neck and coaxing me with a kiss
as long as the marriages of doves,
Phyllis began to ask for a jar of wine.
66. LXVI
You bought your house for a hundred thousand,
which you want to sell for that sum or even less.
But with sly art you corrupt the buyer, Amoenus,
and the hovel lies hidden, ambitious with riches.
Jewelled couches gleam with prime tortoise-shell,
and rare slabs of Moorish citron-wood;
silver and gold a more-than-simple Delphic table bears;
boys stand there, whom I'd pray were my own masters.
Then you sound out two hundred thousand, and say it's not for less.
You sell a furnished house cheap, Amoenus.
67. LXVII
You, the May Ides, gave birth to Mercury,
on the August Ides Diana returns,
the October Ides Maro consecrated.
May you often keep the Ides, both these and those,
you who celebrate the Ides of great Maro.
68. LXVIII
Morning client, the reason I left the city,
if you're wise, you'd court ambitious halls.
I'm no advocate, nor fit for bitter lawsuits,
but lazy and older and a companion of the Muses;
leisure and sleep delight me, which great Rome
denied me: I'll go back, if there's no rest here either.

title: Epigrams
text:
69. LXIX
Just as with your tablets and goblets, Paulus,
you hold all your friends to be original masterpieces.
70. LXX
When the bandy-legged home-bred slave was lately carrying towels for Aper,
and the one-eyed old woman sat over his little toga,
and the ruptured rubber gave him a drop of oil,
he was a grim and harsh censor of the soused:
he kept shouting that the cups should be smashed and the Falernian poured out,
that a knight had just drunk after bathing.
But after three hundred thousand came from his old uncle,
he doesn't know how to go home sober from the baths.
O how much carved cups and five long-haired boys can do!
Then, when he was poor, Aper wasn't thirsty.
71. LXXI
You deny me nothing, Lygdus, when I ask:
yet once, Lygdus, you denied me nothing.
72. LXXII
Having bought acres of a little field hidden near the tombs
and the propped-up roof of a badly-built hovel,
you abandon, Pannychus, your urban lawsuits, your estate,
and the small but sure rewards of a worn toga.
Grain, millet, barley-gruel and beans you used to sell
as a man of business; now you buy them as a farmer.
73. LXXIII
You say I'm your heir, Catullus.
I won't believe it, Catullus, until I've read it.
74. LXXIV
While a Nile-borne convoy brings you crystal,
take cups from the Flaminian Circus.
Are these more daring, or those who send such
gifts? But there's a use in cheap glassware:
these embossed pieces, Flaccus, tempt no thief,
and aren't spoiled by too hot water.
What of it, that the guest drinks while his servant's at ease,
and the trembling hands haven't feared a mishap?
This too is something, that you'll toast in these,
if a cup, Flaccus, must be broken by you.
75. LXXV
Polytimus hastens to the girls;
unwilling, Hypnus confesses himself a boy;
Secundus has buttocks fed on acorns;
Dindymus is soft, but doesn't want to be;
Amphion could have been born a girl.
The charms and the pride of these
and their querulous airs, Avitus, I'd rather have
than five times two hundred thousand as a dowry.

title: Epigrams
text:
76. LXXVI
A jar is given for twenty coins, a peck for four pieces of bronze.
Drunk and bloated, the farmer has nothing.
77. LXXVII
While he greeted Jove with many prayers,
standing bent back right up onto his tiptoes,
Aethon farted in the Capitol.
Men laughed, but the father of the gods himself,
offended, punished his client with a three-night
dine-at-home sentence.
After this disgrace, poor little Aethon,
when he wants to come to the Capitol,
first seeks out the Paterclian privies
and farts ten and twenty times.
But although he's taken care by his cracking,
with clenched buttocks he greets Jove.
78. LXXVIII
I've written nothing against you, Bithynicus. You won't believe it
and bid me swear an oath? I'd rather give satisfaction.
79. LXXIX
I gave you many things you asked for;
I gave you more things than you asked for:
yet you don't stop asking me always.
Whoever denies nothing, Atticilla, sucks.
80. LXXX
So as not to praise the deserving, Callistratus praises everyone.
He for whom no one is bad, how can anyone be good?
81. LXXXI
On winter days and the holidays of Saturn,
poor Umber used to send me a little cloak;
now he sends me spelt-gruel: for he's become rich.
82. LXXXII
There's no escaping Menogenes in the baths and around
the bathhouse, however you may wish to, by every art.
He'll catch the warm ball with right hand and left,
so as to charge you often with the catches he made.
He'll gather and bring back the slack bladder from the dust,
and, even if he's already bathed, even if already in slippers.
If you take up your towels, he'll say they're whiter than snow,
though they be filthier than a baby's bib.
As you comb your scanty hairs with the cut comb,
he'll say you've arranged the locks of Achilles.
He'll himself bring you a swig from the dregs of a smoky flagon,
and keep gathering the sweat of your brow.
He'll praise everything, marvel at everything, until,
having endured a thousand vexations, you say, "Come!"

title: Epigrams
text:
83. LXXXIII
Fabianus, the mocker of ruptures,
whom all balls lately feared
as he spoke against swollen hydroceles,
more than two Catos could say,
suddenly in the Neronian baths
saw himself, poor wretch, and began to keep silent.
84. LXXXIV
I'd not wanted, Polytimus, to violate your hair,
but I'm glad to have granted this to your prayers.
Such were you, lately shorn Pelops, and you gleamed
with your locks laid aside, that the bride could see all the ivory.
85. LXXXV
You say buggerers' mouths smell.
If this is true, Fabullus, as you say:
what do you think cunt-lickers' mouths smell of?
86. LXXXVI
You have thirty boys and as many girls:
you have one prick, and it won't stand. What will you do?
87. LXXXVII
Cotta, having complained twice that he'd lost his slippers,
while he brings a careless home-born slave to his feet,
the only one to attend the poor man and make a crowd,
devised—a shrewd and cunning man—
a way not to suffer such a loss more often:
he began to go to dinner unshod.
88. LXXXVIII
Tongilianus has a nose: I know it, I don't deny it. But now
Tongilianus has nothing but a nose.
89. LXXXIX
That you bind your head with wool, Charinus,
it's not your ears that ache, but your hair.
90. XC
Maro made a vow for a sick friend—but loudly—
who had a heavy and burning semi-tertian fever,
that, if the sick man were not sent to the Stygian shades,
a welcome victim should fall to great Jove.
The doctors began to promise certain recovery.
Now Maro makes vows, so as not to pay his vow.
91. XCI
Since you share a bed with your husband, Magulla,
and share a catamite too,
why, tell me, do you not share a servant as well?
You sigh; the reason is, you fear the wine-jar.
92. XCII
You often ask, Priscus, what sort I'll be,
if I become wealthy and suddenly grow powerful.
Do you think anyone can describe his future character?
Tell me, if you became a lion, what sort would you be?

title: Epigrams
text:
93. XCIII
By what method she could kiss her lover
in her husband's presence, Fabulla found out.
She keeps kissing a little fool:
him, drenched with many kisses, the lover
snatches at once, and, filled up with his own,
sends back straightway to the laughing lady.
How much greater a fool is the husband!
94. XCIV
I was writing epic; you began to write: I gave way,
lest my poems should stand as rivals to yours.
My Thalia transferred herself to the tragic buskins:
you too fitted the long train to yourself.
I moved the strings of the lyre, refined by Calabrian Muses:
ambitious one, you snatch the new quills from me.
I venture satires: you labour to be a Lucilius.
I play at light elegies: you play at the same too.
What could be less? I began to fashion epigrams:
hence too my palm is now sought by you.
Choose what you don't want—for what shame is it to want everything?—
and if there's anything you don't want, Tucca, leave it to me.
95. XCV
The most pathic little books of Mussetius,
which rival the Sybaritic little books,
and the pages dipped in itching salt,
read, Instantius Rufus; but let your girl
be with you, lest you sing the wedding-song
with lustful hands
and become a husband without a woman.
96. XCVI
Since your husband's life and fidelity are known to you,
and no woman oppresses or troubles your bed,
why, foolish one, are you tormented, as if by rivals, over the servants,
in whom love is both brief and fleeting?
I'll prove the boys serve you more than their master:
they make it so that you're your husband's only woman;
they give what you, his wife, don't want to give. "Yet I do give it,"
you say, "lest my husband's wandering love should stray from our bed."
It's not the same thing: I want a Chian fig, I don't want a marisca:
in case you doubt which is the Chian, yours is the marisca.
A matron and a wife ought to know her own limits:
yield their own part to the boys, use your own part.

title: Epigrams
text:
97. XCVII
Though you have a wife such as a shameless husband
could scarcely ask for in his prayers,
rich, noble, learned, chaste,
you burst your flank, Bassus, but on long-haired boys,
whom you got with your wife's dowry.
And so the prick, bought back for many thousands,
returns to its mistress and goes limp;
nor, roused by coaxing words,
nor begged with a soft thumb, does it rise.
Have some shame at last, or let's go to court.
This isn't yours, Bassus: you sold it.
98. XCVIII
Baetis, your hair wreathed with an olive-bearing garland,
you who dye golden fleeces in your gleaming waters;
whom Bromius loves, whom Pallas loves; for whom Albula, ruler
of the waters, spreads a ship-bearing path through the straits:
with glad omens may Instantius enter your shores,
and may this year, as the last, go well for the peoples here.
He's not unaware what a burden it is to follow Macer:
he who measures his own weight can bear it.

title: Epigrams
text:
1. I
So that mackerel-fry want no wrapper and olives no overcoat,
And the grubby bookworm fear no pinching famine,
Squander, my Muses, the Nile's papyrus — my loss is your ruin:
Look, drunken midwinter calls for fresh jokes.
My dice-throw fights no duel with the high-and-mighty piece,
My ivory shakes no double-six against the dog:
This page is my walnuts, this page is my dice-box;
Such gaming brings me neither loss nor gain.
2. II
Turn up your nose as long as you like, be one big nose,
The kind Atlas himself, asked to bear it, would refuse,
And go ahead, outsneer the great sneerer Latinus:
Still you can't say more against my trifles
Than I have said myself. Why grind tooth on tooth
By gnawing? You need meat, if you want to be full.
Don't waste your effort: keep your venom for the men
Who admire themselves — I know these things are nothing.
Yet even this "nothing" is not too little, if you come
With a fair ear and no scowl on your morning face.
3. III
The whole crowd of Xenia in this slender little book
Will cost you four coins, bought and paid.
Four is too much? It could go for two,
And the bookseller Tryphon would still turn a profit.
These couplets you may send to your guests as gifts,
If coins are as scarce for you as they are for me.
You will find each thing's own name written above it as a heading:
Skip whatever is not to your taste.
4. IV. Incense
That Germanicus may rule heaven's court late, and long
Reign on earth — offer pious incense to Jove.
5. V. Pepper
The waxy fig-pecker glowing with its plump rump,
When luck deals it your way — if you're wise, add pepper.
6. VI. Spelt-Gruel
I send spelt-gruel; let a rich man send you mead.
If the rich man won't send it, you'll have to buy.
7. VII. Beans
If the pale beans foam for you in their red crock,
You can often turn down the dinners of the fancy.
8. VIII. Coarse Meal
Steep your plebeian pots with Clusine porridge,
So that, full, you may drink sweet new wine on an empty stomach.
9. IX. Lentils
Take this lentil, the Nile's gift, sent from Pelusium:
It is cheaper than gruel, dearer than the bean.
10. X. Fine Flour
You could count neither the merits nor the uses of fine flour,
Since it serves the baker as often as the cook.
11. XI. Barley
Take what the muleteer would give to his uncomplaining mules.
This gift I gave the innkeeper, not to you.
12. XII. Grain
Take three hundred bushels from the Libyan tenant's harvest,
So that the field by the city does not starve.
13. XIII. Beets
To give the bland beets flavor — the dinners of workmen —
How often, alas, the cook will cry for wine and pepper!
14. XIV. Lettuce
The lettuce that used to close our grandfathers' dinners,
Tell me — why does it now begin our feasts?
15. XV. Smokeless Firewood
If the country near Nomentum is your estate,
Bring your own firewood to the villa, rustic — my advice.
16. XVI. Turnips
These turnips I give you, that rejoice in winter's frost,
Romulus is wont to eat — up there in heaven.
17. XVII. A Bundle of Cabbage-Shoots
Lest the pallid stalks turn your stomach,
Let the green cabbage be greened in soda-water.
18. XVIII. Cut Leeks
As often as you've eaten the strong-smelling threads
Of Tarentine leek, give your kisses with lips sealed.
19. XIX. Headed Leeks
Wooded Aricia sends the finest leeks:
See the green hair upon the snow-white stalk.
20. XX. Wild Turnips
The Amiternine field rears these in its happy gardens:
You may eat the Nursine kind more sparingly.
21. XXI. Asparagus
The tender shoot that grew in seaside Ravenna
Will be no more pleasing than wild asparagus.

title: Epigrams
text:
22. XXII. Hard-Skinned Grapes
A grape unfit for cups and useless to Lyaeus,
Yet to you, if you're not drinking, I'll be nectar.
23. XXIII. Chian Figs
The Chian, like aged wine that Setia sent,
Carries with it both its own liquor and its own salt.
24. XXIV. Quinces
If quinces soaked in Attic honey
Are set before you, say: "These honey-apples please me."
25. XXV. Pine-Nuts
We are Cybele's fruit: keep your distance, traveler,
Lest our downfall crash upon your luckless head.
26. XXVI. Service-Berries
We are service-berries, binding too-loose bowels:
You'll give this fruit to a boy more fittingly than to yourself.
27. XXVII. A Branch of Date-Palms
The golden date is held out on Janus' Kalends;
Yet this is wont to be a poor man's gift.
28. XXVIII. A Jar of Syrian Figs
These that came to you packed in a twisted cone —
Had the cottana been bigger, they'd have been figs.
29. XXIX. A Jar of Damson Plums
Take plums wrinkled with the rot of foreign age:
They tend to ease the burden of a costive belly.
30. XXX. Luna Cheese
Cheese stamped with the image of Etruscan Luna
Will furnish a thousand lunches for your boys.
31. XXXI. Vestine Cheese
If you'd take a frugal breakfast without meat,
This lump comes to you from the Vestine flock.
32. XXXII. Smoked Cheese
Not every hearth, not every kind of smoke,
But the cheese that has drunk Velabran smoke has flavor.
33. XXXIII. Trebulan Cheeses
Trebula bore us; a double grace commends us,
Whether we are tamed by gentle flame or by water.
34. XXXIV. Onion-Bulbs
Since your wife is an old woman and your parts are dead,
Bulbs can do nothing for you but fill your belly.
35. XXXV. Lucanian Sausage
I, the Lucanian, come as daughter of the Picene sow:
From me a welcome garland rings the snow-white gruel.
36. XXXVI. A Small Box of Olives
This olive, brought up smuggled from the Picene presses,
Both opens the feast and the same olive ends it.
37. XXXVII. Citrons
Either these came from the leaves of the Corcyrean garden,
Or these were the fruit of the Massylian dragon.
38. XXXVIII. Beestings
What the shepherd stole, while the kids could not yet stand,
From the mothers' first milk — beestings — we give.
39. XXXIX. A Kid
The wanton beast, no friend to the green vine,
Pays the price; tender as he was, he has already harmed the god.
40. XL. Eggs
If the white flows round the saffron yolks,
Let Spanish mackerel-sauce season the eggs.
41. XLI. A Suckling Pig
Let him set before me a nursling fed on pure milk
By its sluggish mother; let the rich man feed on Aetolian boar.
42. XLII. Cling-Stone and Stoneless Fruit
We do not give you stoneless fruit and clingstones from Libyan boughs,
But from Nomentan trees.
43. XLIII. The Same
Stoneless fruit, gathered from suburban boughs, is sent,
And home-grown clingstones too. What have you to do with Libya's?
44. XLIV. A Sow's Udder
You'd think it not yet an udder: so from its generous teat
It flows, and the nipple swells with living milk.
45. XLV. Pullets
If we had Libyan birds and Phasian pheasants,
You'd be getting those — but now take the fowls of the yard.
46. XLVI. Early Peaches
We were once cheap peaches on our mother boughs:
Now, grafted, we are precious peaches.
47. XLVII. Picentine Loaves
Picentine grain so swells with snowy juice
That a light sponge bloats when it takes up water.
48. XLVIII. Mushrooms
It's easy to send silver and gold, a cloak and a toga:
Mushrooms — those are hard to send.
49. XLIX. Fig-Peckers
Since the fig feeds me, since I graze on sweet grapes,
Why didn't the grape, rather, give me my name?

title: Epigrams
text:
50. L. Truffles
We truffles, who burst the nursing earth with our tender crown,
Are the fruit second only to mushrooms.
51. LI. A Dozen Thrushes
A garland woven of roses, perhaps, for you, or rich nard,
But for me a garland made of thrushes is what pleases.
52. LII. Ducks
Let the whole duck be served; but only in the breast
And neck has it flavor: give the rest back to the cook.
53. LIII. Turtle-Doves
When I have a fat turtle-dove, goodbye, lettuce:
And keep your snails to yourself. I've no wish to spoil my appetite.
54. LIV. A Ham
Let mine be Cerretane, or it may be one sent
From the Menapii: let the elegant gorge on gammon.
55. LV. A Gammon
It's fresh: hurry, don't keep your dear friends waiting,
For with an old gammon I want nothing to do.
56. LVI. A Sow's Womb
You, perhaps, are more taken with a maiden hog's:
The mother-sow's womb, from a pregnant pig, takes me.
57. LVII. Egyptian Beans
You'll laugh at the Nile's vegetable and its clinging strings,
When you drag the troublesome threads with bite and hand.
58. LVIII. Goose-Liver
Look how the liver swells, bigger than the big goose itself!
Amazed, you'll say: "Where, I ask, did this grow?"
59. LIX. Dormice
The whole winter through I sleep, and I am fatter
At that season when nothing but sleep feeds me.
60. LX. Rabbits
The rabbit delights to dwell in burrowed caves.
He it was who showed the foe the hidden paths.
61. LXI. Heath-Cocks
Among the flavors of birds, the taste of the Ionian
Heath-cock is said to be the first.
62. LXII. Fattened Hens
The easy hen is fed on sweet meal,
And fed in the dark. The gullet is ingenious.
63. LXIII. Capons
Lest the cock grow lean from a too-drained loins,
He has lost his stones. Now he shall be a cock for me.
64. LXIV. The Same
In vain the hen submits to her barren mate.
This bird should have belonged to mother Cybele.
65. LXV. Partridges
This bird, set out most rarely on Ausonian tables,
You often watch at play in your fish-pond.
66. LXVI. Doves
Do not wrong the tender doves with perjured tooth,
If the rites of the Cnidian goddess have been entrusted to you.
67. LXVII. Wood-Pigeons
Ringed wood-pigeons slacken and dull the loins:
Let no man eat this bird who hopes to be lusty.
68. LXVIII. Wood-Larks
The yellow-green bird is fooled by limed reeds and by nets,
While the green grape, still raw, swells with its young wine.
69. LXIX. Marten-Skins
Umbria never gave us Pannonian martens:
Pudens would rather send these gifts to his mistress.
70. LXX. Peacocks
You marvel each time it unfolds its jeweled wings —
And can you, hard-hearted, hand this over to the cruel cook?
71. LXXI. Flamingos
My red plumage gives me my name, but my tongue
Is the gourmet's delight. What if my tongue could chatter?
72. LXXII. Pheasants
I was first carried over in the Argo's hull:
Before, I knew nothing but the Phasis.
73. LXXIII. Guinea-Fowl
Though Hannibal had eaten his fill of Roman goose,
The barbarian himself never ate his own native birds.
74. LXXIV. Geese
This was the bird that saved the temple of Tarpeian Jove.
You marvel? He had not yet made the bird a god.
75. LXXV. Cranes
You'll throw your lines into disorder, the whole letter will not fly,
If you lose a single one of Palamedes' birds.
76. LXXVI. Woodcocks
Woodcock or partridge — what does it matter, if the flavor's the same?
The partridge costs more. So it tastes the better.
77. LXXVII. Swans
With failing tongue the swan tunes its sweet songs,
Itself the singer of its own funeral.
78. LXXVIII. Purple Coots
Has so small a bird the name of a great giant?
And it has the name of the Green-faction's Porphyrion too.

title: Epigrams
text:
79. LXXIX. Live Mullets
The mullet breathes in the brought-in sea, but is sluggish now;
It grows faint. Give it live water: it will be strong.
80. LXXX. Lampreys
The great lamprey that swims in the Sicilian deep
Cannot dive when its skin is scorched by the sun.
81. LXXXI. Turbots
Though the broad dish carries a turbot,
Still the turbot is broader than the dish.
82. LXXXII. Oysters
I have just come, a shell drunk with Baian Lucrine:
Now in my luxury I thirst for noble garum.
83. LXXXIII. Prawns
The blue Liris loves us, whom Marica's wood
Shelters: from there we prawns come, a vast throng.
84. LXXXIV. Parrot-Wrasse
This parrot-wrasse, which comes half-eaten from the sea's waves,
Is good in its innards; the rest tastes cheap.
85. LXXXV. Coracinus
You are first snatched up, coracinus, in the Nile's market:
No fish has higher glory for the Pellaean gullet.
86. LXXXVI. Sea-Urchins
Though it pricks your fingers with its sharp shell,
Once the rind is off, the sea-urchin will be soft.
87. LXXXVII. Murex-Shells
Dyed with our blood, ungrateful man, you put on
Your cloaks — and that's not enough: we are food as well.
88. LXXXVIII. Gudgeons
Though banquets be lavish in the Venetian lands,
The gudgeon is wont to be the start of the dinner.
89. LXXXIX. Bass
The woolly bass takes in the mouth of Euganean Timavus,
Fed on fresh waters mingled with the sea's salt.
90. XC. Gilt-Head Bream
Not every gilt-head earns the praise and the price,
But only the one whose sole food is the Lucrine shell.
91. XCI. Sturgeon
Send the sturgeon to the Palatine tables:
Let rare gifts grace the ambrosial feasts.
92. XCII. Hares
Among birds the thrush, if my judgment counts for anything,
Among four-footed beasts the hare is the first tidbit.
93. XCIII. Boar
The bristled beast, dreaded in the Diomedean fields,
That fell to the Aetolian spear — such was its kind.
94. XCIV. Does
The boar is feared for its tusk, horns defend the stag:
We unwarlike does — what are we but prey?
95. XCV. Oryx
Not the least prey of the morning's wild beasts,
The fierce oryx — how many dogs' deaths it costs me!
96. XCVI. Stag
This was that stag tamed by your halter, Cyparissus.
Or was this rather your stag, Silvia?
97. XCVII. The Wild-Ass Foal
While the wild ass is young and the foal still grazes
On its mother alone, it has this name — babyish, but brief.
98. XCVIII. Wild She-Goat
You'll see the wild goat hanging from the cliff's height,
And hope it will fall: it looks down in scorn on the dogs.
99. XCIX. Gazelle
You'll give a pet gazelle to your little son:
The crowd, tossing their togas, is wont to ask for it.
100. C. Wild Ass
Here's a handsome wild ass: the hunt of Erythraean
Tusk must be staged: now away with the curtains.
101. CI. Venafran Oil
This the Campanian Venafrum's berry sweated for you:
Whenever you take perfume, this scents it too.
102. CII. Allies' Garum
From the first blood of the still-gasping mackerel
Take the proud garum — a costly gift.
103. CIII. A Jar of Fish-Brine
I am, I confess, the daughter of the Antibes tunny:
Were I the mackerel's, I'd not have been sent to you.
104. CIV. Attic Honey
This noble nectar was sent you by the bee
That plunders the woods of Theseus' Pallas-loved Hymettus.
105. CV. Sicilian Honeycombs
When you give Sicilian combs from the hills of central Hybla,
You may call them Cecropian if you like.
106. CVI. Raisin-Wine
The Cnossian vintage of Minoan Crete
Bore you this, the mead that tends to be the poor man's drink.
107. CVII. Pitched Wine
That this pitched wine has come from vine-bearing Vienna,
Do not doubt: Romulus himself sent it to me.

title: Epigrams
text:
108. CVIII. Mead
You stir Attic honey into nectarous Falernian.
This drink deserves to be mixed by Ganymede.
109. CIX. Alban
This the mild vintage from Caesar's cellars sent,
The vintage that pleases itself on the Julian hill.
110. CX. Surrentine
You drink Surrentine? Take neither painted murra-ware
Nor gold: these wines will give you cups of their own.
111. CXI. Falernian
The Massic came from the presses of Sinuessa:
You ask under what consul it was laid down? There was none.
112. CXII. Setine
Setia, hanging high, that looks on the Pomptine plains,
Sent these old casks from her tiny town.
113. CXIII. Fundan
This Fundan the happy autumn of Opimius bore.
The consul pressed the must and drank it himself.
114. CXIV. Trifoline
I am not of the first rank, I admit — Trifoline Lyaeus —
Yet among wines I'll be the seventh vine.
115. CXV. Caecuban
The noble Caecuban is mellowed at Fundan Amyclae,
And the vine, born in the middle of the marsh, grows green.
116. CXVI. Signine
You'll drink Signine to bind a loose bowel?
Lest it bind too much, let your thirst be sparing.
117. CXVII. Mamertine
If Mamertine of Nestor's age be given you,
It can bear whatever name you like.
118. CXVIII. Tarraconese
Tarraco, yielding only to Campanian Lyaeus,
Bore these wines that rival the Tuscan casks.
119. CXIX. Nomentan
The Nomentan vintage gives you my Bacchus:
If Quintus loves you, you'll drink something finer.
120. CXX. Spoletine
You'd rather have the matured wine of Spoletine flasks
Than drink the new Falernian must.
121. CXXI. Pelignian
The Pelignian tenants send their muddied Marsic:
Don't you drink it — let your freedman do that.
122. CXXII. Vinegar
Don't think the jar of Nile vinegar beneath you:
When it was wine, it was cheaper still.
123. CXXIII. Massilian
When your dole strikes a hundred citizens off the list,
You may set out the smoky wines of Massilia.
124. CXXIV. Caeretan
Let Nepos serve Caeretan, you'll think it Setine.
He doesn't serve the crowd: he drinks it with three friends.
125. CXXV. Tarentine
Aulon, noble in its wools and happy in its vines,
Gives precious fleeces to you, wines to me.
126. CXXVI. Perfume
Never leave perfume or wine to your heir.
Let him have the cash — give all of these to yourself.
127. CXXVII. Rose-Garlands
Midwinter, Caesar, gives you these hurried garlands:
Once the rose was spring's; now it has become yours.
1. I
While the knight and his lord the senator delight in their dinner-suits,
And the freedman's cap suits our Jove well;
While the slave fears no aedile as he rattles the dice-box,
Seeing the icy ponds so near at hand:
Take the alternating lots of rich and poor:
Let each guest give his own gifts to his own.
"These are trifles and trumpery, and things cheaper still."
Who doesn't know it? Or who denies what's so plain?
But what better to do, Saturn, on your soggy days,
Which your own son gave you in place of heaven?
Would you have me write of Thebes, or Troy, or wicked Mycenae?
"Play," you say, "with nuts." I've no wish to lose my nuts.
2. II
At whatever point you like you can end this little book:
Every piece is wrapped up in two lines.
You ask why headings are written in? I'll explain:
So that, if you prefer, you may read the headings alone.
3. III. Citron-Wood Writing-Tablets
Had we not been cut into thin leaves of wood,
We'd be the noble burden of a Libyan tusk.
4. IV. Five-Leaved Tablets
The lord's happy threshold steams with slaughtered bullocks
When high honor is granted on the fivefold wax.
5. V. Ivory Writing-Tablets
Lest the dull wax darken your tired eyes,
Let black lettering paint the snow-white ivory.

title: Epigrams
text:
6. VI. Three-Leaved Tablets
Then you'll think our triple tablets no cheap gift,
When your girl writes on them that she will come.
7. VII. Parchment Tablets
Take these for wax, though it be called parchment:
You'll erase them whenever you want to write afresh.
8. VIII. Vitellian Tablets
Though a girl has not yet read these,
She knows what the Vitellian tablets want.
9. IX. The Same
Because you see them so small, you think they're sent to a girl.
You're wrong: this tablet asks for money too.
10. X. Larger Sheets
There's no reason to think the gift a paltry one,
When a poet gives you blank sheets of paper.
11. XI. Letter-Paper
Whether sent to a slight acquaintance or a dear comrade,
This paper is wont to call them all its own.
12. XII. Ivory Money-Boxes
These boxes it is wrong to fill with anything
But yellow coin: let cheap wood carry silver.
13. XIII. Wooden Money-Box
If anything is still left in the dregs of our little box,
It will be a gift. There's nothing? Then the box itself will be.
14. XIV. Ivory Dice
When no die has shown you the same face twice,
You'll say I have given you a great gift.
15. XV. Gaming-Dice
Let me, the die, not equal the dice in number, so long
As my throw is often bigger than theirs.
16. XVI. The Dice-Tower
The cheating hand that knows how to throw loaded dice,
If it throws through me, will gain nothing but wishes.
17. XVII. The Gaming-Board
On this side the counter is scored by twice-six pips;
On this the discolored piece dies to a twin foe.
18. XVIII. Counters
If you play the wars of the cunning brigands,
This piece of glass will be your soldier and your foe.
19. XIX. Nuts
Gambling with nuts seems small and harmless;
Yet often it has stripped boys of their backsides.
20. XX. A Pen-Case
Drawing the case, remember to arm it with pens:
We've given the rest; you supply the lighter things.
21. XXI. A Stylus-Case
Here you'll have a stylus-case armed with its own iron:
Give it to a boy, and it will be no slight gift.
22. XXII. A Toothpick
Mastic is better: but if you lack a leafy point,
A quill can clear your teeth.
23. XXIII. An Ear-Pick
If your ear is troubled by a fretful itch,
We give you arms suited to such cravings.
24. XXIV. A Golden Hairpin
Lest your damp hair stain the bright silk,
Let a pin fix and hold up your twisted locks.
25. XXV. Combs
What will this boxwood do, which will find no hair,
Given to you with its many-cleft teeth?
26. XXVI. Hair-Dye
Chattian foam fires the Teutonic hair:
You can be smarter with captive locks.
27. XXVII. Soap
If, gray-haired, you mean to change your long-lived locks,
Take Mattiac balls — but why, when you're bald?
28. XXVIII. A Sunshade
Take this parasol to beat the fierce sun:
Even if there's wind, your own canopy will shield you.
29. XXIX. A Broad-Brimmed Hat
I'll watch with you in the Pompeian theater:
For often the man in charge denies the people the awnings.
30. XXX. Hunting-Spears
They'll meet the boars and wait for the lions,
They'll go in against bears, if only the hand be steady.
31. XXXI. A Hunting-Knife
If you groan that your spear, with its long shaft, is knocked aside,
This short blade will go at the huge boar hand to hand.
32. XXXII. A Belt-Dagger
This will be the soldier's glory and an omen of welcome honor,
A weapon fit to gird a tribune's side.
33. XXXIII. A Dagger
A dagger, which a short groove marks with a curving vein.
Salo dipped it, hissing, in his icy waters.
34. XXXIV. A Sickle
A leader's settled peace bent me to gentle uses.
Now I belong to the farmer; before, I was the soldier's.

title: Epigrams
text:
35. XXXV. A Little Axe
When the sad auction was held to pay off debts,
This was bought for four hundred thousand.
36. XXXVI. Barber's Tools
These tools are fit for trimming your hair;
This one's good for long nails, that one for cheeks.
37. XXXVII. A Book-Box
Unless you give me choice little books,
I'll let in the moths and the savage worms.
38. XXXVIII. A Bundle of Reed-Pens
The Memphian land gives reeds handy for paper;
Let the rest of the marsh be woven into roofing for you.
39. XXXIX. A Bedroom Lamp
The sweet lamp, confidante of your couch:
Do whatever you please, I'll keep silent.
40. XL. A Tallow Candle
Fortune gave you the lamp's handmaid,
Who, wakeful, sees the whole darkness through.
41. XLI. A Many-Nozzled Lamp
Since I light the whole banquet with my flames
And carry so many nozzles, I am called a single lamp.
42. XLII. A Wax Candle
This candle will give you fire by night:
For your boy has filched away the lamp.
43. XLIII. A Corinthian Candelabrum
Candles gave us our ancient name:
The oily lamp knew nothing of our thrifty fathers.
44. XLIV. A Wooden Candelabrum
You see it's wood; unless you watch the lights, you'll have
A great blaze made out of your candelabrum.
45. XLV. A Peasant's Ball
This peasant-ball that swells with stiff feathers
Is less loose than the bladder-ball, less tight than the hard.
46. XLVI. A Triangle-Ball
If you know how to drive me back with skilled left hands,
I'm yours. You don't? Then, bumpkin, give back the ball.
47. XLVII. A Bladder-Ball
Off with you, young men: a gentle age suits me:
The bladder-ball befits boys at play, and old men.
48. XLVIII. Hand-Balls
The swift athlete snatches these up in Antaeus' dust,
Who makes his great neck big with futile toil.
49. XLIX. Dumb-Bells
Why do strong arms waste themselves on the foolish dumb-bell?
Digging a vineyard exercises men better.
50. L. An Oil-Cap
Lest the foul wrestler's grease soil your shining hair,
With this cap you can tuck away your oiled locks.
51. LI. Strigils
Pergamon sent these. Scrape yourself with the curved iron:
The fuller won't wear out your towels so often.
52. LII. A Horn Oil-Flask
A bullock lately wore me on his brow:
Yet you took me for true rhinoceros-horn.
53. LIII. A Rhinoceros
Lately admired in our lord's Ausonian arena,
Here for you is the one for whom the bull was a ball.
54. LIV. A Baby's Rattle
If some wailing little home-born slave hangs at your neck,
Let this chattering rattle shake in his tender hand.
55. LV. A Whip
You'll get nowhere with this whip, lash as you will,
If a horse of the purple team runs for you.
56. LVI. Tooth-Powder
What have I to do with you? Let a girl take me:
I'm not used to polishing bought-in teeth.
57. LVII. Behen-Nut Oil
What neither Virgil nor Homer names in song,
This is made of perfume and of the behen-nut.
58. LVIII. Saltpetre-Foam
Are you a rustic? You don't know my Greek name:
I'm called "foam of nitre." Are you Greek? Then aphronitrum.
59. LIX. Balsam-Oils
Balsams enchant me; these are the perfumes of men:
Reek of Cosmus' luxuries, you young wives.
60. LX. Bean-Meal Wash
A welcome gift it will be, and not useless to a chafed belly,
If you seek Stephanus' baths by broad daylight.
61. LXI. A Horn Lantern
I, the road's guide, am carried golden, my flame shut in,
And the small lamp is safe in my bosom.
62. LXII. A Bladder-Lantern
If I'm not horn, am I any dingier? Or does the man
Who comes against me take me for a bladder?
63. LXIII. Pipes
The drunken flute-girl splits us with her dripping cheeks:
Often she has two at once, often a single pipe.

title: Epigrams
text:
64. LXIV. A Reed-Pipe
Why do you laugh at me, joined of wax and reed?
Such was the first pipe ever built.
65. LXV. Woolen Slippers
If by chance there's no slave-boy and you fancy
Putting on slippers, the foot will be its own boy.
66. LXVI. A Breast-Band
You could have bound your chest with a bull's hide:
For that skin cannot hold those breasts of yours.
67. LXVII. A Peacock Fly-Whisk
That which keeps the filthy flies from licking your lunch
Was once the proud tail of an exquisite bird.
68. LXVIII. An Ox-Tail Fly-Whisk
If your clothes get dirtied with yellow dust,
Let this light tail brush it off with gentle strokes.
69. LXIX. A Rhodian Cake
Don't strike your erring slave's teeth with your fist:
Let him eat the cake bright Rhodes sent you.
70. LXX. A Priapus of Wheat-Bread
If you want to be full, you may eat our Priapus:
Though you gnaw his very loins, you'll stay clean.
71. LXXI. A Pig
This pig will make you a good Saturnalia,
Fattened among the foaming boars on acorns.
72. LXXII. A Sausage
The sausage that comes to you in midwinter's season
Had come seven days before Saturn's feast.
73. LXXIII. A Parrot
I, a parrot, will learn from you the names of others:
This I've learned to say of myself — "Hail, Caesar."
74. LXXIV. A Crow
Crow, the greeter — why are you held a fellator?
No member has ever entered your head.
75. LXXV. A Nightingale
Philomela weeps the crime of incestuous Tereus, and she
Who was a speechless girl is now a chattering bird.
76. LXXVI. A Magpie
I, the talking magpie, greet you, my master, with sure voice:
If you didn't see me, you'd deny I'm a bird.
77. LXXVII. An Ivory Cage
If you have such a bird as Catullus' beloved
Lesbia wept for, here it can live.
78. LXXVIII. A Medicine-Case
You see the medicine-case of the healing art: you'll have
Gifts that Paccius would wish were his own.
79. LXXIX. Whips
Play, wanton slaves, but only play:
These are sealed up for me, just for the five days.
80. LXXX. Canes
Hated too much by boys, dear to schoolmasters,
We are the wood made famous by Prometheus' gift.
81. LXXXI. A Beggar's Wallet
Lest it bring a beggar's lunch to the bearded naked man,
And sleep with a surly dog, the wallet asks for alms.
82. LXXXII. Brooms
The palm-broom bears witness it once was prized.
But now the cleaner-up has left the broom at leisure.
83. LXXXIII. An Ivory Back-Scratcher
This hand will guard your shoulders from the biting nuisance
Of the flea, or anything fouler than a flea.
84. LXXXIV. A Book-Rest
Lest your toga or cloak make your books bristle,
This fir will give your scrolls a long span of life.
85. LXXXV. A Peacock-Couch
The bird of Juno gives the bed-frame its most lovely name
With its painted feathers — but it was Argus before.
86. LXXXVI. A Saddle-Cloth
Hunter, take the housing for your girt-up cob:
For a sore tends to rise from a bare horse.
87. LXXXVII. A Dining-Couch
Take the crescent-couch inlaid with horn:
It seats eight; let whoever is your friend come.
88. LXXXVIII. A Relish-Tray
If you believe a female tortoise is set in me,
You're deceived: I'm the male prey of the sea.
89. LXXXIX. A Citron-Wood Table
Take these blessed woods, gifts of Atlas:
Whoever gives gifts of gold will give less.
90. XC. A Maple Table
I'm not curl-grained, nor a daughter of the Moorish wood,
But my wood too has known elegant feasts.
91. XCI. Ivory Tusks
You who carry the bulls' great bodies, you ask
Whether they could have borne up Libya's beams?
92. XCII. A Five-Foot Rule
The holm-oak rule, marked with points and closed with a sharp tip,
Often serves to expose the contractor's frauds.

title: Epigrams
text:
93. XCIII. Antique Cups
This is no recent glory, nor work of our chisel:
Mentor was the first to drink from these, while he made them.
94. XCIV. Bold Cups
We are the plebeian embossed-ware of bold glass,
And our jewel is not cracked by boiling water.
95. XCV. A Chased Golden Bowl
Though I redden, high-born, with Galician metal,
I glory more in the art: for this is Mys' labor.
96. XCVI. Vatinian Cups
Take the cheap memorial of the cobbler Vatinius —
A cup; but his nose was longer.
97. XCVII. Gold-Inlaid Platters
Don't disgrace the big gold platters with a little mullet:
At the very least it should weigh two pounds.
98. XCVIII. Arretine Ware
We warn you, don't too much scorn Arretine ware:
Porsena was elegant with Tuscan earthenware.
99. XCIX. A Basket
I, a basket, came barbarian from the painted Britons;
But now Rome would rather call me her own.
100. C. A Drinking-Bowl
If the land of learned Catullus is not unknown to you,
You've drunk Raetian wines from my crock.
101. CI. A Mushroom-Dish
Though mushrooms have given me so noble a name,
I serve — for shame, alas! — the first-cut cabbage-shoots.
102. CII. Surrentine Cups
Take cups born from no cheap dust,
But the smooth chiseled work of the Surrentine wheel.
103. CIII. A Snow-Strainer
Break my Setine wine, I advise, with our snow:
With cheaper wine you can wet the linen.
104. CIV. A Snow-Bag
Our linens too know how to thin the snow:
No water leaps from your strainer colder.
105. CV. Serving-Jugs
Cold won't be wanting, nor hot, to him who asks.
But you — spare us your game of fastidious thirst.
106. CVI. An Earthen Pitcher
Here a red pitcher with a splayed handle is given you.
The Stoic Fronto used to ask for cold water in this.
107. CVII. Wine-Baskets
The Satyrs love us, Bacchus loves us, the drunken tigress,
Trained to lick its master's drenched feet.
108. CVIII. Saguntine Cups
What no anxious servant need hold and keep,
Take — cups made of Saguntine clay.
109. CIX. Jeweled Cups
See how the gold gleams jeweled with Scythian fires.
How many fingers this cup has stripped!
110. CX. A Drinking-Flask
From this jewel, which keeps the name of Cosmus,
You may drink, voluptuary, if your thirst is for spikenard.
111. CXI. Crystal Ware
While you fear to break it, you'll break the crystal: hands
Too careless and too anxious both go wrong.
112. CXII. A Glass Storm-Cloud
The cloud that comes from Jove will pour rich waters
For mixing in the cups: this will give you wine.
113. CXIII. Murra-Ware
If you drink hot, the murra suits burning Falernian
And the flavor turns out better than the neat wine.
114. CXIV. A Cuman Bowl
This bowl, ruddy with Cuman clay,
The chaste Sibyl sent you, her fellow townswoman.
115. CXV. Glass Cups
You see the wit of the Nile: how often, while its maker
Longs to add more, ah, he has ruined the work!
116. CXVI. A Snow-Flask
You drink Spoletine, or wine laid down in Marsian cellars:
What do you want with the noble chill of boiled water?
117. CXVII. The Same
Not to drink snow, but to drink fresh water
Brewed from snow — that is ingenious thirst's invention.
118. CXVIII. The Same
Mixing the smoke of Massilia with snow-cooled waves —
Go easy, boy, lest your water cost you more.
119. CXIX. An Earthen Chamber-Pot
While I'm called for with a snap of fingers and the slave delays,
Oh, how often the bolster has become my rival!
120. CXX. A Silver Spoon
Though knights and senators call me a ligula,
The unschooled grammarians call me a lingula.
121. CXXI. Snail-Spoons
I'm handy for snails, but no less useful for eggs.
Do you know, then, why I'm rather called a snail-spoon?

title: Epigrams
text:
122. CXXII. Rings
Once a frequent, now a rare, friend gives us.
Happy the man whose comrade is a knight not stranger-born.
123. CXXIII. A Ring-Case
Often the heavy ring slips from greasy fingers,
But your gem will be safe in my keeping.
124. CXXIV. A Toga
The Romans, lords of the world, the nation of the gown,
He made, who gave the stars to his great father.
125. CXXV. The Same
If you find it easy to lose your morning sleep,
The dole will often come with a threadbare toga.
126. CXXVI. A Greatcoat
It's a poor man's gift, but no poor man's use:
This greatcoat we send you in place of a mantle.
127. CXXVII. Dark Canusian Wool
This Canusian, just like clouded mead,
Will be your gift. Be glad: it won't soon turn old.
128. CXXVIII. A Hooded Cape
Gaul clothes you in a Santonian hooded cape.
It was lately the cloak of long-tailed monkeys.
129. CXXIX. Red Canusian Wool
Rome dresses more in dark, Gaul in red,
And this color pleases boys and soldiers.
130. CXXX. A Leather Cape
Though you set out on the road under an ever-clear sky,
Let the leather never fail you against sudden rains.
131. CXXXI. Scarlet Cloaks
If you back the Blues or Greens, why take scarlet?
Take care lest that lot make you a turncoat.
132. CXXXII. A Felt Cap
If I could, I'd wish to have sent whole cloaks:
As it is, I send a gift only for your head.
133. CXXXIII. Baetic Cloaks
My wool tells no lies, I'm not changed in the cauldron.
Let Tyrian dyes please thus: my own sheep dyed me.
134. CXXXIV. A Breast-Band
Band, hold in check your mistress' growing breasts,
So that there be something for our hand to grasp and cover.
135. CXXXV. White Cloaks
We commend ourselves by their use at the amphitheater,
When the white cloak covers the chilly togas.
136. CXXXVI. Dinner-Clothes
We know no courts and no court-summonses:
Our task is to recline on painted couches.
137. CXXXVII. A Neck-Wrap
If perhaps I give you a little book to recite,
Let this neck-wrap stand surety for your ears.
138. CXXXVIII. A Frieze-Mantle
In wintertime smooth fabrics are not much use:
My shaggy nap warms your cloaks.
139. CXXXIX. A Hand-Towel
Let shaggy linens better guard your citron table:
There can be a ring-mark on our table-tops.
140. CXL. Liburnian Hoods
You never knew, you fool, how to attach cloaks to us:
You'd put on white — strip off the green ones.
141. CXLI. Cilician Foot-Socks
No wool gave these, but the beard of a smelly he-goat:
The sole can hide in the Cinyphian fold.
142. CXLII. A Dinner-Suit
While the toga is glad to rest through the five days,
You may by your own right put on this attire.
143. CXLIII. Paduan Tunics
Paduan triple-weaves use up much wool,
And a saw could cut the thick tunics.
144. CXLIV. A Sponge
This sponge falls to you by lot, useful for wiping tables,
Light as it is when it swells with squeezed-out water.
145. CXLV. A Frieze Cloak
Such whiteness is in me, such grace of nap,
That you'd want to put me on even in mid-harvest.
146. CXLVI. A Bolster
Dip your head in Cosmus' nard, and the bolster will smell of it:
When the hair loses the perfume, the feather keeps it.
147. CXLVII. Frieze Bed-Coverlets
The shaggy spreads gleam with purple tapestries.
What use, if your old wife freezes you?
148. CXLVIII. Blankets
Lest the bare couch lie open with no spread,
We sisters have come, joined, to you.
149. CXLIX. A Shoulder-Wrap
I fear the big-bosomed; hand me to a tender girl,
That the linen may enjoy a snow-white breast.
150. CL. Damask Bedspreads
This the Memphian land gives you as a gift: Babylon's needle
Is already beaten by the loom of the Nile.

title: Epigrams
text:
151. CLI. A Girdle
I'm long enough now; but if the belly swells
With a sweet weight, I'll become a short girdle for you.
152. CLII. A Square Coverlet
The land of learned Catullus sends you blankets:
We come from the region of Helicaon.
153. CLIII. A Half-Apron
Let the rich man give a tunic: I can gird you up.
Were I rich, I'd give both gifts.
154. CLIV. Amethystine Wools
Drunk as I am with the blood of the Sidonian shell,
I don't see why I should be called a sober wool.
155. CLV. White Wools
Apulia is noble for first-rate fleeces, Parma for the second;
The Altinum sheep wins praise for the third.
156. CLVI. Tyrian Wools
A shepherd gave us to his Spartan love:
The purple of mother Leda was inferior.
157. CLVII. Pollentine Wools
This land yields not only mourning wools of dark fleece,
But it is wont to give its own cups as well.
158. CLVIII. The Same
A drab wool, true, but made for the sheared attendants —
The sort the table does not summon from the first rank.
159. CLIX. Leuconian Stuffing
Is the cover too close upon the pressed-down feathers?
Take fleece scraped from the Leuconian saddle-cloths.
160. CLX. Circus Stuffing
Chopped marsh-reed is called Circus stuffing.
The poor man buys this litter in place of Leuconian.
161. CLXI. Down
Weary, you can rest on Amyclaean down,
Given you by the inner wool of the swan.
162. CLXII. Hay
Let the frail mattress swell for you, the mule cheated of its feed.
Pale care does not come to a hard bed.
163. CLXIII. A Bell
Give back the ball: the bath-bell sounds. You keep on playing?
You want to go home washed by the Virgin spring alone.
164. CLXIV. A Discus
When the gleaming weights of the Spartan discus fly,
Keep away, boys: let it harm only once.
165. CLXV. A Lyre
It gave Eurydice back to the bard: but he lost her,
Trusting himself too little, loving without patience.
166. CLXVI. The Same
Often it was thrown out of the Pompeian theater —
The lyre that led the woods and held the beasts spellbound.
167. CLXVII. A Plectrum
Lest a hot blister rise on your rubbed thumb,
Let a white plectrum adorn the docile lyre.
168. CLXVIII. A Hoop
The wheel must be set rolling: you give us a useful gift:
This hoop is for boys, but for me it will be music.
169. CLXIX. The Same
Why does the chattering ring wander round the loose circle?
So the crowd it meets may yield to the tinkling hoops.
170. CLXX. A Golden Statue of Victory
This is given him without a lot, on whom the Rhine
Bestowed a true name. Pour ten cups of Falernian, boy.
171. CLXXI. An Earthenware "Boy of Brutus"
The glory of so small a statuette is not obscure:
Brutus was the lover of this boy.
172. CLXXII. A Corinthian "Lizard-Slayer"
Spare the lizard creeping toward you, treacherous boy:
It longs to perish by your fingers.
173. CLXXIII. A Painted Hyacinthus on a Panel
The Oebalian boy turns his dying eyes from the hated discus —
Phoebus' fault and grief.
174. CLXXIV. A Marble Hermaphroditus
Male he entered the spring, and rose up both:
One part has the father's, the rest the mother's.
175. CLXXV. A Painted Danaë
Why did Danaë take a price from you, ruler of Olympus,
If Leda gave herself to you for nothing?
176. CLXXVI. A German Mask
I am a potter's joke, the mask of a redheaded Batavian.
The face you laugh at, a child fears.
177. CLXXVII. A Corinthian Hercules
The infant crushes the twin snakes and does not even look:
Already the Hydra might have feared his tender hands.
178. CLXXVIII. An Earthenware Hercules
I'm fragile: but you, I warn you, don't scorn the statuette:
Alcides is not ashamed to bear my name.

title: Epigrams
text:
179. CLXXIX. A Silver Minerva
Tell me, fierce maiden, since you have helmet and spear,
Why have you no aegis? "Caesar has it."
180. CLXXX. A Painted Europa
You could have done better to change into a bull, best father of gods,
Back then, when Io was a heifer to you.
181. CLXXXI. A Marble Leander
Bold Leander cried out amid the swelling waves:
"Drown me, you floods, when I am on my way back."
182. CLXXXII. An Earthenware Figure of a Hunchback
Drunk, I think, Prometheus made these monsters on earth:
He too played with the Saturnalia's clay.
183. CLXXXIII. Homer's Battle of the Frogs
Read right through the frogs sung in Maeonian song,
And learn to unknit your brow over my trifles.
184. CLXXXIV. Homer on Parchment Tablets
The Iliad and Ulysses, foe to Priam's realm,
Lie hidden, stored together in many a fold of skin.
185. CLXXXV. Virgil's Gnat
Take, eager reader, the Gnat of eloquent Virgil,
Lest, the nuts put aside, you read "Arms and the man."
186. CLXXXVI. Virgil on Parchment
How small a parchment holds the boundless Virgil!
The first leaf bears his very face.
187. CLXXXVII. Menander's Thaïs
With this play he first toyed with the wanton loves of youth;
Glycera was no boy's mistress — Thaïs was.
188. CLXXXVIII. Cicero on Parchment
If this parchment is your companion, imagine
You're traveling long roads in Cicero's company.
189. CLXXXIX. Propertius' Monobiblos
Cynthia — the youthful song of eloquent Propertius —
Won fame, and gave no less than she received.
190. CXC. Livy on Parchment
Vast Livy is compressed into scanty skins,
Whom my library cannot hold whole.
191. CXCI. Sallust
This man, as the hearts of learned men declare,
Crispus, will be the first in Roman history.
192. CXCII. Ovid's Metamorphoses on Parchment
This mass, built up of many-folded leaves,
Carries Naso's fifteen books of song.
193. CXCIII. Tibullus
Wanton Nemesis fired her lover Tibullus,
Whom it pleased to be nothing in his whole house.
194. CXCIV. Lucan
There are some who say I am no poet:
But the bookseller who sells me thinks I am.
195. CXCV. Catullus
Great Verona owes as much to her Catullus
As little Mantua to her Virgil.
196. CXCVI. Calvus' "On the Use of Cold Water"
This paper, which tells you of springs and the names of waters,
Itself swam better in its own waters once.
197. CXCVII. Dwarf Mules
You need fear no fall from these mules:
You often sit nearly higher on the ground.
198. CXCVIII. A Gallic Lapdog
If you want to hear the charms of the little lapdog,
The whole page is too short for my telling.
199. CXCIX. An Asturian Pony
This little Asturian, who gathers his swift hoof to the beat,
Came from the gold-bearing tribes.
200. CC. A Greyhound
The keen greyhound hunts not for himself but for his master,
And will bring you the hare unharmed in his teeth.
201. CCI. A Wrestling-Master
I don't love him for winning, but because he knows how to lose
And has better learned the art of the bedroom-bout.
202. CCII. An Ape
The clever ape, dodging the spears flung at me —
If I had a tail, I'd be a long-tailed monkey.
203. CCIII. A Girl from Cadiz
She wriggles so quivering, itches so caressing, that she'd make
A masturbator of Hippolytus himself.
204. CCIV. Cymbals
The bronze that mourns the Celaenaean loves of the Mother,
The hungry Gallus is often wont to sell.
205. CCV. A Boy
Let mine be a boy smooth by his years, not by pumice,
For whose sake no girl can please me.
206. CCVI. A Love-Girdle
Bind to your neck, boy, pure love itself,
A girdle warm from Venus' bosom.
207. CCVII. The Same
Take the girdle steeped in Cytherean nectar:
This belt fired even Jove, the lover.

title: Epigrams
text:
208. CCVIII. A Shorthand-Writer
Though the words run fast, the hand is faster still:
The tongue has not yet finished, the right hand has.
209. CCIX. A Cuttlefish-Shell
Let the light Mareotic bark be made of a sea-shell:
The reed-pen will run an unhindered course.
210. CCX. A Fool
His stupor is not feigned, nor cunningly counterfeited.
Whoever is no wiser than he ought, he is wise.
211. CCXI. A Ram's Head
You cut the soft neck of Phrixus' woolly mate.
Did he deserve this, the cruel man who gave you a tunic?
212. CCXII. A Dwarf
If you look only at the man's head, you'd think him Hector:
If you see him standing, you'd take him for Astyanax.
213. CCXIII. A Shield
This shield, often vanquished, rarely victorious,
Will be your buckler, a dwarf's.
214. CCXIV. Boy Comic Actors
None in the troupe will play your "Hated Man":
But anyone can be your "Double Deceiver."
215. CCXV. A Buckle
Tell me plainly, buckle, what you do for comic actors
And lyre-singers. "Make them screw at a higher price."
216. CCXVI. A Fowler
The bird is fooled not only by limed reeds but by song,
While the cunning reed grows up in a silent hand.
217. CCXVII. A Hawk
He was the robber of birds: now, the fowler's slave, the same one
Decoys them, and grieves at the birds he catches not for himself.
218. CCXVIII. A Caterer
Say how many you want for dinner and at what price, and don't add
A single word: the dinner is ready for you.
219. CCXIX. An Ox-Heart
Poor pleader, since you write poems that bring back
No money, take the heart you have.
220. CCXX. A Cook
Art alone is not enough for a cook: I don't want
A slavish palate: a cook should have his master's taste.
221. CCXXI. A Grill with Spits
Let the thin tidbit sweat for you on the curved grill;
Let the foaming boar steam on the long spit.
222. CCXXII. A Pastry-Cook
This man's hand will raise for you a thousand sweet
Shapes of his craft: for him alone the thrifty bee toils.
223. CCXXIII. Lard-Cakes
Get up: the baker is already selling boys their breakfasts,
And the crested birds of dawn are crowing on every side.
